questions.fun_fact: La forma ovalada del balón es justo la que permite que gire así y corte mejor el aire.

quality.notes: In rugby this pass is often called the 'spin pass' or 'pase rotado', but 'en espiral' is understandable. 'Pase de pecho' comes from basketball and is a weak distractor. 'Girando sobre su eje' plus the bullet image points strongly to spiral.

questions.description: En Argentina hay dos temas que no se tocan en la mesa: el fútbol y este.
questions.question: Nació en Argentina el 17 de octubre de 1945, con una enorme manifestación en la Plaza de Mayo. ¿Qué movimiento político es?
hints: Su fundador fue tres veces presidente de Argentina.
Su marcha empieza 'Los muchachos…'.
Su gran símbolo femenino es Evita.

media.credit: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Diego Delso

questions.fun_fact: Sus seguidores celebran cada 17 de octubre como el 'Día de la Lealtad'.

quality.notes: Accurate. It fits the WWII subcategory only loosely. Hint 2 points to the Marcha Peronista, which gives the answer to anyone who knows the song. Hint 3 names Evita, which billetes-del-mundo-17 also uses, but the fact asked is different. Most adults outside Argentina need the hints, so 12.

questions.description: El rey del grafiti: llegó a más países que cualquier mochilero.
questions.question: Este dibujo de un señor narizón asomado a una pared apareció por todo el mundo en los años 40. ¿Quiénes lo pintaban por todas partes?
hints: En los años 40, medio mundo estaba en guerra.
Aparecía donde llegaban las tropas aliadas.
Hasta está escondido en el monumento a la guerra en Washington.

media.note: El dibujo clásico de 'Kilroy was here': un hombre calvo y narizón asomándose por encima de una pared, con la frase en inglés.
media.credit: J.-N. L. · FAL · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: J.-N. L.

questions.fun_fact: Kilroy está grabado en secreto en el Memorial de la Segunda Guerra Mundial en Washington.

quality.notes: A fun, surprising subject. The British had a near-identical doodle, 'Mr. Chad', which makes 'Turistas ingleses' slightly muddy. The essential image is available on Commons, but its English text 'Kilroy was here' helps a little. Few 13-year-olds know Kilroy, so 9 rather than 7. Hint 3 repeats the fun fact.

questions.description: Una palabra alemana que suena a estornudo, y aun así nadie le dijo «salud».
questions.question: Durante la Segunda Guerra Mundial, ¿qué era la Wehrmacht?
hints: Existió entre 1935 y 1945.
Su nombre significa 'fuerza de defensa'.
Fue la que invadió Polonia en 1939.

media.credit: Thomas Wolf, www.foto-tw.de · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thomas Wolf, www.foto-tw.de

questions.fun_fact: La Luftwaffe, la fuerza aérea alemana, era una parte de la Wehrmacht.

quality.notes: Accurate, but a dry definition question. The Gestapo-like distractor is good. Hint 3 (the invasion of Poland) nearly gives it, which is allowed. Teens may know the word from games, so about 8.

questions.description: Una foto tan famosa que medio Nueva York jura que el de la foto era su abuelo.
questions.question: Soy fotógrafo de la revista Life. El día en que Japón se rindió, en 1945, retraté a un marinero besando a una mujer en Times Square. ¿Quién soy?
hints: Nací en el Imperio alemán y emigré a Estados Unidos.
Fui uno de los primeros fotógrafos de Life, desde 1936.
Mi apellido empieza por 'Eisen', que significa 'hierro' en alemán.

media.credit: Terabass · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Terabass

questions.fun_fact: Eisenstaedt no anotó los nombres de la pareja, y durante décadas muchas personas aseguraron ser los protagonistas.

quality.notes: Accurate. Victor Jorgensen also shot the scene for the Navy, but 'Life' makes it unique. Hint 3 gives the first half of the surname, which nearly gives it away (allowed for hint 3). The distractors are strong, Rosenthal especially.

questions.description: Un príncipe danés con demasiado tiempo libre y muchísimas ganas de filosofar.
questions.question: En la escena más famosa de Hamlet, en un cementerio, ¿qué sostiene el príncipe en la mano mientras habla?
hints: Es algo que encontraron los sepultureros.
Perteneció a Yorick, el antiguo bufón del rey.
Es la parte del esqueleto que va encima de los hombros.

media.credit: ArildV · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ArildV

questions.fun_fact: Un pianista polaco, André Tchaikowsky, donó su propia calavera a la Royal Shakespeare Company, y un actor la usó en escena haciendo de Hamlet en 2008.

quality.notes: Solid question. The skull pose is widely known from cartoons. The fun fact (Tchaikowsky's skull, used in the RSC's 2008 Hamlet) is true.

questions.description: Un bigote falso y una voz gruesa: el kit de supervivencia de las heroínas de Shakespeare.
questions.question: Rosalinda se hace llamar Ganimedes, Porcia se viste de abogado e Imogen se vuelve un paje. ¿Quién hacía esos papeles en tiempos de Shakespeare?
hints: En los teatros públicos ingleses de la época, las reglas eran muy distintas a las de hoy.
Por eso el disfraz de hombre era un chiste doble para el público.
Eran actores jóvenes a los que todavía no les había cambiado la voz.

media.credit: Ank Kumar · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ank Kumar

questions.fun_fact: En Inglaterra las mujeres no actuaron legalmente en los teatros públicos hasta 1660, más de 40 años después de la muerte de Shakespeare.

quality.notes: The question is a bit long, about 150 characters. The description's 'voz gruesa' hints a little at the voice angle, but only mildly.

questions.description: Un teatro con pasado: antes de los aplausos, ese edificio tuvo una vida muy distinta.
questions.question: El teatro Blackfriars, donde actuaba la compañía de Shakespeare, estaba en un edificio que antes había sido... ¿qué?
hints: El edificio ya tenía varios siglos cuando lo convirtieron en teatro.
En el siglo XVI, el rey Enrique VIII les quitó el edificio a sus dueños.
Allí vivían religiosos dominicos, que vestían capa negra.

media.credit: Paul Hudson from United Kingdom · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Paul Hudson from United Kingdom

questions.fun_fact: Blackfriars era un teatro cubierto e iluminado con velas, así que la compañía podía actuar allí también en invierno.

quality.notes: The description is vague and not very funny. Anyone who knows the English word 'friars' gets it from the name. The Sam Wanamaker image is safe. The 'language' lens label doesn't fit, but that doesn't matter.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, whose 'frailes negros' translation gave the answer away, with the hint about Henry VIII taking the building.

hints: El edificio ya tenía varios siglos cuando lo convirtieron en teatro.
Su nombre en inglés significa 'frailes negros'.
Allí vivían religiosos dominicos, que vestían capa negra.

questions.description: Hay noches en que ni contando ovejas logra uno pegar el ojo.
questions.question: Completa la frase de Shakespeare: 'Intranquila descansa la cabeza que lleva una…'
hints: La dice un rey preocupado.
Es dorada y a veces tiene piedras preciosas.
La usan los reyes y las reinas en la cabeza.

media.credit: Anthony O'Neil · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Anthony O'Neil

questions.fun_fact: La frase es de la segunda parte de 'Enrique IV', donde el rey se queja de que no puede dormir de tanto preocuparse por su reino.

quality.notes: Difficulty 2 is too low. 6-year-olds won't know this quote. They could only guess 'corona' by reasoning, and 'intranquila descansa' is hard wording for them. It's a fairly dry completion question. Decorative media is fine here, because an illustrative image would likely show a crown.

questions.description: Moda isabelina: si no podías girar la cabeza, ibas bien vestido.
questions.question: Es blanco y plisado, rodea el cuello como una rueda y estaba de moda en la época de Shakespeare. ¿Cómo se llama?
hints: Se almidonaba para que quedara bien tiesa.
Sale en muchos retratos de la reina Isabel I.
Su nombre se parece a 'gorja', una palabra antigua para la garganta.

media.credit: unknown Anglo-Netherlandish artist · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: unknown Anglo-Netherlandish artist

questions.fun_fact: Una gorguera grande podía llevar varios metros de tela de lino, plisada y almidonada a mano.

quality.notes: Many adults won't know the word 'gorguera', so it's maybe a 12. 'Chorrera' is a close neckwear term, a good but tricky distractor that remains clearly wrong for a ruff. It's a vocabulary question, a bit dry.

questions.description: Antes de Wikipedia, los dramaturgos copiaban de libros gordísimos.
questions.question: Soy una historia de Inglaterra, Escocia e Irlanda; Shakespeare sacó de mí ideas para 'Macbeth' y sus obras sobre reyes ingleses. ¿Qué soy?
hints: Me publicaron en 1577 y salió una edición ampliada en 1587.
Llevo el apellido de un cronista inglés llamado Raphael.
El apellido de mi autor empieza por 'Hol'.

media.credit: Amy  Truter · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Amy  Truter

questions.fun_fact: Shakespeare usó la segunda edición, de 1587, y a veces copió frases casi palabra por palabra.

quality.notes: This is a dry specialist fact. Hall's Chronicle was also a source for the history plays, but the title of three kingdoms plus Macbeth clearly points to Holinshed. Hint 2 ('Raphael') nearly gives it away to experts.

questions.description: El personaje con peor fama de todos los cuentos de hadas, y ni siquiera tiene escoba.
questions.question: Se casa con tu papá, no es tu mamá y en 'Cenicienta' es la mala. ¿Qué palabra es, también título de una telenovela?
hints: En 'Blancanieves' también aparece una.
Las hermanastras de Cenicienta son sus hijas.
Empieza como 'madre', pero termina en '-astra'.

media.credit: TSTS Sheng · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: TSTS Sheng

questions.fun_fact: 'La madrastra' de Televisa (2005), con Victoria Ruffo, es una nueva versión de una telenovela chilena de 1981.

quality.notes: The Cinderella image fits and does not give away 'madrastra'. The fun fact about the 2005 remake of the Chilean original from 1981 is accurate.

questions.description: Antes de los mil capítulos y las gemelas malvadas, alguien tuvo que dar el primer paso.
questions.question: Se estrenó en 1958, la escribió Fernanda Villeli y es la primera telenovela de su país. ¿De qué país es 'Senda prohibida'?
hints: Su capital es una de las ciudades más grandes del continente.
Allí nació la gran productora Televisa.
Allí se hicieron 'La usurpadora' y 'María la del barrio'.

media.credit: electromechanic812291 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: electromechanic812291

questions.fun_fact: 'Senda prohibida' tuvo 60 capítulos de unos 30 minutos, emitidos de lunes a viernes en 1958.

quality.notes: I'm not sure about the fun fact's exact count of 60 episodes. Mexico is the default guess for telenovelas, so many players will get it by reasoning rather than knowledge. Fairly dry.

questions.description: El sonido favorito de todo televidente cuando la villana por fin recibe lo suyo.
questions.question: En la telenovela, la protagonista le pega a la villana con la mano abierta en la mejilla. ¿Cómo se llama ese golpe?
hints: Suena fuerte y deja la cara roja.
En las telenovelas suena '¡plaf!' y la villana se queda con la boca abierta.
Viene de la palabra con la que llamamos a la mejilla.

media.credit: Sven Scheuermeier sveninho · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Sven Scheuermeier sveninho

questions.fun_fact: Otra forma de llamarla es 'bofetada', y en España también se dice 'tortazo'.

quality.notes: 'Bofetada' would also be right, but it isn't an option, so there's no conflict. The 'colombia' lens label doesn't matter, because the wording is neutral.

questions.description: Los emperadores chinos venían aquí a pedir buen clima, como tú antes de un paseo.
questions.question: En el Templo del Cielo de Pekín, el gran Salón de Oración por la Buena Cosecha se sostiene sin un solo clavo. ¿De qué está hecho?
hints: Es un material que viene de la naturaleza y se puede tallar.
Sus piezas encajan unas en otras como un rompecabezas.
Sus enormes columnas fueron alguna vez troncos.

media.credit: Omer Toledano · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Omer Toledano

questions.fun_fact: El salón original se quemó por un rayo en 1889 y lo reconstruyeron igual, otra vez sin clavos.

quality.notes: 'Sin un solo clavo' strongly suggests wood. The photo shows painted wood, which helps a little. Shares a topic with maravillas-del-mundo-3 (identifying the Temple of Heaven), but this asks a different fact.

questions.description: Si los edificios fueran personas, esto sería lo que les impide encorvarse.
questions.question: Me llamo igual que la parte de tu espalda llena de vértebras, y en los edificios estoy de pie del piso al techo. ¿Para qué sirvo?
questions.answer: Para sostener el peso del edificio
wrong_answers: Para llevar el agua de la lluvia
Para dejar entrar la luz del sol
hints: Sin mí, los pisos de arriba se vendrían abajo.
En los templos griegos estoy en fila, una al lado de la otra.
Soy la columna: aguanto todo lo que tengo encima.

media.credit: Jebulon · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jebulon

questions.fun_fact: En zonas de terremotos, las columnas se refuerzan con muchos anillos de acero por dentro para que no se rompan al sacudirse.

quality.notes: The right answer is the longest option and the most 'technical' one, so it stands out. 'Separar las habitaciones' is a little arguable. The riddle only asks what a column does, which is plain. Related to q-0945 (cave column), but that asks a different fact.

questions.description: Los científicos también juegan a unir puntos, pero con terremotos.
questions.question: Para ubicar el epicentro de un sismo, ¿cuántas estaciones sismológicas se necesitan como mínimo?
hints: Cada estación solo sabe a qué distancia ocurrió el sismo, no en qué dirección.
Se dibuja un círculo por estación y se busca dónde se cruzan todos.
El método se llama 'triangulación': fíjate en el 'tri…'.

media.credit: Heidi Soosalu · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Heidi Soosalu

questions.fun_fact: Hoy se usan cientos de estaciones a la vez, y una computadora calcula el epicentro en pocos segundos.

quality.notes: Three is the standard school answer. Strictly, the method is trilateration, and real hypocentre fixes need more stations (depth and origin time), so 'como mínimo' is a simplification. Hint 3 nearly gives the answer, which is allowed.

questions.description: Un edificio con nervios de acero, literalmente.
questions.question: Si una casa es 'sismorresistente', ¿qué quiere decir?
questions.answer: Que aguanta los terremotos sin caerse
wrong_answers: Que avisa antes de un terremoto
Que no se mueve nada al temblar
hints: 'Sismo' es otra forma de decir terremoto.
Resistir no es lo mismo que quedarse quieto.
Piensa en un árbol con viento fuerte: se dobla, pero no se cae.

media.credit: Henryeke · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Henryeke

questions.fun_fact: Los edificios sismorresistentes sí se mueven al temblar: están hechos para doblarse un poco en vez de romperse.

quality.notes: The trap option 'no se mueve nada' works, and the fun fact explains it. The description joke is weak. A rather plain word-meaning question.

questions.description: Una camisa tan alegre que hace fiesta desde el cuello.
questions.question: Soy una camisa ancha y colorida de África Occidental, con un bordado en V alrededor del cuello. ¿Qué soy?
hints: No soy una tela ni una túnica larga: soy una camisa.
En los años 60 me hice famosa en Estados Unidos.
Empiezo por 'Da-' y termino en '-ki'.

media.credit: Komavo · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Komavo

questions.fun_fact: En los años 60 y 70 el dashiki se volvió símbolo del orgullo afroamericano en Estados Unidos.

quality.notes: The options are good: Agbada and Boubou are robes and Kente is a cloth, so an expert can tell them apart. The question is mostly vocabulary recall, so it feels dry.

questions.description: Una camisa tan fina que casi se ve a través de ella, y no es de plástico.
questions.question: La tela más fina y valorada de esta camisa filipina se teje con fibras de las hojas de una planta frutal. ¿Cuál?
hints: Es una planta que da fruta.
La fibra sale de sus hojas largas y puntiagudas, no del fruto.
Su fruta lleva una corona de hojas encima.

media.credit: Ron Bulovs · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ron Bulovs

questions.fun_fact: El barong tagalog es el traje formal nacional de Filipinas y se lleva por fuera del pantalón.

quality.notes: Barong cloth is also made from abacá (a kind of banana), but 'la tela más fina' plus 'hojas de una planta frutal' still points only to piña among these options. The 'pop_culture' lens label is odd.

questions.description: Cuando el ánimo se viene al suelo, la ropa también se rinde.
questions.question: Perdiste el partido y andas desanimado. Según el dicho, ¿qué prenda tienes caída?
hints: Es una prenda que cuelga de los hombros.
La usaban los caballeros y los reyes de antes.
Drácula también lleva una.

media.credit: m-louis .® · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: m-louis .®

questions.fun_fact: Se dice que la expresión viene de las capas antiguas: cuando alguien iba triste o vencido, dejaba de llevarla bien puesta.

quality.notes: The fun fact gives a folk etymology; it is hedged with 'se dice', but it is not certain. The idiom 'andar de capa caída' is widely known across the Spanish-speaking world.

questions.description: Un artista que vive con miedo a una sola cosa: el sonido «¡pum!».
questions.question: Retuerzo globos largos y flacos hasta convertirlos en perritos, espadas y flores. ¿Quién soy?
hints: Suelo aparecer en las fiestas de cumpleaños.
Mi material de trabajo se infla con aire.
Mi nombre mezcla «globo» con «flexible».

media.credit: Abuka1012 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Abuka1012

questions.fun_fact: Un perrito de globo se puede hacer con un solo globo largo y apenas unos pocos giros.

quality.notes: The question names the balloons, so the answer is easy to work out from the word 'globo'. That fits difficulty 2. Hint 2 says again what the question already says.

questions.description: El polvo blanco más honrado del circo: solo sirve para no caerse.
questions.question: Trapecistas, gimnastas y escaladores se untan este polvo blanco en las manos. ¿Qué compuesto es?
hints: Absorbe el sudor para que las manos no resbalen.
Su metal arde con una luz blanca muy brillante.
Es el mismo «magnesio» que llevan los escaladores en una bolsita.

media.credit: Joop van Bilsen for Anefo · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Joop van Bilsen for Anefo

questions.fun_fact: El magnesio de los gimnastas no es tiza de tablero: la tiza escolar es casi siempre yeso o carbonato de calcio.

quality.notes: Accurate. Many people know 'magnesio' from climbing, but the full compound name keeps it near 10. The axis says the stimulus is a photo, but the media is illustrative, which is fine.

questions.description: Una ciudad donde el primer circo se montó con más caballos que payasos.
questions.question: En 1768, el exsargento de caballería Philip Astley montó el primer circo moderno, con una pista redonda. ¿En qué ciudad?
hints: Astley abrió después otro circo en París, pero no empezó allí.
La ciudad está a orillas del río Támesis.
Es la capital del Reino Unido.

media.credit: Jorge Royan · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jorge Royan

questions.fun_fact: Astley descubrió que, galopando en círculo, la fuerza centrífuga le ayudaba a mantenerse de pie sobre el caballo.

quality.notes: Astley and 1768 are correct. Paris is a strong distractor. Players can reason towards the answer from Astley's English name.

questions.description: Una palabra que suena a brinco y a mueble al mismo tiempo.
questions.question: ¿Qué es un saltimbanqui?
questions.answer: Un acróbata que actúa en la calle
wrong_answers: Un pájaro que salta entre ramas
hints: La palabra viene del italiano.
Es un oficio, no un objeto ni un animal.
Es un artista que hace volteretas y piruetas para el público.

media.credit: Shuying YU · FAL · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shuying YU

questions.fun_fact: Picasso pintó en 1905 un famoso cuadro llamado «Familia de saltimbanquis».

quality.notes: Historically, 'saltimbanco' also meant a charlatan who sold remedies at fairs, so the option 'vendedor de feria ambulante' is slightly arguable. The options vary somewhat in length.

revision.reason: Replaced the fair-seller wrong answer, which the dictionary meaning partly supports, with a job that is clearly wrong.

wrong_answers: Un pájaro que salta entre ramas

questions.description: Un transporte con elefantes de pasajeros y payasos en primera clase.
questions.question: Durante más de cien años llevé a los grandes circos de Estados Unidos de ciudad en ciudad, con elefantes a bordo. ¿Qué soy?
hints: Viajaba sobre todo de noche, entre función y función.
Tenía muchos vagones.
Iba por rieles y hacía «chucu-chucu».

media.credit: Tim Evanson · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tim Evanson

questions.fun_fact: El tren del circo Ringling Bros. medía más de un kilómetro y medio de largo.

quality.notes: The Ringling train was about one mile long, about 1,6 km, so the fun fact's 'más de un kilómetro y medio' is borderline. Some circuses travelled by riverboat. A vintage elephant-parade image may show train cars.

questions.description: Un órgano que vive en el sótano del hígado y casi nadie sabe qué hace allí.
questions.question: Está debajo del hígado, tiene forma de pera pequeña y se puede vivir sin este órgano. ¿Cuál es?
hints: Ayuda a digerir la comida, sobre todo la grasa.
Guarda un líquido verde amarillento que fabrica el hígado.
Su nombre quiere decir 'bolsita', y su apellido viene de ese líquido.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.fun_fact: A veces dentro de la vesícula se forman 'piedras' que pueden ser tan pequeñas como un grano de arena o tan grandes como una pelota de golf.

quality.notes: People can also live without the spleen (bazo) and the appendix. The location under the liver and the pear shape still single out the gallbladder. The description repeats the location from the question. The axis 'word_meaning' doesn't fit this question. The question is somewhat school-like.

questions.description: Un científico que usó sus propios ojos como experimento.
questions.question: Un químico inglés lo descubrió en sí mismo en el siglo XVIII, y afecta mucho más a hombres que a mujeres. ¿Qué es?
hints: Tiene que ver con cómo se ven los colores.
Se hereda a través del cromosoma X, por eso es más común en hombres.
Se llama así por el apellido de aquel químico, John Dalton.

media.credit: Tilman2007 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tilman2007

questions.fun_fact: Más o menos 1 de cada 12 hombres tiene algún tipo de daltonismo, pero solo 1 de cada 200 mujeres.

quality.notes: Accurate. Hint 1 makes it easy. The facts are correct: Dalton was an English chemist and described colour blindness in 1794.

questions.description: Un señor que se mete al congelador por gusto.
questions.question: El holandés Wim Hof, que se baña en hielo, creó un método famoso que combina el frío con ejercicios de… ¿qué?
hints: Su método busca ayudar al cuerpo a aguantar el frío y a calmar la mente.
Los yoguis y los buzos también entrenan mucho esta habilidad.
Consiste en tomar y soltar aire muchas veces seguidas.

media.credit: kallerna · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: kallerna

questions.fun_fact: Wim Hof subió gran parte del Kilimanjaro vestido solo con pantalones cortos.

quality.notes: Hint 1 already points straight at breathing. The answer can be reasoned out (ice baths plus breath), but Wim Hof himself is mostly known to adults, so this is slightly harder than 7.

revision.reason: Replaced hints 1 and 2, which gave the answer away, with vaguer hints about the method's purpose and who else trains it.

hints: Lo haces miles de veces al día sin pensarlo.
Lo haces con la nariz y la boca.
Consiste en tomar y soltar aire muchas veces seguidas.

questions.description: Un truco secreto que compartes con las focas y no sabías que tenías.
questions.question: Soy un reflejo que compartes con focas y delfines, y me llamo 'reflejo de inmersión'. ¿Qué hago?
wrong_answers: Arrugar la piel de los dedos
hints: Sirve para gastar menos oxígeno bajo el agua.
Es más fuerte cuanto más fría está el agua.
Afecta a los latidos.

media.credit: Steve Rupp · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Steve Rupp

questions.fun_fact: Por este reflejo, echarse agua fría en la cara puede ayudar a calmar el corazón cuando late muy rápido.

quality.notes: The description repeats the seal clue from the question, so it adds little. The answer can be reasoned out (diving means saving oxygen). Hint 3 nearly gives the answer. Fingers wrinkling in water is a real reflex, but it is not the diving reflex, so that option is fair.

questions.description: Una cárcel tan famosa en las películas de gánsteres que casi merece su propia estrella en Hollywood.
questions.question: ¿Qué famosa cárcel está a orillas del río Hudson, al norte de la ciudad de Nueva York?
hints: Por estar río arriba de Nueva York, en inglés ir preso se dijo 'ser enviado río arriba'.
Su nombre viene de un pueblo indígena de la zona.

questions.fun_fact: La expresión inglesa 'sent up the river' (enviado río arriba), que significa ir a la cárcel, nació por los presos que llevaban de Nueva York a Sing Sing.

questions.description: Un puente de Venecia con el nombre más dramático de toda Italia.

questions.fun_fact: El nombre del puente lo hizo famoso el poeta inglés Lord Byron en el siglo XIX.

quality.notes: A modern legend about lovers kissing under the bridge exists, which makes 'enamorados' tempting, but 'según la historia' clearly points to the prisoners. Good question.

Por sus ventanitas veían Venecia por última vez antes de la celda.

questions.description: Un museo que guarda con cariño… marcos vacíos.
questions.question: En 1990, unos ladrones disfrazados de policías robaron 'El concierto' de Vermeer en un museo de Boston. ¿Cuántas obras se llevaron en total?
hints: Fue más de una obra, pero cupo en una sola noche de trabajo.

Es un número que mucha gente considera de mala suerte.

questions.fun_fact: El museo Isabella Stewart Gardner todavía cuelga los marcos vacíos en su lugar, esperando que las obras vuelvan.

quality.notes: An exact count that players cannot reason towards; it is pure memory and closer to 14. Hint 3 (the unlucky number) gives it away. The heist story itself is interesting.

questions.description: Un negocio fantástico… mientras nadie pregunte de dónde salen las ganancias.
questions.question: Pagaba a los inversionistas viejos con el dinero de los nuevos, y Bernie Madoff me hizo el más grande de la historia. ¿Qué soy?
hints: Funciono mientras siga entrando dinero nuevo.
También me dicen estafa piramidal.

questions.fun_fact: Madoff fue condenado en 2009 a 150 años de prisión por un fraude de unos 65 000 millones de dólares.

quality.notes: The first-person riddle mixes tenses: 'Pagaba…me hizo'. Hint 2 (estafa piramidal) is strong for a second hint.

questions.description: El motivo por el que ningún ladrón debería tocar absolutamente nada.
questions.question: Soy la regla de oro de los forenses: 'todo contacto deja un rastro'. ¿Cómo me llamo?
hints: Me formuló un criminólogo francés a comienzos del siglo XX.
Por mí se buscan pelos, fibras y polvo en la escena.
Mi creador fundó un laboratorio de policía en Lyon.

media.author: Heptagon

questions.fun_fact: Edmond Locard montó en 1910, en Lyon, uno de los primeros laboratorios de policía científica del mundo.

quality.notes: The three wrong options are famous principles with well-known, unrelated meanings, so an adult can find Locard by elimination. That makes it easier than 13 and the distractors weak.

questions.description: Un viaje de ocho meses en barco, sin escalas divertidas y sin derecho a devolución.

Antes, Gran Bretaña los enviaba a sus colonias de América.
Los mandaron al otro lado del mundo como castigo.

questions.fun_fact: Gran Bretaña envió más de 160 000 presos a Australia entre 1788 y 1868.

quality.notes: It shares the answer word 'presos' with crimenes-famosos-4, but it asks a different fact. The search 'Sydney harbour historic' may return the Opera House, which is harmless.

questions.description: Un robo tan rápido que los turistas no alcanzaron ni a sacar la foto.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which ruled out all wrong options at once, with a middle-strength hint.

Llegaron en un camión y no tuvieron que escalar.
Usaron una máquina de las que se usan en las mudanzas.

questions.description: Un taladro, un fin de semana largo y una bóveda llena de joyas: la receta de un robo muy británico.

questions.fun_fact: El jefe de la banda tenía 76 años, y la historia inspiró la película 'Rey de ladrones', con Michael Caine.

quality.notes: Facts are correct. 'Lo más curioso' points towards the surprising option, but 'policías en servicio' is surprising too. A difficulty of 6 seems low for a UK crime from 2015, even though players can reason about it.

questions.description: Tres palitos que pasan el partido entero muertos del susto.
questions.question: En críquet, es de madera, está clavado en el suelo detrás del bateador y, si la pelota lo tumba, el bateador queda eliminado. ¿Qué es?

Está formado por tres palos verticales con dos piecitas encima.
Su nombre en inglés empieza por 'wick'.

media.author: Des Blenkinsopp

questions.fun_fact: Las piecitas que van encima de los palos se llaman 'bails' y salen volando cuando la pelota pega.

quality.notes: Hint 3 ('empieza por wick') almost contains the answer. For players who don't know cricket, all four English terms are equally opaque, so it is mostly pure memorisation.

questions.description: Los últimos en la fila, como cuando reparten la torta.
questions.question: En críquet, ¿cómo se llama a los últimos bateadores del orden, que suelen ser lanzadores y batean bastante mal?
hints: Suelen salir a batear cuando el partido ya va muy avanzado.
El nombre los compara con una parte del cuerpo de un animal.
'Tail' significa 'cola' en inglés.

media.author: Acabashi

questions.fun_fact: A veces un tail-ender sorprende a todos y salva el partido con su bate.

quality.notes: This is cricket jargon that few Spanish-speaking adults know, so it's probably above 12. 'Torta' means different things in different regions (cake vs sandwich), which is a minor issue. It's a dry term question.

questions.description: Un pato muy elegante que nadie quiere en su colección.
questions.question: Me llaman 'golden duck' (pato de oro) y ningún bateador de críquet me quiere. ¿Qué soy?
questions.answer: Quedar eliminado con la primera bola, sin anotar
wrong_answers: Romper el bate con el primer golpe del partido
Tropezar y caerse mientras corre entre los palos
Recibir un golpe de la bola en el casco
hints: Le pasa al bateador y da un poco de vergüenza.
Después de esto, el bateador tiene que volver muy pronto al pabellón.
Lo de 'oro' es porque pasó lo más rápido posible.

media.credit: Acabashi · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Acabashi

questions.fun_fact: Se dice 'duck' porque el cero en el marcador se parece a un huevo de pato.

quality.notes: Correct, and the duck's-egg fun fact is true. The answer is slightly the most 'cricket-scoring' option, but players can reason towards it.

revision.reason: Replaced hints 1 and 2 so they no longer point to scoring or zero.

hints: Tiene que ver con el marcador.
En críquet, 'duck' significa terminar con cero carreras.
Lo de 'oro' es porque pasó lo más rápido posible.

questions.description: Si te toca batear contra él, mejor ponte casco y rézale a tu santo favorito.
questions.question: ¿A qué velocidad, más o menos, lanza la pelota un lanzador rápido de críquet profesional?
hints: Es más rápido que un vehículo en la ciudad.
Es parecido a la velocidad de un lanzador de béisbol de las grandes ligas.
Es como un vehículo en la autopista, pero un poco más rápido.

media.credit: Acabashi · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Acabashi

questions.fun_fact: El récord de la bola más rápida en críquet pasa de 160 km/h.

quality.notes: 350 km/h (and arguably 250) is clearly absurd for a human throw, so this is really a 2-way choice. Correct: about 145 km/h, record 161 km/h. A dry estimate.

questions.description: Un club tan antiguo que sus reglas son más viejas que la independencia de Colombia.
questions.question: Si quieres visitar el Marylebone Cricket Club, que escribe las reglas del críquet desde 1788, ¿a qué ciudad viajas?
hints: Está en el país donde nació el críquet.
Su estadio se llama Lord's.
Es la ciudad del Big Ben.

media.credit: Matthew Bowden www.digitallyrefreshing.com · Attribution · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Matthew Bowden www.digitallyrefreshing.com

questions.fun_fact: El estadio del club, Lord's, es conocido como 'la casa del críquet'.

quality.notes: Correct (MCC founded 1787, laws from 1788, Lord's). Defaulting to the capital makes it easy, so the difficulty is lower than 7. Other questions also have the answer Londres but ask different facts. The 'Si quieres visitar…' framing adds little.

questions.description: Un dinosaurio con nombre de barco de guerra y tamaño de edificio.
questions.question: Mi nombre significa 'no teme a nada', pesaba como varios camiones y me presentaron en 2014. ¿En qué país hallaron mis huesos?
hints: Fue en el continente americano.
Me encontraron en el sur del continente, en una zona fría, seca y con mucho viento.
Es el mismo país donde apareció el argentinosaurio.

media.credit: Moheen Reeyad · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Moheen Reeyad

questions.fun_fact: El esqueleto del Dreadnoughtus está entre los más completos que se conocen de un dinosaurio gigante de cuello largo.

quality.notes: Dreadnoughtus is little known, so most players can only guess from 'giant sauropods come from Argentina'. That is closer to 11 than 9. Hint 3 (Argentinosaurus) all but names the answer, which is allowed. A 'sauropod skeleton museum' photo might show an Argentinosaurus with a label, a small risk.

revision.reason: Replaced hint 2, which named Patagonia, with a hint that names no place found only in Argentina.

hints: Fue en el continente americano.
Me encontraron en la Patagonia, una región fría y ventosa.
Es el mismo país donde apareció el argentinosaurio.

questions.description: Una serpiente tan larga que para darle un abrazo se necesita un bus entero.
questions.question: Vivió hace 60 millones de años, medía unos 13 metros y sus fósiles salieron de la mina de carbón del Cerrejón. ¿Cómo se llama?
hints: Es la serpiente más grande que se conoce.
Vivió poco después de la desaparición de los dinosaurios, en una selva caliente.
Su nombre mezcla a unos gigantes de la mitología griega con un tipo de serpiente.

media.credit: Petr Vodička · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Petr Vodička

questions.fun_fact: Se calcula que la titanoboa pesaba más de una tonelada, más que un vehículo pequeño.

quality.notes: Titanoboa is well known from documentaries. Among obscure Latin genus names, it is the one famous name and stands out a little. The description says it is a snake, which the question deliberately leaves out. The bus joke is weak.

questions.description: Un héroe de cuento con más confianza en sí mismo que fuerza en los brazos.
questions.question: En un cuento de los hermanos Grimm, maté siete moscas de un solo golpe y me fui a recorrer el mundo. ¿Cuál es mi oficio?
hints: Las moscas llegaron a mi pan con mermelada mientras trabajaba.
Bordé 'siete de un golpe' en un cinturón que yo mismo hice.
Mi trabajo es tomar medidas y coser trajes.

media.credit: Dguendel · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dguendel

questions.fun_fact: En 1938 Mickey Mouse protagonizó una versión animada de este cuento llamada 'El valiente sastrecillo'.

quality.notes: The usual Spanish title of the Mickey short is 'El sastrecillo valiente'. The fun fact's wording is acceptable but unusual.

questions.description: La chaqueta favorita de las señoras elegantes y de los detectives ingleses.
questions.question: La chaqueta clásica de Chanel lo lleva, nació en Escocia y raspa un poquito. ¿Qué es el tweed?
hints: Se usaba para cazar y pasear por el campo frío.
Sale de un animal que hace 'beee'.
Es un tejido abrigado, de hilos de varios colores.

media.credit: Ymblanter · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ymblanter

questions.fun_fact: Se cuenta que el nombre 'tweed' nació de un error: un comerciante leyó mal 'tweel' y pensó en el río Tweed de Escocia.

quality.notes: 'Raspa un poquito' and 'nació en Escocia' clearly point to the only fabric option, so the distractors are weak. 'La chaqueta... lo lleva' reads awkwardly. The 'tweel' misreading is a legend, but the fun fact presents it as one ('se cuenta'). Dry definition question.

questions.description: Una rueda que nunca ha ido a ninguna parte, pero ha hecho millones de ollas.
questions.question: Giro y giro sin parar, y sobre mí unas manos mojadas levantan vasijas. ¿Qué material moldean sobre mí?
hints: Es un material que sale de la tierra.
Mojado es blandito; al hornearlo queda duro.
Con este mismo barro se hacen las macetas y las tejas.

media.author: Christoph Braun

questions.fun_fact: El torno de alfarero ya se usaba en Mesopotamia hace más de 5000 años.

quality.notes: The description's 'rueda... ollas' plus the question make the answer easy, which is fine at level 3. 'artisan workshop tools' might return pottery images, a minor risk.

questions.description: Una palabra elegante que los vendedores de sillas de oficina repiten como un mantra.
questions.question: Un teclado partido en dos mitades e inclinado se vende como «ergonómico». ¿Qué significa esa palabra?
hints: La palabra viene del griego «ergon», que significa trabajo.
Busca que no te duelan las manos ni la espalda.
Una silla también puede ser así si se acomoda a tu postura.

media.credit: James Petts from London, England · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: James Petts from London, England

questions.fun_fact: Los teclados partidos en dos se diseñan para que las muñecas no se tuerzan hacia afuera al escribir durante horas.

quality.notes: Plain vocabulary question that feels like a school test. The setup sentence is a bit long. The description and hint 3 both mention chairs, which nudges towards the answer, but that's acceptable.

questions.description: Unas ollas que se vistieron de gala: todas de negro, de pies a cabeza.

media.author: Shixart1985

questions.fun_fact: Las vasijas de La Chamba se pulen a mano con piedras antes de quemarlas, por eso brillan tanto.

quality.notes: Reduction firing with dung smoke is correct. A base-bundle question needs La Chamba as context, but it can be answered by reasoning. The answer «humo de la quema» is slightly broad, since the black actually comes from carbon in a reducing atmosphere.

questions.description: Muebles que se pelearon con la escuadra y nunca hicieron las paces.

hints: Piensa en conchas, hojas y huesos.
Su nombre es el mismo que se usa para la comida sin químicos.
La silla Tulip parece una flor.

media.author: Palm Beach Police Department

questions.fun_fact: Eero Saarinen diseñó la silla Tulip con una sola pata porque decía que la maraña de patas de sillas y mesas era un «arrabal de patas» confuso e inquieto.

quality.notes: The question sets curves against straight corners, so the «figuras geométricas» and «máquinas» options are weak. The word «orgánico» itself points to nature. Fairly dry.

questions.description: En los años cuarenta, Italia decidió que ir al trabajo también debía tener estilo.

media.author: Stewart Butterfield from San Francisco, USA!!

questions.fun_fact: Piaggio, la fábrica de la Vespa, hacía aviones antes de la Segunda Guerra Mundial.

quality.notes: The description's «zumba más de lo que pica» narrows the options to stinging insects (wasp or bee). A fun origin story. The query (Rome street) may show Vespas, but that doesn't reveal the insect.

revision.reason: Rewrote the description so it no longer implies a stinging insect, and reworded the question because the image doesn't show the scooter.

questions.description: Un hielo picado con azúcar que fue a la escuela en Europa y volvió con acento elegante.
questions.question: Este postre helado de hielo, azúcar y limón se desayuna con un pan brioche. ¿De qué isla es típico?
hints: La isla pertenece a Italia.
La pequeña isla de Malta queda justo al sur de ella.
Es la isla más grande del Mediterráneo, en la 'punta de la bota'.

media.author: Stella

questions.fun_fact: En Sicilia, la granita con brioche es un desayuno de verano tan normal como el café con pan en otros lugares.

questions.description: Un dibujo del colegio que nos tuvo engañados durante décadas.
questions.question: ¿Cómo se llama el famoso esquema, ya desmentido, de que la punta de la lengua siente lo dulce y el fondo lo amargo?
hints: Salía en muchos libros de ciencias del colegio.
Dividía la lengua en zonas, como un país en regiones.
Es lo que usarías para orientarte, pero dentro de la boca.

media.author: Ari Sherbill ariysherbill

questions.fun_fact: En realidad, todas las zonas de la lengua con papilas pueden sentir todos los sabores básicos.

quality.notes: Players can reason towards the name. Hint 3 nearly gives it away, which is allowed. The rating may be slightly too high.

questions.description: Una época en la que podías pagar el mercado con lo que tenías en la despensa.
questions.question: Entre los aztecas, ¿con qué se podía pagar en el mercado?
hints: Era una semilla que crecía en tierras calientes.
Con ella también preparaban una bebida amarga para los nobles.
Hoy se convierte en barras dulces.

media.credit: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata

questions.fun_fact: Había hasta falsificadores: rellenaban cáscaras vacías de cacao con tierra para hacerlas pasar por semillas.

questions.description: La lengua también se va de vacaciones y vuelve como nueva.
questions.question: Te quemaste la lengua con chocolate caliente. ¿Más o menos en cuánto tiempo se renuevan tus células del gusto?
hints: Tu cuerpo cambia muchas de sus células sin que te des cuenta.

media.author: Personal Creations

questions.fun_fact: Las células del gusto se agrupan en botones gustativos, y cada botón tiene decenas de ellas.

quality.notes: Taste cells turn over roughly every 10–14 days on average (some live longer), so «unas dos semanas» is acceptable but approximate. «Nunca se renuevan» has a different form from the other options. The scenario is the clue, so it's OK.

questions.description: Un bombón que se disfrazó de algo que se busca con hocico.
questions.question: Este bombón se llama como un manjar carísimo que se busca bajo tierra con perros o cerdos. ¿Qué ser vivo es ese manjar?
hints: Crece pegado a las raíces de árboles como el roble.
Se reproduce con esporas.
Es pariente de los champiñones.

media.author: Jason Hollinger

questions.fun_fact: Las trufas de chocolate se inventaron en Francia, y se llaman así porque recuerdan a las trufas negras cubiertas de tierra.

quality.notes: 'Un caracol' is a weak distractor because nobody digs snails up with pigs. The claim that chocolate truffles were invented in France is the usual story (Chambéry, 1895) but it isn't firmly documented. The image isn't truly essential: the question works without it. It shares only the answer 'hongo' with quesos-6, which asks about a different fact.

questions.description: Un dúo que nunca sacó un disco, pero sí salvó millones de vidas.
questions.question: Fleming es a la penicilina como Banting y Best son a…
hints: Lo lograron en Canadá en 1921.

media.author: LukaszKatlewa

questions.fun_fact: Banting, Best y Collip vendieron la patente a la Universidad de Toronto por un dólar cada uno, para que llegara a todo el mundo.

quality.notes: The patent story is told in many versions: Banting wasn't on the patent at first, but the version where each was paid $1 is widely accepted. The analogy uses penicillin from q-0163 only as the given half, so it doesn't overlap.

questions.description: Saruman se metió con los vecinos equivocados.
questions.question: ¿Quiénes atacaron Isengard, rompieron su presa e inundaron la fortaleza de Saruman?
hints: Tardan muchísimo en decidirse, pero cuando se deciden, cuidado.

Parecen árboles que caminan y hablan.

questions.fun_fact: More than 500 billion of these cookies have been sold since 1912, which makes it one of the best-selling cookies ever.

quality.notes: Mondelez has given different sales figures over the years (450 to 500 billion and more), so the number is only fairly reliable. “Which country” with the answer USA repeats a common pattern (q-1691 Scotch tape and others) but asks a different fact. The riddle is fine, but the question is a bit flat.

questions.description: The most famous cat in Hollywood never had to read a script.
questions.question: The lion of the film studio MGM roars before its movies. In which decade could cinema audiences first hear the lion roar?
hints: It happened when movies were just learning to have sound.
Black-and-white films were still the norm.
It was the decade of jazz, about 100 years ago.
questions.fun_fact: The first MGM lion, Slats, appeared in silent films, so audiences couldn't hear him; a lion called Jackie was the first whose roar was heard, in 1928.

quality.notes: Good question that you can reason towards from when films got sound. A lion photo would be a safe illustrative image, so decorative is a weaker choice than needed.

questions.description: The only perfume designed to make sure nobody comes near you.
questions.question: Explorers spray it on their skin before a walk in the Amazon. It smells strong and keeps away tiny biters that buzz. What does it keep away?
hints: The animals it keeps away are very small.
They fly and make a buzzing sound near your ears.
Mosquitoes belong to this group.
questions.fun_fact: Only female mosquitoes bite: they need the blood to make their eggs.

quality.notes: Simple and fine. “Tiny biters that buzz” already points strongly to insects, and spiders and bats are easy to rule out. Fun is so-so: the question is plain bug spray with an Amazon setting. Other questions in the game also have the answer “insects”, but they ask different facts.

questions.description: Party guest, great dancer, terrible at taking off his hat.
questions.question: In an Amazon legend, a river animal turns into a charming man in white who comes to village dances. He never takes off his hat. What is it hiding?
hints: The animal is a mammal that lives in the river.
It breathes air through the top of its head.
The animal is the pink river dolphin.
questions.fun_fact: Amazon river dolphins can turn bright pink, and they get pinker when they are excited.

quality.notes: Lovely legend that players can reason out. A family that knows river dolphins can work out the blowhole, so 11 feels a bit high.

questions.description: Rock star by night, rainforest campaigner by day.
questions.question: In 1989 Sting toured the world with chief Raoni, famous for his big lip plate. Their campaign helped protect the land of which Amazon people?
hints: Their lands lie along the Xingu River in Brazil.
Raoni himself belongs to this people.
The name starts with a K.
questions.fun_fact: The tour also started the Rainforest Foundation, which Sting and his wife Trudie Styler founded in 1989.

quality.notes: The facts are right (1989 tour, Raoni Metuktire is Kayapó). Hint 2 (“Raoni belongs to this people”) adds little and nearly gives it away for anyone who knows him. A rather niche activist fact, so it's fun mainly for specialists.

questions.description: A city so high in the clouds that it forgot to tell anyone it was there.
questions.question: I'm a stone city hidden in the cloud forest of northern Peru, decorated with zigzags and human figures, and found by explorers in the 1960s. Who built me?
hints: They lived there long before the Inca conquered them.
They are sometimes called the “Cloud Warriors”.
They also built the huge fortress of Kuélap.
questions.fun_fact: The ruins of Gran Pajatén are so fragile that the park around them is closed to normal tourists.

quality.notes: Gran Pajatén: the facts look right (Chachapoya, friezes, found in the 1960s, Río Abiseo park closed to tourists). The Inca later occupied the region, but builder = Chachapoya is fair. It's very obscure, though. Only Kuélap-level experts get it, and the riddle is a bit long.

questions.description: No engine, no sail, no problem.
questions.question: I'm made of logs tied side by side with vines, I'm flat, and I float down the river with no motor. What am I?
hints: I'm one of the simplest boats you can build.
You stand or sit on my flat top.
Huckleberry Finn floated down a river on one of me.
questions.fun_fact: Balsa trees from South America are so light that “balsa” means “raft” in Spanish.

quality.notes: Plain definition riddle with little surprise. q-0326 (rafting) is related but asks a different fact. The Huckleberry Finn hint leans on Anglo literature, but it's only a hint.

questions.description: Three countries walk into a river town...
questions.question: On the Amazon River there is a spot where three countries meet. Which country is NOT one of them?
hints: The odd one out has Amazon rainforest but doesn't touch the main river.
The spot is near the Colombian town of Leticia.
The odd one out is named after the line around the middle of the Earth.
questions.fun_fact: At this tripoint you can walk from Colombia to Brazil just by crossing a street.

quality.notes: The description is a trailing joke setup, not a full sentence, and not really funny. The question is good and the facts are correct (Leticia/Tabatinga/Santa Rosa).

questions.description: A romance reader, a magnifying glass and a very angry cat.
questions.question: A wild cat like this one hunts in a 1989 novel about an old man who reads love stories in the Amazon. Who wrote it?
hints: The author was from Chile.
He also wrote a story about a seagull and the cat who taught her to fly.
His first name is Luis.

media.note: A clear photo of an ocelot, the spotted wild cat of South American forests.

questions.fun_fact: Sepúlveda lived with the Shuar people in the Ecuadorian Amazon, and that stay inspired the novel.

quality.notes: The novel's cat is a “tigrilla”, which translations render as ocelot or margay, so calling it an ocelot is a slight doubt. The options are all Latin American writers, a Spanish-world focus, though Sepúlveda is well known in Europe. Essential role is a stretch: the ocelot photo is really illustrative.

questions.description: Where you can pay in euros and still be in the rainforest.
questions.question: It is in South America but uses the euro, and Europe launches its rockets from there. What is the only part of the EU on the South American mainland?
hints: It is not a country of its own.
People there vote in French elections.
Its name tells you which country it belongs to.
questions.fun_fact: Rockets launch from there because places near the Equator give them an extra push from the Earth's spin.

quality.notes: The description just repeats the euro clue from the question, so it isn't much of a joke. The Falkland Islands are not on the mainland, so the question's own wording rules them out. 8 is a bit low for young teens.

questions.description: Your daily walk to school suddenly looks very short.
questions.question: Some caribou herds make the longest migration of any land animal. About how far can a caribou walk in one year?
hints: It is far more than you would ever walk in a year.
It is several times the length of a big country like France.
Think thousands of kilometers, but not tens of thousands.
questions.fun_fact: Caribou can travel up to about 5,000 km (3,000 mi) a year, and their calves can walk within hours of being born.

quality.notes: Studies give up to about 4,800 km a year, so 'about 5,000 km' holds as a rounded figure. Options sit a factor of 10 apart, so players can reason towards the answer. Hint 3 nearly gives it away, which is allowed.

questions.description: A shark that came to the ocean with its own metal detector.
questions.question: This shark's wide head is full of sensors that feel tiny electric signals. Which hidden animals does it use them to find under the sand?
hints: The animals it finds hide flat on the seafloor.
They are flat fish that look like they are flying underwater.
Some of them have a stinger on their tail.

media.note: A short underwater clip of a hammerhead shark swimming, with its wide head clearly visible.

questions.fun_fact: A hammerhead can use its wide head to pin a stingray to the seafloor before eating it.

quality.notes: 'Hidden under the sand' rules out dolphins and turtles, and partly jellyfish, so players can get it by elimination. Knowing that hammerheads hunt rays is beyond most 11-year-olds, so the stated 5 is too low. A hammerhead video on Commons is plausible.

questions.description: Running away is a perfectly good plan if you're fast enough.
questions.question: You're watching a fox chase a hare. Which of these does the hare NOT do to escape?
questions.answer: Dig a burrow and hide underground
wrong_answers: Leap sideways to break its scent trail
hints: Hares trust their legs more than hiding places.
Their cousins, rabbits, are the ones who live in tunnels.
Hares sleep in a shallow dip on the open ground.
questions.fun_fact: Baby hares are born with fur and open eyes in a shallow nest on the ground, while baby rabbits are born bare and blind in burrows.

quality.notes: Hares do make sideways leaps, but mostly to hide their trail before resting, not during a chase. That is slightly loose but acceptable. The NOT format is a bit dry, and the description is generic.

questions.description: An animal that would win any contest for doing nothing.
questions.question: “I'm the slowest mammal on Earth, I hang upside down in trees and I sleep most of the day.” Where do I live?
hints: I need lots of trees and warm weather.
It rains almost every day where I live.
My home is near the Amazon River.
questions.fun_fact: Sloths move so slowly that tiny green algae grow in their fur, helping them hide among the leaves.

quality.notes: Sloths also live in Central America, so 'South America' is incomplete but still clearly the best option. Distractors are very weak. A sloth photo does not show the answer, so it is safe as illustrative; decorative is the wrong role.

questions.description: Why flap when the air will give you a free ride?
questions.question: White storks fly from Europe to Africa, avoid crossing open sea, and circle upward in warm rising air over land. What is the rising air for?
hints: Flapping big wings for thousands of kilometers is tiring.
Warm air does not rise much over the sea.
Gliders and paragliders use the same trick.
questions.fun_fact: In 1822 a stork came back to Germany with an African spear stuck in its neck, helping prove that birds migrate to Africa.

quality.notes: 'Spotting fish' clashes with 'avoid open sea' and 'over land', so it is easy to drop. The Pfeilstorch fun fact is great.

questions.description: The most famous movie star that has never said a single word.
questions.question: This silhouette shows the great white shark, the ocean's most famous hunter. Which animal group does it belong to?
hints: It never comes up to breathe air.
It breathes with gills.
It is in the same group as a goldfish.

media.note: A black silhouette of a great white shark seen from the side.

questions.fun_fact: A great white shark can have about 300 teeth at a time, and it grows new ones whenever old ones fall out.

quality.notes: The question names the great white, so the silhouette is not really essential; illustrative fits better. The fun fact about teeth touches q-0985 (teeth replacement), but the question asks a different fact. A rather standard school fact.

questions.description: Wrinkly, toothy and in no hurry to grow old.
questions.question: You're holding a pet mouse, which may live 2 to 3 years. A naked mole-rat is a rodent of similar size: how long can it live?
hints: It lives much longer than you would expect for its size.
Some in zoos have lived for decades.
It can live longer than ten mice in a row.
questions.fun_fact: Naked mole-rats hardly ever get cancer and can survive for minutes without oxygen.

quality.notes: Hint 3 nearly gives the number, which is allowed. '100 years' is easy to drop.

questions.description: A bug so big it could use a mouse as a pillow.
questions.question: This beetle is one of the heaviest insects in the world. Where does it live in the wild?
hints: It lives in hot tropical rainforests.
Its name comes from a giant in an old story.
It shares its home with gorillas and chimpanzees.

media.note: A clear photo of a Goliath beetle (Goliathus) with its black and white pattern.

questions.fun_fact: The larvae of the Goliath beetle can weigh up to about 100 g (3.5 oz), as much as a small apple.

quality.notes: Hard to work out, but hint 3 (gorillas) helps. A Goliath beetle photo is likely on Commons.

questions.description: A whale that travels so far it picks up hitchhikers.
questions.question: “I swim from Arctic seas to the lagoons of Mexico every year, and my gray skin is covered in white and orange patches.” What causes these patches?
hints: The patches are alive.
Some of them also stick to ships and rocks.
Tiny shelled animals glue themselves to my skin.
questions.fun_fact: Gray whales swim about 16,000 to 20,000 km (10,000 to 12,000 mi) on their round trip every year.

quality.notes: Gray whales do carry white rake scars from orca attacks, so 'bites from killer whales' has a grain of truth. The orange color and the word 'patches' still favor barnacles and lice. 'Hitchhikers' in the description hints that the patches are alive. The Baja lagoon image could be illustrative instead of decorative.

questions.description: An elephant that dressed up for the Ice Age.
questions.question: You're standing in a museum next to a woolly mammoth skeleton. About how tall is it at the shoulder?
hints: It was about as big as an elephant.
It was taller than a grown-up.
It would just fit in a room with a high ceiling.
questions.fun_fact: The last woolly mammoths lived on a small Arctic island until about 4,000 years ago, when the Egyptian pyramids already stood.

quality.notes: The options are spread so widely that it becomes a size guess. q-0303 identifies the mammoth skeleton, but that is a different fact.

questions.description: A star that never shines in the sky.
questions.question: Where would you NOT find a starfish living?
wrong_answers: In a rock pool on the beach
hints: Starfish need one special kind of water.
They can't live without salt water.
All the right places are in the sea.
questions.fun_fact: Many starfish can grow back a lost arm, and some can even grow a whole new body from one arm.

quality.notes: The mountain lake stands out as the only freshwater option. Simple question, and the fun fact makes up for it a little.

questions.description: A walking wool sweater with horns.
questions.question: When wolves come, animals like this one in the Arctic stand in a circle with their horns facing out. What is the circle for?
questions.answer: Protecting the calves in the middle
hints: The wolves are looking for the easiest target.
The weakest members of the herd go inside.
Think of what grown-ups do with their little ones.

media.note: A clear photo of a musk ox with its long shaggy coat and curved horns.

questions.fun_fact: A musk ox's soft underwool, called qiviut, is much warmer than sheep's wool.

quality.notes: Players can reason towards it. A musk ox photo is easy to find on Commons.

questions.description: Every hero needs a villain, and this one comes with a crown and a very big appetite.
questions.question: I'm a greedy, penguin-like king of Dream Land, and in the 2001 anime I keep ordering monsters to beat a pink puffball. Who am I?
hints: I carry a huge wooden hammer.
I've been an enemy in the Kirby video games since the very first one.
My name is a royal title plus three repeated syllables.
questions.fun_fact: In the anime, the king orders his monsters from a shady company that delivers them like takeout.

quality.notes: Facts check out (Kirby: Right Back at Ya!, Holy Nightmare Co.). Once you hear 'penguin-like king' and 'pink puffball', King Dedede is the only Kirby character among the options, so it's easier than 8. Kids know him from Smash Bros. and the Kirby games.

questions.description: Two friends shared one pen name, like sharing one very long pencil.
questions.question: Hayao Miyazaki is to Totoro as Fujiko F. Fujio is to…
hints: This character comes from the 22nd century.
He pulls gadgets out of a pocket on his belly.
He is a blue robot cat with no ears.
questions.fun_fact: Doraemon's official birthday is September 3, 2112.

quality.notes: The description says 'two friends shared one pen name', but 'Fujiko F. Fujio' is Fujimoto's name for himself alone, used after the pair split. That's slightly off. Hint 1 (22nd century) already gives it away to anyone who knows Doraemon. Doraemon is huge in Asia, Latin America and Spain, but less known in the English-speaking world. The creator-name analogy is quite dry.

questions.description: A doorway with no door, no walls and no doorbell.
questions.question: You walk under a tall red gate with two crossbars, like in many anime set in Japan. What are you about to enter?
hints: It's a holy place.
Visitors often clap their hands twice there to greet the spirits.
The gate marks the line between the everyday world and the home of the kami, or spirits.
questions.fun_fact: The Fushimi Inari shrine in Kyoto has about 10,000 of these gates, forming long orange tunnels up a mountain.

quality.notes: The torii image is the question's own subject, so that's fine. Knowing the word 'Shinto' is beyond most 11–12-year-olds, so it's probably harder than 6.

questions.description: Red paint: cheaper than a bigger engine, and apparently just as fast.
questions.question: In Mobile Suit Gundam, Char Aznable flies a red mobile suit. A famous line in the series says it moves how many times faster than normal?
hints: Char is nicknamed the “Red Comet”.
It's a small number, less than the fingers on one hand.
It's the same as the number of colors on a traffic light.
questions.fun_fact: Gundam began in 1979, and its plastic model kits, called Gunpla, have sold more than 500 million units.

quality.notes: This is deep fandom knowledge that you can't reason your way to. It's mostly known in Japan, so it doesn't travel well. The 'three times faster' line is real. The Gunpla sales figure is about right (it's grown well past 500 million). Hint 3 nearly gives it away, which is fine for a third hint.

questions.description: A top student whose homework gets way out of hand.
questions.question: Aladdin is to a magic lamp as Light Yagami is to a magic…
hints: He found it after a god from another world dropped it.
You write in it.
It's the second word in the title of his anime.
questions.fun_fact: Ryuk, the god who drops it, is crazy about apples.

quality.notes: Death Note's premise is killing people by writing their names. The wording avoids it, but the series is quite dark for a family game, even at difficulty 10. The facts are right.

questions.description: When the kids' comics grow up, get a job and start paying taxes.
questions.question: In manga, “shonen” is to teenage boys as which word is to adult men?
hints: Manga like “Berserk” and “Vagabond” belong to it.
It's not the word for manga made for women.
The word means “young adult” in Japanese.
questions.fun_fact: “Akira” and “Ghost in the Shell” both first ran in manga magazines for adult men.

quality.notes: Correct, and the distractors are real manga categories, which is good. As a vocabulary question it's a bit dry. It's Japan-specific, but fits the anime topic.

questions.description: The strongest sorcerer around, and also the best hair in the room.
questions.question: Watching Naruto, you see Kakashi hide one eye under his headband. Satoru Gojo hides both eyes under a what?
hints: He's the strongest teacher in Jujutsu Kaisen.
It's a strip of black cloth.
You'd wear one to play pin the tail on the donkey.
questions.fun_fact: His eyes, called the Six Eyes, see cursed energy in such detail that covering them helps him rest.

quality.notes: 'Helmet visor' and 'Paper mask' are weak options. 'Both eyes' rules out the eyepatch, so you can reason to the answer, which makes it easier than 9. The 'Watching Naruto, you see…' setup is a bit forced. Gojo sometimes wears sunglasses instead, but the blindfold is his signature look. Hint 3 uses a mostly Western party game.

questions.description: Beginning, middle, twist, punchline: done before your coffee cools.
questions.question: “Ukiyo-e” is to Japanese woodblock prints as which word is to four-panel comic strips?
hints: Many funny school anime, like “Azumanga Daioh”, began this way.
Japanese newspapers have printed them for about a century.
The word starts with “yon”, a Japanese word for four.
questions.fun_fact: “Sazae-san” began as a newspaper four-panel strip in 1946, and its anime, on air since 1969, is the longest-running animated TV series in the world.

quality.notes: A niche Japanese term that only manga fans know. It's knowledge of one language and region, which travels badly, and fewer people know it than the 14 suggests. The distractors are real and fair for experts. The Sazae-san fun fact is nice.

questions.description: A house that stands on tiptoe so it never gets its feet wet.
questions.question: Le Corbusier's Villa Savoye rests on thin concrete posts that lift it off the ground. What did he call these posts?
hints: They were one of his “five points” of modern architecture.
They leave the ground floor open, so a car could drive under the house.
The word is French and sounds a bit like a boat's “pilot”.
questions.fun_fact: The curve of Villa Savoye's ground floor was planned around the turning circle of a 1920s car.

quality.notes: Solid specialist question. Hint 3's 'pilot' sound link only works in some languages, but it's hint 3.

questions.description: A park where even the benches look like they escaped from a dream.
questions.question: Who designed this colorful park in Barcelona?
hints: He was an architect, not a painter.
He also designed a giant church in the same city that is still being finished.
That church is the Sagrada Família.

media.note: Photo of Park Güell in Barcelona: the mosaic dragon/lizard on the stairs or the curved mosaic bench; no signs with names.

questions.fun_fact: Park Güell was first planned as a fancy housing estate, but only two houses were ever built.

quality.notes: Shares the topic with q-1362 (Sagrada Família is Gaudí's), and hint 3 leans on that, but it asks a different fact. Gaudí is less known to 13-year-olds worldwide than the rating assumes.

questions.description: A skyscraper named after something you'd find in a jar next to the mustard.
questions.question: This glass skyscraper is nicknamed “the Gherkin”. In which city is it?
hints: The city sits on a river with many famous bridges.
It stands in the city's old financial district.
Big Ben is in the same city.

media.note: Photo of the Gherkin (30 St Mary Axe) with its diamond-patterned glass; avoid views showing Tower Bridge, the Shard or other London landmarks.

questions.fun_fact: Despite its curved shape, the Gherkin has only one piece of curved glass: the lens at the very top.

quality.notes: Good. Sydney is a weak distractor next to the European cities. A photo of the building could show other London landmarks; the note handles this.

questions.description: A temple that took the phrase “gold medal” a bit too literally.
questions.question: In which Japanese city does this golden temple stand?
hints: The city was Japan's capital for more than 1,000 years.
It is famous for its many temples, shrines and geisha districts.
Its name uses the same letters as Tokyo, in a different order.

media.note: Photo of the Golden Pavilion (Kinkaku-ji) reflected in its pond; no signs.

questions.fun_fact: The pavilion you see today is a copy: the original burned down in 1950 and was rebuilt in 1955.

quality.notes: Hint 3's anagram depends on spelling: it works for Kyoto/Tokyo and Kioto/Tokio, but not for German Kyoto/Tokio. Many adults know Kyoto's golden temple, so 11 fits better than 12.

questions.description: The world's least welcoming swimming pool.
questions.question: What is the water around this castle for?
hints: Castles were built to be safe from enemies.
It is hard to climb a wall when you are standing in deep water.
Often the only way in was over a bridge that could be pulled up.

media.note: Photo of a medieval castle surrounded by a water-filled moat, such as Bodiam Castle.

questions.fun_fact: The water ring around a castle is called a moat, and many castles had a drawbridge to cross it.

quality.notes: Good kids' question. Bodiam is a reliable photo.

questions.description: A house you can fold up and put in your pocket.
questions.question: What is this drawing?
hints: Builders look at drawings like this before they start work.
You can see walls, doors and rooms from above.
Architects make these drawings.

media.note: A clear architectural blueprint or floor plan showing walls, doors and rooms from above; no written title naming it.

questions.fun_fact: Old building plans were blue because they were copied with a chemical process that turned the paper blue, which is why they are called blueprints.

quality.notes: Easy to recognise and a bit flat. Rated 5, but kids can tell a floor plan from the options, so ~3. Floor-plan images often carry labels; the note covers the title only.

questions.description: A column wearing two curls, like it just got back from the hairdresser.
questions.question: This column style is named after the region where it first developed. Which region?
hints: Greeks lived in this region across the Aegean Sea from Athens.
The famous Temple of Artemis at Ephesus stood there.
The style's name sounds almost like the region's name.

media.note: Close photo of a Greek Ionic column with its two scroll-shaped volutes clearly visible; no labels.

questions.fun_fact: Ionic columns are thinner than Doric ones, and the ancient writer Vitruvius said they were shaped after a woman's figure.

quality.notes: Once you recognise the Ionic column, the name gives Ionia away. The options are long and descriptive. A bit of a school-test feel.

questions.description: A city so small you could knock it over with a sneeze.
questions.question: Why do architects build small models like this one?
questions.answer: To show the building before it's built
wrong_answers: To use as homes for pets
hints: The real building doesn't exist yet.
It helps people imagine how it will look.
It's like a mini preview of the real thing.

media.note: Photo of an architectural scale model of a building or neighborhood, white or wooden, clearly a model.

questions.fun_fact: Some architects test their models in wind tunnels to see how real wind will blow around the building.

quality.notes: The distractors are silly and easy to dismiss, even for kids. Pleasant but not very surprising.

questions.description: Going around in circles, but officially.
questions.question: Look at this running track. How many meters is one lap in the inside lane?
hints: It's much more than the length of one straight.
The famous sprint on the straight is 100 m, and a lap has two straights and two bends.
Two laps make the 800 m race.

media.note: A clear photo of a full standard outdoor athletics track (oval with lanes), seen from above or from the stands. No visible distance numbers or text.

questions.fun_fact: Only the inside lane measures exactly 400 m; outer lanes are longer, which is why runners in the 400 m start at staggered spots.

quality.notes: The photo doesn't really help answer, so 'essential' is debatable; illustrative would do. Hint 2 already lets players work it out. Feels like a standard school fact, so fun is only moderate.

questions.description: A stick so shy it falls down if you so much as brush it.
questions.question: This bar rests loosely on two supports and drops at the slightest touch. Which kind of athletics events use it?
hints: Athletes try not to touch it at all.
It's raised a little higher after each round.
Athletes go over it, either with a pole or without one.

media.note: A close-up of a high jump or pole vault crossbar resting on the pegs of its upright stand. No athlete, no text.

questions.fun_fact: A jumper can brush the bar and still succeed, as long as it stays up on its supports.

quality.notes: Only high jump and pole vault use the bar. Long jump and triple jump are also jumping events but don't, which is a small looseness in the category answer. A clear crossbar photo is likely on Commons.

questions.description: Red, rubbery and covered in lines: it's not a giant eraser.
questions.question: Look at this close-up. Which sport is done on this surface?
hints: You need sneakers for it.
The lines keep everyone in their own lane.
Sprinters race on it as fast as they can.

media.note: A close-up of a red athletics track surface with white lane lines and painted lane numbers. No people.

questions.fun_fact: Before rubbery tracks, runners raced on cinder tracks made of crushed ash.

quality.notes: Easy recognition question that fits a 1, but it isn't very surprising. A clear photo is easy to find.

questions.description: The race where looking like you're in a hurry is allowed, but running is not.
questions.question: In an Olympic race walk, at least how many feet must touch the ground at every moment?
hints: Think about what makes running different from walking.
When you run, there's a moment when you're flying.
Walkers must never be fully in the air.
questions.fun_fact: Race walkers must also keep their front leg straight from the moment that foot hits the ground.

quality.notes: The description's 'running is not' allowed is a mild nudge. A picture of race walkers would be safe as illustrative, so decorative is an unnecessary choice.

questions.description: A fire that travels more than most tourists.
questions.question: “I'm lit by the sun's rays and a curved mirror, then runners carry me all the way to the Games.” In which country am I lit?
hints: It's the country where the Olympic Games began long ago.
I'm lit at the ruins of an ancient temple.
The town where I'm lit is called Olympia.
questions.fun_fact: The torch relay that carries the flame to the host city started at the 1936 Games in Berlin.

quality.notes: Hint 1 ('the country where the Olympic Games began') is too strong for a first hint. The Greece candidates ask different facts.

questions.description: A beach day, except everyone arrives at full speed.
questions.question: Look at this sand with a white board in front of it. Where is it?
hints: It's at an athletics stadium.
Athletes sprint down a runway before reaching it.
They take off from the white board and fly into the sand.

media.query: long jump sand pit takeoff board
media.note: A photo of an athletics long jump sand pit, clearly showing the white take-off board and the end of the runway. No athlete in the air, no text.

questions.fun_fact: Officials rake the sand flat after every jump, because the jump is measured to the closest mark the body leaves.

quality.notes: Fun fact wording 'closest mark the body leaves' is unclear: the jump is measured to the mark nearest the take-off board. Good essential photo.

questions.description: Three steps to happiness, but only one gets you to the very top.
questions.question: “I have three steps, and the middle one is the highest. Winners stand on me to get their medals.” What am I?
hints: You see me at the end of big races.
Gold, silver and bronze each get a step.
The winner stands on my tallest middle step.
questions.fun_fact: The word “podium” comes from an ancient Greek word for “foot.”

quality.notes: A medals image would be safe as illustrative, so decorative is a weak choice.

questions.description: Always second over the hurdle, but never left behind.
questions.question: “When a hurdler clears a hurdle, the other leg goes first and I follow, folded out to the side.” What am I called?
hints: My partner is called the lead leg.
I'm the one that pushes off the ground.
My name means I come along behind.
questions.fun_fact: Knocking a hurdle down by accident is allowed; it just costs the hurdler a bit of speed.

quality.notes: A narrow coaching term. Hint 3 ('My name means I come along behind') depends on the English word 'trail' and may not work in Spanish. The description ('Always second... never left behind') echoes 'trail'. Feels like a dry name-the-term question.

questions.description: Furniture for people who never want to sit down.
questions.question: Athletes push their feet against this to get going. Which races use it?
hints: These races are short.
Athletes start crouched down, hands on the ground.
Think of the 100 m.

media.note: A close-up photo of athletics starting blocks fixed on a track, with no athlete.

questions.fun_fact: Sensors in the blocks spot false starts: reacting in under a tenth of a second counts as leaving too early.

quality.notes: Good. Starting block photos are easy to find.

questions.description: Twenty euros buys you a cathedral window, at least on paper.
questions.question: This window is printed on the 20 euro note. Which style of architecture does it show?
hints: The style comes from the Middle Ages.
Look at the pointed tops of the windows.
Think of Notre-Dame in Paris.

media.note: Close-up of the front of the 20 euro note showing only the pointed-arch Gothic windows; the number 20 and any text should be cropped out or not dominant.

questions.fun_fact: The buildings on euro notes are invented, so no single country gets its own landmark on the money.

quality.notes: The answer is right: the €20 note shows Gothic windows and arches. The fun fact says the buildings are 'invented'. More precisely, they are made-up examples of each style, which is fine. 'Modern' is a weak distractor, and Romanesque would be stronger. The essential image of the note will probably show '20' and 'EURO', but the question already says that, so it does no harm.

questions.description: Money you can't fold, crumple or lose in the washing machine.
questions.question: A café sign says it accepts ₿, the symbol of bitcoin. In which year were the first bitcoins created?
hints: It happened in the 21st century.
Smartphones were just becoming popular.
It was right after a big world financial crisis that began in 2008.
questions.fun_fact: In 2010, a man paid 10,000 bitcoins for two pizzas, which would later be worth hundreds of millions of dollars.

quality.notes: The café-sign setup is an invented scene that the question doesn't need, so fun gets 3. The options are evenly spaced 10 years apart, and 1989 is easy to rule out. Hint 3, about the 2008 crisis, nearly gives the answer, which hint 3 is allowed to do.

questions.description: A bill so fancy it could almost be made into a shirt.
