questions.question: “I'm the US banknote with Benjamin Franklin on the front, and I'm not made of ordinary paper.” What am I mostly made of?
hints: That's why I survive a trip through the washing machine.
I'm made from plant fibers, but not from trees.
Your T-shirt and jeans are made of my main ingredient.
questions.fun_fact: The $100 bill has a blue 3D security ribbon woven into the note, not printed on it.

quality.notes: The answer is correct: 75% cotton and 25% linen. The question is about US money, but the $100 bill is known worldwide, so this is acceptable. Hint 3 points strongly to cotton. It touches q-0391 (linen) only by topic.

questions.description: Purple and gold, and not a single day spent in another jersey.
questions.question: This player spent his whole 20-year NBA career with the Los Angeles Lakers. Who is he?
hints: He played from 1996 to 2016.
He won five NBA titles and wore both number 8 and number 24.
Kids all over the world shout his first name when they toss paper into a bin.

media.note: A clear photo of Kobe Bryant playing in his Lakers jersey; no visible name caption.

questions.fun_fact: Kobe Bryant once scored 81 points in a single game in 2006, the second-highest total in NBA history.

quality.notes: Facts check out (1996–2016, five titles, #8/#24, 81 points is second only to Wilt's 100). The essential photo is likely available, but the jersey number or name may show. Difficulty 5 is too low for families outside the US: the whole-career-with-the-Lakers clue needs NBA knowledge. Kids may know the paper-toss meme, but that is only hint 3. LeBron also played for the Lakers, so the distractors stay fair.

questions.description: The only thing in the arena that never misses a basket.
questions.question: It hangs high above the court, shows the points of both teams and counts down the time. What is it?
hints: Every fan looks up at it during the game.
It has big glowing numbers on it.
It tells you the “score”.
questions.fun_fact: Many big arenas hang a giant four-sided video screen over the center of the court so every seat can see it.

quality.notes: Trophy and whistle are weak distractors. Hint 3 only works in English (score/scoreboard), so it breaks in translation. A decorative arena picture will probably show the scoreboard, but it is blurred. The question is plain.

questions.description: Points, points and more points: someone has been counting for a very long time.
questions.question: In 2023, I broke a record that had stood since 1984 and became the top scorer in NBA history. Who am I?
hints: I started in the NBA straight out of high school in 2003.
I have played for Cleveland, Miami and Los Angeles.
My nickname is “King James”.
questions.fun_fact: The record he broke belonged to Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, famous for his almost unstoppable “skyhook” shot.

quality.notes: Kareem's record from 1984 was broken in February 2023, so the facts are correct. LeBron is very famous and is the obvious guess for an active record-breaker, so 10 is rated too high (estimate 8). The description is generic. The arena query is fine; it could arguably be decorative.

questions.description: A line that's always behind you, no matter how much you score.
questions.question: In soccer, the line behind the goal is the goal line. In basketball, the line behind the basket is the…?
hints: Tennis courts have a line with the same name.
It runs along the short end of the court.
Think of the “base” of the court.
questions.fun_fact: An NBA court measures 28.65 m (94 ft) from one baseline to the other.

quality.notes: Hint 3 ("base") and the tennis hint depend on the English word, so they won't work in Spanish (línea de fondo) or German. The line is also called the end line. The description is weak. It is a dry terminology question.

questions.description: A slam dunk, with a little help from some very silly friends.
questions.question: In the 2021 film “Space Jam: A New Legacy”, a basketball star teams up with which cartoon gang?
hints: The gang has been around since the 1930s.
One of them is a very fast bird chased by a coyote.
Its most famous member asks “What's up, Doc?”.
questions.fun_fact: The first “Space Jam”, from 1996, starred Michael Jordan alongside the same cartoon gang.

questions.description: The only team member who's allowed to sweat inside a giant fluffy head.
questions.question: A person in a big furry costume dances, gives high fives and throws T-shirts into the crowd during breaks. Why?
hints: This character never plays in the game.
It is often an animal that matches the team's name.
It's all about cheering and fun.
questions.fun_fact: Some mascots do real acrobatics, like flipping off trampolines to dunk the ball during breaks.

quality.notes: The distractors are absurd for a dancing costumed character, so the answer is obvious. Mascots are a fairly US-style custom, but they are known worldwide.

questions.description: It catches every basket and never drops one.
questions.question: Look at the net hanging from this basketball hoop. What is it usually made of?
hints: It's soft and bendy.
It moves with a “swish” when the ball goes through.
A fishing net is made of the same kind of thing.

media.note: A clear close-up of a basketball hoop with a white cord (string) net, not a metal chain net.

questions.fun_fact: Some outdoor courts use nets made of metal chains, because string nets wear out fast in the rain and sun.

quality.notes: Glass, paper and wood are very weak distractors. The photo isn't really essential, and real nets are nylon cord, which is acceptable as "string". The fun fact about chain nets is fine.

questions.description: The polite basketball way to say “no, thank you” to a shot.
questions.question: I'm a “block” in basketball, and the crowd goes wild when I happen near the rim. What am I?
questions.answer: Stopping a shot with your hand
wrong_answers: Taking the ball from a dribbler
A pass that leads to a basket
hints: Defenders love me; shooters don't.
Tall players who can jump high do me the most.
The ball gets swatted away while it's flying toward the basket.
questions.fun_fact: Blocks were not counted as an official NBA statistic until the 1973–74 season.

quality.notes: It is a plain term definition. Hint 3 spells the answer out (allowed for hint 3). Blocks became an official stat in 1973–74, which is correct. The distractors (steal, rebound, assist) are good.

questions.description: Before you read this question, your mind was perfectly empty. Allegedly.
questions.question: Which English philosopher argued that a newborn's mind is a “blank slate”, filled only by experience?
hints: He lived in the 17th century.
His ideas also shaped modern ideas of rights and government.
He wrote “An Essay Concerning Human Understanding” in 1689.
questions.fun_fact: Locke didn't actually write “tabula rasa” in English: he compared the newborn mind to “white paper”.

quality.notes: The question says "English", which rules out Descartes (French). The fun fact is a bit muddled: "tabula rasa" is Latin, and the idea goes back to Aristotle and Avicenna, but it is true that Locke wrote "white paper". The question is a fairly dry school-style recall.

questions.description: The boss of your body, who forgets where you left your keys.
questions.question: Ancient Egyptians threw it away when making mummies. It uses about a fifth of your body's energy. Your awareness comes from it. What is it?
hints: It's in your head.
It's protected by your skull.
You use it to think.
questions.fun_fact: Ancient Egyptians thought the heart was where thoughts lived, so they kept it inside the mummy.

quality.notes: The "awareness" clue makes it quite easy. It is related to q-0390 (Egyptians kept the heart in the mummy), and the fun fact repeats that fact, but the question asks something different. The decorative pyramids image would also work as illustrative.

questions.description: The most famous man in logic books, and he never wrote a single one.
questions.question: On page one of a logic book: “All men are mortal. ___ is a man. So ___ is mortal.” Which Greek philosopher usually fills the gap?
hints: He lived in Athens.
He never wrote any books himself.
His most famous student was Plato.
questions.fun_fact: Socrates left no writings at all: we know his ideas mostly from his student Plato.

quality.notes: The description ("never wrote a single one") and hint 2 hint at Socrates for players who know about him, and the fun fact repeats the same point. Shares only a topic with q-1476. The decorative Greek columns could have been illustrative.

questions.description: A rule so good they made it out of the most precious metal.
questions.question: About 2,500 years ago, this teacher said “Do not do to others what you do not want done to yourself.” Who is he?
hints: He lived in Asia.
His teachings shaped Chinese culture for centuries.
His sayings are collected in a book called “The Analects”.

media.note: A clear statue of Confucius, with no name plate or text visible.

questions.fun_fact: Versions of this “Golden Rule” appear in almost every major religion and culture in the world.

quality.notes: The Buddha lived at about the same time and taught a similar rule, so the photo is the real tie-breaker. The question can be answered without the image, so "essential" is a stretch. A statue showing East Asian features helps rule out Socrates and Buddha.

questions.description: Everybody gets a vote, even on what to have for dinner.
questions.question: Democracy was born in the city in this photo, about 2,500 years ago. Which city is it?
hints: It's in Europe.
It's the capital of its country today.
Its city is named after the goddess of wisdom.

media.note: A clear photo of the Acropolis with the Parthenon, no text or signs.

questions.fun_fact: “Democracy” comes from Greek words meaning “rule by the people”.

quality.notes: The Parthenon photo makes it easier for many players. A Parthenon photo is very likely available, so essential media is fine. Hint 3 is awkwardly worded ("Its city").

questions.description: Grandma's sweater is lovely. Truly. Absolutely.
questions.question: What is a “white lie”?
questions.answer: A small lie told to be kind
wrong_answers: A lie told to get money
A lie told only at night
hints: It's meant to protect someone's feelings.
Saying you love a gift you don't like is one.
It's a lie with a good heart.
questions.fun_fact: The philosopher Immanuel Kant said you should never lie, not even a small kind lie.

quality.notes: The question rests on an English idiom, which other languages put differently ("Notlüge", "mentira piadosa"), so it travels badly. The distractors ("written on paper", "only at night") are weak and silly.

questions.description: If A is a question and B is a quiz, then C is this.
questions.question: When did people first write down the rules of logic?
hints: It's much older than computers.
It happened before the Roman Empire was at its biggest.
Aristotle wrote about it in ancient Greece.
questions.fun_fact: Around the same time, thinkers in India and China also built their own systems of logic.

quality.notes: The answer stands out: it is the only option worded "More than", and it is the oldest. The question is a dry dating exercise. The description is a weak, forced joke.

questions.description: This question was going to be asked anyway. It was always going to be.
questions.question: This French scientist imagined a being that knows where every atom is and so could predict the whole future. Who is he?
hints: He lived around the time of Napoleon.
He worked on probability and the motion of planets.
The imagined being is called his “demon”.

media.note: A painted portrait of Pierre-Simon Laplace, without a name caption.

questions.fun_fact: Laplace reportedly told Napoleon that his book on the heavens had “no need” of the idea of God.

quality.notes: "French" rules out Newton. The portrait is not really essential, since the question can be answered from the text, so "illustrative" would be the better role.

questions.description: Which came first? Don't worry, we're only asking what comes next.
questions.question: I'm a hen. If I sit on my egg and keep it warm for three weeks, what comes out?
hints: It's a baby bird.
It's small, fluffy and yellow.
It says “peep peep” and grows up to be like me.
questions.fun_fact: A chick can already peep from inside its egg a day or two before it hatches.

questions.description: Breakfast for very, very small appetites.
questions.question: Look at these small speckled eggs next to a normal hen's egg. Which bird laid them?
hints: The bird that laid them is small itself.
It's a little round bird that runs more than it flies.
Their eggs are a fancy snack in many countries, often boiled.

media.note: Several small brown-speckled quail eggs next to one ordinary chicken egg for size; no labels.

questions.fun_fact: Quail chicks can run around just a few hours after hatching.

quality.notes: Weak distractors. The photo shows eggs smaller than a hen's egg, but ostrich, turkey and duck all lay bigger eggs, so quail is the only option that fits the picture. A quail-vs-chicken egg comparison photo is probably on Commons, but the note needs it to be unlabeled.

questions.description: Flying in formation: the original carpool.
questions.question: Geese often fly in a V like this on long trips. Which birds in the V work the hardest?
wrong_answers: The birds at the two back ends
The birds in the second row
hints: Each bird gets a little lift from the air moving off the wings ahead of it.
One bird has nobody in front of it.
That's why the geese take turns at this spot.

media.note: A flock of geese flying in a clear V formation across the sky.

questions.fun_fact: Birds in a V time their wingbeats to catch the rising air from the bird ahead, a bit like cyclists riding close together.

quality.notes: The video isn't strictly essential (the question works without it), but V-formation footage is easy to find, so it's acceptable.

questions.description: The sunny side of the question.
questions.question: You crack a hen's egg into a bowl. About how much of the egg's weight is the yellow yolk?
hints: The clear egg white is the biggest part.
The shell is only around a tenth.
It's roughly a third of the egg.
questions.fun_fact: The yolk is the food store for the growing chick, which is why it is packed with fat and protein.

quality.notes: A fairly dry estimation question. Hint 1 already rules out 60% and 90%.

questions.description: Some eggs crack, some just wobble.
questions.question: You crack an egg into a pan, and its shell is hard. Which of these animals does NOT lay eggs with a hard shell?
hints: The odd one out lays its eggs in water.
Its eggs look like little balls of jelly.
Its babies are tadpoles.
questions.fun_fact: An eggshell has thousands of tiny holes, so the chick inside can breathe.

quality.notes: The opening line about cracking an egg into a pan is padding that doesn't help, which makes the question longer than it needs to be. Plain NOT-question format.

questions.description: A tuxedo in a toddler size.
questions.question: The little penguin of Australia and New Zealand is the smallest penguin in the world. About how tall is it?
hints: It's much smaller than the famous emperor penguin.
It's still bigger than a pigeon.
It's about as tall as a school ruler is long.
questions.fun_fact: Little penguins are also called fairy penguins, and their feathers are blue instead of black.

quality.notes: A 'Phillip Island beach' search might return Penguin Parade signs or penguin photos, but that wouldn't show the size, so the risk is minor.

questions.description: A home with no door, no roof and no rent.
questions.question: It can be made of twigs, mud or even spit, and birds build it in trees or under roofs. What is a nest mostly for?
hints: It's used for a few weeks in spring.
Parent birds sit in it to keep things warm.
Baby birds grow up in it until they can fly.
questions.fun_fact: Some swiftlets build their nests almost only from their own spit, and people in Asia make soup from them.

quality.notes: Hint 1 ('a few weeks in spring') isn't true everywhere, for example in the tropics. 'Sleeping every night' is arguably partly true for a few species. An illustrative image of an empty nest would be safe, so decorative isn't really needed. Plain question.

questions.description: A game where asking “Does your person wear a hat?” counts as smart detective work.
questions.question: In the classic game Guess Who?, about how many faces are on each player's board?
hints: Every face has its own little flip-up frame.
There are several rows of faces, all of them easy to see at once.
It's two dozen.
questions.fun_fact: A good Guess Who? player can find the right face in about five yes-or-no questions, because each smart question can rule out half of the faces left.

quality.notes: The facts check out: there are 24 faces, and about 5 yes/no questions is right (log2 24 ≈ 4.6). The wrong answers 4, 300 and 5,000 are so far off that anyone picturing the board picks 24 at once, so the estimate has no tension. The question is a plain count rather than a surprise. It needs players to know Guess Who?, which is widespread but not everywhere.

questions.description: The game where the spinner decides how knotted up the whole family gets.
questions.question: In the game Twister, the spinner tells you where to put a hand or foot. How many different colors can it land on?
hints: The colors are the same as the circles on the big floor mat.
Red is one of them, and so are blue and green.
It's the same as the number of hands and feet you have.
questions.fun_fact: Twister became famous in 1966 when a TV star played it on a late-night show, and millions of people suddenly wanted their own.

quality.notes: The facts are right: the 4 colors, and the 1966 Carson show. It's a simple count with little surprise. Hint 2 names three colors, which only rules out 3.

questions.description: A card suit that looks like a leaf, but nobody ever rakes it.
questions.question: I'm a black suit in a normal deck of playing cards, and my ace is often the fanciest card in the deck. Which suit am I?
hints: Only two of the four suits are black.
My symbol looks like an upside-down heart with a little stem.
My name is also a tool used for digging.
questions.fun_fact: The ace of spades got its fancy design in England, where it once carried a stamp to show the tax on the deck had been paid.

quality.notes: Hint 3 depends on the English word "spade" being a digging tool; it fails in Spanish (picas) and German (Pik), so it doesn't travel. "The fanciest ace" is a soft clue: it holds for decks in the English tradition and less so elsewhere. The description's "looks like a leaf" could also suggest clubs.

questions.description: Castles that move in straight lines and never need a drawbridge.
questions.question: Look at this chess set ready to play. How many rooks, the pieces shaped like little castle towers, are on the board?
hints: They all start in the corners.
Each player has the same number of them.
Count the corners of the board.

media.note: Photo of a full chessboard set up in the starting position, all 32 pieces visible, so the rooks in the four corners can be seen.

questions.fun_fact: The rook is the only chess piece that can take part in castling, a special move together with the king.

quality.notes: This is a plain counting task from a photo and is dry. Hint 1 ("in the corners") nearly gives the count. The fun fact says the rook is "the only piece" that castles "together with the king", which is awkward because the king castles too. A starting-position photo is likely on Commons.

questions.description: A game where slamming your tile on the table is half the fun.
questions.question: Dominoes is a hugely popular game from Colombia to China. How many dots are on this domino tile?
hints: The tile has two halves.
Both halves have the same number of dots.
Each half has six dots.

media.note: Clear photo of a single double-six domino tile, with six dots on each half, all twelve dots easy to count.

questions.fun_fact: A standard set of dominoes has 28 tiles, from the blank double up to the double six.

quality.notes: This is a plain counting task with little to discover. A double-six photo is very likely on Commons. The Colombia mention sits fine in a base question because it is paired with China.

questions.description: A game that's neither from China nor really checkers, but nobody told the marbles.
questions.question: The board of Chinese checkers is shaped like a star. How many points does that star have?
hints: Up to this many players can play at once, each starting in their own point.
It's more than the points on a typical drawn star.
It's the same as the faces on a normal die.
questions.fun_fact: Chinese checkers was actually invented in Germany in 1892 as “Stern-Halma”; the Chinese name came later in the United States as a marketing idea.

quality.notes: The Stern-Halma fact (Germany, 1892) is correct and fun. Hint 2 rules out 4 and 5.

questions.description: A number some people love to brag about at dinner parties.
questions.question: I'm the score from a test, and the average person gets 100. What am I meant to measure?
wrong_answers: How well your eyes can see
How much you know about history
hints: People call me IQ.
My tests are full of puzzles, patterns and logic.
The “I” in my name stands for “intelligence”.
questions.fun_fact: Average scores on IQ tests rose by several points per decade during the 20th century, which is called the Flynn effect.

quality.notes: The heart and eyesight options are easy to rule out. Only the history-knowledge option is tempting. The question feels like a school test.

questions.description: The body's main highway, with no traffic lights and lots of messages.
questions.question: People call me the spinal cord, and I live inside your backbone, but I'm not a bone. What am I?
hints: I carry messages between your brain and your body.
If I'm hurt, parts of the body can stop moving or feeling.
I'm part of the nervous system, just like your brain.
questions.fun_fact: Some reflexes, like pulling your hand away from something hot, are handled by the spinal cord before the brain even knows.

quality.notes: “A tube of fat” is a weak wrong answer. The fact is a bit dry. The word “cord” already hints at something like a cable.

questions.description: Your body's electric cables, no batteries needed.
questions.question: They are long, thin cells, they send tiny electric messages, and your brain holds billions of them. Nerves are made of them. What are they?
hints: They are the cells of the nervous system.
They talk to each other through tiny gaps.
Their name starts like the word “nervous”.
questions.fun_fact: Some nerve cells reach from the bottom of your spine all the way to your toes, about 1 m (3 ft) long.

quality.notes: Hint 3 depends on the neuron/nervous link between words, which doesn't work the same in every language. The decorative image would show the answer itself (blurred). The question is fairly textbook-like.

questions.description: The feeling that makes a clock seem to stop on purpose.
questions.question: I come on long rainy afternoons when there's nothing to do, and time feels very slow. What feeling am I?
hints: You might yawn and stare out of the window.
Kids often say “I have nothing to do!” when they feel me.
A new game or a good book makes me go away.
questions.fun_fact: Some studies found that people who were bored first came up with more creative ideas afterwards.

questions.description: The comfiest piece of furniture in the history of science.
questions.question: I'm a couch where patients lay and talked about their dreams. I stood in Vienna and now I'm in a London museum. Who was my famous owner?
hints: My owner was an Austrian doctor of the mind.
He founded psychoanalysis.
He wrote a famous book called “The Interpretation of Dreams”.
questions.fun_fact: The couch was a gift from a grateful patient, and Freud brought it with him when he moved to London in 1938.

quality.notes: Probably a bit harder than 9 for teens, since the couch is mostly adult general knowledge.

questions.description: The face everyone makes when the cake comes out with candles.
questions.question: Your eyebrows go up, your eyes open wide and your mouth makes an “O”. What feeling is that?
hints: It often happens at a party when everyone jumps out.
It comes very fast and goes away quickly.
People shout “Boo!” to cause it.
questions.fun_fact: Surprise is the shortest emotion: it usually lasts only a second or two before turning into another feeling.

quality.notes: “Boo!” is more about a scare than a surprise. “Shortest emotion” is Ekman's claim and not a settled fact. Sleepiness is a weak wrong answer.

questions.description: A tiny silver lady who has been riding on very expensive cars for over 100 years.
questions.question: A leaping cat is to Jaguar as the “Spirit of Ecstasy”, a small winged lady on the hood, is to…
hints: It's a luxury car brand from Britain.
Its logo is two letters R, one on top of the other.
Its name joins the names of its two founders, Charles Rolls and Henry Royce.
questions.fun_fact: On modern models, the little statue can sink into the car at a touch, so thieves can't snap it off.

quality.notes: The facts are correct: the Spirit of Ecstasy dates from 1911, and on modern cars it retracts. It's mostly adults who know this, so the difficulty is a little higher than stated. q-1260 has the same answer but asks a different fact (which brand isn't German).

questions.description: Before the movie starts, someone has to hold the flashlight.
questions.question: A roaring lion is to MGM as what is to Columbia Pictures?
hints: The studio's logo shows a person, not an animal or a building.
She stands on a pedestal, wrapped in a flowing robe.
She raises a bright flame high, a bit like the Statue of Liberty.
questions.fun_fact: The lady is “Columbia”, an old symbol of the United States, and for the 1992 version of the logo a newspaper artist named Jenny Joseph posed as the model.
questions.concept: Dama de la antorcha de Columbia

quality.notes: The distractors are excellent: they describe the Paramount, 20th Century Fox and Universal logos. The fun fact about Jenny Joseph posing in 1992 is correct. The "flashlight" in the description is a gentle, witty nudge toward the torch but doesn't settle it. US studio logos are seen worldwide before films, so this is acceptable.

questions.description: A cook's secret weapon, sold in a little brown bottle.
questions.question: I was a Swiss miller who, in the 1880s, made quick soup powders and a dark seasoning sauce. My last name is still on the bottles. Who am I?
hints: I wanted to give factory workers cheap, healthy meals that cooked fast.
Today my name is also on instant noodles that are very popular in India.
My seasoning bottle is brown with a yellow and red label.
questions.fun_fact: Maggi seasoning is so popular in Germany that lovage, a garden herb that smells like it, is often called the “Maggi herb” there.

quality.notes: The distractors are good (Knorr, Nestlé, Lindt). Hint 2 (Maggi noodles) almost gives it away for many families. A difficulty of 8 seems a bit low for teens, so I'd put it around 10. The question runs slightly long.

questions.description: The whole planet is on a spinning ride, and nobody bought a ticket.
questions.question: About how long does Earth take to spin once all the way around?
hints: While it spins, one half of Earth has day and the other half has night.
One full spin gives you one morning and one night.
It's the length of one whole day.
questions.fun_fact: At the equator, Earth's spin carries you along at about 1,670 km/h (1,040 mph), and you don't feel a thing.

quality.notes: Accurate (the sidereal day is 23 h 56 min, so "about 24 hours" is right). It reads like a dry school fact; the fun fact is what makes it interesting.

questions.description: The cheapest way to stay young: be born on the rarest date of the year.
questions.question: You were born on February 29, 2008. Counting up to 2024, how many birthdays have you had on the real February 29?
hints: February 29 only comes in leap years.
A leap year comes once every 4 years.
The leap years after 2008 are 2012, 2016, 2020 and 2024.
questions.fun_fact: About 5 million people around the world were born on February 29.

quality.notes: The answer is 4 (2012, 2016, 2020, 2024). Some players may wonder whether the birth date itself counts as a birthday, but "birthdays" makes it clear enough. Hint 3 lists all four years, which is allowed.

questions.description: Once a year, setting fire to a cake is completely normal.
questions.question: On your birthday, you hear the song, close your eyes and blow out every candle in one breath. Tradition says what will then come true?
hints: You think about it with your eyes closed.
You're not supposed to tell anyone what it is.
It's something you really, really hope for.
questions.fun_fact: Putting candles on birthday cakes is an old custom; children's birthday parties with candles were already popular in Germany more than 200 years ago.

quality.notes: The distractors are deliberately silly. That suits difficulty 1, but nobody would seriously pick them. The question is a little long.

questions.description: Gyms are packed in January and strangely empty by March.
questions.question: What do you call the promises people make at the start of a new year to do better, like eating healthier?
hints: They're plans to change yourself.
Many people forget them within a few weeks.
“This year I will exercise more!” is a classic one.
questions.fun_fact: About 4,000 years ago, people in ancient Babylon made promises to their gods at the new year, like paying back what they owed.

quality.notes: Resolutions are mainly a Western custom, but they are widely known. Young kids may not know the term.

questions.description: A date so close you can almost touch it, but not quite.
questions.question: Today is Friday. How many days from now is “the day after tomorrow”?
hints: Tomorrow is 1 day away.
It comes right after tomorrow.
Here it would be Sunday.
questions.fun_fact: Many languages have a single word for the day after tomorrow, like German “übermorgen”.

quality.notes: Simple and correct, but not very exciting; the German fun fact saves it a bit.

questions.description: The only calendar you can never lose is at the end of your arms.
questions.question: In the knuckle trick, you count the months over your fists, and each month on a knuckle has 31 days. How many months land on a knuckle?
hints: The months that fall in the dips between knuckles are shorter.
January, March and May all land on knuckles.
July and August are next to each other, and both land on knuckles.
questions.fun_fact: July and August both have 31 days, which is why the trick jumps from one fist to the other.

quality.notes: The wording is a bit roundabout: it really asks how many months have 31 days. Players can count it on their own fists, which is nice.

questions.description: Two tiny letters that decide if you're late for school or way too early.
questions.question: I'm “a.m.”, written after times like “7:00”, and I come from Latin. What do I tell you?
hints: I have a partner: “p.m.”.
My Latin words are “ante meridiem”.
“Ante” means “before”, and “meridiem” means “midday”.
questions.fun_fact: Noon itself is neither before nor after midday, so “12 a.m.” and “12 p.m.” confuse people all the time.

quality.notes: a.m./p.m. is a 12-hour-clock habit of English-speaking countries and parts of Latin America. Families in Germany and much of Europe use the 24-hour clock, so it doesn't travel well. "That the alarm is on" is a weak distractor.

questions.description: No hands, no ticking, just glowing numbers staring at you in the dark.
questions.question: What is this used for?
hints: You often find one next to a bed or on an oven.
It shows hours and minutes.
It's a kind of clock.

media.note: A clear photo of a digital clock showing a time in large digits, e.g. a bedside digital clock; no brand names visible.

questions.fun_fact: The first digital wristwatches with glowing numbers went on sale in the 1970s.

quality.notes: Very easy and fine for kids. The description hints at a clock ("glowing numbers"), but the photo shows one anyway. A digital clock photo is easy to find.

questions.description: The most loved button in the world is the one that says “just a bit more sleep”.
questions.question: Your alarm rings at 7:00. You press snooze, and it rings again 10 minutes later. What time is it now?
hints: Snooze only gives you a few more minutes.
Add 10 minutes to 7:00.
The hour stays the same.
questions.fun_fact: Many alarm clocks snooze for 9 minutes instead of 10, because of how the first snooze clocks were built.

quality.notes: The fun fact's reason for the 9-minute snooze is vague and partly folklore. "10:00" and "7:01" are weak distractors.

questions.description: A month full of falling leaves in some places and spring flowers in others.
questions.question: How many days does October have?
hints: It's not one of the shortest months.
It's the same as December.
It's the most days a month can have.
questions.fun_fact: October's name comes from the Latin word for “eight”, because it was the eighth month in the oldest Roman calendar.

quality.notes: A dry recall fact; the Latin "eight" fun fact helps.

questions.description: Two jet-lagged Americans who can't sleep, and neither can the karaoke machine.
questions.question: In “Lost in Translation”, Bill Murray and Scarlett Johansson meet in a Tokyo hotel. When did the film come out?
hints: Scarlett Johansson was still a teenager while filming.
It came out in the same decade as the first iPod.
It won an Oscar for best original screenplay in 2004.
questions.fun_fact: Director Sofia Coppola won the Oscar for its screenplay, and her father Francis Ford Coppola directed “The Godfather”.

quality.notes: This is a dry release-year question and has little to do with the capital-cities subcategory. With the options ten years apart, an adult who knows the film or Johansson's career can work it out, so 13 is too high. It needs adult film knowledge.

questions.description: A country that moved house and left its beaches behind.
questions.question: In 1960, Brasília became the capital of Brazil. Which city was the capital just before it?
hints: It is a city by the sea.
It is famous for its carnival and its beaches.
A giant statue of Christ looks down on it from a mountain.
questions.fun_fact: Brasília was built almost from nothing in about four years, and seen from above it is shaped a bit like an airplane.

quality.notes: The description's “left its beaches behind” hints at a coastal city and makes São Paulo and Manaus less likely. Many 11-year-olds outside Brazil would guess São Paulo, so I'd rate it a bit higher than 5.

questions.description: A dog that looks like someone flicked paint all over it.
questions.question: Dogs like this one star in a Disney film set in London, with 101 spotted puppies. What breed is it?
hints: Look at its black spots on white fur.
The villain in the film is Cruella de Vil.
Its name sounds a bit like the film's title, but without the number.

media.note: A clear photo of a spotted Dalmatian dog, no text.

questions.fun_fact: Dalmatian puppies are born completely white; their spots appear after a couple of weeks.

quality.notes: The question mentions “101 spotted puppies”, which together with the photo makes it very easy, but that fits the stated level. Hint 3 is close to the title but allowed.

questions.description: A home with very important tenants and very strict doormen.
questions.question: Buckingham Palace is to the British king as what is to the president of the United States?
hints: We are looking for where the president lives and works.
It is in Washington, D.C.
Its name tells you its color.
questions.fun_fact: The White House has 132 rooms and even its own bowling lane.

quality.notes: It leans toward the US, but the White House is known worldwide. Hint 3 nearly gives the answer, which is fine for hint 3.

questions.description: A bridge where the guards breathe fire, at least in stone.
questions.question: This bridge, guarded by dragon statues, stands in which European capital?
hints: The dragon is the symbol of this city.
It is the capital of a small country between the Alps and the Adriatic Sea.
It is the capital of Slovenia.

media.note: A clear photo of the Dragon Bridge in Ljubljana showing its dragon statues, with no signs or text naming the city.

questions.fun_fact: A legend says the Greek hero Jason, of the Golden Fleece, fought a dragon near where Ljubljana stands today.

quality.notes: Hint 2 (“small country between the Alps and the Adriatic”) already points straight to Slovenia, so it's very strong for a second hint. Well-read adults know about the dragon of Ljubljana, so 13 fits better than 14.

questions.description: A clock so famous it doesn't need a watch.
questions.question: In Disney's “Peter Pan”, the children fly past this famous clock tower. What is it called?
hints: It is in London.
It stands next to the British parliament by the river.
Its name sounds like a tall man called Ben.

media.note: A silhouette of the Big Ben clock tower (Elizabeth Tower) in London, no text.

questions.fun_fact: Big Ben is really the name of the huge bell inside; the tower itself was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012.

quality.notes: The question says “clock tower”, but none of the wrong options is a clock tower, so they can be ruled out by the wording alone. Few families outside the US know the Space Needle, so it's a weak option. “Leaning Tower” is ambiguous on its own.

questions.description: A city with a very famous big brother-in-law.
questions.question: I'm a Caribbean capital and the oldest city Europeans founded in the Americas that still stands. The brother of which explorer founded me?
hints: I am Santo Domingo, in the Dominican Republic.
His famous brother reached the Caribbean in 1492.
That explorer sailed with the Niña, the Pinta and the Santa María.
questions.fun_fact: Santo Domingo has the first cathedral built in the Americas, finished in the 1540s.

quality.notes: The description says “big brother-in-law”, which is wrong: Bartholomew was Columbus's brother, not his brother-in-law. Once players hear “Caribbean” and “explorer”, Columbus is easy to work out. Hint 2 touches the same fact as q-0099 (1492) but is still acceptable.

questions.description: The dial that gets excited every time you step on the gas.
questions.question: This car dial sits next to the speedometer, is often marked “×1000” and has a red zone at the top end. What does it measure?
wrong_answers: How fast the car is going
hints: It is called a tachometer, or rev counter.
Its unit is short for “revolutions per minute”.
It counts how many times the engine's crankshaft turns each minute.
questions.fun_fact: A typical car engine idles at around 800 revolutions per minute, so its crankshaft turns more than 13 times every second while the car stands still.

quality.notes: Dry, school-test feel. Hint 1 names the tachometer outright, which makes it much easier for anyone who has heard the word. The dashboard image will show the dial itself, but that matches what the question already describes. The q-1257 crankshaft question is a different fact.

questions.description: The only part of the car that's always looking back on the past.
questions.question: I hang at the top of the windshield and show the driver what's behind the car, without turning around. What am I?
hints: You can see your own face in me.
I reflect light.
My name says I show the view to the rear.
questions.fun_fact: Some ambulances have their name written backwards on the front so drivers read it the right way in their rearview mirror.

quality.notes: The distractors are weak: none of them shows what is behind the car, and the dashboard doesn't hang at the top. The ambulance fun fact is nice.

questions.description: The sound every passenger's stomach knows too well.
questions.question: Listen: which part of the car is the driver using hard right now?
hints: It happens when a car has to stop quickly.
The driver presses a pedal with a foot.
It is the opposite of the gas pedal.

media.note: A car braking hard: the screech of tires and brakes as it stops suddenly, no horn.

questions.fun_fact: Many electric cars turn the energy of braking back into electricity to recharge their batteries.

quality.notes: Freesound clips of brake screeches often end in a crash, so pick a clean clip as the note says. The screech could be heard as the tires, but no option conflicts with that.

questions.description: A number that tells your foot to calm down.
questions.question: I'm a number inside a red circle on a road sign, and drivers must not go faster than me. What am I?
wrong_answers: The distance to the next town
hints: Police may check me with a special camera.
Near schools I am usually small.
I tell you the most kilometers per hour you may drive.
questions.fun_fact: On some stretches of Germany's highways, the autobahn, there is no general speed limit at all.

quality.notes: The distractors are weak: none of them is shown as a number in a red circle. Red-circle weight-limit signs exist, but they carry a 't'. The lens 'colombia' doesn't fit a base question, though the content travels fine. The fun-fact twist is the most fun part.

questions.description: For the days when the sky is the best roof.
questions.question: On a hot sunny day, open is better. A car is to a convertible as a shoe is to a…
hints: Think of what a convertible has that a normal car doesn't.
A convertible's roof can fold away, so the top is open.
It's the shoe you wear to the beach.
questions.fun_fact: Convertibles are also called cabriolets, a name that comes from a light horse carriage with a folding hood.

quality.notes: The opening line 'On a hot sunny day, open is better.' is clumsy and nearly gives the answer away. The analogy is a bit loose: a boot is also a kind of shoe, though only the sandal is open, so it holds.

questions.description: Somebody's day job is driving the coolest toy truck in town.
questions.question: I drive a big red truck with a long ladder and a hose, and I rush to put out fires. Who am I?
hints: My truck has a loud siren.
I wear a helmet and a heavy jacket.
I spray water on flames.
questions.fun_fact: Not every fire truck is red: some cities paint them bright yellow-green, because that color is easier to see.

quality.notes: The fire truck image makes it very easy, but that is fine at difficulty 1.

questions.description: Some guests move in without asking, and never pay rent.
questions.question: At the vet, a cat gets a pill against worms that live inside its body. Which of these does NOT live inside cats?
hints: Look for the one that lives in a totally different place.
Three of these are parasites; one is a helper in the garden.
This one digs through soil after the rain.
questions.fun_fact: A cat can catch a tapeworm just by swallowing an infected flea while it licks its fur clean.

quality.notes: Facts are right: roundworm, tapeworm and hookworm are all cat parasites. Even kids can spot the earthworm because it is the only familiar one, so 6 is too high. The topic is a bit dry, and the vet scene adds length without adding a clue. An illustrative vet image would be safe, so decorative isn't needed.

questions.description: A noise that means “feed me”, “pet me” and “open the door” all at once.
questions.question: Listen! The ancient Egyptians named this animal after the sound it makes. Which animal is it?
hints: It is a pet that lives in many homes.
It loves to chase mice.
It also purrs when it's happy.

media.note: A clear recording of a domestic cat meowing, a few meows, no other animals.

questions.fun_fact: In ancient Egypt, one word for cat was “miu”, which sounds a lot like a meow.

quality.notes: The Egyptian word “miu” is correct. Once you hear the meow, the answer is trivial (difficulty 1), but that suits kids. Media is missing the required background_query for an audio question.

questions.description: A tiny fluffball that sleeps all day and attacks your toes at night.
questions.question: Dog is to puppy as cat is to…
hints: We're looking for a baby animal.
This baby says “meow”.
It's a very young cat.
questions.fun_fact: Kittens are born with blue eyes, and their real eye color only shows up after a few weeks.

quality.notes: A plain analogy that suits the youngest players but doesn't surprise anyone. Hint 2 nearly names the answer. The decorative puppy image is fine. q-0739 is also about kittens, but it asks a different fact.

questions.description: Two little lights in the dark hallway, and it's not a robot.
questions.question: Drivers see me on dark roads, and I'm named after the way a cat's eyes look at night. People call me a “cat's eye”. What am I?
hints: I have no battery and no electricity.
I only shine when light hits me.
I'm small and sit in a line along the road.
questions.fun_fact: Cats' eyes glow at night because of a mirror-like layer behind the eye that bounces light back, helping them see in very dim light.

quality.notes: “Cat's eye” is mainly a British name for road studs; in the US they are usually called raised pavement markers. Families in some regions may not know these road studs or the name, so this is a mild regional and language problem. Hint 1 rules out two options. Otherwise the players can reason their way to the answer.

questions.description: A house cat dressed up for a jungle costume party, and it never takes the costume off.
questions.question: This spotted pet breed, the Bengal, comes from crossing house cats with which wild cat?
hints: The wild ancestor is small, not much bigger than a house cat.
It lives in forests from India to Southeast Asia.
Its name sounds like a big spotted hunter, but it is a small cat.

media.note: A clear photo of a Bengal cat showing its spotted, leopard-like coat.

questions.fun_fact: Many Bengal cats love water and may jump into a bath or play with a running tap.

quality.notes: The facts are right, and the serval is a good distractor (it is the wild parent of the Savannah cat). The media role is wrong: the question names the Bengal, so the photo is illustrative, not essential. The Bengal's leopard-like coat hints a little at “leopard”. The fact that Bengals love water is widely reported but anecdotal.

questions.description: A cat that has been holding its paw up for years and still won't put it down.
questions.question: The maneki-neko is a cat figure from Japan. It sits in many shops and restaurants and lifts one paw. What does that gesture mean in Japan?
hints: Many visitors think it is waving, but that's not quite it.
The shop owners hope it brings something in.
It is calling customers and good luck inside.
questions.fun_fact: A maneki-neko with its left paw up is said to call customers, and one with its right paw up is said to call money.

quality.notes: The beckoning gesture and the left-paw/right-paw lore are correct. Hint 1 rules out “Goodbye”. The image of a shopping street may show a maneki-neko, which is fine because it doesn't reveal the meaning. The Japan candidates only share the country, not the fact.

questions.description: The sweet secret hiding in your glass of milk, no spoon needed.
questions.question: You're reading food labels: fructose is the sugar of fruit, as which sugar is the sugar of milk?
hints: Many adults around the world have trouble digesting it.
Special “free” versions of milk leave it out or break it down.
Its name comes from “lac”, the Latin word for milk.
questions.fun_fact: Long-aged hard cheeses like Parmesan contain almost no lactose, because it gets used up while they ripen.

quality.notes: Accurate, but it plays as a dry school-style analogy. The opening “You're reading food labels” adds nothing and makes the question longer. Hint 2 (“free” versions of milk) is very strong because lactose-free milk is everywhere, so hint 3 is barely needed. Difficulty is about right; many teens know lactose from lactose-free products, so 7 may fit better.

questions.description: The orange brick of the dairy world, now far more famous than its tiny hometown.
questions.question: This cheese is named after a village famous for its caves and its gorge. In which country is that village?
hints: The country is on an island.
It is the home of Big Ben.
Its capital is London.

media.note: A clear photo of a block or wedge of orange cheddar cheese, with no labels or text.

questions.fun_fact: Cheese is still left to ripen inside the cool caves of Cheddar Gorge today.

quality.notes: Essential media is risky. A plain orange cheese block could be Red Leicester, Mimolette or a colored Gouda, and much cheddar is white. So players have to recognize cheddar from the photo and also know it comes from England. That is two steps and harder than 6. Hint 2 (Big Ben) already gives the answer, which is fine for hint 3 but not hint 2. “England” as a country is acceptable. The fun fact about cheese ripening in the Cheddar Gorge caves is true.

questions.description: The night sky's biggest snack, if you believe the old stories.
questions.question: In old tales and cartoons, what is this said to be made of?
hints: It's a food made from milk.
Cartoon mice would love to take a bite.
Its craters look a bit like the holes in a famous Swiss kind.

media.note: A clear photo of the full Moon in a dark sky.

questions.fun_fact: In the 1989 short film “A Grand Day Out”, Wallace and Gromit fly a homemade rocket to the Moon to get cheese.

quality.notes: The moon-made-of-cheese idea is strongest in English and European folklore and cartoons, though Wallace & Gromit and Looney Tunes carry it widely. “A Grand Day Out” is usually dated 1989 (premiere), with its TV broadcast in 1990, so this is a small date nuance. q-0973 (the picture book about how the moon tastes) shares only the topic.

questions.description: The only cheese plate where the guest leaves very disappointed.
questions.question: What is this used for?
hints: It snaps shut very fast.
People often put a piece of cheese on it as bait.
Cartoon cats and this tool are after the same small, squeaky animal.

media.note: A clear photo of a classic wooden spring mousetrap, set and empty.

questions.fun_fact: The classic wooden spring mousetrap was invented over 100 years ago, and it has hardly changed since.

quality.notes: Clean and easy, and kids know mousetraps from cartoons. The description's “guest leaves very disappointed” hints a little at the trap's purpose, but it stays playful.

questions.description: Breakfast straight from the source, one squeeze at a time.
questions.question: Who usually does this work every day?
hints: This person usually starts work very early in the morning.
They look after big animals that eat grass.
Their work fills the milk cartons at the store.

media.note: A close-up photo of hands milking a cow's udder into a bucket.

questions.fun_fact: A good dairy cow can give about 30 liters (8 gallons) of milk in a single day.

quality.notes: Distractors are weak: a sailor and a baker are easy to rule out, and the beekeeper is the only plausible one. Saying a dairy farmer does hand milking “every day” is a bit dated, since most milking today is done by machine. The question is quite plain. The fun fact (about 30 L a day) is reasonable for high-yield cows but higher than the global average.

questions.description: Four suspects walk into the lab, and one of them is not sour at all.
questions.question: You test four things with litmus paper, and three turn it red because they are acids. Which one is NOT an acid?
hints: The odd one out is a base, the opposite of an acid.
People take it to calm an upset, burning stomach.
It is a white, milky medicine with magnesium in it.
questions.fun_fact: Milk of magnesia calms heartburn because it is a base, and it cancels out some of the acid in your stomach.

quality.notes: The answer stands out: it's the only medicine, the only two-word name, and the only option that isn't a food or venom. Hint 1 already says the answer is a base, which gives a lot away. Fun is 3 because it's a dry, odd-one-out school test. cheese-1 and q-1194 cover lemon juice and vinegar as acids, but this asks a different fact.

questions.description: A family of elements so eager to grab other atoms that they'd make terrible dinner guests.
questions.question: Going down one column of the periodic table, you meet fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine. What is this family called?
hints: These elements react very easily and are almost never found alone in nature.
Their name comes from Greek words meaning “salt maker”.
A bright kind of lamp is named after this family.
questions.fun_fact: Fluorine is the most reactive of all elements: it can even make glass and some metals burst into flame.

quality.notes: Accurate, but fun is 3: it reads like a textbook recall question. Fluorine making glass burn is a documented fact. Difficulty is probably 10 rather than 9.

questions.description: A material that holds up your stockings, your parachute and your toothbrush, all at the same time.
questions.question: I'm a strong man-made fiber from the 1930s. I was used for the first modern toothbrush bristles, for stockings and for parachutes. What am I?
hints: I was invented in the United States at the chemical company DuPont.
During the Second World War, I replaced silk in parachutes.
Fishing lines and guitar strings are often made of me.
questions.fun_fact: When nylon stockings first went on sale in 1940, people lined up for hours, and millions of pairs sold in days.

quality.notes: The question runs about 170 characters, so it's a bit long. The description mostly repeats the question text. Level 7 is a little low: young teens rarely know which fiber was used for what.

questions.description: Tiny racers that never stop doing laps around the center of every atom.
questions.question: This drawing shows an atom with its nucleus in the middle. What tiny particles whirl around it?
hints: They have a negative electric charge.
When they flow through a wire, you get electricity.
Their name sounds a lot like “electric”.

media.note: A simple drawing of an atom: a nucleus in the center with small particles on orbits around it, with no text labels.

questions.fun_fact: An electron is about 1,800 times lighter than a proton, so almost all of an atom's weight is in its tiny nucleus.

quality.notes: Electrons “whirling” on orbits is the simplified Bohr picture, which is acceptable here. Hint 3 is strong but allowed. Fun is 3: a standard school question. A labelled diagram could show “electron”, so the note's no-labels rule matters.

questions.description: A bucket wearing a raincoat made of metal so it never gets rusty.
questions.question: Galvanized steel buckets like this one get a shiny coat that keeps them from rusting. Which metal is that coat made of?
hints: The same metal is used in some white sunscreens.
It is a bluish-gray metal with atomic number 30.
Its name has just four letters and starts with the last letter of the alphabet.

media.note: A clear photo of a galvanized steel bucket with its typical shiny, crystal-patterned gray surface.

questions.fun_fact: Zinc protects steel even when scratched, because it corrodes first and “sacrifices” itself to save the iron.

quality.notes: Good question. The image isn't essential: it should be illustrative, though it shows nothing that gives the answer away. Hint 3 also works in Spanish and German (zinc, Zink).

questions.description: The gas that turns every birthday party into a game of “catch it before it hits the ceiling”.
questions.question: I'm a party balloon, and if you let go of my string, I float up to the sky. What gas am I filled with?
hints: This gas is much lighter than air.
Big airships and weather balloons use it too.
It is the second element in the periodic table.
questions.fun_fact: Helium was found on the Sun, by studying its light in 1868, many years before anyone found it on Earth.

quality.notes: The fun fact (helium found on the Sun first) is a nice touch. A 9-year-old may not know the word “helium”, so level 4 fits better than 3.

questions.description: A planet covered in water that still has to be careful about every drop it drinks.
questions.question: Of all the water on Earth, seen here from space, about how much is fresh water rather than salty?
hints: Most of Earth's water is in the oceans.
Oceans are salty, so you can't drink them.
It is a tiny share: less than one part in twenty.

media.note: The famous photo of the whole Earth from space, showing oceans, clouds and continents.

questions.fun_fact: Most of Earth's fresh water is frozen in ice sheets and glaciers, so only a tiny part is easy for us to drink.

quality.notes: Sources give 2.5–3% fresh water; “about 3%” is fine. The Blue Marble photo is illustrative, not essential: the question doesn't need it. Related to q-0937 (Antarctic ice holds most fresh water), but this asks a different fact.

questions.description: A rescue team that needs walks, treats and belly rubs.
questions.question: In this cartoon, a boy named Ryder leads rescue puppies, and its song says “no job is too big, no pup is too small”. What is it?
hints: The puppies drive their own vehicles.
One pup, Chase, is a police dog; Marshall is a firefighter.
The name joins a dog's foot with a team that keeps watch.
questions.fun_fact: Paw Patrol started in Canada in 2013 and is now watched by children in more than 160 countries.

quality.notes: Shares a topic with q-1164 (Paw Patrol premiere year), and the fun fact gives 2013, which is that question's answer. They ask different facts, but the fun fact gives the other one away. Hint 3 nearly spells out the name, which is allowed.

questions.description: A menu that gets worse with every verse.
questions.question: In the song, an old lady swallows a spider to catch a fly. What does she swallow next, to catch the spider?
hints: Each new animal eats the one before it.
Think about what animal likes to eat spiders.
It has wings and feathers.
questions.fun_fact: The spider in the song “wriggled and jiggled and tickled inside her”, which is why children love acting it out.
questions.concept: There Was an Old Lady Who Swallowed a Fly

quality.notes: 'There Was an Old Lady Who Swallowed a Fly' is a song from English-speaking countries and is little known to Spanish- or German-speaking families. This is an international-angle problem. Players can still reason towards the answer (what eats spiders), but a frog also eats spiders. Cat as a distractor is clever, since it comes next in the song.

questions.description: A song so good that someone else tried to take the credit.
questions.question: I wrote “Remember Me” for my little daughter Coco, but a famous singer took the credit for it. Who am I?
hints: I'm a skeleton in the Land of the Dead.
I'm Miguel's great-great-grandfather.
My friend Ernesto stole my songs and my guitar.

media.query: marigold flowers Day of the Dead

questions.fun_fact: “Remember Me” won the Oscar for Best Original Song in 2018.

quality.notes: The question rules out its own distractors. Ernesto is the famous singer who took the credit, Miguel is a living boy with no daughter, and Imelda is a woman. Anyone who saw Coco can pick Héctor by elimination. The fun fact is correct (the Oscar was awarded at the 2018 ceremony).

questions.description: An instrument that fits in your pocket and still makes a lot of noise.
questions.question: A drum is to hitting as a harmonica is to…
hints: Think about how you make a harmonica sound.
You hold it against your lips.
You use your breath.
questions.fun_fact: A harmonica makes sounds both when you blow into it and when you breathe in through it.

quality.notes: A plain analogy that is fairly dry and not linked to a children's song. A harmonica photo could show someone playing it at the lips, which hints at the answer.

questions.description: A king with a long striped tail and even longer dance moves.
questions.question: The lemur King Julien sings “I Like to Move It” in a film named after the island he lives on. Which island?
hints: The island is off the coast of Africa.
It's the home of almost all the world's lemurs.
In the film, zoo animals from New York wash up there.
questions.fun_fact: “I Like to Move It” was a dance hit in 1993, more than ten years before the film made it famous with children.

quality.notes: Same answer as q-0166 (Madagascar from its silhouette), but a different fact. 'Lemur' in the question plus a lemur image already point strongly to Madagascar for older players, and the film is very famous, so it is probably easier than 5.

questions.description: A song that's also a full workout for your whole body.
questions.question: You're singing and touching your head, then your shoulders, then your knees. What do you touch next?
hints: It's lower than your knees.
You have to bend down to reach them.
They are at the very end of your feet.
questions.fun_fact: The song gets faster and faster each time, until everyone is laughing and out of breath.

quality.notes: The Spanish and German versions of the song end on 'pies'/'Fuß' (feet), so translations should watch the answer. The 'gets faster each time' fun fact is a common way to play it, not a universal rule.

questions.description: A sweet little crime solved by a dad detective.
questions.question: In the nursery rhyme “Johny Johny Yes Papa”, the boy says “No, Papa” but laughs “Ha ha ha!” when he opens his mouth. What was he eating?
hints: It's sweet.
It's white and usually in a bowl or a jar.
People put it in tea and coffee.
questions.fun_fact: Versions of “Johny Johny Yes Papa” have been watched billions of times on YouTube.

quality.notes: Known worldwide through YouTube, but stronger in English-speaking and South Asian homes than in Latin America or Germany. Chocolate and honey are plausible guesses. The 'history' lens on the axes is odd.

questions.description: A magic wand that only works on a hundred musicians at once.
questions.question: An entire orchestra watches the tip of this thin stick. What is it called?
hints: Musicians don't play it. Someone waves it.
The person holding it stands in front of the orchestra and faces the musicians.
Its name is also used for the stick passed between runners in a relay race.

media.note: Close-up of a conductor's hand holding a thin white baton. No instruments or orchestra in focus.

questions.fun_fact: Before batons became common, some conductors kept time by banging a long staff on the floor or by waving a rolled-up sheet of music.

quality.notes: Hint 3 is a pun that only works in English: the relay stick is a “testigo” in Spanish and a “Staffelstab” in German, so it falls flat when translated. It also touches q-0463 (relay baton), but that question asks a different fact. The essential image shows the object being asked about, which is acceptable here. The question is a fairly plain vocabulary test.

questions.description: Shoes that make you stand on your tiptoes all evening, on purpose.
questions.question: Where would you see dancers wearing shoes like these?
hints: These shoes are soft, pink and have ribbons.
The dancers spin and stand on the tips of their toes.
Think of “Swan Lake”.

media.note: Close-up of a pair of pink satin ballet pointe shoes with ribbons, no dancer's full body shown.

questions.fun_fact: A professional ballet dancer can wear out a pair of pointe shoes in a single show.

quality.notes: The distractors are clearly silly, which is fine for a level-1 question but makes it trivial. The question is satisfying for kids but not surprising.

questions.description: A love letter that you can play with ten fingers.
questions.question: I'm a short piano piece, my German name means “For Elise”, and almost every piano student learns me. Who wrote me?
hints: He was German and lived around 1800.
He also wrote a famous Ninth Symphony with the “Ode to Joy”.
He kept composing even after he lost his hearing.
questions.fun_fact: In Taiwan, many garbage trucks play “Für Elise” so people know it's time to bring out their trash.

quality.notes: Saying the title is a German name rules out Chopin and Tchaikovsky, and hint 1 does the same. q-0070 has the same answer (Beethoven) but asks about his deafness, a different fact, so this is acceptable. Hint 3 reuses that deafness fact. Many young teens won't know who wrote Für Elise, so it is probably a bit harder than 6.

questions.description: The loudest way to say “ta-da!” in an orchestra.
questions.question: What are these instruments made of?
hints: They are shiny and golden.
When you crash them together, they ring for a long time.
A spoon, a key and a coin are made of the same kind of material.

media.note: Clear photo of a pair of brass orchestral crash cymbals.

questions.fun_fact: One of the world's best-known cymbal makers was founded in Istanbul in 1623 and is still run by the same family.

quality.notes: Hint 1 (“shiny and golden”) almost gives the answer away. The question is simple and not very surprising, but the fun fact about the cymbal maker founded in 1623 makes up for some of that. It overlaps only loosely with q-0161 (what a saxophone is made of), a different instrument.

questions.description: Tick, tock, tick, tock: the bossiest member of the band.
questions.question: This ticking device helps musicians keep a steady tempo. What is its swinging arm called?
hints: It swings from side to side at a steady speed.
Moving a little weight up or down this arm changes how fast it ticks.
Old grandfather clocks have one too.

media.note: Photo of a classic wooden pyramid-shaped mechanical metronome with its swinging arm visible.

questions.fun_fact: Beethoven was one of the first composers to write metronome speeds into his music.

quality.notes: Strictly, a metronome uses an inverted pendulum, but “pendulum” is the standard name. “Lever” is a vague mechanical word, but it is not a real competitor to the answer. Hint 3 (grandfather clocks) comes close to giving the answer, which is allowed.

questions.description: A composer whose music still turns up at weddings, even though he never got an invitation.
questions.question: Felix Mendelssohn, the German composer who made Bach's music famous again, lived in which century?
hints: Bach had already been dead for a long time when Mendelssohn was born.
He was a young man when Beethoven died.
He was born in 1809.
questions.fun_fact: Mendelssohn wrote the famous “Wedding March” as part of his music for Shakespeare's “A Midsummer Night's Dream”.

quality.notes: The question is a dry “which century” school item. Adults can work out the answer from the clue that he revived Bach plus a rough sense of the Romantic period, so it is easier than 13. Hint 3 gives the birth year, which almost states the answer. The description and fun fact both use the Wedding March angle.

questions.description: Blowing across a bottle, but with much better results.
questions.question: Players hold this instrument sideways and blow across a hole. What is it?
hints: It's a long, thin, silvery tube.
It makes a high, sweet sound, a bit like a bird.
A tiny version of it is called a piccolo.

media.note: Close-up of the silver lip plate and blowing hole of a transverse (concert) flute, with some keys visible.

questions.fun_fact: The oldest flutes ever found are about 40,000 years old and were made from bird bones and mammoth ivory.

quality.notes: Other sideways-blown instruments (the fife, the bansuri, the Chinese dizi) also fit the clue, but they are all flutes, so the answer still holds. The essential close-up shows the answer itself, so the question is basically picture recognition. The 40,000-year-old flute fun fact is good.

questions.description: Five lines where the notes hang out like birds on a wire.
questions.question: Musical notes are written on these five lines. What are the lines called?
hints: Without these lines, you couldn't tell a high note from a low one.
There are always exactly five of them, with four spaces between.
In some languages, its name means “five lines”.

media.note: Close-up of printed sheet music showing the five horizontal lines with a few notes; no title or composer name visible.

questions.fun_fact: Some old church songbooks used a staff with only four lines, and a few choirs still sing from them today.

quality.notes: UK English often says “stave”, but the US word “staff” follows the house style. The question is a vocabulary test with little surprise. In Spanish, hint 3 will nearly give away “pentagrama”, but hint 3 is allowed to come close.

questions.description: A toy that turned 1958 into one big wiggle.
questions.question: A skateboard is to your feet as which toy is to your hips?
hints: You don't hold this toy in your hands while you play.
It's a big plastic ring.
You keep it spinning by swaying your waist.
questions.fun_fact: In 1958, the hula hoop became a craze, and about 25 million were sold in the USA in just a few months.

quality.notes: The analogy is easy for children: hips point straight to the hula hoop, so a 3 fits better than a 5. The fun-fact figure (25 million) is the commonly quoted one, but it's a rough number.

questions.description: The only puppy whose mom has been to space.
questions.question: If you had petted Pushinka, a puppy of the space dog Strelka, in 1961, you would have been at the home of which family?
hints: Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev gave her away as a gift.
She went to live with his biggest rival's family.
Her new home was the White House.
questions.fun_fact: Pushinka later had puppies with the Kennedys' dog Charlie, and the president jokingly called them “pupniks”.

quality.notes: The 'If you had petted…' scenario is a bit convoluted. The description says 'only puppy whose mom has been to space', but Strelka had a whole litter, so the claim isn't true. Adults can guess the Kennedys from 1961 plus a Soviet space dog.

questions.description: A boxing match with the whole Cold War in the ring.
questions.question: You're watching “Rocky IV” as Rocky's huge opponent Ivan Drago steps into the ring. Which country does Drago fight for?
hints: The film came out in 1985.
The final fight takes place in Moscow.
He says the famous line: “I must break you.”
questions.fun_fact: Ivan Drago was played by Swedish actor Dolph Lundgren, who also has a degree in chemical engineering.

quality.notes: The name 'Ivan' plus the Cold War setting make the answer easy to reason out, so about a 6. The 'You're watching…' framing is unnecessary. Lundgren does hold a chemical engineering degree.

questions.description: A flag with a hole in it, and the hole is the point.
questions.question: In 1956, Hungarian rebels waved flags like this one. Why is there a hole in the middle?
questions.answer: They cut out the communist coat of arms
wrong_answers: To let the wind pass through it
To hang it sideways from a pole
To show that a city had surrendered
hints: The rebels were rising up against the Soviet-backed government.
Something used to be printed in that spot.
It was a symbol of the regime they wanted gone.

media.note: The red, white and green Hungarian flag with a round hole cut out of the middle, as used in the 1956 revolution.

questions.fun_fact: The flag with a hole is still a symbol of freedom in Hungary and is flown every year on October 23, the day the revolution began.

quality.notes: A good question that players can reason out. The 1956 flag with the hole is well documented on Commons.

questions.description: The world's most famous place to show your passport.
questions.question: This famous crossing linked West Berlin and East Berlin. Who was allowed to use it?
hints: Ordinary East Germans couldn't simply leave East Berlin.
Its name came from the letter C in the soldiers' alphabet.
US, British and French troops passed through it.

media.note: A clear photo of Checkpoint Charlie, the guard house with the sector sign, in Berlin.

questions.fun_fact: In 1961, US and Soviet tanks stood facing each other at Checkpoint Charlie for about 16 hours before both sides pulled back.

quality.notes: 'Only school groups' and 'Only trucks carrying goods' are weak distractors. 'On holiday' is UK wording; use 'vacation' or reword. Strictly, diplomats could also cross there, but the answer holds.

questions.description: A car with a glass box on top, and a very special passenger inside.
questions.question: What was this unusual vehicle with a glass cabin built for?
hints: Its glass became bulletproof after an attack in 1981.
It was used a lot by a Polish man who traveled the world.
Its nickname starts with the title of the head of the Catholic Church.

media.note: A clear photo of a Popemobile with its glass cabin, ideally empty, without visible text naming it.

questions.fun_fact: John Paul II's first trip home to Poland as pope in 1979 drew millions of people and helped inspire the Solidarity movement.

quality.notes: Commons has Popemobile photos, but they may show the SCV plates or the pope himself.

questions.description: Diplomacy, but make it fluffy.
questions.question: For Communist China, ping-pong was to sports diplomacy as which animal was to animal diplomacy?
hints: China sent pairs of them to zoos around the world as gifts.
Two of them arrived in Washington, D.C., in 1972.
It's black and white and loves bamboo.
questions.fun_fact: In 1972, the giant pandas Ling-Ling and Hsing-Hsing moved to the National Zoo in Washington, D.C., as a gift from China.

quality.notes: The analogy ('animal diplomacy') is close to circular, and the panda is the obvious guess for China, so this is easier than a 6.

questions.description: The Cold War that was anything but cold.
questions.question: It was fought in the jungles of Southeast Asia, sparked huge peace protests around the world and ended in 1975. Which war was it?
hints: The USA sent hundreds of thousands of soldiers there.
Helicopters became its best-known image.
The city of Saigon was later renamed Ho Chi Minh City.
questions.fun_fact: After the war, Saigon was renamed Ho Chi Minh City, though many people there still call it Saigon.

quality.notes: The fun fact repeats hint 3 (Saigon renamed). The question is a fairly standard school-style item.

questions.description: A Russian menu with one item you should not eat.
questions.question: Borscht, pelmeni, shchi and ushanka: three are Russian dishes. Which one is NOT?
hints: The odd one out was worn by Soviet soldiers in winter.
It's made of fur.
Its name comes from the Russian word for “ears”.
questions.fun_fact: The ushanka's flaps can be tied up on top of the head or tied down under the chin to keep the ears warm.

quality.notes: The link to the Cold War is loose. People in the blurred Red Square image might wear ushankas.

questions.description: A flag so simple you could draw it with one crayon and a plate.
questions.question: Japan's flag is white with one red circle. What does the circle stand for?
hints: It's something you see in the sky.
Japan is often called “the Land of the Rising” something.
It shines during the day.

media.note: A close-up of the flag of Japan: the red circle on white, no text.

questions.fun_fact: In Japanese the flag is called “Hinomaru”, which means “circle of the sun”.

quality.notes: Hint 2 ('Land of the Rising…') almost gives the answer away, which is too strong for a second hint. The image is labelled essential but adds nothing, since the question already describes the flag; illustrative would fit better.

questions.description: A paint-box recipe with only two ingredients and no oven.
questions.question: Grapes, eggplants and plums are often purple. Which two paint colors do you mix to make purple?
hints: Yellow is not part of the mix.
One of them is the color of strawberries.
The other is the color of the sky.
questions.fun_fact: For a long time purple dye was so costly that only kings and emperors could wear it.

quality.notes: This is a plain school-style fact. The opening about grapes and eggplants is padding. Mixing purple is a little harder for 6-year-olds than mixing green, so 3 fits better than 2. Hint 1 rules out two options at once.

questions.description: The only light that's always in a hurry.
questions.question: I hang above the street next to red and yellow lights. When I glow green, what do cars do?
hints: Red means the opposite of me.
Drivers are happy to see me.
The cars start moving.
questions.fun_fact: The first electric traffic lights appeared in the United States in 1914, long before most families had a car.

quality.notes: The distractors 'Turn around' and 'Honk' are silly, so 'Stop' is the only real alternative. The question is trivial even for a 1. The image of an intersection may show a lit traffic light. The fun fact is right that the first electric light was in Cleveland in 1914, but the claim about family car ownership is loose. The description joke is weak.

questions.description: A flag that went to the Moon and still needs 50 of these.
questions.question: Besides stripes, which shape appears 50 times on this flag?
hints: Look at the blue corner.
You can see them in the night sky.
They have five points.

media.note: A clear photo of the flag of the United States, with the 50 stars visible.

questions.fun_fact: Each of the 50 stars stands for one US state, and the 13 stripes for the first 13 colonies.

quality.notes: This is just a look-and-count question about a well-known flag, so it isn't very surprising. It is fine as a 1. The US focus is mild.

questions.description: The only flag you're allowed to eat with your hands.
questions.question: Pizza Margherita shows the colors of Italy's flag: red, white and green. Which topping gives the green?
hints: It's a fresh herb.
It's also the main leaf in pesto.
Its leaves smell sweet and are put on after baking.

media.note: A photo of a pizza Margherita with tomato, mozzarella and basil leaves.

questions.fun_fact: The story goes that the pizza was named after Queen Margherita of Italy, who visited Naples in 1889.

quality.notes: The answer is the same as q-0323 (basil, the main leaf in pesto), and hint 2 points to that fact. The photo shows basil leaves, which helps those who know them by sight.

questions.description: A color named after a plant that smells better than most colors.
questions.question: The color lavender is named after this plant. Around which sea does it grow wild?
hints: It likes hot, dry summers.
Think of southern Europe.
This sea touches Spain, Italy and Greece.

media.note: A clear photo of purple lavender flower stems, no field signs or place names.

questions.fun_fact: The name lavender may come from the Latin “lavare”, “to wash”, because Romans put it in their baths.

quality.notes: Mediterranean is the only warm, dry option, so it stands out against the Baltic and Bering Seas. The image should be illustrative, not essential. The fact itself is a bit dry.

questions.description: A flag that carries a smaller flag around like a backpack.
questions.question: Which country's flag sits in the top corner of this flag of Australia?
hints: Australia was once ruled from far away.
Its flag is also called the Union Jack.
Its capital is London.

media.note: A clear photo of the flag of Australia.

questions.fun_fact: The five white stars on the right form the Southern Cross, a star pattern seen from the Southern Hemisphere.
