quality.notes: Hint 2, 'Union Jack', basically gives the answer away and should be the third hint.

questions.description: A little green man who is always running, and for once that's good advice.
questions.question: You see this green sign with a running figure above a door. Where does the door lead?
hints: You hope you never need it.
Use it if there is a fire.
It's the fastest safe way out.

media.note: A close-up of a green emergency exit sign with the running man pictogram, ideally without any word.

questions.fun_fact: The running man sign was designed in Japan in the 1970s and is now used in many countries.

questions.description: Sixteen bits of pure joy, wrapped in gray plastic.
questions.question: You're in a Japanese toy store on the day the Super Nintendo (Super Famicom) first goes on sale. Which year is it?
hints: It came after the first Nintendo console from the 1980s.
Its big rival was the Sega Mega Drive.
It was the first year of a new decade.
questions.fun_fact: The Super Nintendo sold about 49 million consoles around the world.

quality.notes: A dry year question. The toy-store scenario is padding. Hint 3 nearly gives the year away. For a 13-year-old (stated level 7), the release year of a 1990 console is harder than that, so about 9. 1983 (the Famicom's year) is a nice distractor.

questions.description: Everybody jumps out of the plane, and only one gets to be happy.
questions.question: “Fifty players parachute onto my island, and only the last one standing wins. Free Fire is famous for me.” What kind of game am I?
hints: The play area keeps getting smaller.
Fortnite is another famous example.
The name sounds like a fight fit for a king.
questions.fun_fact: A Free Fire match lasts only about 10 minutes, so it can be played quickly on a phone.

quality.notes: “Parachute onto my island, last one standing” is already a strong clue for players who know Fortnite. An illustrative image would be safe here, so decorative is a weaker choice than needed.

questions.description: A little mushroom for your thumb that changed gaming forever.
questions.question: Which of these game controllers has NO analog stick?
hints: Think of the oldest one.
It came out in the 1980s.
It only has a cross-shaped pad and a few buttons.
questions.fun_fact: Nintendo 64 games like Super Mario 64 made analog sticks popular in 1996.

quality.notes: The answer stands out: it is the only old controller and the only option with “original” in it, so players can guess it by age alone. Hint 1 almost gives it away. A fairly dry odd-one-out.

questions.description: He liked one ancient board game so much that he named a company after it.
questions.question: This man founded a famous video game company and named it after a word from a board game. Which board game?
hints: The game is very old and comes from East Asia.
It's played with black and white stones.
The company made Pong and the 2600 console.

media.note: A clear portrait photo of Nolan Bushnell, the founder of Atari, with no company name or logo visible.

questions.fun_fact: Nolan Bushnell also founded Chuck E. Cheese, a pizza restaurant full of arcade games.

quality.notes: Essential media is the wrong role: almost nobody recognizes Nolan Bushnell, and the question can be answered without the photo. It should be illustrative. Without the photo, the question doesn't say which company until hint 3. A nice fact (Atari comes from a Go term). Sharing the answer “Go” with colours-3 is a different fact, so no overlap.

questions.description: A stick full of joy, but it had a serious job long before games.
questions.question: Long before video games, which people already used a control stick called a “joystick”?
hints: Their job happens far above the ground.
Pulling the stick back made them go up.
Flight simulator games still use one.
questions.fun_fact: Pilots were calling their control stick a “joystick” over 100 years ago, in the early days of flying.

quality.notes: Modern crane operators also use joysticks, but “long before video games” keeps pilots the clear answer. The term dates to about 1910 in aviation.

questions.description: A shiny disc that sent cartridges into early retirement.
questions.question: Sony and Philips introduced the CD-ROM, which later held PlayStation games. Around which year?
hints: It came a few years after the music CD.
It was ready before the first PlayStation.
It was in the middle of the 1980s.
questions.fun_fact: One CD-ROM held about 650 MB, hundreds of times more than a typical game cartridge of the time.

quality.notes: The CD-ROM standard (Yellow Book) is usually dated 1985, with 1983–84 sometimes cited, so there is small doubt. A dry year question: a technical date is hard for 16-year-olds, so it is above the stated 9. Hint 3 nearly gives it.

questions.description: A headset that puts a whole world just a few centimeters in front of your nose.
questions.question: Meta Quest headsets were first sold as “Oculus Quest”. What does the Latin word “oculus” mean?
hints: It's a part of your body.
Eye doctors are sometimes called “oculists”.
You use two of them to see.
questions.fun_fact: The Oculus brand began with a crowdfunding campaign in 2012, and Facebook bought it for about 2 billion dollars in 2014.

quality.notes: Hint 2 (“oculists”) nearly gives the answer. In Spanish and German, related words (oculista, okular) make it easier still. A somewhat school-like word question.

questions.description: Perfect for people who refuse to stop and ask for directions.
questions.question: What object is shown in this close-up?
hints: Hikers and sailors carry one so they don't get lost.
It has a needle that turns by itself.
Its needle always points north.

media.note: A close-up of a magnetic compass face: the needle and part of the N/E/S/W markings, without the whole object.

questions.fun_fact: People in China were using magnetic compasses to find their way about 1,000 years ago.

quality.notes: A plain 'identify the object' question. If the close-up shows the N/E/S/W letters, the answer is obvious, which is acceptable at difficulty 2.

questions.description: Bedtime is a lot harder to sell when it's still bright outside.
questions.question: Near the poles in summer, the sun can still shine at midnight, like here. At the North Pole, for about how many months in a row does the sun not set?
hints: Think of the year split between one long day and one long night.
The long day starts in March and ends in September.
It is half of the year.

media.note: A photo of the midnight sun low over the Arctic sea or landscape, clearly daylight; no clocks or text.

questions.fun_fact: At the South Pole it's the other way around: the sun stays up from September to March.

quality.notes: Hint 3 ('half of the year') basically gives the answer, which is allowed for hint 3. Many teens can reason it out, so slightly easier than 9.

questions.description: A huge blue puddle that showed up for a geography test.
questions.question: Which ocean is highlighted on this map?
hints: It touches the east coast of Africa.
The big island of Madagascar sits in it.
It is named after a country in Asia.

media.note: A world map with the Indian Ocean highlighted and no labels or names.

questions.fun_fact: The Indian Ocean is the only ocean named after a country.

quality.notes: The fun fact is widely repeated, but the ocean was named after the region of India long before the modern country existed, so it is a bit loose. The description is generic. A dry map-identification question.

questions.description: A bear that only wears black and white and eats salad all day.
questions.question: On which continent does this animal live in the wild?
hints: It lives in cool mountain forests.
It eats almost only bamboo.
Its home is in China.

media.note: A clear photo of a giant panda; no zoo signs or text.

questions.fun_fact: A giant panda can spend up to 14 hours a day eating bamboo.

quality.notes: Hint 2 (bamboo) touches q-0028, but the fact asked is different. The question is simple and rather dry.

questions.description: A sleepy teddy bear that lives in a tree and isn't a bear at all.
questions.question: On which continent does this animal live in the wild?
hints: It eats almost only eucalyptus leaves.
It shares its home with kangaroos.
It lives on the smallest continent.

media.note: A clear photo of a koala in a tree; no signs or text.

questions.fun_fact: Koalas sleep up to 20 hours a day.

quality.notes: A standard question that is a little dry. The 'history' lens is irrelevant here.

questions.description: A big piece of land that looks a bit like a lopsided ice cream cone.
questions.question: Which continent is highlighted on this map?
hints: It reaches from the frozen Arctic down to warm tropical beaches.
Canada and Mexico are on it.
It is joined to South America by a thin strip of land.

media.note: A world map with North America highlighted and no labels or names.

questions.fun_fact: Greenland, the largest island in the world, is part of North America.

quality.notes: Hint 2 (Canada and Mexico) is already very strong. Players in Latin America learn America as one continent, but the options still work. The fun fact touches q-0167 (Greenland). Dry.

questions.description: A ditch in the desert that saves ships weeks of sailing.
questions.question: This canal in Egypt joins the Mediterranean Sea and the Red Sea. Which long trip does it save ships between Europe and Asia?
hints: Without it, ships must go much farther south.
They would pass the Cape of Good Hope.
It's the continent where Egypt is.

media.note: A short clip of a large ship sailing through the Suez Canal with desert on both sides; no captions.

questions.fun_fact: In March 2021, the giant ship Ever Given got stuck across the Suez Canal and blocked it for six days.

quality.notes: The video isn't really essential; illustrative would be enough. A Suez Canal ship clip is plausible on Wikimedia.

questions.description: A wall so long it never actually ends at a door.
questions.question: Sorting your vacation postcards: Big Ben goes with the United Kingdom, so the Great Wall goes with…
hints: It's in Asia.
It's the home of the giant panda.
Its capital is Beijing.
questions.fun_fact: Despite the famous story, you can't see the Great Wall from the Moon with your own eyes.

quality.notes: The description's joke is weak. The postcard scenario is light framing but okay. Easy and not very surprising.

questions.description: Someone took a lot of metal and knitted a giant.
questions.question: Which famous tower is shown in this close-up?
hints: It's made of iron, with lots of crossing beams.
It is in Europe.
It stands in Paris.

media.note: A close-up of the Eiffel Tower's iron beams, showing only part of the structure; no signs or text.

questions.fun_fact: On hot summer days, the iron of the Eiffel Tower expands and the tower can grow up to about 15 cm (6 in) taller.

quality.notes: Hint 1 (iron lattice) nearly settles it, because the other towers are stone, marble or concrete. That is fine at difficulty 2.

questions.description: Swing and a miss: the word every batter hates to hear.
questions.question: This player is batting in baseball. How many strikes put the batter out?
hints: It's fewer than five.
It's an odd number.
Think of the saying “___ strikes and you're out!”.

media.note: A clear photo of a baseball batter standing at home plate, ready to swing; no scoreboard or text visible.

questions.fun_fact: A baseball batter gets four “balls” before walking to first base, but only three strikes before being out.

quality.notes: Plain rules fact, so it's a bit dry. The photo isn't needed to answer, so it should be marked illustrative, not essential. Baseball rules lean toward the US, but “three strikes” is a saying people know almost everywhere. Hint 3 is close to giving it away, which is allowed.

questions.description: Enough players for a team photo, and still a fight over who stands in front.
questions.question: A cricket team puts eleven players on the field. Which pair of sports also has eleven players per side?
hints: Both are played on big grass fields.
One uses a stick, the other mostly feet.
One of them has the World Cup with the most fans on Earth.

media.note: A photo of a full cricket team on the field (fielders spread out or lined up), so players can see a whole team.

questions.fun_fact: A cricket team is often called an “XI”, the Roman numeral for eleven.

quality.notes: Correct, and American football (also 11) isn't among the options. The photo is illustrative, not essential, and a single photo rarely shows all eleven fielders. Hint 3 points straight to soccer. Fairly ordinary question.

questions.description: A stadium where a whole country once cheered loud enough to wake the sea.
questions.question: In this stadium, India won the 2011 Cricket World Cup final. What is it called?
hints: It stands close to the Arabian Sea.
It's in India's biggest city, Mumbai.
Its name starts with a W.

media.note: A photo of Wankhede Stadium in Mumbai, ideally aerial or the inside of the ground; no visible name signs.

questions.fun_fact: Sachin Tendulkar, who grew up in Mumbai, played his last Test match here in 2013.

quality.notes: Specialist cricket knowledge centered on India; outside cricket countries few families could reason toward it. Most players won't recognize the stadium from the essential photo, and stadium photos often show the name on signs. Hint 3 is a first-letter hint.

questions.description: A big leather hand that never shakes anybody's hand.
questions.question: Bat is to hitting as baseball glove is to…
hints: Fielders wear it on one hand.
It helps you stop a fast ball safely.
You do this when someone throws a ball to you.
questions.fun_fact: In cricket, only the wicket-keeper may wear gloves; all other fielders catch with bare hands.

quality.notes: Easy analogy that kids can work out; a little plain. The fun fact about cricket fielders not wearing gloves is a nice touch.

questions.description: Before fast bowlers, the ball moved about as quickly as a sleepy turtle.
questions.question: The first cricket bowlers rolled the ball along the grass, more than 400 years ago. In which country?
hints: It's in Europe.
Its capital stands on the River Thames.
It's the home country of Shakespeare.
questions.fun_fact: One of the oldest known mentions of cricket is in an English court case from around 1597.

quality.notes: Generally accepted, though some theories give the name a Flemish/Dutch origin, so including Netherlands is slightly delicate. The 1597 court case dates to 1597/1598 depending on the calendar. Hint 2 already identifies England.

questions.description: Every great tradition has a first day, and this one came with sunburn.
questions.question: The very first Test match, Australia against England in 1877, was played at this ground. In which city is it?
hints: It's in the Southern Hemisphere.
It's the capital of the state of Victoria.
It also hosts the Australian Open tennis tournament.

media.note: A photo of the Melbourne Cricket Ground (the stadium and its field), without visible signs naming the ground or city.

questions.fun_fact: Australia won that first Test by 45 runs, and won the 100th-anniversary match there in 1977 by exactly 45 runs too.

quality.notes: The fun fact (45 runs both times) is great. Hint 2 gives it away already. An aerial MCG photo may show the Melbourne skyline, which only some players would recognize. Cricket-heavy, but adults can reason toward Australia's big cities.

questions.description: Gotham's busiest doctor, and she never sends a bill.
questions.question: I'm a doctor who runs a free clinic in Gotham's Crime Alley, and I helped look after young Bruce Wayne. Who am I?
hints: I'm a kind old friend of the Wayne family, not a villain.
Batman sometimes comes to me to get patched up.
My first name rhymes with “Wesley”.
questions.fun_fact: Leslie Thompkins first appeared in a 1976 comic called “There Is No Hope in Crime Alley”.

quality.notes: Deep fan knowledge that few families can reason towards, so it is dry for most players. Hint 3 is a rhyme that only works in English and won't translate.

questions.description: A man who is never late, except to his own dates.
questions.question: I'm a police scientist. Lightning hit my lab, covered me in chemicals and made me the fastest man alive. Who am I?
hints: I wear a red suit with a lightning bolt.
I work in Central City.
I'm the best-known Flash, star of a long TV series.
questions.fun_fact: Barry Allen first appeared in 1956, and comic fans see him as the start of a whole new age of superheroes.

quality.notes: Wally West also got his powers from lightning and chemicals in the same lab. 'Police scientist' tells them apart, but it is close.

questions.description: A villain who can't make up his mind, so he lets luck do it.
questions.question: Two-Face was once Gotham's lawyer Harvey Dent. Half his face is scarred, and he makes every choice with one object. What is it?
hints: He carries it in his pocket.
He flips it in the air: one side means yes, the other no.
One side of it is clean, the other is scratched.
questions.fun_fact: Two-Face first appeared in Batman comics in 1942.

quality.notes: 'A dice' should be 'A die'. The description's 'lets luck do it' narrows the options a bit.

questions.description: She's grounded at home, but on rooftops at night.
questions.question: My father is Gotham's police commissioner, and at night I secretly fight crime next to Batman. What is my hero name?
hints: I'm a hero, not a villain.
My real name is Barbara Gordon.
My costume has pointy ears and a cape, just like Batman's.
questions.fun_fact: Barbara Gordon became Batgirl in 1967, partly so she could join the Batman TV series.

quality.notes: Good question. Hint 1 already rules out two options, but it is fine as a hint.

questions.description: The most famous letter in the whole universe, and it's not even on a mailbox.
questions.question: I'm red and yellow, shaped like a diamond, and I sit on Superman's chest. Which letter is inside me?
hints: It's the first letter of his hero name.
It's the same letter that starts “super”.
It looks a bit like a snake.
questions.fun_fact: In some Superman stories, the S isn't a letter at all: it's his family's symbol on Krypton and means “hope”.

quality.notes: Fine as a level-1 question. Hint 2 nearly gives it away, but that is fine for hint 2 at this level.

questions.description: Birdwatchers keep getting this one wrong.
questions.question: Someone points at the sky and shouts “Look! It's a bird! It's a plane!”. How does the famous line end?
hints: It's something that flies but isn't a bird or a plane.
It's a superhero.
He wears a red cape and comes from Krypton.
questions.fun_fact: Superman first appeared in 1938, in a comic that cost 10 cents.

quality.notes: Good. The other candidates are about Superman topics but ask different facts.

questions.description: A remake so lifelike that you can almost smell the savanna.
questions.question: You're watching the 2019 “The Lion King” with its lifelike animals. Which of these characters do you NOT meet?
hints: Three of them live on the African savanna, close to Pride Rock.
The odd one out comes from a different Disney jungle story.
He is a big, lazy bear who sings about the “Bare Necessities”.
questions.fun_fact: The 2019 “The Lion King” was made almost entirely on computers, but its makers went on a safari in Kenya to study real animals and landscapes.

quality.notes: Solid odd-one-out. Mentioning the 2019 version adds a little filler but does no harm.

questions.description: Three ducklings who would be impossible to tell apart without a little fashion help.
questions.question: Huey, Dewey and Louie, Donald Duck's nephews, each wear their own cap color. Which color is NOT one of them?
hints: Their caps help you tell the three identical brothers apart.
In “DuckTales”, Huey wears red.
The missing color is the color of a banana.
questions.fun_fact: In the old comics the three nephews often wore caps in random colors, and the fixed red, blue and green only became the rule later.

quality.notes: Accurate for modern canon. Players can guess yellow because red, blue and green form a set. Hint 2 rules out one option directly.

questions.description: Never forget to send a party invitation to someone with horns.
questions.question: I'm a horned fairy who wasn't invited to the baby princess's party, so I cursed her. Where did the good fairies hide her from me?
questions.answer: In a cottage in the forest
wrong_answers: In a tower with no door
In a palace under the sea
In a castle made of ice
hints: Three kind fairies raised her there, pretending to be ordinary people.
She grew up among trees and singing animals, not in a palace.
It was a small wooden house deep in the woods.
questions.fun_fact: In “Sleeping Beauty”, the three good fairies hid Princess Aurora under the name Briar Rose until her 16th birthday.

quality.notes: Sleeping Beauty is less familiar to today's kids than newer films, so a little harder than 3. The spinning-wheel image points to the film but not to the answer.

questions.description: The only vegetable with a strict bedtime.
questions.question: You're riding to the royal ball in a coach made from a pumpkin. At what time does the magic end?
hints: Cinderella has to leave the party in a big hurry.
The clock strikes twelve times.
It is in the middle of the night.
questions.fun_fact: In the Disney film, the Fairy Godmother also turns mice into horses and a horse into a coachman for the same night.

quality.notes: Classic, well calibrated.

questions.description: A pirate who is brave against everyone, except one very hungry reptile.
questions.question: It ate Captain Hook's hand, it swallowed a clock, and now it follows him everywhere. What kind of animal is it?
hints: It lives in the water around Neverland.
Hook panics whenever he hears “tick-tock”.
It has a long snout, green scaly skin and lots of teeth.
questions.fun_fact: Peter Pan was first a 1904 stage play by J. M. Barrie, and the ticking crocodile was already in it.

quality.notes: Easy for kids, maybe 3. Hints 1 and 2 make it easier still.

questions.description: A man with more glasses than a kitchen cupboard.
questions.question: This musician wrote the music for “Can You Feel the Love Tonight” from “The Lion King”. Who is he?
hints: He is a British pop star famous for his piano playing.
He is known for colorful costumes and huge sunglasses.
One of his famous songs is “Rocket Man”.

media.note: A clear photo of Elton John, ideally at a piano or on stage with his typical glasses; no name or text visible.

questions.fun_fact: “Can You Feel the Love Tonight” won the Oscar for Best Original Song, with lyrics by Tim Rice.
questions.concept: Can You Feel the Love Tonight

quality.notes: Wikimedia Commons very likely has a clear photo. Young teens may not recognize Elton John's face, so slightly harder than 7. Hints 1 and 2 are strong.

questions.description: Finding out you're a princess beats any surprise on a school day.
questions.question: You're watching the 2001 film “The Princess Diaries”, where a shy teen learns she's royal. Who is NOT in the cast?
hints: The princess's grandmother is played by the star of “Mary Poppins”.
The film was the breakthrough role of the young actress playing Mia.
The odd one out starred in Disney's “Freaky Friday” a couple of years later.
questions.fun_fact: Mia's royal home in the film, Genovia, is an invented tiny European country.

quality.notes: A cast-list question is a fairly dry memory test, and the 'You're watching' opener is filler. Young teens rarely know a 2001 film's cast; it is more of a young-adult/adult question. The description is weak and generic.

questions.description: A big cat with stripes and a very bad attitude toward man-cubs.
questions.question: Shere Khan in “The Jungle Book” is a Bengal tiger, from Mowgli's jungle. In which country do most Bengal tigers live?
hints: The country is in Asia.
The Taj Mahal is there.
Its capital is New Delhi.
questions.fun_fact: No two tigers have the same stripes: their pattern is as unique as a human fingerprint.

quality.notes: The wording 'Bengal tiger, from Mowgli's jungle' is clumsy. Brazil, Kenya and Australia are easy to rule out, since none has wild tigers. It's a geography question in Disney dress.

questions.description: A mother who loves her daughter's hair a little too much.
questions.question: I locked a girl with magic golden hair in a tower and pretended to be her mother. What did I use her hair for?
hints: When the girl sang, her hair started to glow.
The magic came from a golden flower.
Without it, I quickly turned into a very old woman.
questions.fun_fact: In “Tangled”, the magic of Rapunzel's hair comes from a single drop of sunlight that fell to the ground and grew into a golden flower.

quality.notes: Nice riddle, good description.

questions.description: A woodworking project that went much better than planned.
questions.question: An old woodcarver made me and wished on a star that I could be a real boy. Who came and made me move and talk?
hints: I am Pinocchio, the puppet whose nose grows when he lies.
She came down from the sky in the middle of the night.
She is a magical woman named after a color.
questions.fun_fact: Pinocchio was first a story by the Italian writer Carlo Collodi, published in the 1880s.

quality.notes: Geppetto and Jiminy Cricket are good distractors. Hint 3 ('named after a color') almost gives the answer, which is allowed.

questions.description: The only rug that has never been vacuumed while it was at home.
questions.question: I'm a rug with golden tassels, I can't talk, and Aladdin and Jasmine ride on me. What do I do best?
hints: I took them on a ride during “A Whole New World”.
I go high above the city at night.
Birds can do it too, with wings.
questions.fun_fact: In “Aladdin”, Carpet has no face and no voice, so the animators made it act only with its tassels.

quality.notes: Almost obvious, since everyone knows a magic carpet flies. The distractors are weak, and the description joke doesn't quite land.

questions.description: A robot with a name that's really a job title.
questions.question: EVE is a white robot, she comes from space, and her mission is to find a plant on Earth. What does her name stand for?
hints: Her name is made from the first letters of three words.
One of the words fits her mission with plants.
She comes from beyond Earth and checks green, growing things.
questions.fun_fact: WALL·E's name is also short for something: “Waste Allocation Load Lifter: Earth-Class”.

quality.notes: Players can reason it out from 'space' and 'plant', which is good. The fun fact about WALL·E's name is a nice touch.

questions.description: Fashion tip: glass shoes are lovely, but very hard to run in.
questions.question: Cinderella loses one glass slipper on the palace stairs. How many glass slippers does she still have after the ball?
hints: Shoes usually come in pairs.
The prince's helper finds the one she lost.
When the lost one breaks, she pulls the other one out of her pocket.
questions.fun_fact: In Disney's “Cinderella”, the stepmother trips the Grand Duke's footman so the slipper smashes, but Cinderella saves the day with the matching one.

quality.notes: It's simple logic, and someone thinking of the smashed slipper could argue for 0. The fun fact repeats hint 3.

questions.description: Every chocolate bar was once a bean that dreamed big.
questions.question: In a chocolate factory, cocoa beans go in and chocolate bars come out. What are the cocoa beans called?
hints: Think about where the factory's work begins, not where it ends.
It's what a factory starts with before making anything.
Cotton for T-shirts and wood for tables are also called this.
questions.fun_fact: Most of the world's cocoa beans are grown in West Africa, while most chocolate is made far away in Europe and North America.

quality.notes: Correct and clear, but it reads like a dry textbook question: name the economic term. 'By-product' is a plausible distractor for young players.

questions.description: A hand you can't see, but that somehow sets the price of your bread.
questions.question: I'm an 18th-century Scottish thinker, and I said an “invisible hand” guides free markets. Who am I?
hints: He is often called the father of modern economics.
His big book came out in 1776, the same year as the US Declaration of Independence.
The book is “The Wealth of Nations”.
questions.fun_fact: The famous “invisible hand” appears only once in “The Wealth of Nations”, a book of nearly 1,000 pages.

quality.notes: Good distractors (Hume is also a Scottish thinker of the same century). Small risk: an Edinburgh Old Town search could return the Adam Smith statue on the Royal Mile. The fun fact is true for The Wealth of Nations.

questions.description: Villagers don't take cash, but they do love shiny green rocks.
questions.question: You want to craft a block of emeralds in Minecraft. How many emeralds do you need?
hints: You fill the crafting table with them.
The crafting grid is 3 by 3.
It's the same number as for a block of gold or diamond.
questions.fun_fact: In Minecraft, emeralds are the money villagers use when they trade with you.

quality.notes: Correct. Players can reason towards it from the 3×3 crafting grid. Good fit for kids and teens.

questions.description: Some characters count sheep to sleep; these count coins.
questions.question: You're picking a team of cartoon characters who love money. Which one does NOT belong?
hints: One of them would rather have something sweet than something shiny.
One of them dives into a pool of coins.
The odd one out loves honey, not money.
questions.fun_fact: Scrooge McDuck keeps his fortune in a giant money bin and loves to swim in his coins.

quality.notes: Pooh clearly stands out from the other three. Wario is less known to young kids. Hint 3's 'honey, not money' is an English rhyme that won't translate, but it is only a hint.

questions.description: The happy part of running a lemonade stand.
questions.question: You sell lemonade for 5 coins after spending 2 coins on lemons and sugar. What are the 3 coins you keep called?
hints: It's good news for a seller.
It's what is left after paying your costs.
Businesses want this number to be as big as possible.
questions.fun_fact: If you spend more than you earn, the money you lose is called a loss: the opposite of profit.

quality.notes: Clean and correct, but a plain school-style definition.

questions.description: The day the dollar broke up with gold.
questions.question: In 1971, I stopped letting other countries swap US dollars for gold, ending the Bretton Woods system. Who am I?
hints: I was President of the United States at the time.
My announcement became known as a “shock” named after me.
I later resigned after the Watergate scandal.
questions.fun_fact: Since the “Nixon shock”, no major currency has been tied to gold.

quality.notes: Hint 3 (Watergate) touches on q-1406, but this question asks a different fact. Many history-minded adults know the 'Nixon shock', so slightly below 14.

questions.description: Nature built this bridge long before anyone needed to cross.
questions.question: In southern France, canoeists paddle under the Pont d'Arc, a giant natural stone arch. Which river carved it?
hints: The river gives its name to a French department.
Its gorge is close to a cave with some of the oldest known cave paintings.
Its name starts with “Ard…”.
questions.fun_fact: The Chauvet Cave nearby holds paintings about 36,000 years old, and its full-size copy is named after the Pont d'Arc.

quality.notes: Accurate, and the distractors are good French gorge rivers. Fun is only moderate: this is pure regional geography that few people can reason towards. Hint 3 spells out the first three letters, which is close to the limit. The decorative gorge image might show the Ardèche itself, but it carries little risk.

questions.description: A coat hanger so big that trains and cars drive across it.
questions.question: This close-up shows a giant steel arch bridge nicknamed “the Coathanger”. In which city does it stand?
hints: The city is on a big harbor in the Southern Hemisphere.
Huge New Year's fireworks are set off from this bridge.
A famous opera house with sail-shaped roofs stands right next to it.

media.query: Sydney Harbour Bridge steel arch close-up
media.note: Close-up of the steel truss arch of the Sydney Harbour Bridge; no Opera House, no signs or text visible.

questions.fun_fact: Workers climbed the Sydney Harbour Bridge to paint it, and today visitors can climb its arch too.

quality.notes: The “Coathanger” nickname is a strong clue for anyone who knows it. The essential close-up has to avoid showing the Opera House or the skyline, so the media needs careful picking.

questions.description: A bridge with a very grumpy tollkeeper.
questions.question: In a famous fairy tale, three animals like these must cross a bridge. Who lives under it?
hints: The story comes from Norway.
He wants to eat whoever crosses.
The biggest goat butts him into the river.

media.note: Photo of three goats (billy goats) standing together, ideally of different sizes.

questions.fun_fact: “Three Billy Goats Gruff” was collected in Norway in the 1840s by Peter Christen Asbjørnsen and Jørgen Moe.

quality.notes: The tale is well known in English and Nordic countries but less so in Latin America, so it is probably a bit harder than 4 for families elsewhere. The internet-troll question (q-0965) is a different fact.

questions.description: A bird that never forgets your homework, even when you'd like it to.
questions.question: I'm a green owl, and every day I remind you to do your language lesson. Who am I?
hints: I live in an app on your phone.
I'm famous for funny, slightly pushy reminders.
My app is called Duolingo.
questions.fun_fact: Duo has become an internet star thanks to memes about how hard he pushes people to keep their learning streak.

quality.notes: Good, well-known meme topic. Many people know the green owl but not the name 'Duo', so a little harder than 5. The distractors (Hedwig, Archimedes, Owl) are nice.

questions.description: Gotta match 'em all: every Pokémon game seems to come with a twin.
questions.question: On the shelf of an old game shop: Pokémon Red is to Pokémon Blue as Pokémon Gold is to…
hints: The pair came out together a few years after Red and Blue.
Like the first pair, the two names belong together.
Think of medals: first place, then second place.
questions.fun_fact: Pokémon games come in pairs so that players have to trade with each other to catch every Pokémon.

quality.notes: The 'On the shelf of an old game shop' scenario is filler and not the clue (Keep it short). The gold/silver pair is easy to reason out even without knowing Pokémon, so 7 is too high. Bronze isn't a real Pokémon game, which makes it a weaker distractor.

questions.description: Cartoon couples: the cutest relationships with the biggest ears and beaks.
questions.question: You're watching Disney cartoons: Mickey is to Minnie as Donald is to…
hints: We're looking for Donald's girlfriend.
She's a duck, just like him.
Her name is also the name of a small white flower.
questions.fun_fact: Minnie Mouse appeared on screen in 1928, in the same cartoon as Mickey, so she's just as old as he is.

quality.notes: 'You're watching Disney cartoons' is filler. Hint 1 just repeats the question. Daisy is less well known around the world than Minnie, so 4 fits better than 3. Goofy and Pluto are clearly not girlfriends; Clarabelle is the only distractor that really works.

questions.description: Grandma is acting a little strange today.
questions.question: Complete the line from Little Red Riding Hood: “Grandma, what big eyes you have!” “All the better to … you with!”
hints: Think about what eyes are for.
The wolf has a different answer for the ears and for the teeth.
You do it when you look at something.
questions.fun_fact: The best-known versions of Little Red Riding Hood were written by Charles Perrault in France and by the Brothers Grimm in Germany.

quality.notes: Solid. Hint 1 ('what eyes are for') is already strong.

questions.description: Big things start small, sometimes next to the family car.
questions.question: It was founded in 1976 by two friends both named Steve, started out in a garage in California, and sold its first computer as a bare circuit board. Which company?
hints: Today it makes phones, tablets and laptops.
Its two Steves were Jobs and Wozniak.
Its logo is a fruit with a bite out of it.
questions.fun_fact: The first Apple computer had no case, no keyboard and no screen: buyers had to add those themselves.

quality.notes: Ronald Wayne was briefly a third co-founder, so 'founded by two friends' simplifies things a little. Hint 2 names Jobs and Wozniak, which is nearly the answer already.

questions.description: A villain so scary that even his name is off-limits.
questions.question: Harry Potter's enemy Voldemort is so feared that most wizards won't say his name. Harry says it anyway. What do the others call him instead?
hints: It's a way of talking about someone without saying who.
He's also called He-Who-Must-Not-Be-Named.
It's as if you said: “the person you already know I mean.”
questions.fun_fact: Voldemort's real name is Tom Riddle, and “I am Lord Voldemort” is made from the letters of his full name.

quality.notes: Hint 2 gives another name that also correctly answers the question ('He-Who-Must-Not-Be-Named'). 'The Dark Prince' sits close to the real epithet 'the Dark Lord'. The fun fact reveals Tom Riddle, which touches q-0961-unrelated q-1532 (the Tom Riddle diary) only lightly.

questions.description: Two shakers that have never been seen apart.
questions.question: On dinner tables all over the world, two shakers stand side by side. Complete the pair: “salt and…”
hints: It's not sweet.
It can make you sneeze.
It comes in small black grains.
questions.fun_fact: Black pepper was once so valuable that people called it “black gold” and even paid taxes with it.

quality.notes: Very easy and not very surprising. The claim that people paid taxes with pepper is broadly true (medieval tributes and rents) but loosely put. Decorative media is a reasonable choice, since a shaker photo would show the answer.

questions.description: In Agrabah, every royal needs a furry sidekick.
questions.question: In Disney's Aladdin, Aladdin's pet Abu is a monkey. Aladdin is to monkey as Princess Jasmine is to…
hints: Jasmine's pet lives in the palace.
It's a big striped cat.
Its name is Rajah.
questions.fun_fact: Abu once gets turned into an elephant by the Genie in the film.

quality.notes: Hint 2 ('big striped cat') is already very strong.

questions.description: A forest snack that is not on any menu.
questions.question: In The Last of Us, Joel guides Ellie across a ruined America. The disease that changed the world comes from a real living thing that infects ants. What kind?
hints: It is not an animal or a plant.
Its relatives grow in forests after the rain.
Mushrooms belong to this group.
questions.fun_fact: The real Cordyceps fungus can take over an ant's body and make it climb up a plant before the fungus grows out of it.

quality.notes: The real ant fungus is Ophiocordyceps, not 'Cordyceps' as the fun fact says. The Last of Us is a mature-rated horror game and series, which is borderline for a family game. The description ('forest snack') hints at mushrooms. The HBO series made this widely known, so 10 is a bit high.

questions.description: Every great cartoon scientist borrows a little from the classics.
questions.question: I'm a scientist who drags my grandson Morty across the universe. I started out as a cartoon parody of which film inventor?
hints: He's from a film series of the 1980s.
He also takes a teenager on wild trips.
He built a time machine out of a car.
questions.fun_fact: Morty also began as a parody: of Marty McFly, the teenager who travels in time with Doc Brown in Back to the Future.

quality.notes: Rick and Morty is a crude adult cartoon (Adult Swim), so it doesn't fit a family game, especially for the young teens whose window includes 11. The facts about its origin as a parody are correct.

questions.description: Every pair of heroes needs someone to work against.
questions.question: Which of these characters is NOT on Mario and Luigi's side?
hints: He's very big and very grumpy.
He keeps kidnapping a princess.
He's a giant turtle with spikes on his shell.
questions.fun_fact: Luigi got his green clothes because the first Mario Bros. game needed a way to tell two players apart.

quality.notes: Close to q-0512 and q-0876 (Bowser as Mario's enemy), but the fact asked is a different one.

questions.description: Small, sharp and always looking for a hole to get through.
questions.question: It's thin, has a sharp point and a tiny hole called an eye, and you push thread through it. What is it?
hints: You find it in a sewing kit.
It helps fix a torn shirt.
Grandmas use it to sew on buttons.
questions.fun_fact: People sewed with needles made of bone tens of thousands of years ago.

quality.notes: A plain definition question with little surprise, and it doesn't fit famous duos. The description gets it backwards: the thread goes through the needle's hole, not the needle through a hole.

questions.description: A tool for spying on things too small to even notice they're being watched.
questions.question: Scientists use it in labs, it has lenses and a little stage for glass slides, and it lets you see cells. What is it?
hints: It makes things look much bigger.
You look at tiny things with it, not faraway ones.
It helps you see germs.
questions.fun_fact: In the 1670s, Dutch cloth seller Antonie van Leeuwenhoek used his handmade microscopes to see bacteria for the first time.

quality.notes: Solid but plain object identification. “Lets you see cells” makes it easy, so a 3 is probably closer than a 4.

questions.description: A movie star by day, a secret inventor by night.
questions.question: Hedy Lamarr was a Hollywood star, she invented “frequency hopping” with a composer, and she patented it in 1942. What was it meant to do?
questions.answer: Stop enemies jamming torpedo radio signals
wrong_answers: Guide planes landing in thick fog
hints: It was invented during the Second World War.
The signal kept jumping between radio channels so it was hard to block.
It was about controlling a weapon that travels underwater.
questions.fun_fact: Her idea of hopping between frequencies is an ancestor of the wireless technology used in Bluetooth and Wi-Fi.

quality.notes: The correct option is longer and more specific (“torpedo”) than the others, so it stands out. Hint 2 practically spells out anti-jamming, which is acceptable for hint 2 but strong. A great surprising fact.

questions.description: Beep beep beeeep: someone is sending you a message the old-fashioned way.
questions.question: “I'm a code of dots and dashes, and I carry my American inventor's name.” Who was he?
hints: The code was sent along telegraph wires.
In this code, SOS is three dots, three dashes, three dots.
His last name rhymes with “horse”.
questions.fun_fact: Samuel Morse was also a painter before he became famous for the telegraph.

quality.notes: Most people know the name “Morse code”, so the riddle answers itself. Hint 3's rhyme with “horse” only works in English and breaks in translation. q-1514 also has Morse as its answer, but asks a different fact.

questions.description: A parking spot where nobody arrives by car.
questions.question: This big “H” is painted on a roof. What kind of place is it?
hints: Something arrives here from the sky.
It doesn't need a long runway.
The flying machine that lands here has spinning blades on top.

media.note: A clear photo of a helipad on a rooftop with a big painted H, no helicopter visible and no readable text.

questions.fun_fact: Igor Sikorsky's R-4, from 1942, was the first helicopter ever built in large numbers.

quality.notes: Distractors are weak: a bus stop or boat harbor on a roof makes no sense. The fun fact has little to do with helipads.

questions.description: A dessert invented by a kid who forgot to clean up.
questions.question: An 11-year-old invented this treat by accident in 1905, after leaving a drink outside on a cold night. What was the stick first used for?
hints: The stick was already in the cup before it froze.
He had been mixing powder into water.
You'd use a spoon for the same job today.

media.note: A clear photo of a single colorful ice pop on a wooden stick, no brand or packaging.

questions.fun_fact: The boy, Frank Epperson, later patented his frozen treat in 1924.

quality.notes: The Epperson story is widely told but partly legend; it's fine as written. The media is labeled essential, but it's really illustrative of “this treat”. Hint 1 almost gives the answer.

questions.description: The slowest, quietest and most colorful way to leave the ground.
questions.question: You're standing in the basket of a hot air balloon. A boat floats on water; what does your balloon float on?
hints: Look up, not down.
Birds fly through it.
You breathe it all the time.
questions.fun_fact: The first passengers of a hot air balloon, in 1783 in France, were a sheep, a duck and a rooster.

quality.notes: Very obvious, and the snow and sand distractors are throwaways. The fun fact (sheep, duck, rooster) saves it a little.

questions.description: The world's biggest hug, waiting on top of a mountain since 1931.
questions.question: This giant statue stands on a mountain above Rio de Janeiro. Who does it show?
hints: The open arms are a sign of welcome and peace.
He is a religious figure, not a king or an emperor.
Christmas celebrates his birth.

media.note: A clear front view of the Christ the Redeemer statue on Corcovado, arms spread wide.

questions.fun_fact: The statue is about 30 m (98 ft) tall and gets hit by lightning several times a year.

quality.notes: Solid. The essential photo is easy to find. The open-arms pose already hints strongly at Jesus, but that is fine for this level.

questions.description: A city that hugs itself very tightly, and has done so for centuries.
questions.question: Most of the stone walls around the old city of Dubrovnik in Croatia were built in which era?
hints: Dubrovnik was a rich trading republic then, always worried about attackers.
Knights and castles belong to the same time.
Think of the long time between the fall of Rome and around 1500.
questions.fun_fact: The walls run for almost 2 km (1.2 mi) around the old town, and visitors can walk the whole loop on top of them.

quality.notes: Most of the walls date from the 13th–15th centuries, but some were reworked into the 16th–17th, so 'Middle Ages' is right only in broad terms. Fairly dry school-style dating question. Hint 2 (knights and castles) nearly gives it away. Players can reason their way from 'stone city walls' to medieval, so it is easier than 10.

questions.description: A shortcut so good that ships stopped going around a whole continent.
questions.question: About how long is the Panama Canal, from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean?
hints: Panama is very narrow at that point.
A ship takes about 8 to 10 hours to go through.
It is about as long as two marathons.
questions.fun_fact: Locks lift each ship about 26 m (85 ft) up to a lake in the middle, then lower it down again on the other side.

quality.notes: Asks a different fact (length) from the existing Panama Canal questions. The options are powers of ten, which allows good reasoning. Hints and fun fact are accurate.

questions.description: A church that looks like it was decorated by a team of very excited ice cream makers.
questions.question: You're in Moscow's Red Square, looking at the church with colorful onion domes. In which century was it built?
hints: Russia was ruled by a tsar at the time.
It was built under Ivan the Terrible.
It was finished just a few years before Shakespeare was born.
questions.fun_fact: Saint Basil's Cathedral is really nine separate chapels joined together on one base.

quality.notes: Built 1555–1561, so 16th century is correct and the Shakespeare hint checks out. 'Nine chapels' is the usual claim, though a tenth chapel was added in 1588. Dating it to the right century is harder than 8 without the hints. q-1615 is also about Saint Basil's but asks something different.

questions.description: The most famous chimney in the world, and Santa has nothing to do with it.
questions.question: I'm the giant domed church of the Vatican. When white smoke rises from the chimney next door, crowds rush to my square. Why?
questions.answer: A new pope has been chosen
wrong_answers: A new saint has been named
The pope is leaving on a trip
hints: The cardinals have been voting behind locked doors.
Black smoke means “not yet”.
Soon someone will step onto the balcony in white robes for the first time.
questions.fun_fact: The smoke gets its black or white color from special chemicals added when the voting papers are burned.

quality.notes: Accurate: the chimney is on the Sistine Chapel, next to the basilica. Having the basilica speak in first person is a slightly forced riddle frame. Kids aged 6–10 rarely know about conclaves, so it fits young teens and older best.

questions.description: Before it painted the world's fries red, this company wanted to make your eyes water.
questions.question: Heinz ketchup is to tomatoes as Heinz's very first bottled product, from 1869, is to what?
hints: It is a root, not a fruit.
It is famous for being very hot and making your nose sting.
It is often served with roast beef, and wasabi is a close relative.
questions.fun_fact: Henry Heinz sold his horseradish in clear glass bottles so buyers could see it held no cheap fillers.

quality.notes: The analogy feels forced. It's really just asking what Heinz's first product was, and the 'is to' framing adds nothing. The description's 'make your eyes water' narrows the options to spicy things, but all four are spicy, so that's fine. q-1098 has the same answer but asks a different fact (wasabi substitute). Hint 3 mentions wasabi, which links to it. The answer is hard to reason towards, so this is closer to 13.

questions.description: Every morning you put a man's name on your toothbrush and don't even notice.
questions.question: You're squeezing Colgate onto your toothbrush. Who is the brand named after?
hints: Many brands are named after the person who started the business.
He opened his shop in New York in 1806.
His first name was William, and he sold soap and candles.
questions.fun_fact: William Colgate started out selling soap and candles; toothpaste came decades later, in the 1870s.

quality.notes: The options are uneven. The answer is the only one with a qualifier ('Its founder, a soap maker') and stands out by length. 'A tooth fairy story' is a silly filler and doesn't fit 'Who'. 'English king' is a decent decoy. The scenario clause adds nothing.

questions.description: A fiery animal that hugs the whole planet, and still doesn't get burned.
questions.question: “My name is a nickname of the red panda, and my logo wraps around the globe. I'm a web browser.” Who made me?
hints: It isn't one of the giant tech companies that also sell phones or computers.
It is a nonprofit group that also builds free software.
Its name sounds like a mix of a famous movie monster and an old browser called Mosaic.
questions.fun_fact: Before it was called Firefox, the browser was briefly named Phoenix and then Firebird.

quality.notes: The description's 'fiery animal' plus the riddle points to Firefox, but the question is about who makes it, so that's acceptable. Many young teens use Chrome and don't know Mozilla, so 9 is more realistic than 8.

questions.description: The logo is a man with a ball; the court has a few more of them.
questions.question: You're watching an NBA basketball game. How many players from both teams are on the court at the same time?
hints: Both teams have the same number of players on the court.
Each team has fewer players on court than a soccer team.
Each team plays with five.
questions.fun_fact: The player in the NBA logo is widely said to be Jerry West, a star of the 1960s.

quality.notes: The NBA framing leans toward the US league for no reason; basketball itself is universal. It's a dry count question with only a thin link to logos, and the logo connection appears only in the fun fact. The description's 'man with a ball' only makes sense to people who know the NBA logo.

questions.description: Chocolate on the outside, a mystery on the inside, just like a birthday.
questions.question: A piñata is to candy as a Kinder Surprise chocolate egg is to what?
hints: It's the surprise in the name.
It hides in a little yellow capsule.
Kids build it or play with it after eating the chocolate.
questions.fun_fact: “Kinder” is the German word for “children”.

quality.notes: The distractors are weak. A seed or a balloon inside a chocolate egg is not plausible, and the word 'Surprise' strongly suggests a toy. Kinder Surprise isn't sold in the US, but it's known in most of the world.

questions.description: Design a fair cake-sharing rule without knowing which slice you'll get.
questions.question: I asked you to design a fair society from behind a “veil of ignorance”, not knowing if you'd be rich or poor. Who am I?
hints: I was a 20th-century American philosopher.
I set out the idea in my 1971 book “A Theory of Justice”.
My first name is the same as the Beatle Lennon's.
questions.fun_fact: “A Theory of Justice” has sold hundreds of thousands of copies, which is very rare for a heavy philosophy book.

quality.notes: Solid. The description is an imperative rather than a statement but still works. Hint 3 points to 'John', which is acceptable for hint 3.

questions.description: A man who wasn't sure the sun would come up tomorrow, but slept well anyway.
questions.question: This Scottish thinker of the 1700s said that seeing the sun rise every day doesn't prove it will rise tomorrow. Who is he?
hints: He lived in Edinburgh and was a close friend of the economist Adam Smith.
His idea is known as the problem of induction.
Immanuel Kant said this man woke him from his “dogmatic slumber”.

media.note: Allan Ramsay's 1766 portrait of David Hume, with no name or caption visible.

questions.fun_fact: A statue of Hume stands on Edinburgh's Royal Mile, and students rub its toe for luck, which might have amused a man who doubted cause and effect.

quality.notes: The portrait is not really essential: players can't recognize Hume's face, and the text alone carries the question. 'Illustrative' (e.g. Edinburgh or his statue) would fit better. Hint 1 rules out the Adam Smith option. The 'dogmatic slumber' hint is reused in famous-philosophers-8.

questions.description: A philosopher so punctual that the town clocks were jealous.
questions.question: Immanuel Kant took his daily walk so punctually that neighbors in Königsberg could set their clocks by him. In which century did he live?
hints: He lived in the Age of Enlightenment.
He was alive during the American and French Revolutions.
He was born in 1724 and died in 1804.
questions.fun_fact: Kant's hometown of Königsberg is now Kaliningrad in Russia, and he hardly ever traveled far from it in his whole life.

quality.notes: Kant lived until 1804, so strictly he also lived in the 19th century; 'mainly lived' would be cleaner. Asking for a century is a bit dry, though the clock anecdote helps.

questions.description: A book so hard that even its author wrote a shorter version to explain it.
questions.question: I'm a famously difficult German book. My author asked what the mind can know before any experience, after Hume woke him from his “dogmatic slumber”. What am I?
hints: I was published in 1781.
My author lived all his life in Königsberg.
My author is Immanuel Kant.
questions.fun_fact: Kant published a shorter guide to the book in 1783, partly because readers found the original so hard to follow.

quality.notes: Rather dry, close to a school test. The description and the fun fact both tell the same Prolegomena story. The 'dogmatic slumber' clue repeats a hint from famous-philosophers-1. The 'pop_culture' lens doesn't fit the question.

questions.description: A philosopher who took “living simply” about as far as it goes.
questions.question: Diogenes lived in a large clay jar in the street. His school, the Cynics, took its name from the Greek word for which animal?
hints: People mocked him for living shamelessly in public, like an animal.
He happily accepted the nickname.
It's the animal that barks.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says that when Alexander the Great offered Diogenes any wish, he only asked him to step aside because he was blocking the sun.

quality.notes: The dog origin is the usual explanation, though some link the name to the Cynosarges gymnasium. Hint 1 ('like an animal') points the way a little.

questions.description: A short slogan with a very long history.
questions.question: “I think, therefore I am” is to Descartes's “Discourse on Method” as “Workers of the world, unite!” is to which book?
hints: The book came out in 1848.
Its authors were two Germans living abroad.
It was written by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels.
questions.fun_fact: The slogan is carved on Karl Marx's tomb in Highgate Cemetery, London.
questions.concept: Proletarios de todos los países, uníos

quality.notes: The analogy is just padding: the Descartes half adds nothing to 'Which book has this slogan?'. The description is a fragment, not a full sentence, and only mildly funny.

questions.description: The most powerful man in the world kept a diary, and it became a bestseller.
questions.question: The emperor in this statue wrote private notes to himself that became the book “Meditations”. Who is he?
hints: He ruled Rome in the 2nd century AD.
He was a follower of Stoic philosophy.
He is the old emperor in the film “Gladiator”.

media.note: The bronze equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius in Rome, without any visible name plate.

questions.fun_fact: Marcus Aurelius wrote his “Meditations” in Greek, not Latin, often in army camps during wars.

quality.notes: Good. The Capitoline statue is easy to find on Commons. The photo doesn't really help identify him; the text carries the question.

questions.description: A how-to guide for rulers that gave its author's name a bad reputation.
questions.question: Thomas More is to “Utopia” as Niccolò Machiavelli is to which book?
hints: Machiavelli wrote it in Florence around 1513.
It advises rulers on how to gain and keep power.
Its title is a royal title, lower than king.
questions.fun_fact: “The Prince” was only printed in 1532, five years after Machiavelli died.

quality.notes: The description ('gave its author's name a bad reputation') hints at 'Machiavellian' but not at the title. The analogy format is a bit dry.

questions.description: A war guide now read by business bosses and sports coaches.
questions.question: This bamboo book is a copy of “The Art of War”, a famous ancient Chinese guide. Who is said to have written it?
hints: He is said to have been a general about 2,500 years ago.
One of his lines: win without fighting.
His name starts with “Sun”.

media.note: The bamboo-slip copy of The Art of War (UC Riverside), showing the tied bamboo strips with Chinese writing.

questions.fun_fact: Ancient Chinese books were often written on strips of bamboo tied together with string, then rolled up.

quality.notes: Genghis Khan is a weak distractor (not a writer, and Mongol). The bamboo book isn't needed to answer, so the role should be illustrative, not essential.

questions.description: The worst place in the world to lose your sewing kit.
questions.question: I'm a big pile of dried grass in a field, and cows eat me in winter. Finding a needle in me is almost impossible. What am I?
hints: Farmers pile me up after cutting and drying the grass.
Horses and cows love to munch on me.
My first part is the word for dried grass.
questions.fun_fact: Hay is dried grass for animals to eat, while straw is the dry stalks left over after grain is harvested.

quality.notes: Hint 3 depends on the English compound word hay+stack (works in German, not in Spanish 'pajar'). The query 'farm field summer' could turn up a photo with haystacks.

questions.description: The milk factory has a voice, and it uses it.
questions.question: Complete it: “The cow says…”
hints: It's a long, low sound.
You hear it from a big animal in a green field.
Your mouth makes a round “oo” shape when you say it.
questions.fun_fact: Mother cows and their calves can recognize each other just by their moos.

quality.notes: Very basic, and fine for level 1, but not very surprising. Animal sounds are spelled differently in each language, and hint 3 (the round 'oo' shape) is English-specific, though a translation can adapt it.

questions.description: A hen who does all the work and, fairly, eats all the snacks.
questions.question: In a famous folk tale, a little red hen finds some grains, plants them and bakes bread, while her lazy friends won't help. What were the grains?
hints: Think about what most bread is made from.
The hen has to grind it into flour first.
It grows in golden fields with heavy heads of grain.
questions.fun_fact: In many versions, the hen's lazy friends each answer her with “Not I!”, and then they want to eat the bread.

quality.notes: The folk tale is best known in English-speaking countries, but players elsewhere can reason from 'bakes bread' to wheat, so it travels. Hint 1 nearly gives the answer away.

questions.description: A barnyard where the spider is the hero and the pig is the star.
questions.question: You're watching “Charlotte's Web”: Wilbur is to pig as Templeton is to…
hints: Templeton is greedy and loves leftover food.
He digs through trash at the county fair.
He's a rodent with a long, bare tail.
questions.fun_fact: Author E. B. White got the idea while watching a real spider spin its egg sac in his own barn.

quality.notes: The book is translated widely and the 2006 film helps, but it is better known in English-speaking countries. Good distractors: there are geese and sheep in the book too.

questions.description: Goats that decided the ground was just too boring.
questions.question: Goats climb high into argan trees there to eat the fruit, and the nuts give a famous oil used for hair and cooking. In which country?
hints: It's in Africa.
Its coast faces both the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea.
Its cities include Marrakesh and Casablanca.
questions.fun_fact: While chewing, the goats often spit out the hard argan nuts, and people once collected them to make oil.

quality.notes: Most adults know the argan oil–Morocco link, but few teens do, so I'd rate it slightly higher than 10.

questions.description: He has a beard, horns and absolutely no manners.
questions.question: This bearded fellow is a male goat. What is a male goat often called?
hints: A ram is a male sheep, so that's not it.
It sounds like a person's name.
It's also a nickname for William.

media.note: A close-up photo of the head of an adult male goat, showing its beard and horns.

questions.fun_fact: A female goat is called a nanny, and a baby goat is called a kid.

quality.notes: The question lives on English vocabulary: 'billy goat' has no equivalent in Spanish (macho cabrío/chivo) or German (Ziegenbock), and hint 3 (a nickname for William) only works in English. It can't travel as a base question. Also, 'buck' is the more standard term for a male goat.

questions.description: A cow having a permanent bad hair day, and loving it.
questions.question: Look at this shaggy cow with long horns and a fringe over its eyes. Which country does this breed come from?
hints: It comes from a cold, windy, rainy part of Europe.
Its home has mountains, lakes and bagpipes.
The breed is named after the hilly north of this country.

media.note: A close-up of a Highland cow's head showing the long shaggy fringe and wide horns, without any text or flags.

questions.fun_fact: A group of Highland cattle is called a “fold”, not a herd.

quality.notes: Good. Highland cattle photos are easy to find in Commons.

questions.description: A family reunion where one guest clearly took the wrong bus.
questions.question: You're at a farm. Three of these animals are close relatives of the donkey. Which one is NOT?
hints: Look for the animal that doesn't look like a donkey.
Donkey relatives have one big hoof on each foot.
This one has horns and gives milk.
questions.fun_fact: A mule's mother is a horse and its father is a donkey.

quality.notes: The 'You're at a farm' setting is invented and doesn't fit a zebra. The odd one out is very obvious.

questions.description: Lots of wool, one direction, zero independent thinkers.
questions.question: Look at all these woolly backs. What is a group of sheep called?
hints: A pack is for wolves, and a school is for fish.
The same word is used for a group of birds.
It sounds a bit like “block”.

media.note: A close photo of many sheep packed tightly together, mostly woolly backs, no shepherd or dog.

questions.fun_fact: When one sheep in a group starts to move, the others usually follow it.

quality.notes: Collective nouns are vocabulary of one language. 'Flock' covers both sheep and birds in English, but Spanish uses rebaño for sheep and bandada for birds, so hint 2 breaks in translation, and hint 3 ('sounds like block') is an English sound. The essential image doesn't help answer.

questions.description: A tail that went to the hairdresser and asked for curls.
questions.question: Look at this curly tail. Which farm animal does it belong to?
hints: This animal loves rolling in mud.
It's often pink.
It says “oink”.

media.note: A close-up of a pink pig's curly tail, showing only the back end of the pig.

questions.fun_fact: A pig's tail often hangs straight when it is stressed or unwell, and curls up when it feels relaxed.

quality.notes: Some dogs have curly tails too (pugs, Shibas), but the photo makes the answer clear. The fun fact about tail posture is broadly supported, but simplified.

questions.description: A book you can't read but you can definitely pet.
questions.question: Fashion designers flip through this to pick fabrics and colors. What is it called?
hints: It is full of small pieces of real fabric.
Each little piece is a sample of a bigger roll of cloth.
A small sample of fabric is called a “swatch”.

media.note: A clear photo of a fabric sample book: many small fabric pieces bound or fanned out together, no brand text readable.

questions.fun_fact: Paint shops and car makers use swatch books too, so customers can see and feel their choices.

quality.notes: Distractors and the description are fine. Age fit: “swatch book” is a trade term most 13-year-olds have never heard, so 7 looks too low; I'd put it nearer 9. Fun: it's a dry vocabulary question. Hint 3 contains “swatch”, which is close to giving the answer away (allowed for hint 3).

questions.description: The most famous gust of wind in movie history.
questions.question: In a 1955 film, which star stood over a subway grate while her white dress blew up around her?
hints: She was a blonde Hollywood star of the 1950s.
The film was “The Seven Year Itch”.
Andy Warhol made famous colorful prints of her face.
questions.fun_fact: The dress was designed by William Travilla and sold at auction in 2011 for about 4.6 million dollars.

quality.notes: The scene is iconic and the facts check out (Travilla designed the dress; it sold in 2011 for about $4.6 million before fees). Hint 2 names the film, which helps adults a lot, but that's fine for a hint. The lens axis “language” doesn't fit this question.

questions.description: A unicorn who would rather sew a gown than save the day, but does both.
questions.question: You're shopping at Rarity's dress shop, the Carousel Boutique. Which town are you in?
hints: Rarity is a pony from “My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic”.
Twilight Sparkle, Applejack and Pinkie Pie live in the same town.
The town's name starts with the kind of animal that lives there.
questions.fun_fact: Rarity stands for the Element of Harmony called Generosity.

quality.notes: Age fit: the question depends on knowing one TV franchise, and many kids (especially fans of other shows) won't have watched it, so I'd rate it nearer 6. Hint 1 names the show. A decorative image is acceptable here. The lens axis “history” doesn't fit.

questions.description: A ruler that learned to bend so it could hug your waist.
questions.question: In a tailor's shop, a clock is to time as a tape measure is to…
hints: Tailors wrap it around your waist or arm.
It is covered in centimeters or inches.
It tells you how long something is.
questions.fun_fact: Many tailors' tape measures are 150 cm (60 in) long, enough to go around almost anyone.

quality.notes: Fun: a simple analogy with no surprise in it. Distractors: “Heat” is easy to rule out. Hint 3 (“how long”) nearly says the answer, which is allowed for hint 3.

questions.description: A handbag with a royal secret, and a very long waiting list.
questions.question: This Hermès bag is named after Grace Kelly. In photos from 1956, what was she using it to hide?
hints: She had just married Prince Rainier of Monaco.
She held the bag in front of her belly.
Soon after, she became a mother.

media.note: A clear photo of a classic Hermès Kelly handbag (trapezoid shape, top handle, flap with strap closure).

questions.fun_fact: One Kelly bag is sewn by hand by a single craftsperson and can take about 20 hours to make.

quality.notes: Correctness: the bag was only officially renamed “Kelly” later (1977), but the anecdote itself is well documented. Distractors: “Her wedding plans” is weak because she married in April 1956, and the options are uneven in length. Hint 2 practically gives the answer. Essential media: a clear photo of a Kelly bag may be hard to find on Commons or Openverse. Difficulty: you can reason towards the answer, so 12 rather than 13.

questions.description: A perfume that comes with its own little garden on top.
questions.question: I'm Marc Jacobs' best-known perfume, and my bottle cap is covered in white plastic flowers, which give me my name. What flower am I?
hints: The flowers on the cap have white petals and a yellow center.
It is also a popular girl's name.
Children pull its petals off saying “loves me, loves me not”.
questions.fun_fact: Marc Jacobs' Daisy perfume came out in 2007 and became one of the best-selling perfumes in the world.

quality.notes: Correctness: “one of the best-selling perfumes in the world” is a loose claim. Age fit and fun: it's built around a US brand product, which is brand trivia more than culture. “White flowers” narrows the options to daisy or lily, so the stated 12 is too high; I'd say about 10.

questions.description: Shoes that look like cheese and are proud of it.
questions.question: When these foam clogs first came out in 2002, what activity were they made for?
hints: The holes let water drain out.
They don't slip easily on wet floors.
They were first shown at a boat show in Florida.

media.note: A clear photo of a pair of classic Crocs clogs with the holes on top visible, no charms.

questions.fun_fact: Crocs are not made of rubber but of a special soft foam called Croslite.

quality.notes: The facts check out (2002 Fort Lauderdale boat show; Croslite foam, not rubber). Hint 1 (water draining out) is already strong for a first hint. Essential media: Crocs photos are likely on Commons.

questions.description: Scissors so precious, touching them is a family crime.
questions.question: Tailors keep their big fabric scissors sharp. Which of these do they NOT cut with them?
hints: Three of these are kinds of cloth.
Cutting this one makes the blades dull.
You write and draw on it at school.
questions.fun_fact: Fabric shears have a bent handle so the lower blade can rest flat on the table while cutting.

quality.notes: Distractors: paper is the only option that isn't cloth, so the odd one out is obvious. Hint 1 says this outright, which is too strong for a first hint. Fun: easy and predictable.

questions.description: She traded her ice skates for a lot of white lace.
questions.question: This designer was a figure skater and a Vogue editor before becoming famous for wedding dresses. Who is she?
hints: She was born in New York to parents from China.
She opened her first bridal shop in 1990.
Her first name is also a word for “true” in some languages.

media.note: A clear portrait photo of fashion designer Vera Wang, with no name or caption text visible.

questions.fun_fact: She started designing wedding dresses after she couldn't find one she liked for her own wedding.

quality.notes: Good distractors (all famous women designers). Essential portrait: most players can't recognise her face, so the photo adds little, but it does no harm. Commons does have photos of her.

questions.description: A snack that pulls a long string every time you take a bite.
questions.question: These golden sticks are breaded and fried, with a cheese inside that melts into long strings. Which cheese is it usually?
hints: It is a cheese from Italy.
It is the same white cheese that melts on top of most pizzas.
It comes as soft white balls, often kept in water.

media.note: Photo of a plate of breaded, fried cheese sticks, ideally with a dipping sauce; no text or menu labels naming the cheese.

questions.fun_fact: Traditional mozzarella from around Naples is made from the milk of water buffalo.

quality.notes: Hint 2 (the pizza cheese) nearly gives it away, but hints are allowed to get strong. q-0684 also mentions mozzarella, but it asks a different fact.

questions.description: Fries that just came back from a weekend in the countryside.
questions.question: When fries are called “rustic” on a menu, what does that usually mean?
questions.answer: Thick-cut with the skin left on
hints: It is about how the potato is cut and peeled.
They look more homemade than thin fast-food fries.
The cook does not bother to peel the potatoes.
questions.fun_fact: Much of a potato's fiber is found in its skin.

quality.notes: “Rustic” on menus mostly means skin-on, but they aren't always thick-cut, so the answer is slightly loose. The question tests menu vocabulary, which is a bit dry. The fiber fun fact is commonly stated and acceptable.

questions.description: The sandwich that sunbathes in a frying pan until it is golden.
questions.question: This toasted cheese sandwich gets its golden, crispy outside from what, spread on the bread before it goes in the pan?
hints: It is a dairy product, like the cheese inside.
It melts quickly in a hot pan.
It is made by churning cream.

media.note: Photo of a golden grilled cheese sandwich cut in half with melted cheese; no text.

questions.fun_fact: Halloumi cheese from Cyprus is so firm that it can be grilled on its own without melting away.

quality.notes: Honey, ketchup and jam aren't believable as something you spread on a grilled cheese to fry it. Mayonnaise is also commonly used, but it's not among the options, so it's no problem. The halloumi fun fact only loosely relates to the question.

questions.description: A plant with ears that can't hear a thing.
questions.question: People in Mexico have made this food from the plant in the photo for thousands of years. What is it?
hints: The plant in the photo grows tall and has yellow kernels.
This food is flat, round and soft.
You can wrap it around beans or meat to make a taco.

media.note: A clear photo of ripe corn (maize) cobs on the plant, husks partly open so the yellow kernels show. No tortillas or text in the picture.

questions.fun_fact: Thousands of years ago, farmers in Mexico turned a small wild grass called teosinte into the big corn cobs we know today.

quality.notes: Distractors are weak: none of them is a corn food, so once players spot the corn, rice noodles, tofu and potato chips are easy to rule out. In the real world, Mexicans make other foods from corn too (tamales, pozole), but none of them is among the options. The description's 'ears' points to corn, which the essential photo shows anyway.

questions.description: A fruit with a crown, spiky armor and a very sweet heart.
questions.question: The fruit in this photo first grew wild in which part of the world?
hints: Christopher Columbus saw it for the first time on his travels.
It comes from the same continent as the potato and the tomato.
Its home is near the Amazon rainforest.

media.note: A clear photo of a whole pineapple with its leafy crown. No labels, flags or maps.

questions.fun_fact: Pineapples were so rare in 1700s Europe that rich people rented one just to show it off at a party.

quality.notes: The pineapple's wild home is the Paraná–Paraguay region of southern Brazil and Paraguay, so 'near the Amazon rainforest' (hint 3) is a bit loose. Hawaii is a strong distractor.

questions.description: A sweet so soft and powdery it should come with a napkin warning.
questions.question: This sweet, covered in powdered sugar, became famous at the palaces of which empire?
hints: It is often flavored with rose water.
The empire had its capital in Istanbul.
The sweet is named after a country today called Türkiye.

media.note: A close-up photo of a few cubes of Turkish delight (lokum) dusted with powdered sugar. No labels, flags or packaging text.

questions.fun_fact: In “The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe”, the White Witch tempts Edmund with a box of Turkish delight.

quality.notes: 'Famous at the palaces' is roughly right: lokum grew popular in Ottoman Istanbul (Hacı Bekir, 1777), but the palace link is part legend. Hint 2 (Istanbul) makes it easy.

questions.description: Long, thin and very hard to eat without making a mess.
questions.question: This food is famous in Italy. What kind of food is it?
hints: It is made from flour and water.
It's often served with tomato sauce.
Macaroni and lasagna are other kinds of it.

media.note: A close-up photo of cooked spaghetti strands, with or without a little tomato sauce. No text.

questions.fun_fact: Italians traditionally eat spaghetti by twirling it with a fork, without cutting it.

quality.notes: Very easy. Rice, soup and salad are hard to mistake for spaghetti in a photo, and the question has little surprise in it. Close to q-0322 (lasagna from a photo), but that asks a different thing.

questions.description: Golden sticks that disappear faster than you can count them.
questions.question: What are these made from?
hints: They grow under the ground.
You can also mash them.
They're brown on the outside and white inside.

media.note: A clear photo of a portion of French fries. No packaging or logos.

questions.fun_fact: Belgium and France both say they invented French fries.

quality.notes: Simple and a bit dry. Shares a topic with fast-food-5 (French fries) and famous-logos-11 (Pringles → potatoes), but asks a different fact.

questions.description: A tree that cries something delicious onto your pancakes.
questions.question: The sweet syrup often poured on pancakes comes from the tree with this leaf. Which tree is it?
hints: Its leaves turn bright red in the fall.
Farmers collect its sap at the end of winter.
Its leaf is on Canada's flag.

media.note: A clear photo of a single maple leaf, not the Canadian flag, no text.

questions.fun_fact: It takes about 40 liters (10 gallons) of maple sap to make just 1 liter (1 quart) of syrup.
