quality.notes: Many people know the maple leaf from Canada's flag, so it may be a bit easier than rated. q-0632 asks about the maple leaf, but not about syrup.

questions.description: The crunchiest revenge in history.
questions.question: A famous legend says potato chips were invented in 1853 by a cook who got annoyed. Who annoyed him?
hints: The story takes place in a restaurant.
This person kept sending the fries back to the kitchen.
They said the fries were too thick.
questions.fun_fact: Historians think the story is more legend than fact: recipes for thin fried potato slices were printed years before 1853.

quality.notes: Some versions of the George Crum legend name Cornelius Vanderbilt as the customer, but none of the wrong options fits him, so it stays unambiguous. The fun fact rightly calls it a legend.

questions.description: Two sticks walk into a restaurant and leave with dinner.
questions.question: In many Asian countries, what are these used for?
hints: People use them every day at the table.
You hold both in one hand.
They're great for picking up noodles.

media.note: A clear photo of a pair of chopsticks lying on a table, no food being eaten, no text.

questions.fun_fact: People in China have been using chopsticks for more than 3,000 years.

quality.notes: The distractors are joke options (drums, knitting) that nobody would pick. That fits difficulty 1 but makes the question trivial.

questions.description: A small piece of paper that can ruin a footballer's whole afternoon.
questions.question: “The referee shows me to warn a player. Get two of me in one match, and you must leave the field.” What am I?
hints: I'm the same color as a banana.
I'm a warning, not the final punishment.
I'm the middle color of a traffic light.
questions.fun_fact: English referee Ken Aston got the idea for yellow and red cards while waiting at a traffic light, and they were first used at the 1970 World Cup.

quality.notes: Solid. Cards are usually plastic, not paper, which is a small nitpick in the description. Blue and green cards are weak distractors.

questions.description: A city where the beach and the football pitch are never far apart.
questions.question: Germany won the 2014 World Cup final at the famous Maracanã stadium. In which city is it?
hints: The 2014 World Cup was played in Brazil.
This city is famous for its giant carnival.
It's home to Copacabana beach and the Christ the Redeemer statue.
questions.fun_fact: The Maracanã was built for the 1950 World Cup and is said to have held about 200,000 people at that tournament's final match.

quality.notes: The description's beach detail rules out São Paulo and Brasília. It's a fairly dry location fact. A decorative image is fine here, though an illustrative image (German fans, a trophy) could be safe. Same answer as capital-cities-3, but that asks a different fact.

questions.description: The referee's best friend is a TV in a little room far away.
questions.question: At the 2018 World Cup, referees could jog to a screen at the side of the field to watch a replay. What is this system called?
hints: It was used at a World Cup for the first time in Russia.
Its name is three letters long.
The letters stand for Video Assistant Referee.
questions.fun_fact: The 2018 World Cup in Russia was the first ever to use video replays to help the referee.

quality.notes: 'Slow-mo cam' is a weak, made-up distractor. Hawk-Eye supplies replay technology to football, so it is close to VAR. The fun fact only repeats hint 1. Calling 2018 the first World Cup 'to use video replays' is loose, since 2014 already had camera-based goal-line technology.

questions.description: The most nervous walk in sports is just eleven meters long.
questions.question: A match ends in a draw and goes to a penalty shootout. How many kicks does each team take at first?
hints: It's fewer than the number of players on a team.
If it's still a draw after them, the teams keep going one kick at a time.
It's the same as the number of fingers on one hand.
questions.fun_fact: The penalty kick was invented in 1891 by William McCrum, a goalkeeper from Ireland.

quality.notes: 10 is a weak distractor. In the fun fact, McCrum proposed the penalty in 1890 and it was adopted in 1891, and his home is now Northern Ireland, so 'invented in 1891' is a bit loose. The question is a plain rules fact.

questions.description: Red and black stripes, and a very long list of stars who wore them.
questions.question: You're looking at a wall of famous AC Milan shirts. Which of these players never played for the club?
hints: AC Milan plays in Italy.
This player never played for any Italian club.
He spent most of his career at FC Barcelona.
questions.fun_fact: AC Milan shares its stadium, San Siro, with its biggest rival, Inter Milan.

quality.notes: 'You're looking at a wall of shirts' is an unnecessary scene-setting story. Messi stands out because many players know him as a famous one-club Barcelona player.

questions.description: A World Cup with a soundtrack of a million buzzing plastic horns.
questions.question: In which year was the World Cup played in South Africa, the first ever held in Africa?
hints: Spain won it, their first World Cup title.
Shakira sang “Waka Waka” for this World Cup.
It came between the World Cups in Germany and Brazil.
questions.fun_fact: The vuvuzela horns heard all through the 2010 World Cup can be as loud as a chainsaw.

quality.notes: Many young teens were born after 2010, so the year is harder for them than 7. The 'as loud as a chainsaw' comparison is roughly right.

questions.description: Lie back, kick up, and hope you land gently.
questions.question: What is it called when a player jumps, flips backward in the air and kicks the ball over their own head?
hints: The player's back faces the goal.
The legs move in the air like they're pedaling.
Its name comes from a vehicle with two wheels.
questions.fun_fact: In Spanish this move is often called a “chilena”, and Chile and Peru both claim it was first done on their shores.

quality.notes: Hint 2 ('pedaling') nearly gives the answer away. A decorative image is fine. The Rabona, Scorpion kick and Panenka distractors are good.

questions.description: An award whose name doesn't leave much room for modesty.
questions.question: “In 2016 I won FIFA's very first The Best award for men's player, and I won it again in 2017.” Who am I?
hints: In 2016 I also won the European Championship with my country.
I played for Real Madrid at the time.
My nickname is CR7.
questions.fun_fact: FIFA started The Best awards in 2016, after it split from the Ballon d'Or it had shared with a French magazine.

quality.notes: This is a dry award-and-year fact; most players will guess between Ronaldo and Messi. It's harder than 9, since even many adults won't remember who won FIFA's The Best in 2016 and 2017.

questions.description: Sometimes the best place in the world is right behind somebody else.
questions.question: I'm the pocket of calmer air right behind a speeding car, and cyclists use me too. What do I help a racer close behind do?
hints: Think of the wind you feel when a big truck passes you.
The car in front pushes the air out of the way.
Drivers use it just before overtaking on a long straight.
questions.fun_fact: Cyclists ride in tight groups because riders sheltered inside the bunch save a lot of energy.

quality.notes: Slipstreaming is familiar from cycling and from films like Cars, so it may be easier than 10. The answer is a little more general than the wrong options, but that's fine.

questions.description: A brain teaser that has fooled more grown-ups than it would like to admit.
questions.question: A race car passes the car in second place, like in the photo. What place is it in now?
hints: Don't rush: think about who is still ahead.
It took the exact spot of the car it passed.
The leader is still in front of it.

media.note: Two race cars side by side on a track, one passing the other.

questions.fun_fact: This famous riddle catches lots of grown-ups, who quickly answer “first”.

quality.notes: 'Fourth' is a weak distractor; really only First and Third tempt. The photo isn't truly essential, since the riddle works without it (illustrative would fit better). Hint 2 gives the answer away.

questions.description: The part of the car that decides whether the engine sings or screams.
questions.question: You're biking up a hill and click a lever so pedaling gets easier. Which car part does that same job for the engine?
hints: The driver uses it with a stick or with paddles on the wheel.
Race drivers click it up and down many times each lap.
It lets the driver change gears.
questions.fun_fact: A modern Formula 1 car has eight forward gears.

quality.notes: Hint 3 ('change gears') almost contains the answer word, which is acceptable for a third hint. A good bike analogy that players can reason through.

questions.description: The only car in the race that's allowed to lead without winning anything.
questions.question: When the safety car drives onto the track during a race, what must the drivers do?
questions.answer: Slow down and line up behind it
wrong_answers: Stop in the pit lane right away
Race to pass it before it slows
Stop wherever they are on track
hints: Something on the track has to be cleared first.
Passing is not allowed while it's out.
It leads the cars like a mother duck leads her ducklings.
questions.fun_fact: The F1 safety car is a supercar driven by a professional, and it must still go fast so the race cars' tires don't get too cold.

quality.notes: A safety-car photo might show cars already lined up behind it, which hints at the answer. Hint 3 (mother duck) nearly gives it away, which is fine for a third hint.

questions.description: A man who thought power should be cut into slices, like a cake nobody gets to eat alone.
questions.question: This French thinker wrote “The Spirit of the Laws” and said power should be split into three branches. Who is he?
hints: He was a nobleman and a judge from near Bordeaux.
His book came out in 1748, decades before the Revolution.
His idea is called the “separation of powers”, and his name has “mount” in it.

media.note: A classic painted or engraved portrait of Montesquieu (Charles-Louis de Secondat), in profile or three-quarter view, with no name visible.

questions.fun_fact: Montesquieu's idea of separate lawmakers, government and judges went into the US Constitution and many constitutions after it.

quality.notes: Solid, but a dry textbook fact. Hint 3's 'mount' clue relies on English wordplay. The portrait isn't needed to answer, so the role should be illustrative, not essential. Most adults know Montesquieu and the separation of powers, so 12 fits better than 11.

questions.description: Napoleon's comeback tour: shorter than most summer holidays.
questions.question: Which place is NOT linked to Napoleon's “Hundred Days” comeback in 1815?
hints: The Hundred Days began with an escape from an island and ended with a famous defeat in Belgium.
One of these places is the site of a great Napoleonic victory ten years earlier.
The odd one out is a battle from 1805, often called the Battle of the Three Emperors.
questions.fun_fact: Napoleon landed in southern France with only about 1,000 men in March 1815 and reached Paris in under three weeks without a real fight.

quality.notes: The Hundred Days technically began after Napoleon left Elba, but the escape is clearly part of it. Ligny is obscure. Same answer as q-0650 (the Austerlitz victory behind the Arc de Triomphe), but that question asks a different fact. Feels like a school test.

questions.description: A very bad year to be in the crown business.
questions.question: French royalists lost their cause when the Revolution abolished the monarchy. In which year did that happen?
hints: It was not the year the Bastille fell, but a few years later.
It happened in the same year the Marseillaise was written.
It was three years after the storming of the Bastille.
questions.fun_fact: French royalists did get a king back in 1814, but the last French king, Louis-Philippe, lost his throne in 1848.

quality.notes: The opening 'French royalists lost their cause…' is awkward: royalism lived on long after 1792. A plain date question with a dry feel. The crown image is fine.

questions.description: A palace that left behind nothing but a very nice garden.
questions.question: This Paris palace stood right next to the Louvre, housed the royal family after 1789 and burned down in 1871. What was it?
hints: The king's family moved here after crowds brought them from Versailles.
It was stormed by Parisians on August 10, 1792.
Its famous garden, still there today, carries the palace's name.
questions.fun_fact: The name Tuileries comes from the tile factories (“tuileries”) that stood on the site before the palace was built.

quality.notes: Few adults know the vanished Tuileries Palace; most only know the garden, so this is closer to 13. Hint 3 comes close, which is acceptable.

questions.description: Lots of people swearing in a sports hall, and nobody even lost a match.
questions.question: This famous artwork shows deputies swearing an oath in an indoor tennis hall in June 1789. Which artist made it?
hints: The artist was himself a revolutionary and later a member of the Convention.
He also painted the death of Marat in his bathtub.
He later painted Napoleon crossing the Alps on a rearing horse.

media.note: Jacques-Louis David's drawing/painting “The Tennis Court Oath” showing the crowd of deputies raising their arms around a man on a table; no caption or artist name visible.

questions.fun_fact: David never finished the big painting, because several of the heroes in it fell out of favor during the Revolution.

quality.notes: Good. q-2053 (Michelangelo's David) only shares the name. Wikimedia surely has the Tennis Court Oath image.

questions.description: A revolutionary who dressed for horse riding, even in parliament.
questions.question: I was born in today's Belgium, wore a riding outfit in revolutionary Paris, and in 1792 asked for women to be allowed to carry arms. Who am I?
hints: I had been a singer before the Revolution.
I was nicknamed the “Amazon of Liberty”.
My chosen name comes from my home village of Marcourt.
questions.fun_fact: Théroigne de Méricourt's real name was Anne-Josèphe Terwagne; the name she is known by was invented in Paris.

quality.notes: A fair specialist question; the facts check out (Marcourt, Terwagne, singer, 'Amazon of Liberty', the 1792 call to arms). The description only repeats the riding-outfit clue from the question and isn't very funny. It's niche for family play.

questions.description: A king whose bank account started a revolution.
questions.question: France was nearly broke, so in 1789 the king called the Estates-General for the first time since 1614. Which king was it?
hints: His wife was Marie Antoinette.
He was the last king before the monarchy was abolished.
His number is one more than fifteen.
questions.fun_fact: France's money problems came partly from helping the Americans win their war of independence.

quality.notes: Hint 3 nearly gives it away, which is allowed. Estates-General paintings sometimes carry captions, but none names the king's number.

questions.description: A country with no crown, and no one to polish it.
questions.question: The French Revolution first made France into me, and today France is on its fifth version of me. What am I?
hints: In me, nobody inherits the right to rule.
My leaders are chosen, and my head of state is often a president.
My name comes from Latin for “the public thing”.
questions.fun_fact: France's current system, the Fifth Republic, began in 1958 under Charles de Gaulle.

quality.notes: 'First made France into me' is slightly off: the Revolution first made France a constitutional monarchy (1791), and only later a republic. 'A federation' is a weak distractor. A French flag would be safe as illustrative media.

questions.description: An optimistic song: the revolutionary version of “Don't worry, be happy”.
questions.question: I'm a French revolutionary song from 1790, and my title repeats a phrase Benjamin Franklin liked to say in Paris. What am I?
hints: Crowds sang me while preparing the Festival of the Federation.
I am older than France's national anthem.
My title means “It will be fine”.
questions.fun_fact: Franklin, asked in Paris how the American Revolution was going, is said to have answered “Ça ira”: “It will be fine”.

quality.notes: The Franklin connection is a well-known story but probably not true; it is told with 'is said to' in the fun fact, but the question states it as fact. The 'Don't worry, be happy' description hints at the title's meaning, which helps players who know French.

questions.description: Something everyone gets at birth, no wrapping paper needed.
questions.question: Every person has them from birth, nobody can take them away, and France wrote them down in 1789. What are they?
hints: They are about being free and being treated equally.
They belong to all people, rich or poor.
The United Nations made a universal declaration of them in 1948.
questions.fun_fact: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948 has been translated into more than 500 languages.

quality.notes: The wrong options are weak: nobody gets taxes or a passport at birth. It's a different fact from q-2010 (a quote from the Universal Declaration), though on the same topic.

questions.description: Say what you want, just don't shout during the quiz.
questions.question: Article 11 of this 1789 declaration calls one right “one of the most precious rights of man”. Which right is it?
hints: It is about thoughts and opinions.
It lets every citizen speak, write and print freely.
Newspapers and writers depend on it most.

media.query: Declaration of the Rights of Man painting Le Barbier
media.note: The well-known painting of the 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (by Jean-Jacques-François Le Barbier), showing the text on two stone tablets; zoomed out so Article 11 is not readable.

questions.fun_fact: The 1789 Declaration is still part of French constitutional law today.

quality.notes: Article 11 is quoted correctly. The Le Barbier painting isn't needed to answer, so illustrative would fit better than essential; it is safe as long as the text can't be read. Hint 2 nearly gives the answer away. A school-style question.

questions.description: Cinderella's fairy godmother would need a much bigger team of mice for this one.
questions.question: Giant pumpkins like this one can weigh more than a car. What do plant scientists call a pumpkin?
hints: Think about what's inside it.
It grows from a flower.
It's full of seeds, just like an apple or a tomato.

media.note: A photo of one huge, record-size pumpkin, ideally with people next to it for scale.

questions.fun_fact: The record pumpkin, grown by Travis Gienger in 2023, weighed 1,247 kg (2,749 lb).

quality.notes: The facts check out: Gienger's 2023 pumpkin weighed 2,749 lb. Players can guess "A fruit" from everyday talk, because root, stem and leaf sound unlikely for a pumpkin. The media role should be illustrative, not essential: the photo doesn't answer the question.

questions.description: Her serve could get a speeding ticket on most highways.
questions.question: In which year did Serena Williams win the first of her 23 Grand Slam singles titles?
hints: She was still a teenager.
She was 17 years old.
It was the last year of the 1900s.
questions.fun_fact: Serena won the 2017 Australian Open while she was pregnant with her daughter.

quality.notes: It's a dry year question. Hint 1 ("still a teenager") plus her well-known long career rules out the far options, and hint 3 gives the year away. Most young teens won't know the date, so 8 is rated a bit low. A tennis ball image is safe.

questions.description: Some people collect stamps; these people collect bracelets and concert tickets.
questions.question: They trade friendship bracelets, know every “Era”, and in 2023 their dancing in Seattle shook the ground like a small earthquake. Who are they?
hints: They are fans of one singer.
Their singer is famous for “Shake It Off”.
Their singer re-recorded her old albums as “Taylor's Version”.
questions.fun_fact: The Eras Tour earned more than 2 billion US dollars, the most of any concert tour ever.

quality.notes: The Seattle "Swift Quake" and the Eras Tour's earnings of more than 2 billion US dollars are both true. "Eras" in the question and "Shake It Off" in hint 2 point strongly to Taylor Swift. This is pop culture centered on the US, but it is known worldwide.

questions.description: Some people avoid getting their shoes dirty; he made a career out of orange dust.
questions.question: This clay court in Paris hosts a Grand Slam tournament that one man won a record 14 times. Who is he?
hints: He plays left-handed.
He comes from Spain.
His nickname was “The King of Clay”.

media.note: The main orange clay court of Roland Garros in Paris, ideally empty; no players visible.

questions.fun_fact: Nadal won the French Open on his very first try, in 2005, at just 19 years old.

quality.notes: Hint 2 (Spain) settles it among these options. The court photo is illustrative, not essential. It shares only a topic with q-0404 (the clay court surface).

questions.description: A street so rich that even the pigeons check the news every morning.
questions.question: The world's biggest market of its kind sits on this New York street. What is traded there?
hints: What people buy there is not something you can hold in your hand.
Owners of these get a small part of a company's profits.
If you own one, you own a tiny piece of a business like a car maker.

media.note: The green street sign reading “Wall St” in New York, without the stock exchange building's name in view.

questions.fun_fact: Wall Street is named after a wooden wall that Dutch settlers built there in the 1600s.

quality.notes: Solid. The Wall St sign does most of the work for anyone who knows the name, which is fine since it's essential media. Wall Street is world-famous, so the US setting is OK.

questions.description: A machine with trust issues, but only about paper.
questions.question: Shops keep a machine like this next to the cash register. What is it for?
hints: It looks closely at money before the shop accepts it.
It often shines a purple ultraviolet light.
Real banknotes pass, copies made at home do not.

media.note: A banknote checking machine with ultraviolet light, ideally with a banknote inside; no text saying what it does.

questions.fun_fact: Many banknotes have hidden marks that glow only under ultraviolet light.

quality.notes: Essential media is risky: Commons may not have a clear photo of a counter-top UV banknote checker without printed text, and the machines look very different from each other. Fairly dry as trivia.

questions.description: Too heavy for a piggy bank, too shiny to use as a doorstop.
questions.question: What are blocks of pure gold like these called?
hints: They are made by pouring melted metal into a mold.
Banks keep them stacked in vaults.
People often just call them gold bars.

media.note: A stack of shiny rectangular gold bars.

questions.fun_fact: A standard gold bar kept by big banks weighs about 12.4 kg (27 lb).

quality.notes: The word “ingot” is vocabulary that few 11-year-olds know; they would say “gold bars”, so a 5 is too low (about 7). “Nuggets” is a good distractor. The question is a fairly dry vocabulary test.

questions.description: A coin so famous that parrots learned to say its name.
questions.question: Pirates had a nickname for this Spanish silver dollar. What was it?
hints: The nickname comes from how much the coin was worth.
Long John Silver's parrot squawks it in “Treasure Island”.
It was worth 8 smaller Spanish coins called reales.

media.note: Close-up of an old Spanish silver 8 reales coin, showing part of the design.

questions.fun_fact: The Spanish silver dollar was legal money in the United States until 1857.

quality.notes: Calling it a pirate “nickname” is loose: “piece of eight” was the coin's common name everywhere, not pirate slang. If the coin is shown sharp with the big “8” mark on it, that hints at the answer.

questions.description: The only cave in the world with a voice-controlled door.
questions.question: Ali Baba's treasure cave opened when he called out the name of these seeds. What are they?
hints: The story comes from the “Arabian Nights”.
These seeds are often sprinkled on burger buns.
The magic words are “Open …!”

media.note: Close-up of a pile of pale sesame seeds.

questions.fun_fact: Ali Baba's story was added to the “Arabian Nights” in the 1700s by French translator Antoine Galland, who heard it from a Syrian storyteller.

quality.notes: Works across languages (“Ábrete sésamo”, “Sesam öffne dich”). Showing the seeds makes it easier for anyone who knows burger buns. Fine for an essential image.

questions.description: A coin so loved that Shakespeare had a character cry out for it.
questions.question: This gold coin from Venice, showing a kneeling ruler before Saint Mark, was used across Europe for centuries. What was it called?
hints: Venice minted it for over 500 years.
Shylock worries about these in “The Merchant of Venice”.
Its name is related to the ruler's title: duke.

media.note: Close-up of a gold Venetian ducat showing the kneeling Doge and Saint Mark, without a caption.

questions.fun_fact: Venice minted ducats from 1284 until the republic fell in 1797.

quality.notes: Good distractors (florin especially). The coin's Latin legend (DVX) may be readable in a sharp image, which is a slight hint.

questions.description: A wall that hands out money, if you ask it nicely.
questions.question: What do people get from a machine like this one?
hints: You need a bank card to use it.
You put the money in your wallet afterwards.
It gives out banknotes.

media.note: A street cash machine with keypad and card slot, no text on screen saying “cash”.

questions.fun_fact: The world's first cash machine opened in London in 1967.

quality.notes: Very easy and a bit flat. ATM photos often show a bank logo or “Cash” text on screen. The first ATM (Barclays, 1967) was in Enfield, Greater London, so the fun fact is fine.

questions.description: The oldest boat ticket in history, and it's one way only.
questions.question: In Greek myths, the dead were given a small coin like this one. Who was it meant to pay?
hints: He worked on a river.
He rowed souls across the river Styx.
He was the ferryman of the underworld.

media.note: A small ancient Greek silver obol coin, both sides if possible.

questions.fun_fact: An obol was a small silver coin: six of them made one drachma.

quality.notes: The description (“boat ticket”) hints at a ferryman but doesn't give the name. Readers of Percy Jackson and fans of mythology may know it younger. The lens tag “everyday” doesn't fit.

questions.description: A piece of paper that promises money, and hopes the bank agrees.
questions.question: Before bank cards, which signed slip of paper told your bank to pay someone from your account?
hints: You wrote the amount in numbers and in words.
It came in a little booklet from your bank.
If there wasn't enough money, it would “bounce”.
questions.fun_fact: The oldest known handwritten check in England dates from 1659.

quality.notes: “Before bank cards” is a bit loose, since checks are still used. Young players rarely see checks, so 7 may be slightly low. “Bounce” in hint 3 is an English idiom. An illustrative image (e.g. an old bank counter) might have been possible instead of decorative. Fairly dry.

questions.description: A city with better drains than some apartments today.
questions.question: You walk the neat brick streets of Mohenjo-daro, with covered drains under your feet. About how many years ago were they built?
hints: The city belongs to one of the oldest civilizations in the world, in today's Pakistan.
It was around at the same time as the first pyramids of Egypt.
Think of roughly 2500 BC.
questions.fun_fact: Mohenjo-daro had one of the world's first city-wide drain systems, and its bricks were all made in the same size.

quality.notes: Solid estimate question. 12,000 years is easy to rule out, but players can reason their way there, which fits the style.

questions.description: A time so long and so proper that it got named after one lady.
questions.question: Steam trains, Sherlock Holmes's London and Charles Dickens's novels all belong to a period named after a British queen. What is it called?
hints: It covers most of the 1800s.
The queen ruled for 63 years and became Empress of India.
Her name sounds like the word for winning.
questions.fun_fact: Queen Victoria reigned for 63 years, and many of her 42 grandchildren married into the royal families of Europe.

quality.notes: Hint 3 depends on wordplay (Victoria/victory) that doesn't work in German. Steam trains and Dickens's first novel started slightly before 1837, but Victorian is clearly the best answer. The question feels a bit like a school test.

questions.description: The French throw a big party every year for an old prison break-in.
questions.question: You're watching fireworks over Paris on the day France remembers the storming of the Bastille. What date is it?
hints: It's in the middle of summer in France.
It's in the same month as the US Independence Day, but later.
The French call it “le 14 juillet”.
questions.fun_fact: When the crowd stormed the Bastille in 1789, they found only seven prisoners inside.

quality.notes: Hint 3 'le 14 juillet' literally contains the answer in French. Hint 2 uses the US Independence Day as a reference point, which is an Anglo/US bias. The fun fact about seven prisoners is great.

questions.description: A king with so many crowns he needed an extra shelf.
questions.question: Charlemagne was crowned ruler of three of these peoples. Which one did he never rule?
hints: Charlemagne lived around the year 800.
The Pope crowned him emperor in Rome on Christmas Day.
These raiders came from the far north and attacked his empire's coasts.
questions.fun_fact: Charlemagne was crowned Emperor of the Romans by the Pope on December 25, 800.

quality.notes: Vikings can be reasoned out as the odd one, which is good. The fun fact only repeats hint 2 (crowned on Christmas Day 800), so it isn't surprising.

questions.description: One big red country that turned into fifteen smaller ones overnight.
questions.question: On a world map from 1985, three of these groups of countries were part of the Soviet Union. Which one was not?
hints: The Soviet Union broke up in 1991.
Estonia, Georgia and Kazakhstan all became independent then.
Think of Sweden, Norway and Denmark.
questions.fun_fact: When the Soviet Union broke up in 1991, it split into 15 independent countries.

quality.notes: Accurate, but reads like a dry geography test. The fun fact (15 countries) repeats what the description already hints at.

questions.description: The heaviest outfit you could ever wear to work.
questions.question: Knights wore metal suits like this one. What were they for?
hints: Knights went to battle in them.
They are hard and strong.
Swords bounced off them.

media.note: Clear photo of a full medieval suit of plate armor, as in a museum.

questions.fun_fact: A full suit of knight's armor weighed about 25 kg (55 lb), and knights could still run and climb in it.

quality.notes: The distractors are deliberately silly, which is fine for difficulty 1 but trivial. Armor weight is usually given as 15–25 kg, so 'about 25 kg' is the upper end.

questions.description: Ancient Rome's favorite show, with no TV needed.
questions.question: In ancient Rome, crowds filled this huge arena to watch fighters. What were these fighters called?
hints: They fought with swords, nets and shields.
Some of them became as famous as sports stars.
Their name comes from “gladius”, the Roman sword.

media.note: Clear photo of the Colosseum in Rome; no text.

questions.fun_fact: The Colosseum could hold about 50,000 people and had a giant cloth roof to shade them from the sun.

quality.notes: Samurai, Vikings and cowboys are obviously out of place in ancient Rome. Hint 3 (gladius) touches on q-1929 but asks a different fact.

questions.description: A pharaoh who made peace and then carved his own face on a mountain.
questions.question: This giant face at Abu Simbel shows Ramesses II. After the Battle of Kadesh he signed one of the oldest known peace treaties. With which people?
hints: The battle took place in today's Syria, around 1274 BC.
This empire was centered in today's Turkey.
Their capital was Hattusa.

media.note: Close-up of one of the giant seated statues' faces at the Abu Simbel temple; no text.

questions.fun_fact: A copy of the Egyptian–Hittite peace treaty hangs at the United Nations headquarters in New York.

quality.notes: The question is two sentences and a bit long. The Abu Simbel photo is illustrative, not essential (you can answer without it).

questions.description: A teenager who didn't wait to be told she was too young.
questions.question: This golden statue in Paris shows Joan of Arc. In 1429 she led French soldiers to free the city of Orléans. From which army?
hints: It happened during the Hundred Years' War.
The enemy came from across the sea, to the north.
Their king lived in London.

media.note: Photo of the gilded equestrian statue of Joan of Arc at Place des Pyramides in Paris.

questions.fun_fact: Joan of Arc was only about 17 years old when she helped free Orléans.

quality.notes: A Viking army in 1429 is implausible, which weakens the distractors. The statue is illustrative rather than essential. The topic is a common school fact.

questions.description: A king who never needed to ask for compliments.
questions.question: This ancient mosaic shows King Alexander of Macedonia, who built a huge empire. How do we usually call him: Alexander the…?
hints: His empire reached from Greece to India.
He never lost a major battle.
The nickname means very big or very important.

media.note: The Alexander Mosaic from Pompeii, or its detail showing Alexander on his horse.

questions.fun_fact: Alexander founded more than a dozen cities named after himself, and the most famous is Alexandria in Egypt.

quality.notes: Awkward English: 'How do we usually call him' should be 'What do we usually call him'. The mosaic works better as an illustrative image than an essential one.

questions.description: Medieval job offer: no salary, no vacation, no moving out.
questions.question: This detail from a medieval calendar shows farm workers who were tied to their lord's land and could not leave it. What were they called?
hints: They were not slaves, but they were not free either.
They had to work the lord's fields as well as their own.
The word is related to “servant”.

media.note: Detail from the Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry (e.g. October) showing peasants sowing and working in the fields; crop out any text.

questions.fun_fact: In Russia, serfdom lasted until 1861, centuries after it ended in most of Western Europe.

quality.notes: The image is illustrative, not essential. 'Peasants' would have made a more tempting distractor than knights.

questions.description: Before ballpoints, writers borrowed their pens from birds.
questions.question: For hundreds of years, people wrote with feather pens like this one. Where on the bird did the best feathers come from?
hints: They needed long, strong feathers.
These feathers help a bird fly.
A goose flaps them.

media.note: Clear photo of a feather quill pen, ideally with an inkwell; no visible bird.

questions.fun_fact: The word “pen” comes from the Latin word “penna”, which means feather.

quality.notes: Hint 2 ('help a bird fly') gives it away almost completely, although tail feathers also play a role in flight.

questions.description: Superheroes wear masks to hide their face; this one hides something much smaller.
questions.question: Doctors and nurses often wear this over their nose and mouth. What does it help stop?
hints: It's about staying healthy.
They are far too tiny to see.
They can make you sick when someone coughs or sneezes.

media.note: A clear photo of a single surgical face mask, or a person wearing one, with no text on it.

questions.fun_fact: One sneeze can send thousands of tiny droplets into the air, and a mask catches many of them.

quality.notes: Correct and clear, and a mask photo is easy to find. The question is fairly plain, though fine for little kids. Hint 3 nearly gives the answer, which is allowed.

questions.description: An exercise that lets you lift a whole person off the floor: you.
questions.question: You do push-ups every day for a month. Which muscles get much stronger?
hints: Think about which part of you pushes the floor away.
Your hands do all the pushing.
They're above your belly.
questions.fun_fact: During a push-up your belly muscles work too, keeping your body straight like a plank.

quality.notes: The wrong answers are clearly wrong even for kids. The question is a bit plain.

questions.description: Your nose's way of shouting “Get out!” at a speck of dust.
questions.question: This photo shows a sneeze up close. What is the cloud coming out of the mouth made of?
hints: That's why you should sneeze into your elbow.
It's a little wet.
It's mostly spit and mucus mixed with air.

media.note: The well-known high-speed photo of a person sneezing with a visible spray of droplets (e.g. the public-domain CDC photo).

questions.fun_fact: Your eyes close by themselves when you sneeze: it's a reflex that's very hard to stop.

quality.notes: The answer is longer and more detailed than the wrong ones, so it stands out. 'Only dry air' is a weak wrong answer. The CDC sneeze photo is likely on Commons. The fun fact (eyes always close when you sneeze) holds for nearly everyone but is stated as an absolute.

questions.description: The longest wait for a delivery that everyone is happy about.
questions.question: Before it is born, a human baby grows inside its mother for about how many months?
hints: It's less than a year.
It's more than half a year.
It's the same as three times three.
questions.fun_fact: An elephant baby grows inside its mother for about 22 months, almost two years.

quality.notes: A good, clean question; the elephant fun fact is a nice touch.

questions.description: A sleeping bag that a caterpillar knits for itself.
questions.question: A chick grows inside an egg. A silkworm turns into a moth inside a…?
hints: The silkworm makes it all by itself.
It's made from a very long thread.
People unwind it to make silk.
questions.fun_fact: A single silkworm cocoon can be made of one thread about 1 km (0.6 mi) long.

quality.notes: The 1 km thread is at the high end (usually 300–1,500 m), but 'about' covers it.

questions.description: A garden worm with a very big glow-up planned.
questions.question: A fat white grub lives in the garden soil. What will it become when it grows up?
hints: It will grow six legs.
It will get hard wing covers.
Ladybugs belong to the same group.
questions.fun_fact: Some beetle grubs live underground for several years before they become adults.

quality.notes: A fairly dry school fact. The word 'grub' may be unfamiliar to young kids. An illustrative photo of a grub would be safe, so decorative is the weaker choice. Hint 3 (ladybugs) nearly gives it away, which is fine for hint 3.

questions.description: The longest line in the world, and nobody is complaining.
questions.question: Why do ants often walk one behind the other in a line like this?
hints: The first ant leaves something behind.
You can't see it, but ants can sense it.
It works through their antennae, like a nose.

media.note: Photo of a line of ants walking one after another along a path or surface.

questions.fun_fact: If you wipe a finger across an ant trail, the ants behind get lost for a moment because the smell is gone.

quality.notes: 'They follow the moon' is a weak distractor. The image isn't really essential (the question works without it), but an ant-line photo is easy to find, so it's acceptable.

questions.description: Interior design for people who think glitter is too boring.
questions.question: Artist Jan Fabre covered a ceiling of the Royal Palace in Brussels with shiny green jewel beetle wing cases. About how many?
hints: It covers a whole large hall.
Each wing case is smaller than a fingernail.
It's more than a million.
questions.fun_fact: Jewel beetle wing cases keep their shine for centuries, so people in Asia have used them in jewelry and textiles for a long time.

quality.notes: Heaven of Delight (2002), about 1.6 million elytra: correct. A nice estimation question. Hint 3 effectively gives the answer, which is allowed.

questions.description: A flying flower that counts better than you.
questions.question: A butterfly lands on a flower right in front of you. How many wings does it have?
hints: It's more than a bird has.
Look closely: the wings come in pairs.
Two at the front, two at the back.
questions.fun_fact: A butterfly's wing colors come from tiny scales, like dust, that rub off on your fingers.

quality.notes: Many kids would answer 2, so it's slightly harder than rated. Hint 1 rules out 2. The description ('counts better than you') is weak and hardly related. The question itself is plain.

questions.description: His trophy shelf needed its own shelf.
questions.question: This player has won the Ballon d'Or, the prize for the best player of the year, more times than anyone. How many times?
hints: It's more than his great rival Cristiano Ronaldo, who has five.
His first came in 2009 and his last in 2023.
It's the number of legs on a spider.

media.note: A clear photo of Lionel Messi, ideally in an Argentina or Barcelona shirt, without any visible Ballon d'Or trophies or captions.

questions.fun_fact: Lionel Messi won his eighth Ballon d'Or in 2023, after leading Argentina to the 2022 World Cup title.
questions.concept: Ocho Balones de Oro de Messi

quality.notes: Essential Messi photo is easy to find. Hint 3 (spider legs) gives the answer straight away, which is allowed for the last hint.

questions.description: A silver cup so big it has ears.
questions.question: You're watching the Champions League final and a captain lifts a huge silver cup with big handles. What did his team do to get it?
hints: It only happens at the very end of the match.
The other team goes home without it.
They beat their opponent in the last match of the tournament.
questions.fun_fact: The Champions League trophy is nicknamed “big ears” because of its huge handles.

quality.notes: Very easy and a bit flat. The wrong answers are silly on purpose, which suits kids.

questions.description: A kick that's named after where it happens, which is very handy.
questions.question: Where on the field does a player stand to take a corner kick?
questions.answer: At a corner of the field
hints: It's right next to a small flag.
It's as far to the side as you can go.
The name of the kick tells you.
questions.fun_fact: A goal scored straight from a corner kick is called an “Olympic goal,” after one scored this way by Argentina against Olympic champions Uruguay in 1924.

quality.notes: The name of the kick gives it away, but that is intended at level 1. The “colombia” lens doesn't fit the question. The Olympic goal fun fact is nice.

questions.description: A World Cup so big it needed three countries to fit.
questions.question: This country had 11 of the 16 host cities of the 2026 World Cup, hosted its final, and also hosted the 1994 World Cup. Which country?
hints: It shared the 2026 tournament with its two neighbors.
The final was played near New York.
Its flag has stars and stripes.
questions.fun_fact: The 2026 World Cup was the first with 48 teams, up from 32.
questions.concept: Mundial de Estados Unidos, México y Canadá 2026

quality.notes: Brazil is a weak wrong answer, since it was not a 2026 host. The question is a fairly dry list of facts.

questions.description: Three trophies in one season: some clubs just don't know when to stop.
questions.question: In 2023, Manchester City won the English league, the FA Cup and the Champions League in one season. What is this feat called?
hints: It's named after the number of trophies.
A hat-trick is three goals, not three trophies.
It comes from an old word meaning “three times”.
questions.fun_fact: Manchester United had won the same treble in 1999, so City became the second English club to do it.

quality.notes: A dry vocabulary question. Treble works in other languages too (triplete, Triple). Hint 1 is fairly strong.

questions.description: In Germany, one club treated the league title like a yearly subscription.
questions.question: This club plays in red, comes from southern Germany and won the Bundesliga 11 seasons in a row, from 2013 to 2023. Which club?
hints: Its stadium glows red at night.
Its city is famous for Oktoberfest.
It's from the capital of Bavaria.
questions.fun_fact: Bayer Leverkusen ended the streak in 2024, winning the Bundesliga without losing a single match.

questions.description: A coach who paces the touchline like he's lost his car keys.
questions.question: This coach won the Champions League with both Barcelona and Manchester City. Who is he?
hints: He was also a midfielder for Barcelona.
He's from Catalonia, in Spain.
He's famous for his shaved head and short-passing football.

media.note: A clear photo of Pep Guardiola's face, without captions or club badges that show his name.

questions.fun_fact: Guardiola has also coached Bayern Munich, where he won the Bundesliga three times in a row.

quality.notes: Essential face photo is easy to find. The question is a straight recall question.

questions.description: Brazil's team chose its shirt the way a canary chooses its feathers.
questions.question: Brazil's team is called the Canarinha, “little canary,” after its yellow shirt. In which decade did it first wear yellow?
hints: Brazil played the World Cup it hosted in white shirts.
After that home World Cup, a contest picked a new design.
It was a few years before Pelé's first World Cup win in 1958.
questions.fun_fact: The yellow shirt was designed in 1953 by a 19-year-old who won a newspaper contest after Brazil lost the 1950 World Cup in white.

quality.notes: The fun fact mostly repeats what the hints already say.

questions.description: A noise that makes every parent in the house shout “Don’t move! Shoes on!”
questions.question: Listen: what material makes this sound when it breaks?
hints: It makes a sharp, high, tinkling sound.
Windows and drinking cups are often made of it.
It is clear, you can see through it, and it is made from melted sand.

media.note: A clear recording of a glass (a drinking glass or a window pane) shattering, with the tinkling of falling pieces. No voices.

questions.fun_fact: Most glass is made by melting sand with a few other ingredients in a furnace at about 1,500 °C (2,700 °F).

quality.notes: Solid sound question. Breaking glass is easy to find on Freesound. Most young kids know the sound, so it is closer to a 2.

questions.description: A machine that can do a million sums a second but still asks you to restart it.
questions.question: “I sit on a desk, you can write, play games and watch videos on me.” Which set of parts do I have?
hints: You use it for school work and for games.
One of the parts shares its name with a small animal.
You type on one part and look at another part.
questions.fun_fact: The first computer mouse, built in the 1960s, was a wooden box with two metal wheels.

quality.notes: The riddle clearly names a computer, so the question becomes 'match the parts list'. The camera, bicycle and piano lists are easy to rule out. The form is awkward and dry. Laptops and tablets often have no mouse, so there is a small quibble.

questions.description: Gravity tries its best, and this thing keeps saying “Nope, up again!”
questions.question: In the garden: a swing is to swinging as a trampoline is to…?
hints: Think about what your legs do on it.
You go up and down, again and again.
It is what a rubber ball does when you drop it.
questions.fun_fact: The modern trampoline was built in the 1930s by George Nissen, a young gymnast in the United States.

quality.notes: This is an easy, plain analogy with little surprise. 'Jumping' would also fit, but it is not an option, so this is fine.

questions.description: It has a lot of teeth and never goes to the dentist.
questions.question: “I have many sharp teeth, but I never eat. I go back and forth to cut wood.” What am I?
hints: You find me in a toolbox.
Carpenters use me.
I make a “zzzt, zzzt” sound and leave sawdust behind.
questions.fun_fact: The ancient Egyptians already used copper saws to cut wood more than 4,000 years ago.

quality.notes: Hint 3 contains 'sawdust', which literally includes the answer 'saw'. This breaks the hint-3 rule and is also tied to English. Rephrase it, e.g. 'leave little wood crumbs behind'.

questions.description: The only monster in the house that eats dust bunnies.
questions.question: Listen: which machine in the house makes this noise?
hints: It is used for cleaning.
It is pushed across the floor.
It sucks up dust and crumbs from the carpet.

media.note: The steady whooshing roar of a household vacuum cleaner running, ideally switched on and moving over a floor.

questions.fun_fact: One of the first powered vacuum cleaners, built in London in 1901, was so big that horses pulled it from house to house.

quality.notes: The description's 'eats dust bunnies' points fairly clearly at the vacuum cleaner, which makes it easier, though kids would know the sound anyway. The fun fact about Booth's horse-drawn 'Puffing Billy' is true.

questions.description: The “What did you say?” of the 1800s, now in a handy size.
questions.question: Long before small electronic hearing aids, what did people who couldn’t hear well hold to their ear?
hints: It was a simple object, with no electricity.
It was shaped like a horn, wide at one end and narrow at the other.
Its name is also the name of a brass instrument.
questions.fun_fact: The composer Ludwig van Beethoven used several ear trumpets as he slowly lost his hearing.

quality.notes: The seashell is a nice playful distractor. The fun fact touches Beethoven's deafness (q-0070), but the question asks a different fact. Young players may not know the term 'ear trumpet', so slightly harder than rated.

questions.description: A clock that stops working every time a cloud walks by.
questions.question: Clocks like this one tell the time with a shadow. In which ancient land were the oldest known ones made?
hints: It was a sunny land with a very old civilization.
The same people built giant stone monuments.
Think of pharaohs and pyramids.

media.note: A clear photo of a sundial with its shadow-casting pointer and hour marks; no Egyptian, Greek or Roman setting visible.

questions.fun_fact: Sundials in the Southern Hemisphere run the other way round, because the shadow moves counterclockwise there.

quality.notes: Egypt has the oldest known sundials (about 1500 BC), though Babylon is sometimes also named; Babylon is not an option, so this is fine. Players can reason to 'Egypt = oldest', but kids rarely know this, so about 7. The fun fact about Southern Hemisphere sundials is correct.

questions.description: A machine that makes things the way you build a sandwich: layer after layer.
questions.question: This close-up shows a machine at work, laying down thin lines of melted plastic. What is the machine?
hints: It is controlled by a computer.
It can make toys, cups and spare parts from a design file.
It is like a normal printer, but it prints in three dimensions.

media.note: A close-up of a 3D printer nozzle laying plastic on a half-built object, layers visible; no brand name readable.

questions.fun_fact: Doctors have used 3D printers to make custom hand and arm parts for children.

quality.notes: The question text ('laying down thin lines of melted plastic') together with the 'layer after layer' description makes it fairly easy, but that is acceptable.

questions.description: A leg with a spring in its step, literally.
questions.question: Running blades like this one help athletes sprint. What light, springy material are they mostly made of?
hints: It must be very light and very strong.
Racing cars and bicycles use it too.
It is made of thin black threads glued together in layers.

media.note: A clear photo of a curved J-shaped running blade prosthesis (alone or worn by an athlete, face not the focus).

questions.fun_fact: A running blade works like a spring: it bends when it hits the ground and pushes back as it straightens.

quality.notes: 'Light, springy' in the question rules out steel, oak and copper, so carbon fiber stands out as the only modern, high-tech material. A photo of a running blade is likely on Commons.

questions.description: She's French, she's calm, and she's the only one who ever got 007 to slow down.
questions.question: This French actress played Madeleine Swann, the woman Bond falls for in two films. Who is she?
hints: She played Bond's love interest in the Daniel Craig years, after Vesper Lynd.
She also starred in “Blue Is the Warmest Color” and “Dune: Part Two”.
Her first name has three letters and starts with L.

media.note: A clear portrait photo of actress Léa Seydoux, with no caption or name visible.

questions.fun_fact: Madeleine Swann first appeared in “Spectre” (2015) and came back in “No Time to Die” (2021), which makes her one of very few Bond loves to appear in two films.

quality.notes: Recognizing a face from a portrait is fairly dry for most players. Wikimedia should have a usable portrait, but it needs one with no caption. Hint 3 (three letters, starts with L) comes very close to the answer, which is allowed. The 'history' lens is mislabelled.

questions.description: Even secret agents have that one old friend who goes completely off the rails.
questions.question: You're watching agent 006, Alec Trevelyan, turn against his friend 007. In which year did this Bond film come out?
hints: It was the first Bond film after a six-year break.
It was Pierce Brosnan's first time playing 007.
The film shares its name with a famous Nintendo 64 game from 1997.
questions.fun_fact: Alec Trevelyan was played by Sean Bean, who later became famous as Boromir in “The Lord of the Rings”.

quality.notes: The 'You're watching…' opening isn't needed. Otherwise the wrong answers are well chosen (other Bond release years) and the hints build up well.

questions.description: The man who hands out exploding pens and never gets them back in one piece.
questions.question: Q's letter comes from “quartermaster”, an old job title used in armies and on ships. What does a quartermaster look after?
hints: Think about what Q does for Bond before every mission.
Soldiers come to the quartermaster when they need boots, food or tools.
It's all the stuff an army needs to do its job.
questions.fun_fact: Desmond Llewelyn played Q in 17 Bond films, more than any other actor in the same role in the series.

quality.notes: Knowing what Q does in the films makes it easy to work out, so it's a little easier than 10. The correct answer is a bit longer than the others.

questions.description: He got the most famous job in film and quit after just one try.
questions.question: George Lazenby played James Bond in only one film. In which year did it come out?
hints: He came right after the first Bond actor, before Roger Moore.
In the film, Bond gets married.
It came out the same year humans first walked on the Moon.
questions.fun_fact: George Lazenby was an Australian model with almost no acting experience when he was cast as 007.

quality.notes: Asking for a release year is fairly dry, though the Moon-landing hint helps. Hint 1 skips over Connery's return in 1971, but it is still true. The 'language' lens is mislabelled.

questions.description: The fluffiest member of the world's most dangerous evil team.
questions.question: It's white and fluffy, it sits on Bond villain Blofeld's lap, and he strokes it while making evil plans. What is it?
hints: It's a pet many people keep at home.
It has long fur and purrs.
It's a cat, but which kind?
questions.fun_fact: In the early films Blofeld's face was hidden, so audiences only saw his hands stroking the cat.

quality.notes: 'A Persian cat' is the only option that names a breed, so it stands out. Hint 3 ('It's a cat') leaves only one option. The evil-boss-with-a-cat trope is very well known from cartoons and Austin Powers, so this is easier than 7.

questions.description: An island so famous for one film that tourists forgot its real name.
questions.question: You're on a boat in Thailand's Phang Nga Bay, looking at a rock islet nicknamed “James Bond Island”. In which decade was the film shot there?
hints: Roger Moore was playing 007 at the time.
The villain has a third nipple and a very fancy weapon.
The villain's weapon is a golden gun.
questions.fun_fact: The island's real name is Khao Phing Kan, and the tall rock next to it, Ko Tapu, is only about 4 m (13 ft) wide at the bottom.

quality.notes: The 'third nipple' detail in hint 2 is a bit cheeky for a family game with kids watching. Swap in a different clue.

questions.description: Long before emojis, people were already texting with tiny pictures.
questions.question: You see a little running-man sign over an exit: a pictogram. Writing that began with picture signs like this started about how long ago?
hints: It happened long before the Romans.
It began in Mesopotamia and Egypt, around the time the first cities grew.
Think of the age of the oldest pyramids, then go back a little more.
questions.fun_fact: Many letters we use today started as pictures: the letter A comes from an old drawing of an ox's head.

quality.notes: The exit-sign setup is forced and makes the question long. It's really just a dates question. The facts are correct (about 3200 BCE; A from aleph).

questions.description: The world's oldest notebook: heavy, muddy and impossible to erase once it dries.
questions.question: This clay tablet is covered in wedge-shaped writing. In which ancient land was this writing invented?
hints: It was a land between two rivers.
Those rivers are the Tigris and the Euphrates.
Today this region is mostly in Iraq.

media.note: A clear photo of a clay tablet with cuneiform writing, without museum labels naming its origin.

questions.fun_fact: One of the oldest known complaints in the world is on a clay tablet: a customer grumbling about bad copper.

quality.notes: Mesopotamia is school knowledge and harder for young teens than 7. The Ea-nasir fun fact is correct and fun. Make sure the tablet photo has no museum label.

questions.description: A tiny hat that some letters wear to look fancy.
questions.question: I'm a little mark on top of a letter, like on the e in “café”. What am I for?
questions.answer: Showing how to say the word
wrong_answers: Showing the word is a name
hints: Without me, people might read the word wrong.
I change the sound or the stress of the word.
Read me aloud and you'll notice.
questions.fun_fact: Vietnamese uses so many marks that one letter can carry two of them at once.

quality.notes: It's about written accents, which partly depend on the language. In Spanish an accent can also tell two meanings apart (tú/tu), so “how to say it” is not the whole story. Quite dry.

questions.description: The night-time group chat of the forest.
questions.question: Wolves make this long sound with their noses up, often at night, and cartoons love it under a full moon. What is it called?
hints: It sounds like “aoooooo”.
Dogs sometimes do it too when they hear a siren.
Sing a very long “oooo” to the sky.
questions.fun_fact: Wolves don't actually howl at the moon: they point their heads up so the sound carries far, up to about 10 km (6 miles).

quality.notes: Plain vocabulary question, not much surprise. Hint 1 (“aoooooo”) almost gives it away. The 10 km range holds only in open terrain.

questions.description: A language you can use across a noisy room, or through a window.
questions.question: Many deaf people talk in a language like this one. What is it made of?
hints: It makes no sound at all.
You need your eyes to understand it.
Look at the person's hands.

media.note: A clear photo of a person communicating in sign language with their hands.

questions.fun_fact: There is not one sign language but more than 300, and American and British Sign Language are very different.

quality.notes: The essential photo shows the hands, so the answer is clear from it; that's fine at this level. Simple question.

questions.description: Grammar class, where words get sorted into teams like players at recess.
questions.question: Sorting words in class: “cat” is to noun as “jump” is to…
hints: “Cat” names a thing.
“Jump” is something you do.
It's the word kind for actions.
questions.fun_fact: Some words can be both: “dance” is a noun in “a dance” and a verb in “we dance”.

quality.notes: Dry grammar-class item. “Jump” can also be a noun, and the fun fact itself points this out. The “dance” fun fact works in English but not in every language.

questions.description: The free morning concert nobody asked for, starting at 5 a.m.
questions.question: You hear a bird singing outside your window at dawn. Where in the bird does the song come from?
questions.answer: A voice box deep in its chest
hints: It works a bit like your own voice.
Air from the lungs passes through it.
It's inside the bird, not on the outside.
questions.fun_fact: A bird's voice box, the syrinx, has two sides, so some birds can sing two different notes at the same time.

quality.notes: The answer is longer and more detailed than the short body-part distractors, so it stands out.

questions.description: A summer night serenade played on wings instead of a violin.
questions.question: You hear this insect chirping on a summer night. Which ones make the sound?
hints: The song is a way of showing off.
It's mostly meant to attract a partner.
Think of a male bird singing in spring.

media.note: A clear close-up photo of a cricket (the insect).

questions.fun_fact: Crickets chirp by rubbing their wings together, and they chirp faster when it's warmer.

quality.notes: Hints 2 and 3 nearly give it away, which is acceptable. It's close to q-0749 (cricket stridulation), and the fun fact repeats that fact, but it asks a different thing. The question says “you hear” but shows a photo, which is a little odd.

questions.description: Japanese has more alphabets than most people have pencils.
questions.question: I'm a curvy Japanese script with 46 basic signs. Over 1,000 years ago, women at the royal court wrote famous stories in me. What am I?
hints: I am one of the scripts used in Japan today.
My twin script has the same sounds but looks sharp and angular.
Japanese children learn me first, before the Chinese-style characters.
questions.fun_fact: Hiragana grew out of quickly brushed Chinese characters, which is why its letters look so soft and round.

quality.notes: Accurate: hiragana has 46 basic signs, and Heian court women (Murasaki Shikibu) wrote in it. Hangul is a weak distractor because the question says the script is Japanese. Anime fans know hiragana, so a 10 may fit better. The description calls scripts “alphabets”, which is loose.

questions.description: A word so friendly it practically gives you a hug.
questions.question: The greeting “Hola!” comes from the language of the country with this flag. Which language is it?
hints: The flag is red and yellow.
It's the language of flamenco and paella.
It's also spoken in Mexico and Argentina.

media.note: The national flag of Spain, with no text.

questions.fun_fact: Spanish is spoken as a first language by about 500 million people, more than English.

quality.notes: “Hola” alone answers it, so the flag isn't really needed. That's acceptable at difficulty 2, but it's a dry question. The description is generic. The fun fact holds: about 500 million native speakers, more than English's roughly 380 million.

questions.description: The magic word, with a Parisian accent.
questions.question: “Thank you” is to English as … is to French.
hints: It's a short, polite word.
You might hear it in a bakery in Paris.
It sounds a bit like “mare-see”.
questions.fun_fact: French people often say “merci beaucoup”, which means “thanks a lot”.

quality.notes: Simple and correct, but a plain vocabulary question. It shares only a theme with q-0381 (Danke).

questions.description: Someone who can hear you with their eyes.
questions.question: I understand what you say without hearing a sound, just by watching your mouth move. Who am I?
hints: Many deaf people learn my skill.
I keep my eyes on your face while you talk.
I “read”, but not from a book.

media.query: two people talking face to face

questions.fun_fact: Many speech sounds look the same on the lips, like “p”, “b” and “m”, so lip readers also guess from context.

quality.notes: Clean riddle. An illustrative image would also have been safe here, so decorative isn't needed.

questions.description: Four names that sound like cousins, but one lives on a different island chain.
questions.question: Māori is an official language of New Zealand, and many places there have Māori names. Which of these is NOT in New Zealand?
hints: The odd one out also has a Polynesian name.
It's a famous beach, far to the north of New Zealand.
You'll find it in Honolulu, Hawaii.
questions.fun_fact: Māori and Hawaiian are close relatives: both are Polynesian languages, and “wai” means water in both.

quality.notes: Good, plausible distractors. Waikiki is famous enough that players can reason it out.

questions.description: An island language that looks European but has a surprising family tree.
questions.question: Reading a café menu in Malta, you meet Maltese words. Spanish is to Latin as Maltese is to…
hints: Maltese is written in the Latin alphabet, but that's a disguise.
Its oldest roots arrived in the Middle Ages from North Africa.
It's the only Semitic language that is an official language of the European Union.
questions.fun_fact: Maltese counts to three as “wieħed, tnejn, tlieta”, very close to Arabic, but borrows many words from Italian and English.

quality.notes: The café-menu scenario is filler and makes the text longer for nothing. It's odd to have Latin as a distractor when it already appears in the analogy. The facts check out (Siculo-Arabic roots; the only Semitic official language of the EU).

questions.description: A chase that has lasted since 1940, and nobody has won yet.
questions.question: Jerry is to mouse as Tom is to…?
hints: Think of a famous cartoon pair that is always chasing each other.
Tom is always trying to catch Jerry.
This pet purrs and says “meow”.
questions.fun_fact: Tom and Jerry won seven Oscars for best animated short film.

quality.notes: Hint 2 just repeats the question. The three wrong answers are obviously wrong to anyone who has seen the cartoon, so the fun is mild. Facts check out: the first cartoon came out in 1940, and the series won 7 Oscars. A decorative TV image is fine.

questions.description: Small, spotted and still learning how to use all four legs at once.
questions.question: It's a baby deer, it often has white spots on its back, and Bambi is one. What is it called?
hints: The word is only used for young deer.
The white spots help it hide among sunlit leaves.
It sounds like the start of the word “fawning”.
questions.fun_fact: A fawn has almost no smell, so predators find it hard to sniff out while its mother is away.

quality.notes: Hint 3 (“fawning”) literally contains the answer, which breaks the hint rule. It is also English wordplay that won't work in other languages. The question is mostly an English vocabulary test of animal-baby words, which makes it less fun and harder to translate. Decorative image is fine.

questions.description: The one animal nobody ever wants to give a hug.
questions.question: I'm a rodent covered in sharp quills. I can't shoot them, but they stick in anyone who bites me. What am I?
hints: I'm a cousin of mice and beavers.
My quills come out easily and get stuck in the attacker.
My name means “spiny pig”.
questions.fun_fact: A porcupine can have about 30,000 quills.

quality.notes: Solid riddle. The “spiny pig” origin is correct (Latin porcus + spina). Hedgehog, armadillo and echidna are good look-alikes. An illustrative image, such as a forest den, would also have been safe.

questions.description: A philosophy of life from a warthog who loves bugs for lunch.
questions.question: Pumbaa the warthog and his friend Timon sing a Swahili phrase in “The Lion King”: “Hakuna Matata”. What does it mean?
hints: Timon and Pumbaa teach it to young Simba.
It's about living a happy, relaxed life.
The song says it means this “for the rest of your days”.
questions.fun_fact: “Hakuna matata” is a real phrase that people say every day in East Africa.

quality.notes: Hints 1 and 2 add little, and the “relaxed life” hint almost gives it away. The phrase is real Swahili and the facts are correct. The question is a bit long, but fine.

questions.description: Some animals wear their weapons right on their face.
questions.question: Elephant is to tusk as rhinoceros is to…?
hints: Look at the rhino's nose.
Some rhinos have one, others have two.
A unicorn has one on its forehead.
questions.fun_fact: A rhino's horn is made of keratin, the same stuff as your hair and fingernails.

quality.notes: Simple analogy and not very surprising. The keratin fun fact repeats what q-1473 (rhino horn) says in its own text, but that question asks a different thing. A rhino-free savanna image could be illustrative rather than decorative.

questions.description: The quietest superhero move in the world.
questions.question: In a library, someone makes this gesture at you. What do they want?
hints: Look at where the finger is.
Libraries are places for reading and thinking.
They might also whisper “shhh”.

media.note: A person holding one index finger against closed lips (the “shh” gesture).

questions.fun_fact: Many libraries now have special rooms where people can talk, so the reading rooms stay quiet.

quality.notes: Mentioning the library already points to the answer. Fine for difficulty 1 but not much fun. The description is weak: “superhero move” doesn't really link to the gesture. Shh-gesture photos are easy to find.

questions.description: The only day when throwing your hat in the air is a sign of good behavior.
questions.question: Who are these people, throwing their caps in the air?
hints: Look at their long gowns and square caps.
They have just reached the end of something long.
They worked hard for years to get a diploma.

media.note: Graduates in gowns throwing square graduation caps into the air.

questions.fun_fact: The flat square graduation cap is often called a “mortarboard”, after a builder's board for holding mortar.

quality.notes: Throwing caps in the air comes mostly from US and UK custom, but films have made it known worldwide. The photo plus hint 1 make it easy.

questions.description: Two French words that sound even better with a full plate in front of you.
questions.question: You sit down to eat and someone says “Bon appétit!”. What do they mean?
hints: It comes from French.
People say it right before eating.
It's a wish that your food tastes good.
questions.fun_fact: Many languages have their own version, like “buen provecho” in Spanish and “guten Appetit” in German.

questions.description: Every table has a boss seat, unless it's round and the knights are touchy.
questions.question: Complete the analogy: a king is to his throne as the host of a dinner is to the…
hints: Think of the most important seat.
It's usually at one short end of a long table.
It shares its name with the top part of your body.
questions.fun_fact: In the legends, King Arthur's Round Table had no head, so none of his knights could claim the best seat.

quality.notes: Hint 3 nearly gives it away, which is allowed. Many children know “head of the table”, so it's slightly lower than 6.

questions.description: A French bakery runs on butter, flour and one magic word.
questions.question: I'm the word you're expected to say when you walk into a shop in France: “Bonjour!”. If you skip me, what often happens?
questions.answer: The staff may think you're rude
wrong_answers: You must pay before you choose
The staff only speak English to you
hints: It's about how people see you.
In France, greeting first is basic politeness.
Going straight to your order feels cold there.
questions.fun_fact: In France, people also say “Bonjour” when getting on a bus or entering a doctor's waiting room.

quality.notes: The free croissant option is a joke and drops out at once. The riddle wording (“I'm the word… “Bonjour!”. If you skip me…”) is clunky to read aloud.

questions.description: It's the sharpest guest at every dinner.
questions.question: I have a handle and a sharp edge, and at dinner I help you cut your food. What am I?
hints: I don't scoop and I don't poke.
I'm used for slicing.
You use me to cut a steak or spread butter.
questions.fun_fact: Table knives often have round tips; that's said to go back to the 1600s, when France tried to make dinners safer.

quality.notes: Very easy and not very interesting: “sharp edge, cut your food” is the definition of a knife. The description repeats “sharp”. The round-tip story (Richelieu, Louis XIV) is told with “said to”, which is fine.

questions.description: It says “Happy birthday” without saying a word.
questions.question: People send cards like this for birthdays and holidays. What is it usually made of?
hints: It's light and easy to fold.
You can write on it with a pen.
Books and notebooks are made of it too.

media.note: A folded paper greeting card, e.g. a birthday card, standing open.

questions.fun_fact: Billions of greeting cards are sent around the world every year.

quality.notes: Trivial, and the glass, metal and stone options aren't believable. It has little to do with manners and the fun fact is flat.

questions.description: It's the hero your shirt never knew it needed.
questions.question: I lie on your lap at dinner, and when you spill sauce, I keep your clothes clean. What am I?
hints: I'm made of cloth or paper.
You can also wipe your mouth with me.
I'm often folded next to your plate.
questions.fun_fact: Long ago in ancient Rome, guests took food home wrapped in their napkins.

quality.notes: A simple riddle that isn't very exciting. The Roman fun fact is nice.

questions.description: A family reunion of heroes, ruined by one very mischievous relative.
questions.question: In the first Avengers film, I opened a portal over New York, led an alien army, and got smashed around by Hulk. Who am I?
hints: I wear a helmet with long golden horns.
I love tricks and lies.
Thor is my adopted brother.
questions.fun_fact: Hulk's line “Puny god” after smashing Loki got some of the biggest laughs in cinemas in 2012.

quality.notes: Hints 1 and 3 (horned helmet, adopted brother of Thor) repeat the clues of q-0252 (also Loki), but this question asks a different fact.

questions.description: A villain who celebrates Halloween all year long, and not in a nice way.
questions.question: I fly on a glider and throw pumpkin bombs at Spider-Man. Who am I?
hints: I have a scary laugh and a mask.
In real life, I'm a rich businessman.
My son Harry is Peter Parker's best friend.
questions.fun_fact: The Green Goblin's real name is Norman Osborn, and in the comics he found out who Spider-Man really is.

quality.notes: Solid question. The pumpkin image and the Halloween description only echo the question text.

questions.description: Who needs an airplane ticket when you have the right accessory?
questions.question: You see heroes rushing across the city. Spider-Man swings with his webs, as Thor flies with his…
hints: It's a weapon.
It brings lightning.
Only the worthy can lift it.
questions.fun_fact: Thor's hammer is called Mjolnir, and Thor flies by spinning it very fast and then throwing it while holding on.

quality.notes: The 'You see heroes rushing across the city' scenario adds nothing (Keep it short). Thor does wear a cape, but he flies with the hammer, so the answer is still clear.

questions.description: The smartest man in the room, and also the stretchiest.
questions.question: I stretch my body like rubber and I lead the Fantastic Four. What is my real name?
hints: I'm a genius scientist.
My hero name is Mister Fantastic.
I'm married to Sue Storm, the Invisible Woman.
questions.fun_fact: The Fantastic Four's first comic in 1961 started the Marvel age of superheroes.

quality.notes: Good distractors from inside the Fantastic Four.

questions.description: Same spider, different bite, totally new superhero.
questions.question: In my universe, the radioactive spider bit me instead of Peter Parker, and I swing around in a white hooded suit. Who am I?
hints: I appear in the film “Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse”.
I play drums in a band.
My father is a police captain named George.
questions.fun_fact: Gwen Stacy as a spider-hero first appeared in a 2014 comic and became so popular she got her own series.

quality.notes: Fair question. The Spider-Verse films make it reachable for teens.

questions.description: She bakes, she worries, and she has no idea her nephew climbs buildings.
questions.question: Because Peter Parker's parents are gone, he grows up with his Aunt May. In which city do they live?
hints: The city has huge skyscrapers.
The Avengers Tower is there too.
They live in a part of it called Queens.
questions.fun_fact: Aunt May was first drawn as a very old lady, but the films have shown her younger and younger.

quality.notes: The distractors (London, Paris, Tokyo) are generic world capitals that are easy to dismiss. The 'Because…' framing is awkward, and the question is fairly plain.

questions.description: Saturday mornings, cereal and mutants: a winning combination.
questions.question: In which year did “X-Men: The Animated Series” first air on TV?
hints: It came out before the first X-Men film.
It was a hit cartoon of the early 1990s.
Its sequel, “X-Men '97”, is named after the year the original ended.
questions.fun_fact: The show was so popular that its sequel series, “X-Men '97”, picked up the story in 2024 almost exactly where it ended.

quality.notes: An exact air year is dry, close to rote memorization. Hint 1 already rules out 2000 and 2008.

questions.description: The man behind the most famous life lesson in superhero history.
questions.question: I raised a boy from Queens and told him: “With great power comes great responsibility.” Who am I?
hints: I'm family, not a superhero.
My wife is called May.
The boy I raised is Peter Parker.
questions.fun_fact: In the first Spider-Man comic from 1962, the famous line about great power was not said by Uncle Ben but written in the last caption.

quality.notes: The image is safe, so illustrative would work better than decorative.

questions.description: Two hidden kingdoms, one very wet.
questions.question: In the film “Black Panther: Wakanda Forever”, Black Panther is to Wakanda as Namor is to…
hints: It's a hidden kingdom.
It lies deep under the ocean.
Its people take inspiration from the ancient Maya.
questions.fun_fact: In the comics, Namor rules Atlantis, but the film changed his kingdom to Talokan, inspired by Mesoamerican cultures.
