quality.notes: Talokan is a fairly niche MCU name, so 9 is underrated. Sokovia is not a hidden kingdom, which makes it a slightly weak distractor. Wakanda appears in q-0507, but this question asks a different fact.

questions.description: A superhero whose cape got swapped for comfy shoes.
questions.question: Look at the photo: who usually does this job in a hospital?
hints: This person works where sick people get better.
They check your temperature and look after patients all day.
They help the doctors take care of patients.

media.note: A clear photo of a nurse in scrubs caring for a patient in a hospital bed (e.g. taking blood pressure). No text naming the job.

questions.fun_fact: Florence Nightingale, a famous nurse in the 1800s, was nicknamed “The Lady with the Lamp” because she checked on patients at night.

quality.notes: A photo of a nurse could also be read as a doctor, but no doctor option exists. The distractors are very weak, though that is fine at level 1. The fun fact about Nightingale touches q-1289, but only in passing.

questions.description: A bed that comes to you when you can't get to it.
questions.question: It has two long poles, a strip of strong cloth stretched between them, and two people carry a patient on it. What is it?
hints: You lie down on it, you don't sit.
Ambulance workers use it to move injured people.
Its name comes from the cloth being pulled tight across it.
questions.fun_fact: In an emergency, people have made stretchers out of two sticks and a couple of buttoned-up jackets.

quality.notes: Hint 3 depends on English wordplay (stretched cloth → stretcher), so it doesn't travel to other languages. The question is a fairly plain definition. An illustrative image (for example an ambulance) would be safe, so decorative is more cautious than needed.

questions.description: Greasy, sticky and somehow good for you.
questions.question: You scraped your knee, and you rub a thick, greasy medicine from a little tube onto it. What is it called?
hints: You don't swallow it.
It goes right on the skin.
It is like a cream, only thicker and oilier.
questions.fun_fact: Ancient Egyptians put honey on wounds, and today some hospitals still use special medical honey.

quality.notes: Syrup, tablet and inhaler are never rubbed on the skin, so the only real challenge is knowing the word "ointment". The distractors should be skin products (cream, gel, lotion) instead, though cream would overlap with the answer, so pick carefully.

questions.description: The one homework your pillow can do for you.
questions.question: About how many hours of sleep a night do doctors suggest for children aged 6 to 12?
hints: It's more than adults need.
It's less than half a day.
Going to bed at 8 and waking up at 6 is about right.
questions.fun_fact: Your body releases most of its growth hormone while you sleep, so you really do grow at night.

quality.notes: 15 and 20 hours are absurd, so it comes down to 5 versus 10. Health-advice questions feel like a school test.

questions.description: A sickness that taught the world to check the water before drinking it.
questions.question: “I spread through dirty drinking water and make people lose water fast. In 1854, a London doctor stopped me by removing a pump's handle.” What disease am I?
hints: I'm caused by bacteria, not by a mosquito.
Clean water and good sewers almost wiped me out in rich countries.
The doctor was John Snow, who drew a famous map of my cases.
questions.fun_fact: John Snow's 1854 map of cholera cases in London is one of the most famous maps in the history of science.

quality.notes: Good question. "Dirty water" makes it possible to reason toward the answer. Hint 3 names John Snow, which helps adults.

questions.description: The person who can read your doctor's handwriting.
questions.question: This health worker studies medicines for years, prepares and hands out the medicine a doctor prescribes, and tells you when to take it. What is this job?
hints: You find them behind a counter in a shop.
Their shop often has a green cross or a sign with a bowl and a snake.
They work in a pharmacy.
questions.fun_fact: The snake wrapped around a bowl, a symbol of pharmacy, is linked to Hygieia, the Greek goddess of health.

quality.notes: The description is a good joke. The question itself is a plain job definition.

questions.description: Tiny, colorful, and absolutely not candy.
questions.question: What are the things in this photo for?
hints: You usually take them with a glass of water.
A doctor or pharmacist tells you how many to take.
They help you feel better when you're sick.

media.note: A clear photo of tablets/pills, ideally some in a blister pack, with no brand names visible.

questions.fun_fact: Ancient Egyptians made some of the first pills by mixing medicine with bread dough or honey.

quality.notes: The Egyptian bread-dough pill claim is widely repeated but loosely sourced. The question is very easy, and a blister pack rules out every other option.

questions.description: A very long winter that forgot to end on time.
questions.question: You're standing on a glacier left over from the last ice age. About how long ago did that ice age end?
hints: People were already living on Earth back then.
It was long before the pyramids, but long after the dinosaurs.
It's a five-digit number of years.
questions.fun_fact: During the last ice age the sea was about 120 m (390 ft) lower, so people could walk from Asia to America.

quality.notes: About 11,700 years is correct. Small caveat: many alpine glaciers mostly grew back during the Holocene and aren't really leftovers of the ice age. Hint 2 rules out two options at once, which leaves only 12,000 vs 1 million. 11-year-olds rarely know this, so it's closer to a 7.

questions.description: A volcano that skipped the small talk and went straight to the big news.
questions.question: You're watching geysers in Yellowstone, which sits on a supervolcano. When did it last have a giant eruption?
hints: No one wrote it down, because there was no writing yet.
The dinosaurs were long gone by then.
Early humans lived in Africa, but none were in America yet.
questions.fun_fact: The heat of Yellowstone's supervolcano powers more than half of all the geysers in the world.

quality.notes: The last caldera-forming eruption (Lava Creek) is dated at about 631,000–640,000 years ago, so “about 600,000” is a loose rounding. Most players can only reason towards it, so it's closer to an 11.

questions.description: A sport for people who think stairs are too easy.
questions.question: You're watching sport climbing at the Olympics. Which of these is NOT one of its disciplines?
hints: Sport climbing joined the Olympics at the Tokyo Games.
Three of these are about getting up a wall.
The odd one out is from skiing and canoeing.
questions.fun_fact: The best speed climbers race up a 15 m (49 ft) wall in less than 5 seconds.

quality.notes: Slalom is well known from skiing, so players can easily guess it as the odd one out. “Lead” is the only distractor that's really plausible. The speed record is a changing fact: men are under 5 s, women aren't. Somewhat dry list question.

questions.description: The slowest bumper cars in the universe.
questions.question: I'm a huge slab of Earth's outer shell, and when I push into my neighbor, the Himalayas grow. What am I made of?
hints: I'm hard, not runny.
Continents and ocean floors sit on top of me.
Mountains are made of the same stuff.
questions.fun_fact: Tectonic plates move about as fast as your fingernails grow.

quality.notes: Nice misconception distractor (liquid lava), but “what is it made of” is rather dry. Hint 3 nearly gives the answer away.

questions.description: All the thrill of flying, and nobody loses your suitcase.
questions.question: I have a cockpit and screens, but I never leave the ground. I'm a “flight simulator”. What do I let you do?
questions.answer: Feel like you're flying a plane
wrong_answers: Talk to a pilot in the sky
hints: “Simulate” means to copy something or pretend.
Pilots practice with me before they fly the real thing.
You sit at the controls and clouds rush past on the screen.
questions.fun_fact: Airline pilots train for many hours in simulators so real that they practice storms and engine problems without any danger.

quality.notes: The term 'flight simulator' nearly explains itself, so the question is easy and not very surprising. The decorative image is fine.

questions.description: A bird that missed its last flight forever.
questions.question: The dodo, a star of natural history museums, belonged to three of these groups. Which one did it NOT belong to?
hints: It lived only on the island of Mauritius, in the Indian Ocean.
DNA tests showed its closest living relatives coo in city squares.
Its beak was big and hooked, but it was no talking bird.
questions.fun_fact: The dodo's closest living relative is the Nicobar pigeon, a shiny green bird from islands in Asia.

quality.notes: A nice surprise with the pigeon family. Hint 2 rules out one wrong option clearly, which is fine. Young players may not know the dodo was in the pigeon family, so it is a bit harder than 7.

questions.description: A night so windy that even the stars are spinning.
questions.question: Van Gogh painted this famous night sky in 1889. What kind of paint did he use?
hints: Look how thick and swirly the brushstrokes are.
It's the same kind of paint used for the Mona Lisa.
This paint shares its name with what you fry food in.

media.note: The full painting The Starry Night by Vincent van Gogh.

questions.fun_fact: Van Gogh based it on the view from his window at a hospital in southern France.

quality.notes: 'Spray paint' and 'Poster paint' are weak distractors for a famous 1889 painting. It is a fairly dry question about materials. q-0118 asks about the same painting but a different fact (who painted it).

questions.description: He's huge, he's ancient, and he's not allowed to eat the visitors.
questions.question: I'm a giant dinosaur in the museum hall, but I have no skin, no eyes and no roar at all. What am I made of?
hints: You can't see yours, but you have them inside you too.
Dogs love to chew on these.
Your body has 206 of them.
questions.fun_fact: Many dinosaur skeletons in museums are copies, because the real fossil bones are too heavy and precious to stand on display.

quality.notes: Feathers, seashells and leaves are very weak distractors, though this is okay at kids' level. Hint 3 reuses the 206-bones fact from q-0045, but the question asks something different.

questions.description: Some museums have stairs; this one has a slide in very slow motion.
questions.question: You walk down a long spiral ramp looking at art, inside a round white museum in New York. Who designed this building?
hints: He was an American architect famous for buildings that blend with nature.
He also designed Fallingwater, a house built over a waterfall.
He shares a first name with the architect of the Guggenheim in Bilbao, but it's not him.
questions.fun_fact: The museum opened in 1959, six months after its architect died, so he never saw it finished.

quality.notes: Hint 3 is odd: it names Frank Gehry as a wrong answer and narrows the choice to the two Franks. Strong famous-architect distractors.

questions.description: Digging in the dirt, but make it science.
questions.question: Who uses a small brush like this to free old objects from the ground?
hints: This person loves digging up the past.
Indiana Jones and Lara Croft do this job in films and games.
They study ruins, tombs and lost cities.

media.note: Close-up of a small brush clearing soil from an old pot or bone at a dig site; no text.

questions.fun_fact: Archaeologists often use tools as small as toothbrushes and dental picks so they don't break what they find.

quality.notes: Paleontologists use the same brushes, but they are not among the options. The astronaut and chef distractors are very weak. The description ('Digging in the dirt, but make it science') points straight at the answer.

questions.description: A rock with a message for anyone patient enough.
questions.question: In 1799, soldiers in Egypt found a stone with one text carved in three scripts, including Greek and hieroglyphs. What did it make possible?
hints: Scholars already knew how to read ancient Greek.
A Frenchman, Jean-François Champollion, studied it for years.
For over a thousand years, nobody could understand those Egyptian signs.
questions.fun_fact: Champollion cracked the code in 1822 and is said to have shouted “I've got it!” before fainting.

quality.notes: Champollion fainting is a legend; the fun fact rightly says 'is said to'. The stone has two languages in three scripts, so the wording 'one text carved in three scripts' is fine.

questions.description: The only place where celebrities never complain about their photos.
questions.question: Why would a heat wave worry the staff at Madame Tussauds in London?
questions.answer: The figures could soften and droop
wrong_answers: The figures could start to rust
The figures' hair could turn white
The figures' glass eyes could crack
hints: The famous faces there look real, but they aren't alive.
Think of what happens to a candle left in the sun.
The figures are made of the same stuff as candles.
questions.fun_fact: Each figure takes months to make, and every single hair is put in one by one.

quality.notes: The figures are wax, and Tussauds controls the temperature, so the premise is reasonable. Players who know the figures are wax will find it easy.

questions.description: A famous name that's telling a little fib.
questions.question: This plaque is one of the famous “Benin Bronzes”, now in museums worldwide. Many of them are actually made of which other metal?
hints: Metal for them often arrived as bracelets traded by Portuguese merchants.
It's a mix of copper and zinc.
Trumpets and door handles are often made of it.

media.note: Photo of a metal plaque from the Kingdom of Benin showing carved figures; no labels or captions.

questions.fun_fact: They come from the old Kingdom of Benin, in what is now Nigeria, not from the modern country called Benin.

quality.notes: Make sure the essential plaque photo has no museum label. Tin is a component of bronze, but the answer is still clearly brass.

questions.description: The only instrument that needs its own building, and maybe its own electricity bill.
questions.question: Air is pushed through my hundreds of tubes, you play me with your hands and your feet, and I fill big churches with sound. What am I?
hints: I am a keyboard instrument, but I don't use strings.
Some of my tubes are taller than a house.
Bach wrote famous music for me.
questions.fun_fact: The organ in Boardwalk Hall in Atlantic City, USA, has more than 33,000 pipes.

quality.notes: The query "cathedral interior nave" could easily return a photo with the organ pipes in view, which would show the answer. q-1610 asks about Bach, not the organ, so it is only related. The Boardwalk Hall figure of about 33,000 pipes is right.

questions.description: A tiny triangle that has started more rock songs than any alarm clock.
questions.question: Guitar players strum with this little thing. What is it usually made of today?
hints: It has to bend a little without breaking.
It is light, cheap and comes in every color.
Many toys and bottles are made of the same material.

media.note: A clear photo of one or a few ordinary guitar picks (plectrums), no brand text readable.

questions.fun_fact: Long ago, many guitar picks were made from turtle shells; plastic took over and helped protect the turtles.

quality.notes: Glass, stone and clay are obviously wrong for something that has to bend, so the distractors are weak. It's a fairly dry "what is it made of?" question. Several other questions in the game also have the answer plastic (a bank card, beach toys), but they're about different objects.

questions.description: A small instrument that likes to say everything twice, very fast.
questions.question: Listen: which instrument is playing?
hints: It is a string instrument plucked with a pick.
Its body looks a bit like half a pear.
It is a famous instrument from Italy, often heard in Naples.

media.note: A solo mandolin playing a melody, ideally with its typical fast tremolo; no other instruments.

questions.fun_fact: A mandolin has eight strings, but they come in pairs, so it plays like it has only four.

quality.notes: Telling a mandolin from a banjo or ukulele by ear is hard, so it would be a fair bit harder if the recording has no tremolo. Freesound probably has solo mandolin recordings.

questions.description: A thin strip of plant that makes saxophones sing.
questions.question: This thin piece of cane vibrates when a clarinet or saxophone player blows. What is it called?
hints: It is made from a tall grass-like plant.
Players often wet it in their mouth before playing.
It shares its name with plants that grow by rivers and ponds.

media.note: A close-up of one loose clarinet or saxophone reed (thin flat cane strip), not attached to the instrument.

questions.fun_fact: Many reeds are cut from a giant cane plant called Arundo donax, which grows in warm places like southern France.

quality.notes: The description mostly repeats the question ("thin strip of plant… saxophones") and isn't very funny. As a recall question it's fairly dry. Reed Richards (marvel-superheroes-8) only shares the word.

questions.description: The drum that loves a dramatic moment just before the big reveal.
questions.question: Listen: which drum is playing?
hints: It is played with two thin sticks.
Under it, metal wires buzz against the skin.
Marching bands carry it on a strap, and it rolls before big announcements.

media.note: A solo snare drum roll or crisp snare hits, with the clear rattling wire sound.

questions.fun_fact: The rattle comes from metal wires called snares stretched across the bottom skin.

quality.notes: The drum roll in the description could also point to timpani, which keeps the options open. Snare recordings on Freesound are easy to find.

questions.description: A piano that needs a plug instead of a piano mover.
questions.question: Inside a piano, hammers hit strings. You press a key on an electronic keyboard: what makes the sound come out?
hints: It needs electricity to work.
There is nothing inside to hit or blow into.
Your TV and phone use the same parts to play sound.
questions.fun_fact: Many electronic keyboards can sound like hundreds of instruments, from violins to dog barks.

quality.notes: The sound is made electronically and the speakers only output it, and some keyboards have no speakers and use headphones, so the answer is a slight simplification. Bells and pipes are weak distractors. The question is somewhat dry. A sharp photo of the keyboard may show the speaker grilles.

questions.description: A guitar with a hole in it is not broken, we promise.
questions.question: Why does an acoustic guitar have a big round hole in its front?
hints: It has to do with the hollow body behind it.
The air inside the guitar vibrates with the strings.
Electric guitars, which use amplifiers, don't need one.
questions.fun_fact: Violins have two sound holes shaped like the letter f, so they are called f-holes.

quality.notes: "To make the sound louder" is a simplification. The sound hole mainly lets the air inside resonate (it boosts the low notes) and projects the sound out, but the answer is acceptable at this level.

questions.description: A tuba's little sibling with a very flattering name.
questions.question: The euphonium, a brass instrument, takes its name from Greek. What does that name mean?
hints: The name praises the instrument.
The same Greek start is in “euphoria”, a very good feeling.
It describes how pleasant it is to listen to.
questions.fun_fact: The euphonium was invented in Germany in the 1840s and is a star of brass bands.

quality.notes: Players can reason it out from "eu-" (as in "euphoria", which hint 2 even names), so it's slightly easier than 11. The euphonium did come from Germany: Sommer, around 1843.

questions.description: Rock and roll's favorite piece of furniture.
questions.question: What is the body of an electric guitar like this one usually made of?
hints: It is a natural material.
Guitar makers love maple, ash and mahogany.
It comes from trees.

media.note: A clear photo of a solid-body electric guitar, ideally with a visible wood grain finish.

questions.fun_fact: Unlike an acoustic guitar, most electric guitars have a solid body with no hollow space inside.

quality.notes: It's a fairly dry "what is it made of?" question. Asking for wood-grain finish in the image note makes it easier. Other questions have wood as the answer too, but they're about different objects.

questions.description: He can shoot hoops, sing and swing on a trapeze, but probably not all at once.
questions.question: I played a basketball star who loves singing in “High School Musical”, and later I flew on a trapeze in “The Greatest Showman”. Who am I?
hints: My character in the school musical was called Troy Bolton.
I later starred in “Hairspray” and “Baywatch”.
My first name has only three letters.
questions.fun_fact: In the first “High School Musical” film, some of Troy's singing was dubbed by another singer, Drew Seeley.

quality.notes: “Flew on a trapeze” is loose: Zendaya's character is the trapeze artist, and Efron only swings on ropes with her in one scene. Hint 3 (letter count) is weak. High School Musical is fading for today's kids, so 6 may be a bit low.

questions.description: A song with sequins, a bowler hat and a lot of attitude.
questions.question: The song “All That Jazz” opens a Kander and Ebb musical whose 1996 Broadway revival is the longest-running revival in Broadway history. Which city is that musical named after?
hints: The story takes place in the 1920s Jazz Age.
Its two heroines are nightclub stars who end up in jail.
The city is on the shore of Lake Michigan.
questions.fun_fact: The 2002 film version of the musical won the Oscar for Best Picture.

quality.notes: The question is long-winded (about 190 characters, stacked with facts). Many adults know “Chicago” and “All That Jazz”, so 13 is too high; it is closer to 11.

questions.description: A dance where your head is allowed to do the work of your feet.
questions.question: You see dancers spinning on their heads on cardboard mats to hip-hop beats in the Bronx, New York. In which decade was this dance born?
hints: It grew up together with hip-hop music.
DJs looped the drum breaks of funk records for dancers.
Disco was also popular at the time.
questions.fun_fact: Breaking became an Olympic sport for the first time at the 2024 Paris Olympics.

quality.notes: Hint 3 (disco) points very strongly to the 1970s.

questions.description: The only dance where your shoes get louder applause than you.
questions.question: I'm a dance where metal plates on your shoes make the music, mixing African and Irish steps. In which country was I born?
hints: I became a star in Broadway shows and Hollywood films.
Gene Kelly and Gregory Hines danced me.
I grew up in cities like New York in the 1800s and 1900s.
questions.fun_fact: The metal plates on tap shoes are called “taps”, and they gave the dance its name.

quality.notes: The fun fact is doubtful: the name “tap” more likely comes from the tapping sound, and metal taps were added later.

questions.description: A travel guide for a land where the roads are made of yellow bricks.
questions.question: You're touring Elphaba's homeland from “Wicked”. Which of these places is NOT in it?
hints: Elphaba's homeland is the land of Oz.
Elphaba and Glinda meet as students at one of these places.
The odd one out is reached through a wardrobe.
questions.fun_fact: Elphaba's name comes from the initials of L. Frank Baum, who wrote “The Wonderful Wizard of Oz”: L-F-B.

quality.notes: The description (yellow brick road) and hint 1 both reveal Oz, after which Narnia stands out. The recent Wicked films make this easier than 8.

questions.description: A factory where the rivers are chocolate and the safety rules are optional.
questions.question: The 1971 musical film “Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory”, with the song “Pure Imagination”, is based on a book by which author?
hints: He also wrote “Matilda” and “The BFG”.
He was British, with parents from Norway.
His first name sounds like “Ronald” without the N.
questions.fun_fact: The book's title is “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory”; the film put Willy Wonka's name first.
questions.concept: Willy Wonka y la fábrica de chocolate

quality.notes: Hint 3 is an English-only sound clue, which is weak in other languages.

questions.description: Leather jackets, hair gel and a lot of combs in back pockets.
questions.question: Danny Zuko leads the T-Birds gang in “Grease”. Which of these characters is NOT one of the T-Birds?
hints: The odd one out belongs to another group at Rydell High.
That group wears pink jackets.
The odd one out leads the Pink Ladies.
questions.fun_fact: John Travolta, who played Danny in the 1978 film, had played a T-Bird in a touring stage version of “Grease” years before.

quality.notes: A fan-detail question, but fair: an expert can tell the answer from the wrong options.

questions.description: The longest “I'll just stay for a little while” in world literature.
questions.question: You plan a three-week visit to a mountain sanatorium, like Hans Castorp in Thomas Mann's “The Magic Mountain”. How many years did he end up staying?
hints: He stays for far more than one year.
It's a number that shows up a lot in fairy tales.
The answer is a single digit, more than five.
questions.fun_fact: Mann's 1929 Nobel Prize mainly praised his first novel, “Buddenbrooks”, which he published when he was just 26.

quality.notes: The “You plan a three-week visit…” framing is an invented scenario and makes the question longer than it needs to be. Hint 3 leaves only 7 among the options, which is fine for a final hint.

questions.description: A palace with more than a thousand rooms and one very calm former resident.
questions.question: This palace was once the winter home of which winner of the 1989 Nobel Peace Prize?
hints: The palace stands high in the Himalayas.
He is a Buddhist leader who has lived in India since 1959.
He's the spiritual leader of Tibet.

media.note: A clear photo of the Potala Palace in Lhasa, with no signs or text naming it.

questions.fun_fact: Mahatma Gandhi never won the Nobel Peace Prize, though he was nominated five times.

quality.notes: A clear photo of the Potala Palace is easy to find on Wikimedia Commons. Hint 2 practically names the Dalai Lama. Gandhi died before 1989, so he is easy to rule out. Recognizing the Potala is harder than 8 for young teens.

questions.description: A dreamer who got the world's biggest peace award at an age when many people are still paying off their first car.
questions.question: When Martin Luther King Jr. won the 1964 Nobel Peace Prize, he was the youngest winner of that prize so far. How old was he?
hints: He was not a teenager.
He was younger than most grandparents.
He was born in 1929.
questions.fun_fact: King gave all the prize money, about 54,000 dollars, to the civil rights movement.

quality.notes: The options are so far apart (19/60/82) that 35 is easy to guess. The description's “paying off their first car” also points to a young adult. Hint 3 lets you work it out exactly, which is fine for a final hint.

questions.description: The only cookie-sized thing in your house you'd never dare to bite.
questions.question: You get to hold a real Nobel Prize medal, made of gold and about as big as a cookie. About how much does it weigh?
hints: Gold is very heavy for its size.
It's heavier than a coin but lighter than a big bottle of water.
It weighs about as much as an apple or two.
questions.fun_fact: In 2022 the journalist Dmitry Muratov sold his Nobel Peace Prize medal for 103.5 million dollars to help children from Ukraine.

quality.notes: Modern Nobel medals weigh about 175–185 g, so “about 200 grams” is a loose but fair rounding.

questions.description: A word that does a handstand and doesn't even get dizzy.
questions.question: You turn a page upside down and the word “Illuminati” still reads exactly the same. Which author's thriller are you reading?
hints: The story takes place in Rome and the Vatican.
The hero is a professor who studies symbols.
The same author wrote “The Da Vinci Code”.
questions.fun_fact: The ambigrams in “Angels & Demons” were drawn by artist John Langdon, and the book's hero, Robert Langdon, is named after him.

quality.notes: Solid. The scenario framing (“which author's thriller are you reading?”) is a bit forced. The St. Peter's Square image hints at the book's setting but doesn't name it.

questions.description: A paper loop that got its life twisted.
questions.question: Call me a Möbius strip: I'm a band of paper with a half twist, taped into a loop. What's special about me?
wrong_answers: I can't be cut with scissors
I always fall flat on a table
hints: Try it with a strip of paper and some tape.
Draw a line along the middle without lifting your pen.
Your line covers both “sides” without ever crossing an edge.
questions.fun_fact: The three chasing arrows of the recycling symbol are often drawn as a Möbius strip.

quality.notes: The riddle opening “Call me a Möbius strip” reads a little oddly. The distractors are clearly wrong for anyone who has handled one.

questions.description: An actor so shy that the audience only ever sees its outline.
questions.question: I'm cut from leather or paper and move behind a lit screen, so you only see my dark outline. China and Indonesia have used me for centuries. What am I?
hints: I need a lamp to perform.
The audience never sees my colors, only my shape.
Your own hands can make my simplest kind on a wall.
questions.fun_fact: Indonesia's wayang puppet theater, which includes shadow puppets, is on UNESCO's list of the world's living cultural treasures.

quality.notes: “Dark outline” in the question and “outline” in the description point strongly to shadow, but it's fine for a 4. Decorative media is a reasonable choice.

questions.description: An artist who makes holes in the street without ever picking up a shovel.
questions.question: I'm an English artist nicknamed the “Pavement Picasso”. My chalk drawings on sidewalks seem to open deep holes or rise out of the ground. Who am I?
hints: I've drawn in cities around the world since the 1990s.
My pictures only work from one spot, often seen through a camera.
My first name matches the calendar named after Julius Caesar.
questions.fun_fact: Because his drawings are made right on the ground, a single rain shower can wash away days of work.

quality.notes: Very niche. Only street-art fans will know the name, though experts can tell Beever (English) from Wenner, Müller and Keer. Hint 3 (Julian/Julius) basically gives it away among the options. The media query could return a work by one of the distractor artists, but without a name on it.

questions.description: A painting that only tells you its secret if you stand in the corner.
questions.question: You stand to the side of a famous 1533 painting in London's National Gallery, and a stretched smear turns into a skull. Who painted it?
hints: He was a German painter who worked in England.
He painted famous portraits of King Henry VIII.
His name ends with “the Younger”.
questions.fun_fact: The painting is called “The Ambassadors” and shows two real French diplomats.

quality.notes: Shares the anamorphosis topic with q-1093 but asks a different fact (the painter). Hint 3 (“the Younger”) gives the answer away among the options, which is allowed for hint 3.

questions.description: Glasses that can't decide which color they like best.
questions.question: What are glasses like these used for?
wrong_answers: Protecting your eyes from the sun
hints: You might get them at the movies.
Each eye gets a slightly different picture.
With them on, things seem to jump out of the screen.

media.note: A clear photo of a pair of red-and-blue (red-cyan) paper or plastic 3D glasses, with no text or logos.

questions.fun_fact: Red-and-blue 3D pictures, called anaglyphs, were first made in the 1850s.

quality.notes: Easy and a bit plain. Clear photos of red-cyan glasses are common on Wikimedia Commons, so the essential image is fine.

questions.description: A face in the sky that has been staring at us since before the dinosaurs.
questions.question: People see me as a face on the full Moon, but nobody is really there. What makes my eyes and mouth?
hints: These areas are called “seas”, though they hold no water.
They formed billions of years ago.
Melted rock flooded huge basins and hardened.
questions.fun_fact: In East Asia, many people see a rabbit in the very same dark patches.

quality.notes: Nice question. The rating of 7 may be slightly low: many teens would guess craters or shadows.

questions.description: Stairs: the only thing in Hollywood that never asks for an autograph.
questions.question: I won the Best Actress Oscar at 22 and tripped on the stairs going up to get it. I played the blue shape-shifter Mystique. In which film series?
hints: I'm also famous as Katniss in “The Hunger Games”.
In this series, Professor Xavier runs a school for young people with special powers.
Wolverine, with metal claws, is its most famous hero.
questions.fun_fact: Jennifer Lawrence won her Oscar in 2013 for “Silver Linings Playbook”, and she joked about her fall on the stairs during her speech.

quality.notes: Correct: Jennifer Lawrence was 22 at the 2013 Oscars. The Oscar story is really just decoration. 'Mystique' on its own points to X-Men, so teens who watch Marvel films will get it more easily than a 9 suggests.

questions.description: Some people win an Oscar and walk to the stage; others take the scenic route over the chairs.
questions.question: This Italian film won three Oscars in 1999. Its star and director, Roberto Benigni, climbed over the seats to the stage. A father turns hard times into a game for his son. What film is it?
hints: It is set in Italy during the Second World War.
Benigni won Best Actor, the first man to win it for a role not in English.
Its title says something hopeful about life.
questions.fun_fact: Roberto Benigni was so happy at the Oscars that he said he wanted to “kiss everybody”, and he stepped on the tops of the seats on his way to the stage.

quality.notes: Facts are right: 3 Oscars at the 1999 ceremony, the first man to win Best Actor for a non-English role, and the walk over the seats. The question is too long (three sentences, about 200 characters) and stacks several clues. The fun fact repeats the seat-climbing detail that is already in the question. The Holocaust setting is handled gently enough.

questions.description: Glare on a lake: the nemesis of every vacation photo.
questions.question: A filter like this cuts glare from water and windows. The man who invented cheap polarizing plastic sheets later founded a famous instant-camera company. Who?
hints: He was an American inventor of the 20th century.
His company's cameras spat out the photo right after you pressed the button.
The company name comes from the word “polarizer”.

media.note: A round camera polarizing filter, ideally held in front of water or a window to show reduced glare. No brand names visible.

questions.fun_fact: Edwin Land dropped out of Harvard and created his first polarizing sheet in 1929, when he was only about 20 years old.

quality.notes: Most adults don't know Edwin Land by name; many know Polaroid but not its founder, so it's closer to a 13. The question is long (about 165 characters). The essential image of a polarizer filter adds little: a photo can't easily show reduced glare, and Commons photos may show brand names. An illustrative role would fit better.

questions.description: Your eyes have been doing autofocus since long before cameras existed.
questions.question: When you look up from a book to a far tree, your eye's lens refocuses light onto the retina. A camera's lens focuses light onto the…
hints: Like the retina, it is at the back.
It turns light into the picture.
In old cameras, film did this job.
questions.fun_fact: Your eye focuses by changing the shape of its lens, while most cameras focus by moving their glass lenses forward or back.

quality.notes: The question runs about 140 characters and has a two-part setup. "Image sensor" stands out as the only technical-sounding option. "Flash" and "shutter button" are weak distractors, and only "memory card" is really tempting. It's a solid analogy, but a bit dry.

questions.description: A portrait so tough you could mail it in a letter and it would survive the trip.
questions.question: In the 1860s, cheap portraits were made in minutes on thin, black-lacquered metal plates that could be cut with shears. Which metal?
hints: The famous name of these photos is misleading.
This metal was cheap and could rust.
Magnets stick to it.
questions.fun_fact: These photos are called tintypes, even though they contain no tin at all.

quality.notes: This is a good expert question, and the "tin" option is a nice trap that is clearly wrong once you know the answer. Some well-read adults could reason towards iron from the hints, so it may be closer to 14. The decorative image is fine, though an illustrative "tintype portrait" image would also be safe.

questions.description: The ocean does the wave, and physicists grab a measuring tape.
questions.question: A wave is made of crests and troughs. What do physicists call the distance from one crest to the next?
hints: It is a length, so you measure it in meters.
Red light and blue light differ in exactly this distance.
The word joins the name of the thing with a word for “how long”.

media.note: A clear photo of a row of ocean waves where several crests can be seen one after another. No text or diagrams.

questions.fun_fact: Radio waves can have wavelengths longer than a soccer field, while X-rays are smaller than an atom.

quality.notes: Fun 3: a fairly dry school definition. The 'essential' role is a stretch because the question works without the photo; 'illustrative' would fit better. Wavelength is probably a bit easier than 10.

questions.description: The physics of the very, very tiny, hiding in your very, very ordinary stuff.
questions.question: Three of these inventions only work thanks to quantum physics. Which one does NOT need it?
hints: Quantum physics was only worked out in the 1900s.
The odd one out was already powering trains and factories long before that.
It runs on boiling water and pistons.
questions.fun_fact: Every computer chip in your phone relies on quantum effects in billions of tiny transistors.

quality.notes: Hint 2 practically gives the answer away, but that is acceptable.

questions.description: Breakfast physics: why your bread turns into toast instead of staying sad and soft.
questions.question: Complete the sentence: the thin wires in a toaster glow hot because they have a high electrical…
hints: It is measured in ohms.
It is how much a material fights against the flow of current.
In Ohm's law, voltage equals current times this.
questions.fun_fact: Old light bulbs work the same way: a thin wire with high resistance gets so hot that it glows.

quality.notes: Fun 3: a fill-in-the-blank school test. Hint 1 (ohms) is strong. This is related to q-1488 (the ohm) and q-0529 (the filament), but it asks a different fact.

questions.description: Push a wall, and the wall quietly pushes back. Rude, but fair.
questions.question: Complete Newton's third law: “For every action, there is an equal and opposite…”
hints: It explains why a rocket goes up when gas shoots down.
When you push a wall, the wall pushes back on you.
The word is “action” with two letters in front.
questions.fun_fact: Newton published his three laws of motion in 1687 in a book called the “Principia”.

quality.notes: Fun 3: completing a memorized textbook phrase. Hint 3 depends on English spelling ('action' with two letters in front). Hint 2 repeats the description. Many teens know the phrase, but 8 is a fairer rating than 7.

questions.description: The red dot that cats have been chasing and never catching.
questions.question: Beams like these shoot across the sky at concerts. What is a laser beam made of?
hints: It travels in a perfectly straight line.
You can block it with your hand or bounce it off a mirror.
It is the same thing that comes from the Sun, just very focused.

media.note: A photo of a laser light show with several bright colored beams crossing the sky or a stage.

questions.fun_fact: Scientists have bounced laser beams off mirrors left on the Moon by astronauts to measure its distance.

quality.notes: The photo is not really essential; 'illustrative' would fit better. The description mentions a laser pointer, which is a nudge but not a giveaway.

questions.description: Nothing has never been so strong.
questions.question: Two teams of horses could not pull apart two metal half-spheres with the air pumped out. When was this famous show?
hints: It happened in Germany, in the town of Magdeburg.
It was in the time of Galileo's students, when the first air pumps were invented.
It was about 30 years before Newton's laws of motion were published.
questions.fun_fact: Otto von Guericke, the mayor of Magdeburg, invented the air pump he used in the show.

quality.notes: Age fit 3: few 16-year-olds can date the Magdeburg hemispheres, so 12 is a better rating than 10. Players can reason toward the answer from the options, though. The facts check out: the show took place around 1654–1657.

questions.description: A color so shy that your eyes have never seen it.
questions.question: Your TV remote sends signals with it, heat cameras in spy films see it, and you feel it as warmth. Which invisible light is it?
hints: It sits just past one end of the rainbow.
Some snakes can sense it to find warm animals in the dark.
Its name means “below red”.
questions.fun_fact: Point a TV remote at your phone camera and press a button: many cameras show the invisible light as a flashing glow.

quality.notes: A strong three-clue question. Hint 2 (snakes) touches the fact in q-1842 (viper heat pits), but the questions ask different facts.

questions.description: The tiny wall button that turns night into day.
questions.question: I live on the wall and go click. With one push I make the room bright, with another I make it dark. What am I?
hints: You usually find me next to a door.
I open and close the path of electricity to a lamp.
You flip me up or down to turn the lamp on or off.
questions.fun_fact: Before light switches, people had to turn a little key on each gas lamp to light their homes.

quality.notes: Description 3: the 'wall button that turns night into day' basically restates the riddle. Fun 3: very easy. Fun fact: gas lamps were turned on with taps or valves; calling it a 'key' is loose, and many homes used candles or oil lamps, not gas. The 'nature' lens doesn't fit.

questions.description: Superheroes save the world in seconds, but a sequel takes its time.
questions.question: You buy a cinema ticket to see “Incredibles 2” in its first week. In which year are you?
hints: It came out many years after the first film.
The first film came out in 2004.
The sequel came out 14 years after the first.
questions.fun_fact: “Incredibles 2” starts at the exact moment the first film ends, even though it came out 14 years later.

quality.notes: A release-year question is dry, and the cinema-ticket setup is invented filler. Release years are harder than the stated 6. Hints 2 and 3 together give 2018 by simple maths.

questions.description: A kitchen where the head chef hides under a hat.
questions.question: At the end of “Ratatouille”, Gusteau's has closed. What is the new restaurant where Remy cooks called?
hints: It is a small bistro, not a fancy restaurant.
Its name is also the name of a dish.
It shares its name with the film.
questions.fun_fact: Ratatouille is a vegetable stew from the south of France, made with eggplant, zucchini, peppers and tomatoes.

quality.notes: Players can guess the answer because it shares the film's title. Still, the bistro's name is a small detail, harder than the stated 6.

questions.description: A soul with a number instead of a name, and no hurry to grow up.
questions.question: I am soul 22. I never wanted to go to Earth, so I stayed for ages where new souls get their personalities. Where am I?
hints: It is from the film “Soul”.
It is a place for souls not yet born.
Its name is the opposite of “the Great Beyond”.
questions.fun_fact: In “Soul”, famous mentors like Abraham Lincoln and Mother Teresa all failed to inspire 22.

quality.notes: The film also calls this place the "You Seminar". It is not among the options, so this is only a small issue. Good distractors taken from other Pixar films.

questions.description: Two brothers, one magic staff and only half a dad.
questions.question: My magic spell went wrong and brought back only my dad's legs, so my brother and I went on a quest. What kind of creature am I?
hints: The film is “Onward”.
In their world, unicorns eat trash.
They have pointy ears and blue skin.
questions.fun_fact: “Onward” was inspired by director Dan Scanlon's own father, who died when he was a baby.

quality.notes: Grammar mismatch: "What kind of creature am I?" is singular, but the answer "Elves" is plural. The fun fact is about a parent's death, which is slightly somber for a reveal. q-1443 (Legolas, elves) only shares the answer word.

questions.description: A fish that loses her keys, her way and her family, but never her smile.
questions.question: Dory is this kind of fish. In “Finding Dory”, she swims far to find her family. Where does she find them?
hints: It is on the other side of the ocean from Nemo's home.
She remembers “the Jewel of Morro Bay”.
It is a US state on the Pacific coast.

media.note: A clear photo of a real blue tang (Paracanthurus hepatus) swimming; no text, no cartoon.

questions.fun_fact: Dory is a blue tang, and real blue tangs can change their blue to a darker shade when stressed.

quality.notes: Media role is wrong: the photo isn't needed to answer, so it should be illustrative, not essential. "Dory is this kind of fish" is padding. Hint 2 (Morro Bay) almost gives the answer away. Fun is moderate.

questions.description: Giddy up! But first, a little math in the saddle.
questions.question: In “Toy Story”, Woody and Jessie ride their horse Bullseye. How many legs do the three have in total?
hints: Woody and Jessie are people-shaped toys.
A horse walks on all fours.
Add 2 plus 2 plus 4.
questions.fun_fact: Bullseye never speaks in the films; he shows his feelings like a real horse, with his body.

quality.notes: Small inaccuracy: Jessie and Bullseye first appear in Toy Story 2, not the first "Toy Story". Saying "the Toy Story films" would fix it.

questions.description: A guy who goes with the flow, and cries at every sad story.
questions.question: I am made of water and cry very easily. I fell in love with a girl made of fire. Who am I?
hints: The film is “Elemental”.
I work as a city inspector.
My last name is Ripple.
questions.fun_fact: In “Elemental”, Wade's whole family loves a game where they try not to cry, and they always lose.

quality.notes: I'm unsure about the fun fact's wording of the Ripples' crying game. As I recall, the players try to make each other cry, so "try not to cry" may be inaccurate.

questions.description: The moment your toaster starts looking grumpy, a poet is to blame.
questions.question: I'm a figure of speech: I make the wind whisper, the sun smile and old stairs complain. What two things do I mix together?
wrong_answers: Words that start with the same sound
A huge exaggeration and a fact
hints: Think about who usually whispers, smiles or complains.
Only people really do those things, but here a wind and a sun do them.
My name has the word “person” inside it.
questions.fun_fact: “Mother Nature” and “Father Time” are personifications so common that most people don't notice them anymore.

quality.notes: Personification is a 'mix' only in a loose sense, so the question 'What two things do I mix together?' is a bit forced. The answer wording is clunky. Otherwise sound, but it reads like a school definition test. Hint 3 depends on the word 'person', which works in the main game languages.

questions.description: A man who saved so much time he didn't even bother with the word “and”.
questions.question: This Roman is behind the most quoted example of asyndeton, a list with the “and” left out. Who is he?
hints: The famous line is a boast about winning a battle very fast.
It has three short Latin verbs in a row.
“I came, I saw, I conquered.”

media.note: A clear photo of a well-known ancient marble bust of Julius Caesar, with no label or name visible.

questions.fun_fact: Caesar wrote “Veni, vidi, vici” in 47 BC after winning the Battle of Zela in only about five days.

quality.notes: The term 'asyndeton' is obscure, but the clue 'and left out' plus the famous boast makes this workable for many adults, so I'd put it closer to 12 than 14. The essential bust isn't really needed because the text alone answers it; an illustrative role would fit better. A sharp Caesar bust may help some players.

questions.description: Poets use the alphabet like a secret code, and they only need the first few letters.
questions.question: In poetry, what does a rhyme scheme like “ABAB” tell you?
questions.answer: Which lines rhyme with each other
wrong_answers: How many syllables each line has
Where the reader should take a breath
hints: Each letter stands for one line of the poem.
Lines that share the same letter have something in common.
In ABAB, the first and third lines end with the same sound.
questions.fun_fact: A Shakespearean sonnet follows the scheme ABAB CDCD EFEF GG, ending with a rhyming pair of lines.

quality.notes: Correct and clear, but a dry school-style definition question.

questions.description: A mountain so poetic that even its rocks probably write sad verses.
questions.question: You're hiking up Mount Parnassus, above Delphi in Greece. Which Greek god was said to live there with the Muses?
hints: The Muses inspired poets, musicians and artists.
This god was the god of music, poetry and light.
His famous oracle spoke at Delphi, and he played the lyre.
questions.fun_fact: The Montparnasse district of Paris got its name from students who jokingly called a hill there “Mount Parnassus”.

quality.notes: Ares, Hephaestus and Poseidon have no link to the Muses or Delphi, so Apollo stands out to anyone who knows a little myth. Naming Delphi makes it easier still. Dionysus is also linked to Parnassus, but the Muses clue settles it.

questions.description: A poem that ignored all the rules and still got into the books.
questions.question: I'm a poem with no fixed rhyme and no fixed rhythm: my lines are as long or short as I like. What kind of verse am I made of?
hints: I break the old rules of meter.
I became very popular in the 19th and 20th centuries.
My name says I'm not tied to anything.
questions.fun_fact: Walt Whitman's “Leaves of Grass”, first published in 1855, made free verse famous around the world.

quality.notes: 'Sonnet verse' and 'Haiku verse' are made-up terms, which makes them weak; only blank verse is a strong distractor. The Whitman portrait is a mild hint, since he is known for free verse.

questions.description: A living library that sings instead of shushing you.
questions.question: Skald is to Viking Scandinavia as what is to West Africa?
hints: Both are poet-storytellers who kept history alive by memory.
In West Africa, this role is often passed down within families.
They often sing to the sound of a kora, a harp-like instrument.
questions.fun_fact: Griots kept alive the Epic of Sundiata, the story of the founder of the Mali Empire, for about 800 years by memory.

quality.notes: Good world-spanning analogy with fair distractors. A kora-player image may come with a 'griot' caption at the source, but the image itself is fine.

questions.description: A poem with a secret message hidden in plain sight.
questions.question: Read my lines from top to bottom, and their first letters spell a hidden word or name. Lewis Carroll hid Alice's real name in one. What kind of poem am I?
hints: Many children write one using the letters of their own name.
Look down the left edge of the poem.
My name begins with “acro”, from the Greek word for the tip or top.
questions.fun_fact: The poem at the end of “Through the Looking-Glass” spells “Alice Pleasance Liddell”, the girl who inspired the books.

quality.notes: The description ('hidden in plain sight') hints at the concept but is fair. Writing acrostics of your own name is a school exercise in some countries, but not everywhere, so slightly harder than 6. The question is a bit long.

questions.description: Before podcasts, people told long stories by singing them in the village square.
questions.question: I'm a poem that tells a story in short four-line stanzas, often with a repeated chorus, and people once sang me. What am I?
hints: Folk singers loved me long before radio.
Today my name is also used for slow love songs.
My name comes from an old word meaning “to dance”.
questions.fun_fact: The word “ballad” comes, through Old French and Occitan, from the Latin “ballare”, meaning “to dance”.

quality.notes: Hint 2 (slow love songs) is very strong. Four-line stanzas also fit other forms, but the story-plus-song clue settles it. Somewhat school-like.

questions.description: Decisions are hard, especially when the forest gives you two roads and no map.
questions.question: You're where two roads split in a yellow wood, like the traveler in Robert Frost's famous poem. Which road did he take?
wrong_answers: The one that led back home
The one his friend had taken
hints: The poem is called “The Road Not Taken”.
He says this choice “has made all the difference”.
He picked the road that fewer people had walked.
questions.fun_fact: Robert Frost recited a poem at President John F. Kennedy's inauguration in 1961.

quality.notes: Robert Frost is US/English-school canon, so families outside English-speaking countries know it far less (International angle). The answer is the famous phrase in its exact wording, so it stands out from the plain distractors. The poem itself suggests both roads were about the same, so 'less traveled' is the speaker's later claim. The scenario framing is a bit forced.

questions.description: The part of the show where someone suddenly remembers they left the oven on at home.
questions.question: It happens near the end of an episode, the host announces it, and one contestant must leave the show. What is it called?
hints: Nobody on the show wants it to happen to them.
After it, there is one less player in the game.
The contestant is “voted out” or “sent home”.
questions.fun_fact: Some shows bring eliminated contestants back for a second chance later in the season.

quality.notes: A dry vocabulary question with little surprise. It is close to q-1804 (immunity protects against elimination) but asks a different fact. The illustrative 'TV studio stage' image is harmless.

questions.description: Cameras everywhere, and the only place to vent is in front of another camera.
questions.question: In Big Brother, housemates go alone into this room, sit in a big chair and tell the cameras their secrets. What is it called?
hints: What's said there is shown to viewers, not to other housemates.
Housemates also use it to name who they want to nominate.
Its name is a kind of book where you write private thoughts.
questions.fun_fact: In many countries, this room is called the “confession room”.

quality.notes: The name 'Diary Room' comes from the UK/US versions. In many countries it is the 'confession room', as the fun fact itself says, so the base question depends on the English-language version. Hint 3 nearly spells it out. The description is only mildly funny. q-1532 shares only the word 'diary'.

questions.description: A snack so powerful it should come with a warning label.
questions.question: In Super Mario games, what happens when Mario grabs a red mushroom with white spots like this one?
hints: It's a good thing, not a bad one.
After he takes a hit, he's small Mario again.
Small Mario becomes Super Mario.

media.note: A clear photo of a real red mushroom with white spots (fly agaric).

questions.fun_fact: Mario's growing mushroom is often compared to Alice in Wonderland, where Alice grows and shrinks by eating a mushroom.

quality.notes: The media role should be illustrative, not essential: the question doesn't need the photo to be answered. Hint 2 (“small Mario again”) strongly suggests that he grew. The Alice in Wonderland link is commonly cited, but it is loosely worded.

questions.description: The only quest where the hardest part was waiting in line at the shop.
questions.question: You're in a huge line outside a Tokyo shop on a weekday morning, waiting to buy Dragon Quest III on the day it comes out. Which decade is it?
hints: It came out for the console known in Japan as the Famicom.
That's the same decade the first Super Mario Bros. came out.
The year was 1988.
questions.fun_fact: So many students skipped school to buy Dragon Quest III in 1988 that police picked up hundreds of them.

quality.notes: Hint 1 (Famicom) and hint 2 (same decade as Super Mario Bros.) both pin the decade early. The figure for truant students picked up by police varies between reports; “hundreds” is safe. A modern Akihabara photo may have signs on it, but they won't give the decade away.

questions.description: Money that only works in one building, which is great for the building.
questions.question: Many arcades sold these coin-like metal discs to put into their game machines instead of real money. What are they called?
hints: Subways and buses in some cities used them too.
The word can also mean a small sign or symbol of something, as in “a ... of thanks”.
It starts with a T.

media.note: A close-up photo of a few metal arcade game tokens.

questions.fun_fact: Arcades liked tokens because they couldn't be spent anywhere else, so players often came back to use their leftovers.

quality.notes: Hints 2 (“a token of thanks”) and 3 (“starts with a T”) only work in English. This is a base question that will be translated (e.g. Spanish “fichas”), so these hints won't travel. The media role should be illustrative, not essential.

questions.description: A game where the best move is often to do nothing at all and hold your breath.
questions.question: “In my games, you hide in shadows and sneak past guards, and if one spots you, an alarm goes off.” What kind of game am I?
hints: Metal Gear, from 1987, made this kind of game famous.
Being quiet and unseen is the whole point.
A word that also describes planes that radar can't see.
questions.fun_fact: In Metal Gear Solid, an exclamation mark pops up over a guard's head when he spots you, and it became one of gaming's most famous sounds.

quality.notes: Hint 3 (stealth planes) depends on the English word and won't carry over to other languages. The riddle describes the genre itself, so it is guessable but a bit dry.

questions.description: A bottle on a mission to stop the only snow that falls indoors.
questions.question: Which shampoo brand was first sold in 1961, made especially to fight dandruff?
hints: Its name is in English in almost every country where it is sold.
Its ads often show someone brushing white flakes off a dark jacket.
Its name lists two body parts: the top one and the one just below your neck.
questions.fun_fact: It is made by Procter & Gamble, the same company that makes Pantene and Pampers.

quality.notes: Brand knowledge is fairly dry, and the 1961 date adds little. The brand is global and anti-dandruff is its well-known identity, so adults get it easily.

questions.description: Chocolate in a tiny suit of armor.
questions.question: I was first sold in 1941, and soldiers carried me because my sugar shell stops the chocolate from melting. What am I?
hints: I was first made in the United States.
My ads say I melt in your mouth, not in your hand.
My name is just two letters, and they are the same letter.
questions.fun_fact: The two Ms stand for Forrest Mars and Bruce Murrie, the two men who started making them.
questions.concept: Se derrite en tu boca, no en tu mano (M&M's)

quality.notes: Smarties (1937) are also chocolate in a sugar shell, so only the 1941 date and the soldiers set M&M's apart. The hint 2 slogan is the US one.

questions.description: How much forest can you cut before the forest stops being a forest?
questions.question: Scientists warn the Amazon has a “tipping point” where it turns into dry savanna. About how much of the forest would have to be lost?
hints: It is a smaller share than most people would guess.
Close to a fifth of the forest is already gone.
It is more than a fifth but less than a third.
questions.fun_fact: The Amazon makes about half of its own rain, so cutting trees can make the rest of the forest drier.

quality.notes: Lovejoy & Nobre gave 20–25%, so '25%' is a fair choice, but it is an estimate scientists still debate. The topic is sobering more than fun. 'About half of its own rain' is a commonly quoted but rough figure.

questions.description: A piece of metal that spends its whole life being stepped on.
questions.question: Look at this U-shaped piece of metal. What is it used for?
wrong_answers: Holding a cart wheel in place
hints: It is nailed onto something.
It belongs to a big animal you can ride.
The animal it is made for says “neigh”.

media.note: A clear photo of a single metal horseshoe, not attached to a horse.

questions.fun_fact: Fixing a horseshoe doesn't hurt the horse, because the outer part of its hoof has no feeling, just like your fingernails.

quality.notes: A simple object-recognition question with little surprise. Most people recognise a horseshoe from its shape. Shares the object with q-1600 (horseshoe luck) but asks a different fact. A clear horseshoe photo is easy to find on Commons.

questions.description: Round, white and friendly hippo lookalikes from the far north.
questions.question: It's late autumn in Moominvalley, and the Moomins fill their tummies with pine needles. What do they do next, all winter long?
hints: They don't leave Moominvalley at all.
The full tummies have to last them through the long, cold months.
They wake up again when the snow melts.
questions.fun_fact: The Moomins were created by Finnish artist Tove Jansson, and their first book came out in 1945.

quality.notes: The Moomins are well known in Finland, Japan and parts of Europe but much less elsewhere. Players can still work it out from 'fill their tummies' plus winter, which points to hibernation, and hint 2 makes it close to obvious.

questions.description: A story of swords, roses and very tall wigs.
questions.question: A 1970s manga and anime follows Oscar, a woman raised as a man, who commands Marie Antoinette's royal guard. Which palace is in its title?
hints: The story takes place before and during the French Revolution.
The palace is famous for its Hall of Mirrors.
It lies just outside Paris and was built up by Louis XIV.
questions.fun_fact: The all-female Takarazuka Revue in Japan has performed a stage musical of this story since 1974.

quality.notes: Marie Antoinette's royal guard points strongly to Versailles even for players who don't know the manga, so it is easier than 10. A portrait of Marie Antoinette may show a palace interior, but that is low risk. Asks a different fact from q-2131 (Versailles from a photo).

questions.description: Some artists quit their club so dramatically that they built a whole new clubhouse with a golden hairdo.
questions.question: This exhibition hall with a dome of golden leaves was built by the city's Secession art group. In which city is it?
hints: The city is the capital of a country in central Europe.
Gustav Klimt helped found the group that built this hall in 1898.
The city is famous for waltzes, Mozart and the old Habsburg emperors.

media.note: Exterior photo of the Secession Building with its golden laurel-leaf dome; no visible city name or signs naming the city.

questions.fun_fact: Locals nicknamed the golden dome “the cabbage” because of its round, leafy look.

quality.notes: The description is long and wordy for a one-liner intro. 'Secession' in the question points to Vienna for anyone who knows the term, but Munich and Prague had Secession groups too, so the options stay fair. Photos of the building are easy to find and have no city name on them (the facade shows only a motto).

questions.description: Wonder Woman's family tree has some very famous branches on Mount Olympus.
questions.question: I'm a Greek goddess the Romans called Venus. In the first Wonder Woman comics, I protected the Amazons and brought baby Diana to life. Who am I?
hints: I'm one of the gods who live on Mount Olympus.
Diana's mother shaped her from clay, and I gave her life.
I'm the goddess of love and beauty.
questions.fun_fact: Wonder Woman's creator, William Moulton Marston, also helped develop an early lie detector test.

quality.notes: Golden Age origin is right: Hippolyta shaped Diana from clay and Aphrodite gave her life. The Venus clue is fair, but anyone who knows the Roman names gets it at once. The Venus planet questions share only the name, not the fact. A Greek temple image would be safe as illustrative, so decorative isn't really needed.

questions.description: A villain who leaves more homework than a math teacher.
questions.question: The Riddler wears green with question marks and leaves puzzles at his crimes. In which city does he cause trouble?
hints: It's a dark, rainy city.
Superman lives somewhere else.
The Joker and the Penguin live there too.
questions.fun_fact: The Riddler first appeared in a Batman comic in 1948.

quality.notes: Riddler's debut was Detective Comics #140 in 1948, which is correct. Hint 2 is weak because it only rules out Metropolis. It is close to the Batman question, but that one asks a different fact.

questions.description: Finally a reward for getting old that isn't a creaky knee.
questions.question: In 1889, this became the first country with a national pension for retired workers. Which one?
hints: It's a country in Europe.
Bismarck had united it only about 20 years earlier.
Its capital is Berlin.
questions.fun_fact: Bismarck's pension started at age 70, at a time when few workers lived that long.

quality.notes: Bismarck's 1889 old-age insurance with a starting age of 70 is correct. Hint 2, which names Bismarck, already gives the answer to many adults. Most players will reason their way to it rather than know it, so it is probably closer to 11.

questions.description: A boss who handed out shorter days and fatter paychecks, which sounds made up but isn't.
questions.question: In 1914, this industrialist gave his factory workers an 8-hour day and doubled their pay. Who is he?
hints: He was American and ran a huge factory in Detroit.
He made the assembly line famous.
His company built the Model T.

media.note: A clear portrait photo of Henry Ford, without any caption or name visible.

questions.fun_fact: Ford's “five-dollar day” in 1914 was so famous that thousands of people lined up outside his factory looking for jobs.

quality.notes: The five-dollar day and the 8-hour day in 1914 are correct. The essential portrait isn't really needed, since the text already answers the question, but Commons has many clear Ford portraits. Hint 3 names the Model T, which links to q-0215, but that question asks a different fact.

questions.description: The worst boss in cartoon history, and he has had a very long time to practice.
questions.question: I own the nuclear power plant in Springfield, so Homer Simpson's paycheck comes from me. Who am I?
hints: He is the richest man in town.
He taps his fingertips together when he plots something.
His assistant is the loyal Smithers.
questions.fun_fact: Mr. Burns is said to be over 100 years old in the show, yet he still runs the plant.

quality.notes: The Simpsons is shown worldwide, but it is still a US show and less familiar to young kids in some regions. It is close to the Springfield question q-0409 in topic only.

questions.description: Your bananas have probably traveled more than you have.
questions.question: Goods bought from another country arrive at the port and go through customs. What is this kind of trade called?
hints: Countries do it with things they can't make or grow enough of themselves.
The money leaves the country, while the goods arrive.
Its opposite is selling goods to other countries, called “export”.
questions.fun_fact: Most goods that countries buy from abroad arrive by ship in big metal containers.

quality.notes: This is a dry definition question that feels like a school test. Hint 3 rules out Export by naming it. Tariff and Subsidy are not kinds of trade, so they are weaker distractors.

questions.description: What goes up must come down, and here it comes down very fast.
questions.question: Home prices rise far above their real value because buyers expect them to keep rising, then they crash. What do economists call this?
hints: Japan had one around 1990, and the US one burst before 2008.
Its name compares it to something that is mostly empty inside.
Children blow the same thing with soap.
questions.fun_fact: When the US housing market crashed in 2007 and 2008, it helped start a worldwide financial crisis.

quality.notes: The term is widely known from the news, so adults get it more easily than teens. Hints 2 and 3 strongly point to the answer.

questions.description: Haircuts, bus rides and doctors: things you buy but can't put in your pocket.
questions.question: Economists group jobs like banking, tourism and cutting hair into one sector of the economy. What is it called?
hints: Services don't grow or build things, they help people.
Farming and mining come first, factories come second.
Its name comes from the Latin word for “third”.
questions.fun_fact: In many rich countries, more than 7 out of 10 workers have jobs in services.

quality.notes: This is a school-test definition. Some models put banking in a quaternary sector, and a barber can work in the informal sector, so the answer is slightly fuzzy. The description hints at services. The answer_kind axis says 'number', which doesn't match a sector name.

questions.description: The shortest and most stressful job interview in the world.
questions.question: A famous job-interview challenge for salespeople goes “Sell me this…” what?
hints: It's a small, everyday object.
You'd find one on almost any office desk.
You can use it to sign a contract.
questions.fun_fact: The challenge became famous worldwide through a 2013 Hollywood film about a real stockbroker named Jordan Belfort.

quality.notes: Accurate: the line was made famous by The Wolf of Wall Street. Hint 2 (office desk) fits Stapler and Phone too, so it's fine. Hint 3 nearly gives it away, which is allowed. Adults who saw the film get it easily, so about 10–11 is right.

questions.description: A bridge in the Scottish Highlands that has never once had a traffic jam.
questions.question: This curved concrete bridge in Scotland was built for one kind of traffic. Which one?
hints: The bridge is very narrow, with no room for sidewalks.
Its traffic runs on a timetable.
In the Harry Potter films, the Hogwarts Express crosses it.

media.note: Photo of the Glenfinnan Viaduct with its curved row of arches, with no train on it.

questions.fun_fact: The Glenfinnan Viaduct, finished in 1901, was one of the first big bridges made of concrete.

quality.notes: Difficulty 3 is too low. With no train in the photo, a 9-year-old has to reason from the bridge's shape or recognise it from Harry Potter. That's more like 5. Commons has many photos of the Glenfinnan Viaduct, but most show the Jacobite steam train. The essential photo must be checked so it has no train, though rails may still show.

questions.description: A Welsh bridge with a lot of nerve and not much railing.
questions.question: Engineers Thomas Telford and William Jessop finished this bridge in Wales in 1805, on these tall stone pillars. What does it carry?
hints: The traffic on it moves very slowly.
Its top is a long iron trough.
It is a kind of aqueduct.

media.note: Photo of the tall stone pillars of the Pontcysyllte Aqueduct seen from the valley below; no boats or water trough visible.

questions.fun_fact: The Pontcysyllte Aqueduct is about 38 m (126 ft) high, and boats still cross it today.

quality.notes: The facts check out: Telford and Jessop, 1805, about 38 m. The question is a bit long and dry, and the engineers' names add little. The 'not much railing' description hints at the famous open edge of the trough. Many photos of the pillars also show the water trough or boats, so the photo needs care.

questions.description: A bridge that has watched about 1,400 years of people cross it.
questions.question: China's Zhaozhou Bridge, built around 605, still stands. Besides its one big stone arch, what special feature is it famous for?
questions.answer: Four small arches in its sides
wrong_answers: Hollow wooden beams in its deck
A roof covering its whole deck
Stone pillars standing in the river
hints: The extra parts make the bridge lighter.
They also let floodwater pass through.
Look at the “shoulders” above the big arch.
questions.fun_fact: Europe built its first bridges with such open side arches many centuries after the Zhaozhou Bridge.

quality.notes: Accurate: it has open spandrels, two small arches at each end. The bridge is also famous for its flat, shallow arch, but that isn't an option, so the answer stays clear. Fairly dry and technical. The description is plain, not funny. The decorative query could find the Zhaozhou Bridge itself, which is fine since the image is blurred.

questions.description: The stuff of log bridges, pencils and kitchen tables.
questions.question: Wool comes from a sheep. Wood comes from a…
hints: It grows in a forest.
It has leaves and branches.
Squirrels climb it.
questions.fun_fact: The Chapel Bridge in Lucerne, Switzerland, was first built in the 1300s and is one of Europe's oldest covered wooden bridges.

quality.notes: A simple analogy that works for a 1. It's not very fun, and the bridge theme only appears in the fun fact. The description describes wood, which the question already names, and it isn't really funny. The MrBeast tree question shares the answer but asks a different fact.

questions.description: A sports store with a name that sounds like ten times the workout.
questions.question: The sports store Decathlon takes its name from Greek. “Deca” means “ten”. What does “athlon” mean?
hints: The same Greek root is in the word “athlete”.
In the Olympic decathlon, athletes run, jump and throw over two days.
Athletes take part in one of these to win a prize.
questions.fun_fact: Decathlon opened its first store in 1976 near Lille, in northern France.

quality.notes: Greek athlos/athlon does mean contest. 'Day' is a weak distractor, and 'Runner' is wrongly drawn towards by hint 1. It's a fairly dry word-root question. Teens may find it harder than 7.

questions.description: A car that never cared much whether there was a road.
questions.question: The first Land Rover, from 1948, was mainly made for which group of people?
hints: Its designer got the idea while working on his own land.
It could pull a plough and drive across fields.
Think of tractors, barns and muddy fields.
questions.fun_fact: The first Land Rover design was reportedly drawn in the sand on a beach in Wales.

quality.notes: Hint 2 uses the UK spelling 'plough'; it should be 'plow'. The farm-use origin is correct: Maurice Wilks and his farm on Anglesey. The sand-drawing story is legend, but it's flagged as 'reportedly'. 'Desert explorers' is a tempting distractor, and arguably early Land Rovers served explorers too, but the main target was farmers. Rated 7, but I'd put it nearer 9.

questions.description: Three of these would make a chocolate lover happy, one would leave them confused.
questions.question: Which of these candies has no chocolate in it?
hints: It comes in many bright colors.
Its flavors are fruits like strawberry and orange.
Its slogan is “Taste the rainbow”.
questions.fun_fact: Skittles were first sold in the United Kingdom in 1974, before they came to the United States.

quality.notes: Facts check out: Skittles went on sale in the UK in 1974, before the US in 1979. The candy brands lean US/UK. Kit Kat, Snickers and M&M's are sold worldwide, but Skittles is less known in some markets. A 'colorful candy jar' image could easily show Skittles or M&M's. The idea is pleasant but plain.

questions.description: Love is a chase, especially when one of you is a ninja.
questions.question: Pucca chases him all over the village to kiss him, he's a ninja who wants to be the best, and he always runs away. What's his name?
hints: He's from a cartoon made in South Korea.
He rarely speaks and carries a sword.
His name has four letters and starts with G.
questions.fun_fact: Pucca started as a character on the internet in South Korea before getting her own TV series.

quality.notes: Hint 1 says it was 'made in South Korea'. The concept is from Korea's Vooz, but the 2006 TV series was co-produced with Jetix and Studio B (Canada), so the hint is only partly accurate. The distractors are real Pucca characters (Abyo, Tobe, Dada), which works well. Pucca was popular in the mid-2000s, mainly in Latin America, Europe and Asia, so the question rests on nostalgia.

questions.description: Old technology that once had the whole family sitting in one row every evening.
questions.question: What do people use this machine for?
hints: It usually sits in the living room.
It has a screen on the front.
Cartoons and the news come on it.

media.note: A clear photo of an old television set with a visible screen, switched off, no logos or text on screen.

questions.fun_fact: In 1926, Scottish inventor John Logie Baird showed one of the first working televisions, and the pictures were blurry and tiny.

quality.notes: This is a very easy question with essential media; a photo of a vintage TV is easy to find on Commons. A very old set may look unfamiliar to 6-year-olds, but the screen makes it clear. Not very surprising: a plain 'what is this' question.

questions.description: A hot little machine with a pointy nose and a very flat personality.
questions.question: A broom is used on the floor. In the same way, an iron is used on…
hints: It gets very hot.
It makes things smooth and flat.
Think of a wrinkled shirt.
questions.fun_fact: Long before electricity, people heated heavy metal irons on a stove or in a fire before using them.

quality.notes: A simple analogy that works. 'Carpets' fits loosely, since steam irons are sometimes used on carpets, but this does not seriously compete. It is a plain everyday question with little surprise.

questions.description: The quiet hero of every family dinner, at least until it starts humming.
questions.question: Clothes go in the washing machine. In the same way, dirty plates go in the…
hints: It's in the kitchen.
It uses water and soap.
It cleans cups, forks and plates for you.
questions.fun_fact: Josephine Cochrane patented her dishwasher in 1886 because she was tired of her fine china getting chipped when washed by hand.
