quality.notes: Stacks of dirty plates are often photographed inside dishwasher racks, so the image has a slight risk of showing the answer. Home dishwashers are much less common in many regions, though children still know the word. This is the same analogy pattern as famous-inventors-2 but with a different answer, so there is no overlap of facts. Fun is limited; the fun fact helps.

questions.description: Rome's most famous bathtub, and nobody is allowed to swim in it.
questions.question: Lovers once left padlocks on the Pont des Arts bridge in Paris. What do visitors leave in Rome's Trevi Fountain?
hints: Visitors throw them over their shoulder into the water.
Legend says it means you will come back to Rome.
You could pay for an ice cream with them.
questions.fun_fact: More than a million euros are fished out of the Trevi Fountain every year and given to charity.

quality.notes: The facts are correct; about €1.4 million a year goes to Caritas. The setup with the padlocked bridge adds length but works as an analogy. The Trevi coin custom is known from films and travel, more by teens and adults than by young children.

questions.description: A very tall Canadian who never stops looking down on Toronto.
questions.question: I'm a concrete needle 553 m (1,815 ft) tall in Toronto, with a glass floor high above the city. What kind of tower am I?
hints: Nobody lives or works in my thin concrete shaft.
I was built because the city's tall buildings kept getting in the way.
The antenna on my top sends programs to millions of homes.
questions.fun_fact: From 1975 to 2007, Toronto's CN Tower was the tallest free-standing structure in the world.

quality.notes: The facts check out: 553 m (1,815 ft), the glass floor, and the tower was built because skyscrapers blocked broadcast signals. The skyline photo will show the tower's antenna, which is a mild hint, but it is the subject of the question. Players can reason their way to the answer without knowing Toronto.

questions.description: The only kind of battle that ends with everyone laughing on the sofa.
questions.question: Kids shoot soft foam darts from colorful toy blasters. Which toy brand is famous for them?
hints: Its blasters are a favorite for battles in the backyard.
Its name has only four letters.
Its logo is often on orange and blue blasters.
questions.fun_fact: The very first Nerf product, in 1969, was a foam ball sold as the world's first official indoor ball.

quality.notes: The other brands obviously don't make foam darts, so anyone who knows the brands rules them out quickly. Nerf is a US brand, but it's widely sold around the world. A decorative 'foam toy darts' image may still show a Nerf logo, even blurred.

questions.description: A philosopher who'd send back a birthday cake for having too many candles.
questions.question: German thinker Arthur Schopenhauer said life swings like a pendulum between pain and boredom. Which outlook is he famous for?
hints: He lived in the 19th century and loved Indian philosophy.
His outlook expects the worst of life.
It's the opposite of optimism.
questions.fun_fact: Schopenhauer had a series of pet poodles, and he called them Atma or Butz.

quality.notes: The decorative image (a pendulum) comes from a metaphor in the quote, which the house style rules out. It should show Schopenhauer's world instead, such as 19th-century Frankfurt. Adults who know Schopenhauer know he was a pessimist, but teens mostly won't, so this is closer to 11. Fairly dry.

questions.description: Three words that philosophy students have argued about for 140 years.
questions.question: Friedrich Nietzsche wrote “God is dead… and we have killed him.” What did he mean?
questions.answer: Faith no longer guided how modern people lived
wrong_answers: Science had proved that God never existed
Christianity had replaced the old Greek gods
Churches would soon be closed by law
hints: Nietzsche was a 19th-century German philosopher.
He was describing a change in society, not a single event.
He worried that without belief, people had lost their shared values.
questions.fun_fact: The line appears in Nietzsche's book “The Gay Science” of 1882, spoken by a madman who runs into a market with a lantern in broad daylight.

quality.notes: The answer is a fair simplification of a reading that is still debated. 'God is dead' may make religious families uncomfortable during a family game night. The book title 'The Gay Science' in the fun fact may cause giggles or confusion for kids. The question is a dry interpretation exercise.

questions.description: An old philosopher's ideas, given a fresh coat of paint 600 years later.
questions.question: Plotinus, born in Egypt, taught in Rome in the 200s that everything flows from “the One”. Whose older ideas did his school revive?
hints: Plotinus's student Porphyry gathered his writings into the “Enneads”.
The older thinker lived in Athens about 600 years before Plotinus.
The older thinker wrote “The Republic” and described a famous cave.
questions.fun_fact: Porphyry says Plotinus seemed ashamed of having a body and refused to tell anyone his birthday.

quality.notes: Plato is the most famous option, and 'Plotinus' sounds a bit like 'Plato', so guessers have an edge. The real gap is about 650 years, not 600, which is close enough. Fairly dry.

questions.description: The runner-up wise man of China, and proud of it.
questions.question: I'm called China's “Second Sage” after Confucius, and I taught that people are born good. Who am I?
hints: I lived in the 300s BC.
My rival Xunzi said human nature is bad.
My Chinese name is Mengzi.
questions.fun_fact: A famous Chinese story says Mencius's mother moved house three times to find the best neighborhood for his education.

quality.notes: The facts are accurate and the distractors are strong. The question is hard but fair for well-read adults.

questions.description: The chattiest animal ever to share a swamp.
questions.question: I never stop talking, my best friend is a green ogre, and I married a dragon. Who am I?
hints: I'm from an animated film.
My ogre friend lives in a swamp.
My name is just what I am.
questions.fun_fact: In the English version of the film, Donkey is voiced by the comedian Eddie Murphy.

quality.notes: Calling him an 'animal' in the description rules out the Gingerbread Man and Pinocchio, leaving only Puss in Boots as a rival. Shrek is from 2001, so a few of today's 6-year-olds may not know it; 2 fits better than 1.

questions.description: A small triangle with a big say in how your pants turn out.
questions.question: What does a tailor use this for?
hints: Tailors use it before they cut.
It leaves a mark that brushes off easily.
It shows where the scissors should go.

media.note: A clear photo of flat triangular tailor's chalk pieces, ideally on plain fabric, without lines that show a cutting pattern.

questions.fun_fact: Some tailor's chalk is made of wax, and its marks melt away when you iron the fabric.

quality.notes: Fair and correct, but not very exciting. Commons should have a clear photo of tailor's chalk. The fact that it's a tailor's tool makes 'marking' easy to guess.

questions.description: A job where the dress code includes a hat, an apron and a few extra holes.
questions.question: Riddle: “I live in a pineapple under the sea, and I work at the Krusty Krab.” What is my job called?
hints: I work in a kitchen.
My favorite tool is a spatula.
I make Krabby Patties on a hot grill.
questions.fun_fact: SpongeBob SquarePants first appeared on TV in 1999.

quality.notes: Young kids may not know the job title 'fry cook', and it translates loosely ('cocinero'). The 'Riddle:' label at the start isn't needed. Squidward is the cashier, which makes that a good wrong answer.

questions.description: Proof that ice cream can be a drink if you're patient enough with a straw.
questions.question: What is this cold, thick drink, shown up close?
hints: It is a classic at burger restaurants.
It often comes in vanilla, chocolate or strawberry.
It is made by blending milk with ice cream.

media.note: Close-up of a creamy milkshake in a glass with a straw, ideally with whipped cream on top; no fruit pieces, no text.

questions.fun_fact: The paper drinking straw was patented in 1888 by Marvin Stone.

quality.notes: Very easy photo question. The fun fact is about straws, not milkshakes. Saying 'cold, thick' in the question already rules out hot chocolate.

questions.description: Chicken putting on a crunchy jacket before going into the hot tub.
questions.question: What is this cooking step called, done before the chicken goes into hot oil?
hints: It gives fried food a crunchy outside.
Fish sticks and chicken nuggets get it too.
A schnitzel gets the same crunchy coat.

media.note: Photo of raw chicken pieces being coated in breadcrumbs, with bowls of egg and crumbs; no text.

questions.fun_fact: Japanese panko crumbs are made from crustless bread, which keeps them light and flaky.

quality.notes: The wording is a bit clumsy and dry. Kids often know the food but not the word 'breading', so this suits young teens and up. The photo is easy to find.

questions.description: Lunch built like a tower, by two very hungry mystery solvers.
questions.question: What super tall snack do Scooby-Doo and Shaggy love to make?
hints: You can take them to school in a lunchbox.
Shaggy piles on everything he finds in the fridge.
They have bread on the top and the bottom.
questions.fun_fact: The sandwich is named after John Montagu, the 4th Earl of Sandwich, an 18th-century British nobleman.

quality.notes: Scooby-Doo is old, but it's still widely known. Hint 3 almost defines a sandwich, which is allowed for a third hint.

questions.description: A drink that started its career by accident, like many great inventions.
questions.question: Legend says I was born when a leaf fell into a Chinese emperor's cup of hot water. Which drink am I?
hints: I am usually drunk hot.
I come in green, black and many other colors.
People drink me from a cup, often with a little bag inside.
questions.fun_fact: After water, tea is the most popular drink in the world.

quality.notes: This is the Shennong legend. 'Leaf' plus 'hot water' makes tea easy to work out. The Forbidden City is from a much later age than the legend, but it's a fine image of China.

questions.description: A wrinkly black pod with a very fancy taste.
questions.question: These dried pods give their flavor to a very popular kind of ice cream. Which flavor?
hints: The ice cream it flavors is usually white or pale yellow.
The pods come from a kind of orchid flower.
It's the most common flavor of ice cream in a cone.

media.note: A clear photo of dried dark vanilla pods (beans). No labels or ice cream.

questions.fun_fact: Vanilla comes from Mexico, where the Totonac people grew it long before Europeans arrived.

quality.notes: Solid. Hint 1 (white or pale yellow ice cream) already almost settles it. Clear vanilla-bean photos are easy to find on Commons. I'd rate it slightly easier than 4.

questions.description: The ancient world's favorite way to shine, cook and light up the night.
questions.question: Ancient Greeks rubbed me on their athletes and burned me in their lamps. Which fruit am I pressed from?
hints: My tree has silvery-green leaves.
A branch of my tree is a symbol of peace.
My fruit can be green or black, and is often put on pizza.
questions.fun_fact: Winners at the ancient Panathenaic Games in Athens won big jars full of olive oil as a prize.

quality.notes: Good riddle. Hint 2 (olive branch for peace) is already strong. Shares a topic with q-0571 (olive crown) but asks a different fact.

questions.description: A club that collected superstars like stickers in an album.
questions.question: Which club had Messi, Neymar and Mbappé in its team at the same time?
hints: The three were teammates for two seasons, from 2021 to 2023.
The club is from France.
It plays its home games in the city of the Eiffel Tower.
questions.fun_fact: Paris Saint-Germain was only founded in 1970, which makes it a very young club next to most of Europe's giants.

quality.notes: The facts are right (2021–23; PSG founded 1970). Football fans of any age know it, but families without a fan may not, so I put it a bit above 5. The 'body_senses' lens tag doesn't fit the question, though that doesn't affect play.

questions.description: The very first World Cup, back when football boots were basically work shoes.
questions.question: Which of these was NOT true of the first World Cup, in Uruguay in 1930?
questions.answer: Teams had to win qualifying games
wrong_answers: All games were played in Montevideo
Uruguay beat Argentina in the final
hints: Getting to Uruguay from Europe meant about two weeks on a ship.
Many European teams said no to the long trip.
FIFA simply invited teams to come.
questions.fun_fact: Uruguay built the Estadio Centenario for the tournament, named for the 100th anniversary of the country's first constitution.

quality.notes: All three true statements check out (13 teams, all games in Montevideo, 4–2 against Argentina). Hints 1–2 point strongly at 'no qualifying'. A NOT-question about statements feels like a school test. The description says 'football boots', a US/UK word clash the house style says to reword. The description is also mild and only half a joke.

questions.description: A victory tradition that would get you strange looks at the supermarket.
questions.question: Winners of a famous race held every May kneel and kiss this strip of old bricks at the finish line. Which race is it?
hints: The track is a big oval in the US.
The whole track was once paved with bricks.
Its nickname is “the Brickyard”.

media.note: Close-up of the strip of bricks across the finish line at Indianapolis Motor Speedway; no visible signs or text naming the track or race.

questions.fun_fact: In 1909 the track was paved with about 3.2 million bricks; today only a one-yard strip remains.

quality.notes: Kissing the bricks is a US tradition. Indy 500 knowledge is mostly American, so it is harder for families elsewhere (international angle). Hint 1 already cuts the options to Indy and Daytona. The essential photo of the brick strip exists, but it may show 'Indianapolis' signs or text, so it needs a careful pick.

questions.description: The king's weekend cabin got slightly out of hand.
questions.question: This huge palace started as a small royal hunting lodge. Near which city does it stand?
hints: French kings lived here until the Revolution began in 1789.
Louis XIV moved the whole royal court here.
It is only about 20 km from the Eiffel Tower.

media.note: A clear wide photo of the Palace of Versailles, ideally aerial or from the gardens, without any signs or captions.

questions.fun_fact: The Hall of Mirrors at Versailles has 357 mirrors.

quality.notes: Paris is the obvious guess for any famous French palace, so players can answer without recognising Versailles. Lyon, Marseille and Bordeaux are weak distractors. Hint 1 simplifies: Louis XV did not live at Versailles in his early years. The hunting-lodge and 357-mirror facts are correct.

questions.description: A snack so big you'd need a crane to lift it out of the oven.
questions.question: This close-up shows a treat that once set a world record at over 18,000 kg (40,000 lb). What is it?
hints: It's a sweet snack, often baked at home.
It tastes great dunked in a glass of milk.
It's round, flat and crunchy, with sweet dark bits inside.

media.note: A close-up of the surface of one chocolate chip cookie, with the chocolate chips clearly visible.

questions.fun_fact: The record cookie was baked in North Carolina, USA, in 2003 and was about 31 m (102 ft) wide.

quality.notes: The 2003 North Carolina record (102 ft, about 40,000 lb) is correct. The essential close-up makes this an easy recognition question, which suits difficulty 2.

questions.description: Like your chores: once one falls over, all the others follow.
questions.question: Domino-toppling record setters line up millions of tiles like these. In which country were dominoes invented?
hints: They reached Europe only in the 1700s, from far away.
They were invented in Asia.
The same country gave the world paper, tea and kites.
questions.fun_fact: On Domino Day 2009 in the Netherlands, about 4.5 million dominoes fell in one chain reaction.

quality.notes: Chinese dominoes are the oldest known. European dominoes first appeared in 18th-century Italy, possibly on their own, so the Italy distractor has a small claim. Domino Day 2009 had about 4.49 million, so the fun fact is correct.

questions.description: The only keyboard where grown-ups type with one finger.
questions.question: When you pay with a bank card, what do you type on a keypad like this one?
hints: Nobody else should see it.
It usually has four digits.
It's called a PIN, and you should never share it.

media.note: A card payment terminal or ATM number keypad, with no text on the screen.

questions.fun_fact: John Shepherd-Barron, who helped invent the cash machine, said he picked four-digit codes because his wife could only remember four.

quality.notes: US gas-station terminals do ask for a ZIP/postal code, so the “postal code” distractor is weakly arguable. The Shepherd-Barron anecdote about his wife is correct. Same topic as history-of-money-15 (ATM gives cash), but a different fact.

questions.description: He keeps his money so tight that even his coins feel cold.
questions.question: In a famous Christmas story, a stingy old man is visited by three ghosts. In which century was the book written?
hints: The author also wrote “Oliver Twist”.
It came out the same year as the first Christmas cards were sold.
Charles Dickens wrote it in the 1840s.
questions.fun_fact: Dickens published “A Christmas Carol” in December 1843, and the first copies sold out within days.

quality.notes: 1843 and the first Christmas cards (Henry Cole, 1843) are correct. Asking for a century is a bit dry. Hint 3 gives the decade, which is allowed.

questions.description: Furniture with a much bigger job than holding books.
questions.question: In this Amsterdam house, Anne Frank's family hid during World War II. What did the bookcase on its stairs secretly cover?
hints: One of the family's helpers built it.
The bookcase could swing open.
Behind it were stairs up to the Secret Annex.
questions.fun_fact: Anne Frank's diary has been translated into more than 70 languages.

quality.notes: Facts are correct (Voskuijl built the bookcase, translated into 70+ languages). The theme is sensitive but handled tactfully. “Hidden bookcase → secret door” is easy to work out, and “Anne's diary and pens” is a weak distractor. The lens is set to “language”, which is odd.

questions.description: The armor your smile wears every day, even while you eat candy.
questions.question: It's the hardest material in the human body, it covers the outside of your teeth, and your body can't grow it back. What is it?
hints: You see it every time you smile.
Toothpaste with fluoride helps keep it strong.
It's the shiny white outer layer of a tooth.
questions.fun_fact: Enamel has no living cells, which is why a hole in a tooth can't heal by itself.

quality.notes: Solid question. The dentist image is safe.

questions.description: A sign of great wisdom, or of raising teenagers.
questions.question: Hair like this has lost something it had when its owner was young. What has it lost?
hints: It happens slowly as people get older.
You can see the difference right away.
Some people use dye to bring it back.

media.note: A close-up photo of gray or white hair on a head, no face needed.

questions.fun_fact: Gray hair is often a mix: some strands are white and some still have color, and together they look gray.

quality.notes: Distractors: 'Its water' and 'Its roots' are weak, and the answer is obvious from the photo, but that fits a difficulty of 2.

questions.description: Thousands of bees in one house, and only one of them gets breakfast in bed.
questions.question: In a beehive, one bee lives for years instead of weeks and lays all the eggs. Which bee is it?
hints: There is usually only one of her in the hive.
The others feed and look after her.
She has a royal title.
questions.fun_fact: A queen bee can lay around 2,000 eggs in a single day.

quality.notes: 'A larva' is a weak distractor. The hive-frame image could safely be illustrative, since the queen is hard to spot in it, so decorative is overly cautious.

questions.description: A tiny vampire wearing striped socks.
questions.question: This striped mosquito spreads a disease also called “breakbone fever”. What is it?
hints: It's caused by a virus.
It's common in warm, rainy parts of the world.
Its name starts with a D.

media.note: Close-up of an Aedes aegypti mosquito showing its white-striped legs and body markings.

questions.fun_fact: This mosquito bites mostly during the day, unlike the malaria mosquito, which bites mostly at night.

quality.notes: 'What is it?' could refer to the mosquito or the disease; 'Which disease is it?' would be clearer. Hint 3 (first letter) is a cheap spelling hint. Fun is middling: the question is fairly dry. Dengue is very familiar in tropical regions and less so elsewhere.

questions.description: A coach who explains football with a music playlist.
questions.question: Klopp once said Wenger's Arsenal played football like an orchestra. Which kind of music did he compare his own style to?
hints: Klopp said the orchestra was a quiet song, and he wanted something louder.
His teams run, press and attack nonstop.
Think long hair, electric guitars and loud drums.
questions.fun_fact: Klopp's fast, attacking style became known as “heavy metal football,” and he won the Champions League with Liverpool in 2019.

quality.notes: 'Lullabies' is a joke option that nobody would pick. Hint 1 already suggests 'louder' music, which leaves only heavy metal.

questions.description: Most people his age worry about homework, not European finals.
questions.question: In 2024, Lamine Yamal became the youngest player ever to score at a European Championship. How old was he?
hints: He was still a teenager.
He turned one year older the day before Spain won the final.
He wasn't old enough to drive a car yet.
questions.fun_fact: Yamal scored his record goal against France in the semifinal, and Spain went on to win Euro 2024.

quality.notes: Hint 3 (too young to drive) doesn't travel well: in the US, 16-year-olds can drive. Otherwise the facts check out: he scored at 16 years 362 days and turned 17 the day before the final.

questions.description: A calm face hiding a very crowded trophy cabinet.
questions.question: This coach has won the Champions League more times than any other coach. Who is he?
hints: He won it twice with AC Milan.
He won it three more times with Real Madrid.
His first name is the Italian form of “Charles”.

media.note: A clear photo of Carlo Ancelotti's face, without captions or name text visible.

questions.fun_fact: Ancelotti is also the first coach to win the league title in all five of Europe's biggest leagues: Italy, England, Germany, France and Spain.

quality.notes: Facts check out: 5 titles (Milan 2003 and 2007, Real Madrid 2014, 2022 and 2024), and he has won all five big leagues. The problem is the level. Knowing coaches is niche club-football knowledge. Families worldwide who don't follow club football won't know it, so 8 is too low; 10–11 fits better. The face photo helps fans recognise him. Hint 1 (Milan) narrows it a lot.

questions.description: One of the loudest stadiums on Earth has a surprisingly gentle nickname.
questions.question: Boca Juniors' stadium in Buenos Aires has tall, steep stands that make it box-shaped. Its nickname compares it to a box of what?
hints: It's a box people often give as a present.
What's inside is sweet.
Think of little treats wrapped in shiny paper.
questions.fun_fact: Fans say La Bombonera's stands shake when Boca supporters jump together.

quality.notes: La Bombonera means a box of chocolates (bonbons), which is right. Hint 2 (“What's inside is sweet”) already settles it, which is too strong for a second hint. For Spanish-speaking players the nickname is well known, so it is easier for them. “Cigars” is a slightly odd choice for a family game, but harmless.

questions.description: A country that collects World Cup stars like stickers.
questions.question: When Brazil won the 2002 World Cup, it became the first country to have won the World Cup how many times?
hints: Brazil's first win came in 1958, in Sweden.
Brazil also won in 1994, in the USA.
Before 2002, Brazil had won four times.
questions.fun_fact: Brazil is the only country that has played at every World Cup.

quality.notes: Correct. The wording “first country to have won the World Cup how many times?” is clumsy. This is a dry counting question. Hint 3 (“four times before 2002”) is basically arithmetic to the answer, which is allowed for hint 3.

questions.description: A striker who talks about himself like a movie hero, and wins anyway.
questions.question: When I left Paris Saint-Germain in 2016, I said “I came like a king, left like a legend.” Who am I?
hints: I'm very tall and famous for acrobatic kicks.
I also played for Juventus, Barcelona and AC Milan.
My first name starts with Z.
questions.fun_fact: When Zlatan left PSG he was the club's top scorer of all time, a record later broken by Cavani and then Mbappé.

quality.notes: The quote and the top-scorer fun fact are both correct. All three distractors played for PSG, which is good. Hint 1 (very tall, acrobatic kicks) is already a strong pointer.

questions.description: A war on a checkered table where nobody gets hurt, only very quiet.
questions.question: In this game, which piece must you protect: if it gets trapped, you lose?
hints: The game is chess.
It is a slow piece: it moves only one square at a time.
It is the ruler of the board, married to the queen.

media.note: A clear photo of a full chess set standing on a chessboard, all kinds of pieces visible.

questions.fun_fact: The word “checkmate” comes from Persian “shah mat”, which means “the king is helpless”.

quality.notes: Hint 1 (“The game is chess”) just repeats what the photo already shows. This is a plain school-style fact. The description's grammar is awkward (“nobody gets hurt, only very quiet”). The “made_of” axis and the inventions category are an odd fit.

questions.description: The soundtrack of old offices, long before anyone had heard a mouse click.
questions.question: Listen: which old machine makes this sound?
hints: It was used in offices for about 100 years.
It printed letters straight onto paper.
Each key hits the paper, and a bell rings at the end of the line.

media.note: A mechanical typewriter in use: fast clacking keys, the bell ding and the carriage return.

questions.fun_fact: The QWERTY key layout we still use on computers was first made for typewriters in the 1870s.

quality.notes: Freesound has clear typewriter recordings, and the bell plus carriage return set it apart from a telegraph. No background_query is given; an audio question needs one.

questions.description: A tiny machine that keeps working hard even while you sleep.
questions.question: This close-up shows part of a small object. What is the object?
hints: Many people wear it every day.
Its hands keep moving round and round.
It tells you the time, right on your arm.

media.note: A close-up of an analog wristwatch face: hands and hour numbers clearly visible, edge of the strap may show; no brand name readable.

questions.fun_fact: Wristwatches became popular with men during the First World War, because soldiers couldn't pull out a pocket watch in battle.

quality.notes: Fun 3: a plain look-and-name question with little surprise. It's close to q-1695 (Omega watch → a watch), but that asks something else. A clear wristwatch photo is easy to find, but a close-up of an analog watch face gives the answer away almost at once, so this is really a 1.

questions.description: A toy older than electricity, and still not interested in being charged.
questions.question: Which of these toys does NOT need batteries to work?
hints: It flies in the sky.
You hold it on a long string.
It needs a windy day at the beach or in the park.
questions.fun_fact: Kites were invented in China more than 2,000 years ago.

quality.notes: Fun 3: simple and a bit dry, but fine for small kids. The three wrong options are all obviously electronic, so the kite stands out once you think about it, which is fine at this level.

questions.description: An engine idea so loud and stubborn that it is still rumbling 130 years later.
questions.question: “I was a German engineer. In the 1890s I built an engine that lights its fuel just by squeezing air, with no spark.” Who am I?
hints: My engine still powers most big trucks and ships today.
My engine is heavy and strong, and burns a thick, oily fuel.
At the gas station, you can fill up with my last name.
questions.fun_fact: At the 1900 Paris World's Fair, a diesel engine was shown running on peanut oil.

quality.notes: Good distractors. Hint 3 nearly gives it away, which is allowed. q-1181 asks about diesel trains (the fuel), not the inventor, so it only shares a topic. Young teens may need the hints, so I'd put it slightly higher than 8.

questions.description: The only thing in the bathroom with lots of teeth and no bite at all.
questions.question: In the bathroom: a toothbrush is for teeth as a comb is for…?
hints: You use it in the morning to look nice.
It can be long or short, curly or straight.
It grows on top of your head.
questions.fun_fact: Combs are among the oldest tools in the world: people have used them for thousands of years.

quality.notes: Fun 3: a very basic analogy with not much payoff, but fine for 6-year-olds. The description ("lots of teeth and no bite") is a nice joke.

questions.description: The very first Bond villain: a doctor by title, with no plans to cure anyone.
questions.question: Jaws is to his steel teeth as Dr. No is to his…
hints: Dr. No was the villain of the very first Bond film, from 1962.
He lost a body part in an accident with radiation.
He can crush things with his fingers.
questions.fun_fact: Dr. No's metal hands turn out to be his weakness: at the end, he can't grip the slippery pipes and slides into a cooling pool.

quality.notes: The distractors are clever (Largo's eye patch, Scaramanga's golden gun, Blofeld's scar). In the film, Dr. No can't get a grip on the smooth metal frame of the reactor pool, so "slippery pipes" is a slight simplification. Correct 4 because of that.

questions.description: The longest nap in film history, and he still woke up grumpy.
questions.question: In “Austin Powers”, Dr. Evil is frozen in 1967. In which decade does he wake up?
hints: His plan to ask for “one million dollars” sounds silly because prices went up while he slept.
He wakes up in the same decade the first film came out.
He sleeps for 30 years.
questions.fun_fact: Mike Myers played both Austin Powers and Dr. Evil, and based Dr. Evil's voice on TV producer Lorne Michaels.

quality.notes: The facts are right (frozen 1967, wakes 1997; the Lorne Michaels voice). Hint 2 is strong: anyone who knows the film came out in 1997 has the answer. An Austin Powers question in a James Bond subcategory is fine as a parody.

questions.description: Your body's own built-in instrument, and you never need to tune it.
questions.question: I'm a pair hidden in your throat, and I shake hundreds of times a second when you sing. What am I made of?
hints: I sit inside your voice box.
Doctors call me the vocal cords.
You can tighten or relax me, just like your arm when you make a fist.
questions.fun_fact: Men's vocal cords are usually longer than women's, which is why their voices tend to sound deeper.

quality.notes: Mostly right: vocal folds are muscle, ligament and mucous lining, so "muscle and soft tissue" is fair, but correct gets 4 for the simplification. Hint 3 ("like your arm") points straight at muscle. Fun 3: an anatomy question about what something is made of feels like school. It also fits the "language" subcategory only loosely.

questions.description: A clock that speaks fluent pilot.
questions.question: Pilots and sailors around the world use “Zulu time”. What is Zulu time?
wrong_answers: The local time below the plane
The local time in South Africa
hints: It's the same number everywhere on Earth at the same moment.
Zulu is the radio word for Z, and Z stands for a zero line on the map.
That line runs through Greenwich in London.
questions.fun_fact: Every time zone has a letter in the radio alphabet: Zulu is zero, and New York in winter is “Romeo”.

quality.notes: Strong distractors: "local time in South Africa" is a tempting false lead. The fun fact (Romeo = UTC−5) is accurate. Hint 1 already rules out the two local-time options fairly strongly. Most adults would need to reason it out, so 11–12.

questions.description: A family reunion where one guest clearly came to the wrong party.
questions.question: Road signs in Ireland show both English and Irish. Which of these languages is NOT a relative of Irish?
hints: Irish belongs to the Celtic family of languages.
Its closest relative is Scottish Gaelic.
The odd one out is spoken near the border of Spain and France and has no known relatives at all.
questions.fun_fact: Basque is a “language isolate”: nobody has ever proven it is related to any other language on Earth.

quality.notes: Accurate, and the distractors are good: Breton is a well-chosen Celtic option. Hint 3 nearly gives the answer away, which is allowed. The bilingual road sign image is safe. q-1544 (beret, Basques) only shares a topic.

questions.description: A race where trust matters just as much as speed.
questions.question: In Paralympic 100 m races for totally blind runners, how many people run together in each lane?
hints: The runner can't see the track.
Someone helps keep the runner on the right path.
A guide runs alongside, tied to the runner's hand by a short cord.
questions.fun_fact: Since the London 2012 Paralympics, guide runners get a medal too when their athlete wins one.

quality.notes: Decorative is the wrong role here: a running-track image would be safe as illustrative. The 'language' lens tag doesn't fit.

questions.description: An expression that sprinted out of the stadium and straight into the news.
questions.question: People call a close election or game “a photo finish.” What does that mean?
questions.answer: The two sides ended almost exactly level
wrong_answers: The winner was clear long before the end
The result was decided by a vote
The contest was stopped before the end
hints: The expression comes from races on the track.
Sometimes judges can't tell the winner with their own eyes.
A special camera at the line shows who crossed it first by a hair.
questions.fun_fact: A photo-finish camera looks only at a thin slice of the finish line and takes thousands of pictures every second.

quality.notes: The wrong answers are weak: once you hear 'close election', the 'ended level' option is easy to pick. The question is a dry word-meaning item. The phrase 'photo finish' exists in many languages, so it travels well enough.

questions.description: A record you can break even if you finish last.
questions.question: A world record is to the whole world as a personal best is to…
hints: Think about whose times are being compared.
Nobody else's results count for this one.
It's your own best ever, across your whole life.
questions.fun_fact: Athletes call it a PB, and they also keep a “season's best” for their top result of the current year.

quality.notes: 'One season' is a bit close to the real 'season's best'. The analogy is easy to work out and not very exciting.

questions.description: A green island floating in a red sea of rubber.
questions.question: Which of these athletics events does NOT take place in the area inside the running track?
hints: The area inside the track is for field events.
Three of these are throwing or jumping.
The odd one out is a race.
questions.fun_fact: Discus and hammer throwers throw from inside a tall net cage, so a bad throw can't fly into the crowd.

quality.notes: The answer stands out as the only race among the options, so the question can be solved by spotting the different one. Hint 2 nearly gives the answer away.

questions.description: Beat a trainer, get paid, buy more Poké Balls: the circle of life.
questions.question: You win this money by beating trainers in Pokémon games, spend it at Poké Marts, and lose some when you black out. What is it called?
hints: Its name mixes the word Poké with a real currency.
That real currency is used in the USA.
Its symbol looks like a P with two lines across it.
questions.fun_fact: The Pokédollar symbol looks like the Russian ruble sign ₽, but with two lines through the P instead of one.

quality.notes: Easy for Pokémon players but harder for families who don't play. Hint 2's 'used in the USA' is loose, since dollars are used in many countries. The 'school' lens tag doesn't fit.

questions.description: He'd sell his own shell if the price were right.
questions.question: SpongeBob's boss, who loves money more than anything, is this kind of animal. Which one?
hints: He runs a restaurant under the sea.
He walks sideways.
His name gives it away: Mr. K…
questions.fun_fact: Mr. Krabs keeps the very first dollar he ever earned framed on his office wall.

quality.notes: The coral reef image could happen to show a crab, a small risk.

questions.description: Steady hands, sharp tools and the patience of a monk.
questions.question: Banknote engravers carve tiny portraits into steel plates by hand. About how long does it take to train a master engraver?
hints: It's much longer than learning to drive.
There are only a few such engravers in the world.
It takes about as long as a child spends in school from age 6 to 16.
questions.fun_fact: One portrait can take an engraver months, and a single slip of the tool can ruin the whole plate.

quality.notes: The '~10 years' figure is often quoted (for example for US engravers), but it varies by country and is approximate. In an estimate question like this, the longest option is the natural guess. The topic is fairly dry.

questions.description: A greeting that keeps your cheeks busier than a hamster's.
questions.question: In Spain, friends often greet each other like this. How many cheek kisses do they usually give?
hints: It's more than one.
It's fewer than four.
You start on one cheek, switch to the other, and that's it.
questions.fun_fact: In parts of France, the number of greeting kisses changes from town to town, from one up to four.

quality.notes: The question is about one country's greeting custom. It is widely known, but it still leans on Spain, and in much of Latin America people give one kiss, so the answer isn't obvious everywhere. Hints 1 and 2 together leave only 2 or 3, which is strong for early hints. Not very surprising as a fact. The 'history' lens doesn't fit. A cheek-kiss photo is fine.

questions.description: Who needs a phone when you have a really deep valley and a lot of breath?
questions.question: I turn Spanish words into high and low notes that can carry for kilometers across the valleys of La Gomera. What am I?
hints: Shepherds used me to talk across steep canyons in the Canary Islands.
The island's steep valleys carry my sound much farther than a shout.
I'm called Silbo, and children on the island still learn me at school.
questions.fun_fact: Silbo Gomero is on UNESCO's list of the world's intangible cultural heritage.

quality.notes: 'Lots of breath' in the description leans a little toward whistling. Drum languages also turn words into high and low notes, but 'Spanish words' and La Gomera settle it. Adults can partly reason toward the answer, so it's about an 11.

questions.description: Ancient email: heavy, made of mud, and somehow still delivered.
questions.question: Letters like this one, sent to Egypt's pharaoh around 1350 BC, were written in Akkadian. Why Akkadian?
questions.answer: It was the language of diplomacy
wrong_answers: It was the pharaoh's mother tongue
It was the language of Egypt's priests
hints: The senders and the pharaoh spoke different languages at home.
Kings of Babylon, the Hittites and Egypt all wrote to each other in it.
It played the role French later played between European courts.

media.note: A photo of one of the Amarna letters: a clay tablet with cuneiform writing.

questions.fun_fact: The Amarna letters were found in Egypt in 1887, and more than 350 of these clay tablets survive.

quality.notes: The distractors are weak: 'pharaoh's mother tongue' and 'Egypt ruled all of Mesopotamia' are easy to rule out with basic knowledge, so players can reason to 'diplomacy'. 'Egypt ruled…' also has a different form from the other 'It was…' options. Amarna tablet photos are easy to find on Wikimedia Commons.

questions.description: A country famous for chocolate, clocks and very careful decisions.
questions.question: Swiss coins like this one say “Helvetia”, an old Latin name for Switzerland. Why use Latin?
questions.answer: So no national language is favored
wrong_answers: Latin is the language of Swiss courts
The first Swiss coins came from Rome
To make the coins harder to fake
hints: Switzerland has more than one official language.
People there speak German, French, Italian and Romansh.
Latin is neutral: none of the Swiss speak it at home.

media.note: A Swiss franc coin where the word HELVETIA is clearly readable.

questions.fun_fact: The “CH” on Swiss cars and websites also comes from Latin: Confoederatio Helvetica.

quality.notes: Neutrality between the national languages is the usual explanation. Hint 2 already points strongly to the answer. A coin showing HELVETIA is easy to find.

questions.description: The story behind the clothes you wear to dream.
questions.question: The word “pajamas” comes from clothes like these from South Asia. What were they first worn for?
hints: The word means “leg clothing” in Persian.
They were loose, light trousers, made for a hot climate.
The British in India only later turned them into nightwear.
questions.fun_fact: British people in colonial India brought pajamas home in the 1800s, and they slowly replaced the nightshirt.

quality.notes: The surprising answer is a nice twist. The kurta pajama photo shows people dressed for the day, which is a mild nudge toward the answer. 'Sleeping at night' is a good trap option.

questions.description: A tiny athlete who trains all night while you sleep.
questions.question: About how long does a pet hamster usually live?
hints: It's a small animal, and small animals often have short lives.
It's longer than a school year.
It's much shorter than a cat's or a dog's life.
questions.fun_fact: A hamster can run several kilometers (a few miles) in one night on its wheel.

quality.notes: A plain pet-care fact without much surprise, so fun is only acceptable.

questions.description: A noisy group chat that doesn't need a single phone.
questions.question: Listen: which animal makes this sound?
hints: It lives on the African savanna.
In “The Lion King”, three of them work for Scar.
People say this animal “laughs”.

media.note: The giggling/laughing call of a spotted hyena.

questions.fun_fact: A hyena's “laugh” tells other hyenas how old it is and how important it is in the group.

quality.notes: Hyena giggle recordings exist on Freesound and Wikimedia Commons.

questions.description: Somebody on the savanna has very big news to share.
questions.question: Listen! Which animal makes this loud call?
hints: It's the biggest animal that lives on land.
It has big ears and long white tusks.
Its long nose is called a trunk.

media.note: An elephant trumpeting call.

questions.fun_fact: An elephant's trunk has tens of thousands of muscles and can pick up a single peanut.

questions.description: A gesture that speaks straight from the chest.
questions.question: Around the world, people put a hand on their heart to send a message. Which one is NOT a usual meaning?
hints: Think about the feelings this gesture usually shows.
The odd one out would need a very different gesture.
For that one, people usually tap their wrist or wave their hand quickly.
questions.fun_fact: In many countries, people put a hand on their heart after a handshake to show they really mean the greeting.

quality.notes: 'Hurry up!' stands out at once from the three emotional meanings, so the distractors are weak. Fun is low: the question is trivially easy and not surprising. The decorative 'heart shape hands' image takes the heart from the wording, not the real gesture. An illustrative 'hand on heart' photo would be safe, so decorative is the wrong role.

questions.description: Dinner is served, and so are the rules.
questions.question: Which of these is NOT seen as good table manners in many countries?
questions.answer: Resting your elbows on the table
hints: Three of these would make a grandparent proud.
The odd one out is something people do when they feel tired or relaxed.
It's a joint halfway along your arm.
questions.fun_fact: In Japan, people say “itadakimasu” before eating, a way of giving thanks for the food.

quality.notes: The elbows rule is mostly a Western one, but saying "in many countries" covers that. Distractors: the three wrong options are all plainly polite, so kids spot the odd one out at once. Fun: reads like a plain school-style quiz. The fun fact about “itadakimasu” is a nice global touch, though it has nothing to do with elbows.

questions.description: Your lips are the door, and the food party stays inside.
questions.question: Why do people chew with their mouth closed?
hints: It's about the other people at the table.
Seeing food being chewed is not nice.
It's good manners.
questions.fun_fact: Chewing with your mouth closed also keeps the noise down: no loud smacking sounds!

quality.notes: Distractors: the wrong answers are silly, which suits level 1 but leaves almost no challenge. Fun: very obvious and preachy. Hint 3 (“It's good manners”) is basically the answer reworded. The axis "three_facts" doesn't match the question.

questions.description: Mwah, mwah! Or maybe just a polite nod.
questions.question: In which of these countries is a kiss on the cheek NOT a usual greeting between friends?
hints: There, people usually keep a little space when they greet.
People there often bow instead.
It's famous for sushi and anime.
questions.fun_fact: In France, the number of cheek kisses changes by region: two in Paris, but up to four in some places!

quality.notes: Cheek kisses are common in all three distractor countries, so they are fair. Hint 3 (sushi and anime) gives the answer away, but that is allowed for hint 3. The Japan candidates ask different facts. The lens "history" is a poor fit.

questions.description: A greeting where your hand goes up, but not to wave hello.
questions.question: Which people are best known for greeting each other with a stiff hand raised to the forehead?
hints: They often wear uniforms.
They march in parades.
They work in an army.
questions.fun_fact: Not every army salutes the same way: in Poland, soldiers salute with just two fingers.

quality.notes: Unambiguous: police officers and scouts also salute, but "best known" and the four options make it clear enough. Fun: simple and a bit dry; the Polish two-finger salute in the fun fact helps. Decorative flag image is fine, since a salute photo would show the answer.

questions.description: Big blue fur, big brain, and the best manners of any monster on the team.
questions.question: Beast first appeared in X-Men #1, together with the original team. In which decade did that comic come out?
hints: It came out during the Cold War.
Stan Lee and Jack Kirby made it in the same decade as Spider-Man's first comic.
Think of the decade of the Beatles.
questions.fun_fact: In his first comics, Beast wasn't blue or furry at all: he got his fur in 1972 and turned blue in 1975.

quality.notes: X-Men #1 came out in 1963, so the answer is right. Correct: the fun fact's dates for Beast's fur (1972) and blue color (1975) are roughly right but simplified; he was first drawn with gray fur. Age fit and fun: this is mostly date memorization, which young teens rarely have; most people would only guess. Hint 1 (Cold War) also fits the 1980s, so it is weak.

questions.description: A cartoon so small and friendly that even the bad guys seem to need a nap.
questions.question: I wear red and blue, I shoot webs, and in a cartoon for little kids I team up with two young spider friends. Who am I?
hints: I can climb up walls.
A spider gave me my powers.
My nickname is Spidey.
questions.fun_fact: Marvel's “Spidey and His Amazing Friends” started on Disney Junior in 2021 and was made for preschool kids.

quality.notes: "Shoots webs" gives the answer away on its own, which is fine for level 1. The fun fact is correct (Disney Junior, 2021). The lens "history" is odd.

questions.description: Before he was a grumpy X-Man, he was a grumpy government employee.
questions.question: Before Logan joined the X-Men in the comics, he worked as a secret agent for which country's government?
hints: It is one of the largest countries in the world by area.
It has two official languages, English and French.
Its flag shows a red maple leaf.
questions.fun_fact: Wolverine first appeared fighting the Hulk, in a comic where he was sent by the Canadian government.

quality.notes: The answer is correct: Department H, then Weapon X; his first full appearance was Hulk #181. The illustrative wolverine animal photo is safe, unless it happens to show a Canadian sign. Hint 1 ("one of the largest countries") also fits the US, but it is only hint 1.

questions.description: Some heroes fly, some swing, and some just throw things very, very hard.
questions.question: Spider-Man shoots webs, as Captain America throws his…
hints: It's round.
It has a star in the middle.
He uses it to block attacks, then throws it.
questions.fun_fact: In his very first comic in 1941, Captain America's shield was not round but shaped like a badge.

quality.notes: Same analogy template as marvel-superheroes-6 (Thor and his hammer), with a different answer, and "Hammer" appears here as a distractor. The fun fact about the badge-shaped first shield is true.

questions.description: A magic spell with more side effects than a medicine box.
questions.question: In “Spider-Man: No Way Home”, a spell to make the world forget Peter Parker goes wrong. Who comes through?
hints: The visitors all know who Peter Parker is.
Some of them came from older Spider-Man films.
Doctor Octopus and the Green Goblin were among them.
questions.fun_fact: In “No Way Home”, three different actors who played Spider-Man appear together on screen.

quality.notes: The answer is slightly simplified: the villains arrive first and the other Spider-Men come later, but it is fair. The answer is the longest and most specific option, so it stands out a little.

questions.description: A warning system better than any alarm clock.
questions.question: I get a tingling feeling in my head that warns me of danger just before it happens. Who am I?
hints: I live in New York.
I got my powers from an animal.
My friends call me Spidey.
questions.fun_fact: Spider-Man's danger warning is called his spider-sense, and in the comics it even helps him dodge in the dark.

quality.notes: Same answer as marvel-superheroes-2, but it asks a different fact (spider-sense). Hint 2 (powers from an animal) points strongly to Spider-Man.

questions.description: A grumpy hero with claws, big sideburns and a very wild haircut.
questions.question: Storm is to controlling the weather as Wolverine is to…
hints: It helps him survive almost anything.
It also makes him age very slowly.
Cuts on his skin close in seconds.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to his healing power, Wolverine is over 100 years old in the comics but still looks middle-aged.

quality.notes: The description is a noun phrase, not a full sentence. It also mostly repeats who Wolverine is rather than adding a joke. The answer is a bit longer and more specific than the other options. Every distractor is another X-Men power (Professor X, Cyclops), which is good.

questions.description: Delicious, crunchy, and your dentist's least favorite topic of conversation.
questions.question: I'm tasty and easy to grab, full of fat, salt and sugar but low in vitamins. What do people call me?
hints: Your parents probably want you to eat less of me.
Chips, candy and sugary soda are good examples of me.
My name says I'm worth about as much as garbage.
questions.fun_fact: Your taste buds love salt, sugar and fat because long ago they were rare and helped people survive.

quality.notes: Comfort food can also be fatty, salty and sweet, but its definition is about emotion, so this is acceptable. Hint 3 depends on the English word “junk”. It mostly works in other languages too (chatarra), but not perfectly. This is a fairly dry definition question.

questions.description: Your body's plumbing, and today it has a small traffic jam.
questions.question: “When a band is tied tight around your arm before a blood test, we swell up below it, because blood can't flow back to the heart.” What are we?
hints: We carry blood toward the heart, not away from it.
We have little valves so blood doesn't flow backward.
Nurses take blood from us, often in the crook of your elbow.
questions.fun_fact: In 1628, William Harvey used almost the same arm-band trick to help prove that blood goes around the body in a circle.

quality.notes: At about 170 characters, the question is longer than the guideline. The fun fact about Harvey's ligature experiment is accurate and a nice touch.

questions.description: Every runner's favorite way to look busy before the starting gun.
questions.question: What is this runner doing before the race?
hints: The runner is standing still and holding one position.
It makes muscles less stiff.
Cats do this every time they wake up.

media.note: A clear photo of a runner holding a stretch, e.g. standing and pulling one foot back toward the buttocks (quad stretch).

questions.fun_fact: The big full-body stretch that cats, dogs and people do after a nap has a scientific name: “pandiculation”.

quality.notes: The answer is a general activity, while the distractors are named exercises, so the forms don't match well. A photo of a stretch is easy to find. The question itself is dry, though the fun fact about pandiculation helps.

questions.description: Taking a seat has never been this speedy.
questions.question: I have a seat and two big wheels, and I help people who can't walk get around. What am I?
hints: You sit on me, not stand.
People push my wheels with their hands.
My name is a chair plus wheels.
questions.fun_fact: Wheelchair basketball has been played at the Paralympic Games since the very first ones in 1960.

quality.notes: This is very easy and not very surprising. A photo of an accessible ramp may show the wheelchair symbol, but the decorative image is blurred, so the risk is low. The overlap with rugby-10 is only a shared topic.

questions.description: A doctor whose job title is a bit of a tongue twister.
questions.question: A neurologist treats problems in which group of body parts?
hints: These parts carry messages around your body.
They let you feel pain and move your muscles.
Together they form the nervous system.
questions.fun_fact: Some nerve signals travel at over 100 m (330 ft) per second, which is about 360 km/h (224 mph).

quality.notes: “Neuro” sounds like “nerves”, which helps players guess. The description's tongue-twister joke is weak. A reflex hammer would work fine as an illustrative image, so decorative is a needlessly cautious choice. The question is fairly dry and school-like. human-body-5 asks a different fact.

questions.description: Camping's version of a hotel room, just without room service.
questions.question: It is often filled with down feathers, it is rated for how cold a night it can handle, and one shape is called “mummy”. What is it?
hints: You use it at night.
Campers take it into a tent.
You zip yourself into it.
questions.fun_fact: The narrow mummy shape keeps you warmer because there is less empty air inside for your body to heat up.

quality.notes: A duvet is also filled with down and rated for warmth, so only the “mummy” clue settles it. Hint 1 fits a duvet as well. The illustrative image query (hiking trail) is only loosely connected to the question.

questions.description: Winter fashion that is mostly about not disappearing into the ground.
questions.question: Look at the photo: what kind of winter gear is this?
hints: You wear them on your feet.
They stop you from sinking into deep, soft snow.
They spread your weight over a big, flat area, like a duck's webbed feet.

media.note: A clear photo of a pair of traditional wooden snowshoes with webbing, not being worn.

questions.fun_fact: The snowshoe hare got its name because its huge furry back feet work just like snowshoes.

quality.notes: Wikimedia Commons is very likely to have a clear photo of traditional wooden snowshoes. Crampons are a good distractor.

questions.description: The tea on top of the world is never quite hot enough.
questions.question: I'm a pot of water on top of Mount Everest, and I boil at only about 70 °C (158 °F). Why?
hints: It's about the air, but not about its temperature.
The higher you go, the less air is above you.
Pressure cookers do the opposite to boil water hotter.
questions.fun_fact: Because water boils at a lower temperature up high, pasta and rice take much longer to cook on big mountains.

quality.notes: “Gravity is weaker” is very slightly true at the summit, but it is not the reason, so this is acceptable. Having the pot speak as “I” is a slightly awkward riddle frame. The distractors are strong and invite reasoning.

questions.description: The world's most crowded place to set an alarm clock.
questions.question: Every summer, crowds climb Mount Fuji in Japan during the night. What do most of them want to see at the top?
hints: It happens early in the morning.
Many climbers start walking around midnight to get there in time.
It's the first light of a new day.
questions.fun_fact: The sunrise seen from the top of Mount Fuji has its own name in Japanese: “goraiko”.

quality.notes: The alarm-clock description and the night climb point strongly to morning, and a 'Mount Fuji' search often returns sunrise shots. A safer query would be 'Mount Fuji trail climbers'. It's a different fact from q-0199, which asks to identify Fuji.

questions.description: A greenhouse so big it had room for all the world's gadgets.
questions.question: London's Great Exhibition, the first world's fair, showed off inventions in a giant glass hall, the Crystal Palace. In which decade?
hints: Queen Victoria opened it.
Trains were spreading fast, but cars didn't exist yet.
It was right in the middle of the 19th century.
questions.fun_fact: Its profits helped build London's museum district in South Kensington, home of the Natural History Museum, the Science Museum and the V&A.

quality.notes: The wrong decades are far apart: once you know it's Victorian, or that Crystal Palace was built of glass and iron, 1850s stands out. It feels like a dry date question. An illustrative image (a Crystal Palace engraving without dates) could have worked instead of a decorative one. The 'colombia' lens tag doesn't fit.

questions.description: It's shiny, it's loud, and it never misses a parade.
questions.question: How many valves does a standard trumpet have?
hints: It is fewer than the fingers on one hand.
The player uses one hand only to press them.
The thumb stays out of it, and so does the little finger.
questions.fun_fact: With just three valves and the shape of the lips, a trumpet player can play every note of the scale.

quality.notes: Few 13-year-olds know the valve count unless they play brass, so 7 looks too low. It's a plain counting fact. The 'scenario' tag doesn't match the question.

questions.description: Small enough for your pocket, loud enough for a whole dance floor.
questions.question: Listen: which instrument is playing?
hints: It is played with the fingers.
It fits in the palm of your hand and comes in pairs.
Flamenco dancers from Spain click them.

media.note: Solo castanets clicking in a rhythm, no other instruments.

questions.fun_fact: A player usually holds a higher-pitched pair in the right hand and a lower one in the left.

quality.notes: Freesound very likely has a solo castanets recording. The background_query field is missing; it's needed for audio questions.

questions.description: A song about scrubbing floors that somehow makes you want to dance.
questions.question: In the musical “Annie”, who sings “It's the Hard-Knock Life” while scrubbing floors for the strict Miss Hannigan?
hints: They are children.
They all sleep in one big room in a New York home.
Annie herself is one of them, until a rich man takes her in.
questions.fun_fact: Annie started as a newspaper comic strip, “Little Orphan Annie”, first printed in 1924.

quality.notes: Annie is a US Broadway story and less known in many countries. Once you know Annie is an orphan, the other options are easy to drop. A Broadway marquee photo may show show titles, possibly 'Annie'. The 'history' lens tag doesn't fit.

questions.description: A piece of music with a French name and a very specific job.
questions.question: A musical begins with the orchestra playing the overture. When does the orchestra play the “entr'acte”?
hints: The show is not over yet when it plays.
Its French name means “between the acts”.
It opens the second act.
questions.fun_fact: Many entr'actes are a quick medley of the show's best tunes, to remind the audience what they loved in the first act.

quality.notes: You can work out the answer from the French word, which is nice, but it's a dry theater-term question. Hint 2 translates the term and nearly gives the answer. The answer_kind tag 'number' is wrong.

questions.description: Champagne, waltzes and plots so silly that nobody minds.
questions.question: Offenbach's “Orpheus in the Underworld” and Strauss's “Die Fledermaus” are light, funny stage works of which kind?
hints: It was a big hit in Paris and Vienna in the 1800s.
Gilbert and Sullivan wrote famous ones in English.
Its name means “little opera” in Italian.
questions.fun_fact: The famous can-can dance tune comes from Offenbach's “Orpheus in the Underworld”.

quality.notes: Facts are right. The description is a fragment, not a full sentence. It is also more of a mood than a joke. The question reads like a dry genre label test, though the can-can fun fact helps. Hint 3 nearly translates the answer, which is allowed. Probably a 12 rather than a 13.

questions.description: A skirt that sticks out like it got a big surprise.
questions.question: I'm a stiff, puffy skirt that sticks straight out, and ballerinas wear me when they dance. What am I?
hints: I am often pink or white.
I'm made of many layers of thin net.
My name is the same short word said twice.
questions.fun_fact: A classic stiff tutu can have more than ten layers of net.

quality.notes: Easy, fair kids' riddle, but not very surprising. The description is a fragment and just repeats the question's 'skirt that sticks out'. Ballet-studio decorative image is fine. It differs from the ballet-shoe candidates.

questions.description: Opening night is just the tip of a very big iceberg.
questions.question: In a musical, actors first win their parts at an audition. What comes next, before opening night?
hints: It takes many weeks.
The cast learns songs, steps and lines.
The last one is called the “dress” one.
questions.fun_fact: A big Broadway musical usually rehearses for about four to six weeks before its first preview.

quality.notes: Dry 'what comes next' question. All three wrong answers happen during or after a show, so they are easy to rule out by logic. The Broadway rehearsal time in the fun fact is roughly right.

questions.description: Even the Nobel committee likes a surprise, and this winner didn't even show up to collect it.
questions.question: Bob Dylan won the 2016 Nobel Prize in Literature and skipped the ceremony in Stockholm. What kind of writing won it?
hints: His work first became famous in the 1960s, long before the prize.
Most people know his work through their ears, not by reading it.
He usually performs it himself with a guitar and a harmonica.
questions.fun_fact: Dylan didn't go to Stockholm in December, so the singer Patti Smith performed one of his songs at the ceremony instead.

quality.notes: The description repeats the question's 'skipped the ceremony' instead of adding a joke. Young teens may not know who Bob Dylan is, but a Nobel for songs is a fun surprise. The Patti Smith fact is correct.

questions.description: Blood with a passport that gets it into almost every body.
questions.question: In an emergency, doctors can give type O negative blood to almost any patient. What are people with this blood type called?
hints: Blood banks are always especially happy to see these people.
Their red blood cells carry no A, B or Rh markers that could upset a patient's body.
People with type AB positive have the opposite title: they can take blood from everyone.
questions.fun_fact: Karl Landsteiner won the 1930 Nobel Prize in Medicine for discovering blood groups, which made blood transfusions safe.

quality.notes: Correct. The Nobel link only appears in the fun fact. 'Living donors' and 'Plasma donors' are weak distractors, and hint 3 rules out 'Universal recipients'. Feels like a school-biology question. It differs from q-1312 (Rh null).

questions.description: A room full of Swedish professors deciding who gets the phone call of their life.
questions.question: Besides economics, which two Nobel Prizes does the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences award?
hints: The academy is full of scientists, so think of science subjects.
They are the first two prizes named in Alfred Nobel's will.
Marie Curie won one of each.
questions.fun_fact: The Peace Prize is the odd one out: it is chosen by a Norwegian committee and handed out in Oslo.

quality.notes: Correct. Two distractors each contain one right subject, which is fair but fiddly. 'Literature and Peace' is easy to rule out from 'Academy of Sciences'. Knowing that the Karolinska picks Medicine is a niche committee fact: dry, and harder than 11.

questions.description: The prize that crashed Alfred Nobel's party almost 70 years late.
questions.question: It was first given in 1969 and Alfred Nobel's will never mentions it, yet people call it a Nobel Prize. Which one?
hints: It was not among the first prizes handed out in 1901.
Sweden's central bank pays for it.
Its winners study money, markets and trade.
questions.fun_fact: Its official name is “The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel”.

quality.notes: Correct (set up in 1968, first given in 1969). It is a satisfying 'gotcha' fact. The Alfred Nobel portrait is a safe image.

questions.description: A medicine found in a handful of dirt that turned into a gift for millions.
questions.question: Ivermectin, honored by the 2015 Nobel Prize in Medicine, protects millions of people from river blindness. What does it kill?
hints: The culprit is spread by the bites of small black flies.
Antibiotics can't kill this disease's main culprit.
Vets give the same drug to dogs against heartworm.
questions.fun_fact: Satoshi Ōmura found the bacteria that make the drug's raw ingredient in a soil sample from near a golf course in Japan.

quality.notes: Facts are right (black flies, heartworm, Ōmura's golf-course soil sample). The answer stands out in form: 'Parasitic worms' against three 'Harmful …' options. The overlap candidates with 'Japan' as the answer don't matter here.

questions.description: The fish have seen plenty of tourists, but this kind still makes them stare.
questions.question: Visitors to coral reefs all over the world love using gear like this. What is it for?
hints: You use it under the water, not on top of it.
It lets you breathe while you swim with the fish.
You wear a mask, fins and an air tank.

media.note: Close-up of a scuba diving air tank with regulator and hose.

questions.fun_fact: “Scuba” started as an abbreviation for “self-contained underwater breathing apparatus”.

quality.notes: Fine as a 2, but dry. A tank in the photo plus “coral reefs” in the text makes the answer obvious on its own. Surfing, sailing and water skiing are easy to rule out because they all happen on top of the water. The lens is tagged “colombia”, but nothing in the question is about Colombia.

questions.description: Your eyes are so slow that a pile of photos turns into a movie.
questions.question: To trick your eyes into seeing smooth motion, how many still pictures per second does a classic cinema film show?
hints: It's an even number.
It's fewer than 30.
It's two dozen.
questions.fun_fact: Silent films were often shot at about 16 to 18 pictures per second, one reason people in them seem to rush around when shown today.

quality.notes: Hint 1 (“even number”) is useless because all four options are even. This is film-nerd knowledge more than school knowledge, so it's slightly harder than 10.

questions.description: The great-great-grandparent of your favorite cartoon, and all it does is spin.
questions.question: The phenakistiscope, a spinning disc with slits that makes drawings seem to move, was invented in which century?
hints: Electric light bulbs didn't exist yet.
Steam trains were just starting to carry passengers.
The first photographs were made in the same decade.
questions.fun_fact: The word “stroboscope” comes from Greek words meaning “whirling” and “to look”.

quality.notes: The phenakistiscope dates from 1832. Hint 3 (“first photographs in the same decade”) is a stretch: Niépce's first photo is from the 1820s, and Daguerre and Talbot only arrive at the end of the 1830s. The fun fact is about the word “stroboscope”, not the phenakistiscope, so it misses the topic. The question itself is a dry date question.

questions.description: An object that tells your mirror a completely different story.
questions.question: A 3D-printed tube looks round when seen directly but square in a mirror. It came second in the 2016 Best Illusion of the Year contest. Which country is its creator from?
hints: The country is in Asia.
It's a nation of islands.
The creator is mathematician Kokichi Sugihara, from the land of sushi and bullet trains.
questions.fun_fact: Sugihara is also famous for slopes on which balls seem to roll uphill, as if pulled by a magnet.

quality.notes: The fact is obscure; nobody knows who won second place in an illusion contest, so the hardness comes from obscurity, not from fewer people being able to work it out. Players can only guess the answer from a Japan stereotype. The question runs about 170 characters, which is long. Japan is a common answer in the pool, but the fact asked here is different.

questions.description: A camera trick older than your great-grandma's TV set.
questions.question: Filmmakers use “forced perspective”, a camera trick that needs no computer. What does it change about things on screen?
wrong_answers: How fast things seem to move
hints: Distance from the camera is the secret.
A friend far away can look small enough to stand on your hand.
Something close to the camera looks huge.
questions.fun_fact: For some scenes in “The Lord of the Rings”, the actors sat at different distances from the camera but seemed to share one table.

quality.notes: Hint 2 practically gives the answer away. “How loud things sound” is a weak distractor, because a camera trick can't change sound.

questions.description: She dressed more movie stars than most closets ever will.
questions.question: Costume designer Edith Head won eight Oscars. In which decade did she win her last one, for the film “The Sting”?
hints: Her career in Hollywood lasted almost 60 years.
“The Sting” starred Paul Newman and Robert Redford.
It was the decade of disco and bell-bottom pants.
questions.fun_fact: Edith Head was nominated 35 times, and many people say she inspired Edna Mode, the tiny costume designer in “The Incredibles”.

quality.notes: This is a dry, minor-date question that most adults can't place. You'd need to know that “The Sting” is from 1973. The Edna Mode fun fact is nice.

questions.description: Fashion tip: dark sunglasses go with everything, even a visitor from another planet.
questions.question: We wear matching suits and dark sunglasses, and we secretly keep track of aliens living on Earth. Our film won an Oscar for its alien makeup. What are we called?
hints: Will Smith is one of us.
We use a flashing gadget that makes people forget what they just saw.
Our name describes the color of our clothes.
questions.fun_fact: Rick Baker shared that makeup Oscar with David LeRoy Anderson, and Baker went on to win seven Oscars for makeup, more than anyone else.

quality.notes: The film is from 1997, so many kids won't know it. Young teens and adults will. The suits plus aliens clue is strong, and hint 3 gives the answer away. The description repeats the sunglasses and alien clues from the question text.

questions.description: A room where a red light means “go”, not “stop”.
questions.question: I'm a room kept almost dark, lit only by a dim red lamp, where people dip paper into trays of liquid. What am I used for?
hints: Far fewer rooms like me are used today than 40 years ago.
The trays hold chemicals that make an image show up on paper.
Film from a camera had to go through this before you could see your pictures.
questions.fun_fact: Darkrooms use red light because black-and-white photo paper barely reacts to it, so the photographer can see without ruining the prints.

quality.notes: Good riddle. Decorative media is justified here, because a darkroom photo would show the answer.

questions.description: A whole planet you can spin with one finger, no rocket needed.
questions.question: On Google Earth you can spin a 3D globe, zoom into your own street and fly over mountains. What is its picture of Earth made of?
hints: The pictures are real, not drawn.
They were taken from high above the ground.
Some cameras that took them orbit around our planet.
questions.fun_fact: Google Earth stitches together millions of separate pictures so smoothly that it looks like one giant photo of the planet.

quality.notes: Distractors are weak: 'Video game graphics' and 'Photos taken from the Moon' are easy to rule out, and the answer is the longest, most specific option. The question is a fairly dry tech fact, and the setup sentence makes it long.

questions.description: The camera's eyeball, minus the blinking.
questions.question: It clicks onto the front of a camera, you twist it to zoom or focus, and it gets a cap when not in use. What is mostly inside it?
hints: Light passes through it on its way into the camera.
Glasses and magnifying glasses work in a similar way.
The pieces bend the light, like the lens in your eye.
questions.fun_fact: A big zoom lens can hold more than 15 separate glass pieces, all lined up perfectly.

quality.notes: Once players work out the object is a lens, the answer follows almost directly, so it feels more like a school test than a surprise. Hint 3 uses the word 'lens', which is fine.

questions.description: A building that has been waving its arms for centuries and never gets tired.
questions.question: Long ago, which building used big spinning sails to grind grain into flour?
hints: It works best on a breezy day.
Its arms turn round and round, slowly.
The Netherlands is famous for them.
questions.fun_fact: Some windmills in the Netherlands are more than 300 years old and still grind flour today.

quality.notes: Solid easy question. Hint 3 (Netherlands) is strong, but that is allowed.

questions.description: Fast enough to win gold, not fast enough to get a speeding ticket.
questions.question: About how fast can the fastest human sprinters run at top speed?
hints: Walking is a lot slower.
A car on a city street goes a bit faster.
It is about as fast as a horse galloping.
questions.fun_fact: Usain Bolt reached about 44 km/h (27 mph) during his world record 100 m race in 2009.

quality.notes: Related to q-0430 (Bolt's record), but it asks a different fact. 40 km/h is a fair 'about' value against Bolt's real peak of ~44.7 km/h.

questions.description: The only dog in the toy box who never needs a leash.
questions.question: In “Toy Story”, what is Slinky Dog's long middle made of?
hints: It can stretch and snap back.
It is a famous toy that can “walk” down stairs.
It is a coiled piece of metal.
questions.fun_fact: The real Slinky spring toy was invented by accident in the 1940s, when an engineer saw a spring “walk” after it fell off a shelf.

quality.notes: Hint 2 basically describes the Slinky, which is fine for a hint. The options are written in lowercase, which is inconsistent with the house style.

questions.description: A ball that has rolled into more films than most actors.
questions.question: I am yellow with a blue stripe and a red star, and I hide in many Pixar films. In which short did I first appear?
hints: The short came out in 1986.
It was one of Pixar's very first films as a studio.
A little desk lamp plays with me, and that lamp now hops in Pixar's logo.
questions.fun_fact: “Luxo Jr.” was the first computer-animated film nominated for an Oscar.

quality.notes: Close in topic to q-1621 (the Luxo lamp in the logo), but it asks a different fact. Knowing the Luxo ball's origin is Pixar-fan or adult knowledge, so it is harder than 10.

questions.description: Small hero, big plan, and a team that is not quite what it seems.
questions.question: I am a clumsy ant inventor. I found “warriors” to fight the grasshoppers, but the bugs I brought home really came from…
hints: The film is “A Bug's Life”.
The bugs were performers, not fighters.
Their boss was a flea, and they did tricks for a crowd.
questions.fun_fact: “A Bug's Life” was Pixar's second feature film, after “Toy Story”.

quality.notes: 'A toy store' is a weak distractor. The first-person riddle is a bit long. A decorative ant image is too cautious: an illustrative ant picture would be safe, so decorative is the wrong role.

questions.description: Medieval influencers who traveled from castle to castle with nothing but songs.
questions.question: What were the medieval poet-singers of southern France, famous for songs of courtly love, called?
hints: They were active about 900 years ago.
Some of them were nobles, even dukes.
Their name comes from an old word of their region meaning “to find” or “to invent”.
questions.fun_fact: Troubadours wrote in Occitan, a language that is still spoken today in parts of southern France.

quality.notes: Strong distractors (minnesingers, bards, griots), and the hints and fun fact are accurate. Fine for adults; hard for young adults.

questions.description: An ancient adventure with a monkey army and no GPS.
questions.question: This Sanskrit epic, credited to Valmiki, follows a prince who rescues his wife Sita from Lanka. What does its title mean?
hints: The title is the hero's name plus one more Sanskrit word.
Think about what the prince does for most of the story.
The prince spends 14 years in exile, wandering through forests.
questions.fun_fact: The Ramayana has about 24,000 verses, and its story is still acted out every year at festivals across South and Southeast Asia.
