quality.notes: Ramayana = Rama + ayana (going, journey); correct. Hint 3 points almost straight at the answer, which is allowed. Players can reason it out from the exile story, so it's slightly easier than 14.

questions.description: A present that comes with a time limit and a judge staring at you.
questions.question: You're on MasterChef and lift the lid of the mystery box. What do you have to do next?
questions.answer: Cook a dish with what's inside
wrong_answers: Guess the price of what's inside
hints: What's inside isn't a gift to keep.
The clock starts ticking as soon as the lid comes up.
Soon the judges will taste what you made from it.
questions.fun_fact: In some mystery box rounds, contestants must use every single ingredient in the box, even the strange ones.

quality.notes: Plain format question, a bit flat. The correct option is slightly longer and more generic than the others. MasterChef (and Junior) is known worldwide, but a 9-year-old may not know the mystery box, so maybe 5 rather than 4.

questions.description: The most nervous handout ceremony on television.
questions.question: On The Bachelor, what does the bachelor give to each woman he wants to keep on the show?
hints: It's handed out in a ceremony at the end of each episode.
Anyone who doesn't get one has to pack their bags.
It's a flower, usually red.
questions.fun_fact: Thousands of roses can be used for a single season of The Bachelor.

quality.notes: A dating show is a borderline topic for kids and young teens, and it comes from the US (though it has versions in many countries). Hint 3 nearly says it, which is allowed.

questions.description: Juggling, singing, dancing dogs: somebody had to invent this.
questions.question: Which British TV judge created the “Got Talent” format, now made in dozens of countries?
hints: He first became famous as a judge on a singing contest.
He's known for being a very honest, sometimes harsh judge.
He also created The X Factor and judged American Idol.
questions.fun_fact: The first “Got Talent” show to air was America's Got Talent in 2006, before Britain's own version.

quality.notes: Simon Fuller is a strong distractor. Shares a topic with q-1805 (Susan Boyle) but asks a different fact. 'British TV judge' leans a little Anglo, but the shows are global.

questions.description: A button so shiny it rains confetti.
questions.question: In “Got Talent” shows, the golden buzzer sends an act straight to the live shows. How many times can each judge usually press it in a season?
hints: It's meant to be very special.
Pressing it makes gold confetti fall over the act.
Judges must save it for the single act they love most.
questions.fun_fact: In many versions, the hosts also get a golden buzzer of their own.

quality.notes: The rules differ a little between versions, but 'usually' covers that. Hint 3 ('single act') says it outright; allowed for hint 3. Same topic as reality-tv-6 but a different fact.

questions.description: Chairs that spin only if they like what they hear.
questions.question: In the blind auditions of The Voice, coaches sit with their backs to the singer. How many coaches are there in most versions?
hints: Each coach builds a team of singers.
It's an even number.
It's the same as the number of legs on a chair.
questions.fun_fact: The Voice started in the Netherlands in 2010 and has been made in more than 70 countries.

quality.notes: Some versions have had 3 or 5 coaches, but 'most versions' handles that. Hint 3 is weak, since chairs don't always have 4 legs. A fairly dry counting question.

questions.description: The quietest minute in any house with children.
questions.question: Supernanny often used a method where a misbehaving child sits alone and quiet for one minute per year of age. What is it called?
hints: It's also a word used in sports.
A coach can call one to stop the game for a short break.
It's a short pause, away from the action.
questions.fun_fact: On the British show, Jo Frost often used a special “naughty step” for the time-out.

quality.notes: The description says it plainly enough that kids can answer from home life without knowing Supernanny. 'Grounding' is a nearby punishment but clearly different. The Supernanny framing adds little.

questions.description: A music contest older than your grandparents' record player.
questions.question: The Eurovision Song Contest is one of the longest-running TV shows. In which decade was it first held?
hints: It is older than the first Moon landing.
Television was still black and white then.
It started in the same decade Elvis Presley became a star.
questions.fun_fact: The first Eurovision, in Lugano, Switzerland, had just seven countries, and Switzerland won.

quality.notes: First held in 1956 in Lugano; the facts are correct. Hint 1 already rules out two options. Shares a topic with several Eurovision candidates (q-1867, colour in 1968) but asks a different fact.

questions.description: Two people punch each other on a screen, and somehow this is a fun night out.
questions.question: You're at an arcade playing a fighting game, and you win the match by winning two out of three of these. What are they called?
hints: Each one ends when a fighter's health bar runs out.
Boxing matches are split into them too.
“… 1… Fight!”
questions.fun_fact: In Street Fighter II, both fighters can knock each other out at the same moment, which is called a “double K.O.”

quality.notes: Fun 3: a fairly plain vocabulary question, and it opens with a scenario (“You're at an arcade…”) that adds little. Hint 2 (boxing) nearly gives the answer away. The summer-olympics-0 boxing question shares the topic but asks a different fact.

questions.description: A snack that becomes a dangerous trap after lunch.
questions.question: In Mario Kart, players drop this behind their kart to make the racers behind them spin out. What is it?
hints: It comes from a fruit.
In cartoons, people slip on it all the time.
The fruit is long, curved and yellow.
questions.fun_fact: Banana peels have been in the series since the very first one, Super Mario Kart, from 1992.

quality.notes: Distractors 3: the banana-peel slip is such a famous cartoon joke that the three other fruit scraps don't really compete. Hint 1 (“comes from a fruit”) is useless because all four options come from fruit.

questions.description: Finally, a theme park where you can live inside a video game without anyone telling you to turn it off.
questions.question: In 2021, a theme park in Osaka, Japan, opened a land where visitors walk through the world of which video game hero?
hints: The land opened inside Universal Studios Japan.
Visitors can hit question blocks and collect coins.
He's a plumber with a red cap.
questions.fun_fact: Visitors to Super Nintendo World can wear a special wristband that lets them collect coins in the park, just like in the game.

quality.notes: Super Nintendo World opened at Universal Studios Japan in 2021: correct. Mario is the obvious guess for “Japanese video game hero”. Other questions ask about Mario as a character, but this one asks a different fact.

questions.description: A quiet island, a few books and no instructions: the perfect holiday for puzzle lovers.
questions.question: The 1993 island puzzle game Myst was so popular that many families got a computer drive just to play its disc. What kind of disc was it?
hints: It looks like the discs that music was sold on in the 1990s.
DVDs only came a few years later.
Its name ends in “ROM”, for “read-only memory”.
questions.fun_fact: Myst was the best-selling computer game in the world for almost ten years, until The Sims beat it in 2002.

quality.notes: Correct 4: the claim that Myst was the best-selling PC game until The Sims is widely repeated but loosely sourced. Fun 3: a fairly dry tech fact, and young players won't know Myst, though they can reason from 1993 to the CD-ROM. The answer topic (CD-ROM) is close to consoles-and-game-companies-14, which asks when the CD-ROM came out, but the fact asked is different. The media is decorative, but an illustrative image (an old PC or a CD-ROM drive) would be safe.

questions.description: Peach's castle has plenty of rooms, and Mario refuses to enter any of them the normal way.
questions.question: In Super Mario 64, Mario reaches new worlds from inside Peach's castle by jumping into what?
hints: They hang on the castle walls.
When Mario jumps into one, its surface ripples like water.
You'd usually find them in an art museum.
questions.fun_fact: Super Mario 64 came out in 1996 with the Nintendo 64, and collecting all 120 Power Stars unlocks a special surprise: Yoshi waiting on the castle roof.

quality.notes: The game is from 1996, so only some young teens will have played it, but adults who did will remember it well. Hint 2 (the surface ripples like water) is strong. The description hints that doors are wrong, which is a minor issue.

questions.description: The sound of music history clearing its throat before the song begins.
questions.question: Listen: which machine makes this sound?
hints: It plays music stored on a flat round disc.
A needle touches the disc while it spins.
DJs scratch the black vinyl discs it plays.

media.note: A clear, recognizable record scratch or needle drop on a spinning vinyl record, with no music playing. Plain hiss or static is not enough.

questions.fun_fact: Vinyl records came back so strongly that in recent years they have outsold CDs in some countries.

quality.notes: A record-scratch sound is easy to find on Freesound. Hint 3 nearly gives the answer away, which is allowed.

questions.description: A band so royal it even named itself after a monarch.
questions.question: Freddie Mercury was the singer of Queen. How many members did the classic Queen lineup have?
hints: Every member of the band wrote at least one of its big hits.
It's the same number of members as the Beatles had.
Besides Freddie, there were Brian May on guitar, Roger Taylor on drums and John Deacon on bass.
questions.fun_fact: Queen's guitarist Brian May later earned a PhD in astrophysics.

quality.notes: Fun 3: a dry counting question, and 4 is the default guess for any band size. Hint 2 (the same number as the Beatles) plus hint 3 (all four names) make it very easy at the end. Difficulty is probably a bit higher than 6 for kids.

questions.description: A space hero who saves the galaxy but still hasn't upgraded his music player.
questions.question: In “Guardians of the Galaxy”, Star-Lord's “Awesome Mix” is on a tape like this. What kind of music is on it?
questions.answer: Pop and rock hits from the 1960s and 1970s
wrong_answers: Grunge and rap hits from the 1990s
Punk and new wave hits from the 1980s
Jazz and swing hits from the 1940s
hints: His mother made it for him on Earth before he was taken into space.
The songs are older than Star-Lord himself.
Songs on it include “Hooked on a Feeling” and “Ain't No Mountain High Enough”.

media.note: A clear photo of an ordinary audio cassette tape, with no film branding or readable song titles.

questions.fun_fact: The soundtrack of the first film topped the US album charts without a single new song on it.

quality.notes: The media role is labelled essential, but the question doesn't need the photo to be answered; it is really illustrative. The cassette points to the 1970s and 1980s, which makes the 1980s option tempting, and that's fine. Facts are correct: the soundtrack topped the Billboard 200 with only older songs.

questions.description: The one piece of paper a rock band is never allowed to lose.
questions.question: Bands often tape a sheet of paper to the stage floor, right by the singer's feet. What is it for?
questions.answer: It lists the songs to play, in order
wrong_answers: It shows the lyrics of every song
It lists the guests allowed backstage
It marks where each musician must stand
hints: Musicians glance at it between songs.
Fans love to grab it after the show as a souvenir.
Its name is “set list”.
questions.fun_fact: Set lists from famous concerts have sold at auction for thousands of dollars.

quality.notes: Some singers do tape lyric sheets on the floor, and tape marks for where musicians stand are real, so there is slight room for argument. Hint 3 states the name “set list” outright, which is allowed. Kids rarely know this, so it is probably harder than 6.

questions.description: A style that walked into the guitar shop with a DJ and a rapper.
questions.question: Linkin Park's “In the End” mixes heavy guitars, DJ scratches and rapped verses. Which rock style from around 2000 is this?
hints: Many of its fans wore baggy clothes and skater shoes.
Bands like Korn and Limp Bizkit also played it.
Its name means a “new” kind of heavy music.
questions.fun_fact: “In the End” is from Linkin Park's first album, one of the best-selling debut albums of the 2000s.

quality.notes: Good distractors. Adults who were teens around 2000 know this well, so it is probably 12 rather than 13. Hint 3 (“new” heavy music) makes it easy.

questions.description: Every guitar hero knows these by touch, even with the lights off.
questions.question: Most electric guitars have 21 to 24 of them. What are the frets on a guitar?
questions.answer: Thin metal strips across the neck
wrong_answers: The tuning pegs at the top of the neck
The magnets under the strings on the body
The knobs on the body that change the volume
hints: They split the neck into steps, one note each.
You can feel them as little ridges when you slide your hand.
They run from one side of the neck to the other.
questions.fun_fact: Each fret raises the note by a half step, so 12 frets take you up one full octave.

quality.notes: Accurate but a bit of a dry definition question. The options are long and descriptive but balanced. The decorative role is fine, since any guitar photo would show every part named in the options.

questions.description: A Martian souvenir that came with an ancient Greek nickname.
questions.question: “I'm hematite, an iron ore, and NASA's Opportunity rover found me on Mars as tiny balls.” What does my Greek name mean?
hints: Ground into a powder, I'm red-brown.
Doctors use the same Greek root in many medical words.
Think of what flows through your veins.
questions.fun_fact: The tiny hematite balls Opportunity found in 2004 were nicknamed “blueberries”, and they suggested Mars once had liquid water.

quality.notes: The quoted riddle is a bit long. Hint 1 (red-brown powder) already points toward blood. Players who know "hemo-" from hemoglobin can reason their way there, so it could be rated a little lower.

questions.description: A mountain that spent thousands of years getting ready for its selfies.
questions.question: “Iron and sulfur minerals paint my slopes in stripes. Thousands hike in Peru's Andes to over 5,000 m (16,400 ft) to see me.” What am I?
hints: Before the 2010s, few tourists knew about me.
Llamas and alpacas often walk the trail next to the hikers.
Count the colors of my stripes and think of the sky after a rain shower.
questions.fun_fact: The red stripes get their color from iron oxide, which is basically rust.

quality.notes: Vinicunca is about 5,200 m, which is fine. The mineral explanation is simplified. Peru also has a second "rainbow mountain" (Palccoyo), though Vinicunca is the famous one. The distractors are all outside Peru, so geography fans can rule them out. The decorative Cusco plaza image is a weak fit: an illustrative Andes/llama trail image would be safe and closer to the question's world.

questions.description: In the game they're blocky and blue; in real life they cost a fortune.
questions.question: In Minecraft, players hunt for diamonds. Where do real diamonds come from?
hints: People get them from mines.
They form where it's extremely hot and the pressure is huge.
Just like in the game, you have to dig down for them.
questions.fun_fact: Most natural diamonds formed about 150 to 200 km (90 to 125 miles) below the surface, and many are over a billion years old.

quality.notes: Hint 1 (mines) nearly gives it away, but at this level that's acceptable. Nice Minecraft hook. The pearl and amber distractors are clever.

questions.description: Ancient swamp plants that waited 300 million years for their second career.
questions.question: It's a black rock that burns. It formed from plants in swamps about 300 million years ago, and power plants still burn it for electricity. What is it?
hints: It's one of the fossil fuels, like oil and gas.
Old steam trains burned it.
Miners dig it out, and some naughty kids get it as a gift in stories.
questions.fun_fact: Charcoal looks similar, but it's made in a few days by heating wood, not over millions of years.

quality.notes: Fairly plain school fact. Charcoal is a near-miss distractor, but the 300-million-year clue rules it out (the fun fact explains this nicely). The "naughty kids" hint relies on a Western Christmas tradition.

questions.description: Sand's most famous mineral has a tiny, very busy side job.
questions.question: Quartz is the most common mineral in sand. With electricity, a tiny quartz crystal vibrates exactly 32,768 times per second. Which everyday object uses that?
hints: The steady vibration is used to count.
The object counts seconds.
You often wear it on your arm.
questions.fun_fact: 32,768 is 2 multiplied by itself 15 times, so a chip can halve it 15 times to get exactly one tick per second.

quality.notes: "Times per second" in the question text already points toward a clock. Hint 2 is strong. inventions-12 also has wristwatch as its answer, but it asks a different fact (photo identification).

questions.description: Rome wasn't built in a day, but legend gives it an exact birthday.
questions.question: Romans counted their years from the founding of their city. According to legend, when was Rome founded?
hints: Legend places it several centuries after the fall of Troy.
Romulus is said to have been its first king.
It happened in the 8th century BC.
questions.fun_fact: Rome still celebrates its birthday every year on April 21.

quality.notes: Well-chosen historical distractors (Troy, the Republic, Alexander). It's a pure date-recall question, so it's a little dry. Most adults half-remember 753, so it rates around 11.

questions.description: From way, way downtown, and then a little further.
questions.question: I became a star with the Golden State Warriors, and I've made more three-pointers than anyone in NBA history. Who am I?
hints: I wear number 30.
My father Dell also played in the NBA.
My nickname is “Steph”.
questions.fun_fact: In 2016, Curry became the first NBA player ever voted Most Valuable Player by every single voter.

quality.notes: Hint 2 (father Dell) nearly identifies him, which is a bit strong for a middle hint. The NBA is known worldwide, so this travels well enough. The Golden Gate image is safe.

questions.description: Loyalty level: one city, one team, one very tall German.
questions.question: At his last game in 2019, Dirk Nowitzki had played every one of his NBA seasons for Dallas. How many seasons was that?
hints: No other player has spent more seasons with a single NBA team.
It's more than Kobe Bryant's 20 years with the Lakers.
He joined the Dallas Mavericks in 1998.
questions.fun_fact: Dirk Nowitzki, who grew up in Würzburg, Germany, led Dallas to its first NBA title in 2011.

quality.notes: Most players can only guess or remember a number here, and an estimate of a season count isn't very satisfying. Hint 2 leaves only 21 or 24, and hint 3 (1998 to 2019) lets you work it out, which is fine for hint 3.

questions.description: Basketball's way of saying “hands off!”.
questions.question: In the NBA, a player who commits six of these must leave the game. What are they?
hints: It has to do with touching another player.
Pushing, holding or hitting someone's arm all count.
The referee blows the whistle, and the other team may get free throws.
questions.fun_fact: In international games under FIBA rules, a player is sent out after only five fouls, not six.

quality.notes: The answer is the only “foul”; the three distractors are all “violations”, so it stands out by form. The description's “hands off!” hints at contact. Dry rules knowledge, though the FIBA fun fact is nice.

questions.description: Thinking about thinking, so you don't have to.
questions.question: The word “philosophy” was made from two ancient words. What does it mean?
hints: The two words come from ancient Greek.
Philosophers are people who want to know.
The first part means “love”.
questions.fun_fact: Pythagoras is said to be the first to call himself a “philosopher”, a lover of wisdom rather than a wise man.

quality.notes: Works in every language because the word is borrowed everywhere. Hint 3 nearly gives it, which is fine for hint 3. The Pythagoras fact is suitably hedged with “is said”.

questions.description: The unstoppable salesman meets the unbreakable sales pitch.
questions.question: A seller claimed his spear could pierce anything and his shield could stop anything. That story gave “contradiction” its name in which country?
hints: The story is over 2,000 years old.
The same country later gave the world paper and printing.
In that language, “contradiction” is written with the signs for spear and shield.
questions.fun_fact: In Chinese, “contradiction” is “máodùn”: literally “spear-shield”.

quality.notes: “Gave ‘contradiction’ its name” is slightly misleading: the English word comes from Latin, and only the Chinese word 矛盾 comes from the story. Hint 2 (paper and printing) is a strong middle hint. The spearhead museum image could carry a label, but that's a minor risk.

questions.description: Mirror, mirror on the wall, who's the smartest bird of all?
questions.question: In 2008, which bird became the first non-mammal shown to recognize itself in a mirror?
hints: It belongs to the crow family, a very clever bunch.
It is a common sight in European parks and fields.
In old stories, it is said to steal shiny things.
questions.fun_fact: In a 2008 test, magpies with a colored dot on their neck kept trying to scratch it off after seeing it in a mirror.

quality.notes: Good, surprising fact, and parrot is a strong distractor. Hint 3 (stealing shiny things) nearly gives it, which is fine for hint 3.

questions.description: Nature's doorbell, except this one is telling you to leave.
questions.question: Watch: what is this goose doing to tell you to stay away?
hints: It's an angry sound.
A snake makes this sound too.
It sounds like “ssss”.

media.note: A goose with neck stretched forward and beak open, hissing at the camera.

questions.fun_fact: Geese are so good at raising the alarm that people have used them as guards for thousands of years.

quality.notes: Essential video: a clear clip of a goose hissing on Commons or Openverse is likely but not certain, and the clip needs sound. The fun fact repeats the answer of farm-animals-2 (geese as guards), but the question asks a different fact.

questions.description: Ancient Rome's most exclusive neighborhood: emperors only, please.
questions.question: The Roman emperors built their homes on this one of Rome's seven hills. Which hill is it?
hints: It rises between the Roman Forum and the Circus Maximus.
Augustus, the first emperor, lived there.
Its name gave us the word “palace”.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says Romulus built the very first walls of Rome on this hill.

quality.notes: Solid. q-1569 names the Palatine as one of the seven hills, but it asks a different fact (that they are hills). Hint 3 (“palace”) almost gives it away, which is allowed for hint 3. The Prima Porta statue is a safe image.

questions.description: A brand-new dance, and the old one didn't even have to move out.
questions.question: In 2005 the All Blacks first performed a new haka, Kapa o Pango. Which older, much more famous haka do they still perform too?
hints: The older haka is about 200 years old.
It is said to have been composed by the Maori chief Te Rauparaha.
Its famous chant means “It is death! It is life!”
questions.fun_fact: Ka Mate is said to have been composed around 1820 by the Maori chief Te Rauparaha, while he hid from his enemies in a food storage pit.

quality.notes: The facts are right (Kapa o Pango 2005, Te Rauparaha, about 1820). The Pacific war-dance distractors are good for experts. Ka Mate is well known to rugby fans, so this is perhaps a 13. For non-fans it is close to a pure-memory question. The description joke is weak.

questions.description: A ball that clearly never learned how to roll in a straight line.
questions.question: Old rugby balls were made from a pig's bladder covered in leather. What shape is a rugby ball?
hints: It is easy to hold under one arm while running.
That shape is why it bounces in strange directions.
Think of what a hen lays.
questions.fun_fact: The pig's bladders came in different sizes, so early rugby balls were all a little different until rubber bladders arrived in the 1860s.

quality.notes: The square and flat options are throwaways. The pig-bladder lead-in doesn't connect to the shape question, so the question reads oddly and isn't very fun. “Like an egg” in the answer is fine for this level.

questions.description: A full-back so elegant he made running backwards toward his own goal look like ballet.
questions.question: Serge Blanco, the legendary full-back who played 93 tests for France, was born in which country?
hints: He was not born in Europe.
His birth country is on the Caribbean coast of South America.
He was born in Caracas.
questions.fun_fact: Blanco grew up in Biarritz, France, and played his whole club career for the town's team, Biarritz Olympique.

quality.notes: Correct: Blanco was born in Caracas and has 93 caps. This is niche sports trivia that you can't reason towards, so it is more of a 14 than a 13. Hint 2 (Caribbean coast) already decides it among the options. The description is about full-back play and is only mildly funny.

questions.description: Players so fast the defenders mostly see the backs of their shirts.
questions.question: I wear number 11 or 14 and sprint along the edge of the field to score tries. My position has the name of a part of a bird. Which part?
hints: I am usually one of the fastest players on the team.
Soccer has a player with almost the same name, who also runs along the side.
Birds flap two of them to fly.
questions.fun_fact: In rugby union, wings are usually the team's top try scorers because they get the ball with open space in front of them.

quality.notes: history-17 also has “the wing” as its answer, but it asks a different fact. The name works in other languages too (ala, Flügel). The bird-part reasoning makes this reachable, though kids need a little sports knowledge.

questions.description: The most famous reunion spot in the desert, no phones needed.
questions.question: Islamic tradition says that two people found each other again on Mount Arafat, near Mecca, after a long separation. Who were they?
hints: Their story goes back to the very beginning, long before Islam.
In Arabic, the hill's name is linked to the word for “to recognize”.
They were the first man and the first woman, sent out of Paradise.
questions.fun_fact: Standing on the plain of Arafat on the ninth day of the Hajj is the most important part of the whole pilgrimage.

quality.notes: The tradition and the 'arafa / “to recognize” link are both right. Hint 1 (“the very beginning”) already points strongly to Adam and Eve. The fact is fairly obscure, so this is closer to 13.

questions.description: Monks who have kept the lights on in the desert for about 1,500 years without a single day off.
questions.question: This monastery at the foot of Mount Sinai, in Egypt, has had monks since the 6th century. Which church do they belong to today?
hints: It was founded by the Byzantine emperor Justinian.
It is the same church as the monasteries of Mount Athos.
Its monks pray in the language of the New Testament.
questions.fun_fact: Saint Catherine's Monastery is often called the oldest Christian monastery still in use, and its library holds some of the oldest books in the world.
questions.concept: Monasterio de Santa Catalina del Sinaí

quality.notes: Hint 2 is loose. Sinai is an autonomous church under the Patriarchate of Jerusalem, and Mount Athos also has Russian, Serbian and Bulgarian monasteries, so “same church” only holds in a broad sense. Coptic is an excellent distractor. The fact is dry.

questions.description: A temple where the morning prayers come with high kicks.
questions.question: Monks at this Buddhist temple in the mountains of China became world-famous for which martial art?
hints: Films about these warrior monks made their fighting style famous around the world.
Bruce Lee and Jackie Chan made it famous in films.
A panda named Po learns it in a film series.
questions.fun_fact: The Shaolin Temple was founded about 1,500 years ago, and its monks still put on kung fu shows for visitors today.

quality.notes: Hints 1 and 2 both point to films, so they repeat each other. Tai chi is also Chinese, but it is clearly linked to Wudang, not Shaolin, so it is wrong but arguable for laypeople. The Shaolin gate may carry a Chinese name sign, which is harmless. Kung Fu Panda makes this easier, so about a 6.

questions.description: Some of the oldest garden residents in Jerusalem, and they have not moved once.
questions.question: These gnarled trees grow in the Garden of Gethsemane in Jerusalem, where Jesus prayed. What kind of trees are they?
hints: These trees can live for well over a thousand years.
The garden lies at the foot of a hill named after them.
Their fruit is pressed for oil.

media.note: Show a close-up of the twisted old trunks of the trees in the Garden of Gethsemane, without fruit and without signs.

questions.fun_fact: The name Gethsemane comes from words meaning “oil press”, and some of its trees are thought to be about 900 years old.

quality.notes: Facts hold up: Gethsemane comes from the Aramaic for 'oil press', and a 2012 study dated some of the trees to about 900 years old. Hint 2 (the hill named after the trees) nearly gives it away, but it is a hint, so that's allowed. An olive trunk is easy to recognise in an essential photo, which makes it easier, though not trivial. Wikimedia Commons has photos of these trees. q-0571 also has olive as its answer, but it asks a different fact.

questions.description: A skinny glass gadget that has been telling the truth for 300 years.
questions.question: What is this tool used for?
hints: Doctors and nurses use it a lot.
Your parents might use it when you feel sick.
It tells you how hot or cold something is.

media.note: A clear photo of a classic glass liquid thermometer; ideally no visible °C or °F label.

questions.fun_fact: Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit made the first reliable mercury thermometer in 1714.

quality.notes: A fairly dry identify-the-object question. Fahrenheit's mercury thermometer of 1714 is correct. Candidate physics-5 says 'A thermometer shows degrees' in its text, which brushes against this answer, but it asks a different fact.

questions.description: A question with good vibrations, measured very precisely.
questions.question: At a concert, loudness is to decibel as pitch is to…
hints: Pitch depends on how many times per second something vibrates.
Radio stations use this unit, often with “mega” in front.
It is named after Heinrich, a German physicist who studied radio waves.
questions.fun_fact: Humans can hear from about 20 to 20,000 hertz, and dogs can hear much higher sounds.

quality.notes: q-1483 asks how the hertz is defined. Same topic, different fact. A tuning fork image is safe.

questions.description: A shopping trip where one item plays by different rules.
questions.question: At the supermarket, three of these are usually sold by the liter (or gallon). Which one is not?
hints: Liters and gallons are used for liquids.
The odd one out is a dry powder.
It's sold in kilograms (or pounds) and used to bake bread.
questions.fun_fact: One liter of water weighs about 1 kilogram.

quality.notes: Plain and a bit dry. Juice is sometimes sold by the carton, but that doesn't really count against it. A blurred supermarket aisle as the decorative image is fine.

questions.description: Two circles, one nose, and a lot of magic.
questions.question: Which famous young wizard from books and films wears round glasses with thin dark frames?
hints: The boy goes to Hogwarts.
He plays Seeker for Gryffindor.
He has a lightning-shaped scar on his forehead.
questions.fun_fact: Harry's round glasses became so famous that this style is often simply called “Harry Potter glasses”.

quality.notes: Hint 1 (Hogwarts) fits all four options, so it is weak but fair. The fun fact's claim that the style is 'often called Harry Potter glasses' is informal but holds up.

questions.description: Hands-free storage, as worn by tourists everywhere.
questions.question: Backpack is to back as … is to waist?
hints: It's a bag you don't hold in your hand.
It clips around your middle.
Many people wear it at the front, near the belly button.
questions.fun_fact: Ötzi the Iceman, who lived about 5,300 years ago, carried a small pouch on his belt.

quality.notes: 'Belt bag' is the only option that hints at the waist (belt ↔ waist), so the answer stands out. Briefcase and suitcase are weak distractors. Younger kids may not know the term 'belt bag', since 'fanny pack' and 'bum bag' are the regional names. The fun fact about Ötzi's belt pouch is correct.

questions.description: A tiny suitcase that only travels to school.
questions.question: It has a zipper, rides to school in your backpack and holds your pens. What is it?
hints: You need it in class.
Inside are things for writing and drawing.
It often holds an eraser and a sharpener too.
questions.fun_fact: Many children in the 1800s wrote on small slates with chalk instead of using paper and pencils.

quality.notes: Very easy and not very surprising, but fine for a level 1 question.

questions.description: The hottest spot in your house is a few thousand kilometers under the basement.
questions.question: Earth's inner core is a ball of solid iron and nickel. About how hot is it?
hints: It is far hotter than any oven or volcano lava.
Lava comes out at roughly 1,000 °C, and the core is much hotter.
It is about as hot as the surface of the Sun.
questions.fun_fact: The inner core is about as hot as the Sun's surface, around 5,000 °C (9,000 °F), yet it stays solid because of the huge pressure.

quality.notes: The 50,000 °C option is easy to rule out with hint 2. The estimate of about 5,200 °C makes 'about 5,000 °C' fair. An iron-nickel meteorite is a safe illustrative image.

questions.description: A dwarf planet shaped like an egg, spinning like it's late for breakfast.
questions.question: Haumea is an egg-shaped dwarf planet that spins very fast beyond Neptune. In which decade was it discovered?
hints: It was found long after Pluto.
It was found by modern telescopes and computers, not by eye.
It was found at about the same time as Eris, just before Pluto stopped being a planet.
questions.fun_fact: Haumea spins once about every 4 hours, so fast that it got stretched into an egg shape.

quality.notes: Discovery was disputed (Brown team 2004, Ortiz team announced 2005), but both dates fall in the 2000s, so the answer holds. 'Dwarf planet' plus hint 3 (Eris, just before Pluto's demotion) make the answer easy to work out. The question is mostly date memorization, with some room to reason. Touches the Pluto-reclassification topic but asks a different fact.

questions.description: A planet that blushes all day, every day.
questions.question: “I coat the dust of the reddest planet in the solar system and give it its color.” What am I?
hints: You can find me on Earth very often too.
I form when a metal meets oxygen.
On Earth I appear on old nails and bikes left out in the rain.
questions.fun_fact: Martian dust is so fine that it gets blown around the whole planet in giant dust storms.

quality.notes: Rated 10, but 'Mars is red because of rust' is common in kids' science shows and books, so it is more like a 7. Related to q-0051 (red planet) but asks why it is red, which is a different fact.

questions.description: A fishbowl for people, but without the water.
questions.question: It's round, it has a see-through front, and astronauts wear it on their heads. What is it?
hints: It protects the most important part of your body.
Bike riders wear one too.
It's like a bike rider's, but much bigger and with a big window.
questions.fun_fact: Space helmets have a small foam pad inside that astronauts use to pop their ears, and also to scratch an itchy nose.

quality.notes: Backpack, glove and boot are not worn on the head and aren't round with a see-through front, so they are weak even for 6-year-olds. Hint 2 ('bike riders wear one too') nearly gives it away. Fine as a level-1 question but not very fun. Decorative image is a reasonable choice, since any astronaut photo would show the helmet.

questions.description: The only job where wearing gold on your face is part of the uniform.
questions.question: Look at this astronaut's helmet. What is the thin layer of gold on the visor for?
hints: In space, there is no air to soften the Sun.
It works like a mirror.
It protects the astronaut's eyes and keeps heat out.

media.note: An astronaut in a spacesuit with the gold sun visor lowered, reflecting the surroundings.

questions.fun_fact: The gold layer is so thin that you can still see through it.

quality.notes: The gold layer also reflects infrared heat (covered by hint 3), so the answer is fine. Hint 1 already points very strongly to sunlight. A NASA gold-visor photo is easy to find.

questions.description: The newspaper corner that knows your future, or says it does.
questions.question: How many star signs are there in the usual Western horoscope?
hints: There's one for each part of the year.
It's the same as the number of months.
It's a dozen.
questions.fun_fact: The Chinese zodiac also has 12 signs, but they're animals for whole years, not months.

quality.notes: A dry counting fact. Probably a bit easier than 5, since many kids know their star sign and that there are 12. Astrology is a slightly odd fit for a stars-and-galaxies question.

questions.description: A sport so small it fits on your dining table.
questions.question: The shuttlecock is to badminton as what is to table tennis?
hints: It's the thing players hit back and forth.
It's very light: it weighs less than 3 grams.
It's round, white or orange, and bounces on the table.
questions.fun_fact: A table tennis ball weighs only 2.7 grams, yet top players can smash it at over 100 km/h (62 mph).

quality.notes: The answer is the only plastic, light-sounding option, and 'leather' and 'wooden' are easy to rule out. Descriptive answers make an analogy feel clumsy; 'a ping-pong ball' would be more natural, but then the options would be trivial. The analogy itself is not very surprising.

questions.description: Gymnastics equipment where letting go is part of the plan.
questions.question: In women's gymnastics, on which apparatus do gymnasts swing and fly between two rails?
hints: The men have a cousin of this apparatus.
The men's version has two rails at the same height.
One rail is clearly higher than the other.
questions.fun_fact: In 1976, Nadia Comăneci scored the first perfect 10 in Olympic gymnastics on this apparatus, and the scoreboard showed “1.00” because it couldn't display a 10.

quality.notes: Hint 2 describes the parallel bars and so rules out the strongest distractor early. 'Two rails' fits the parallel bars too, but 'women's gymnastics' settles it. The Comăneci fun fact is accurate and great.

questions.description: Black, twisty, and loved by exactly half of every family.
questions.question: I'm a chewy black candy, and my name comes from old Greek words for the plant part I'm made from. What does my name mean?
hints: My plant grows wild in southern Europe and Asia.
The first part of my old name is related to the word “glucose”.
Farmers have to dig into the soil to get me out.
questions.fun_fact: The main sweet substance in licorice is up to 50 times sweeter than sugar.

quality.notes: Black licorice candy is common in Northern Europe, the UK and the US, but much less familiar in Latin America and parts of Asia, so players there may not recognize it from the riddle. The etymology needs reasoning (glyc- = sweet), so it is harder than 8. 'Bitter bark' is easy to rule out for a sweet candy.

questions.description: A swimming style for people who skipped every single lesson.
questions.question: I'm the first way many kids swim: head up, paddling with arms and legs under the water. Which animal am I named after?
hints: The animal is a popular pet.
It loves to fetch sticks, even from a lake.
It barks.
questions.fun_fact: Most dogs can do the doggy paddle without ever being taught.

quality.notes: Hint 2 (fetching sticks) almost gives the answer, which is fine at difficulty 2. The fun fact says most dogs paddle without being taught: the paddle is instinctive, but some breeds swim badly, so it's slightly too broad. The doggy-paddle name works in Spanish and German too. An illustrative image would have been safe, so the decorative role isn't needed.

questions.description: Pond vocabulary class is now in session.
questions.question: What is a duckling?
hints: You might see one in spring.
It follows its mother in a line.
It hatches from an egg.
questions.fun_fact: Ducklings can swim just a few hours after they hatch.

quality.notes: This is a dry word-meaning question that reads like a vocabulary drill. It also leans on an English word, though most languages have a matching diminutive. Hint 3 (“hatches from an egg”) rules out the egg option. The wrong answers are weak because they are all “a duck's ___”. The description is bland.

questions.description: The only swimming style where you never see where you're going.
questions.question: In an outdoor pool, freestyle is to seeing the pool floor as backstroke is to seeing…?
hints: You lie face up.
Indoors, you'd see the ceiling.
Outdoors you might spot clouds and birds.
questions.fun_fact: Backstroke swimmers count their strokes from the flags above the pool so they don't bump their heads on the wall.

quality.notes: The analogy is clumsy to read aloud. “The swimmer next to you” is a weak option, and kids could argue for “your own feet”. The answer is easy to reason out but not very satisfying. The illustrative lane-rope image shows a wrong option, though that doesn't really mislead.

questions.description: Your arms are doing all the walking for once.
questions.question: A step is to walking as a … is to swimming?
hints: It's one single movement, not a whole length of the pool.
You do it with your arms.
Each pull of your arm through the water counts as one.
questions.fun_fact: Top freestyle sprinters can make about one arm stroke every half second.

quality.notes: A dry vocabulary analogy. Hint 2 (“with your arms”) is debatable, since strokes also involve the legs. The fun-fact stroke rate is roughly right but not exact. “Stroke” as swimming jargon is probably a bit harder for kids than difficulty 5.

questions.description: The oldest soap trick: everyone cries at your funeral, and then you walk in.
questions.question: My author sent me over a Swiss waterfall in 1893. Readers protested, and in 1903 I came back: I had faked my death. Who am I?
hints: I'm famous for solving mysteries.
I live in London at 221B Baker Street.
My loyal friend is Dr. Watson.
questions.fun_fact: The story of his return, “The Adventure of the Empty House”, explains that he hid for three years while the world thought he was gone.

quality.notes: A strong riddle, and the facts are right (Reichenbach in 1893, the Empty House in 1903). Hint 1 narrows the options to Holmes or Poirot. The query “Swiss Alps waterfall” might return Reichenbach Falls with a Sherlock plaque. The other Holmes questions in the candidates ask different facts. Many adults know the waterfall death, so this feels more like a 10 than an 11.

questions.description: The loudest thing in town, and somehow nobody ever complained.
questions.question: Long before everyone had a watch, what did church bells like this one tell the whole town?
wrong_answers: What prices were at the market
hints: Today your phone tells you this.
They often rang once for every hour.
Think of a clock.

media.note: A clear photo of a big bronze church bell hanging in a bell tower.

questions.fun_fact: Big Ben in London is not the name of the clock tower but of its biggest bell.

quality.notes: The wrong answers (weather, market prices, river depth) are silly, so “what time it was” stands out at once. Bells also called people to services and warned of fires, but the time is the best answer among these options. The Big Ben fun fact is nice and true.

questions.description: The first big churches didn't start from scratch; they flipped through Rome's old building catalog.
questions.question: When Christianity became legal in Rome, the first large churches copied the shape of which kind of Roman building?
hints: Roman temples were too small inside for big crowds.
These long halls were used for courts and business.
Romans called them basilicas.
questions.fun_fact: That's why so many churches today are still called basilicas, a name first used for Roman public halls.

quality.notes: The fact is true (basilica plan). The answer is phrased as a description (“public meeting halls”), which makes it look different from the other options. The “building catalog” description is weak. An illustrative image (Roman forum) is safe, so the decorative role isn't needed. It's a standard art-history fact, closer to 13 than 14.

questions.description: A racket that forgot its strings and got holes instead.
questions.question: Look at this racket: solid, full of holes, no strings. It's used in a doubles sport played on a court with glass walls. Which sport?
hints: The ball looks almost exactly like a tennis ball.
The ball may bounce off the walls, a bit like in squash.
It's hugely popular in Spain and Argentina.

media.note: A clear photo of a padel racket showing its solid, perforated face with no strings.

questions.fun_fact: Padel was invented in Acapulco, Mexico, in 1969, when a man added walls around a court at his home.

quality.notes: Padel is huge in Spain and Latin America but much less known in some regions, so it is probably a little harder than 7. Commons very likely has a clear padel racket photo.

questions.description: Real estate listing: cozy, underground and full of snacks.
questions.question: In “The Hobbit”, Tolkien describes Bilbo's hobbit hole in detail. Which of these did it NOT have?
hints: The answer is about the shape of the house, not what's inside it.
Bilbo's home was dug sideways into a hill.
Hobbits did not like climbing inside their homes.
questions.fun_fact: Tolkien writes that in Bilbo's home “no going upstairs” was needed: bedrooms, bathrooms, cellars and kitchens were all on one floor.

quality.notes: Hint 1 (“the shape of the house”) is a bit vague, because round windows also have to do with shape. The Hobbiton image will show round windows, which quietly rules that option out.

questions.description: The language everyone in Middle-earth speaks, which is why nobody ever mentions it.
questions.question: It's the Common Speech of Middle-earth, Tolkien “translated” it into English for his books, and in it Frodo's real name is Maura Labingi. What is it called?
hints: You would hear it at the inn in Bree.
Its name sounds like an old English word.
Its name points to a direction on the compass.
questions.fun_fact: Tolkien pretended to be only the translator of the Red Book of Westmarch, so the English you read stands in for Westron.

quality.notes: Hint 2 (“sounds like an old English word”) is unclear and doesn't really help. Hint 3 (“a direction on the compass”) nearly gives the answer away, which is allowed for hint 3.

questions.description: The best taxi service in Middle-earth, if only they took more bookings.
questions.question: They rescue Bilbo and the dwarves from goblins and wolves, carry Frodo and Sam away from Mount Doom, and save Gandalf from Saruman's tower. What are they?
hints: They come when Gandalf calls for help.
They live high in the Misty Mountains.
They are the kings of the birds.
questions.fun_fact: Fans often joke that the eagles could have flown the Ring to Mordor, but Tolkien's eagles help only rarely.

quality.notes: Solid question. The decorative mountain image is fine.

questions.description: Fashion meets the dictionary, and the dictionary speaks Arabic.
questions.question: Many Muslim women wear a headscarf called a hijab. What does the Arabic word “hijab” mean?
hints: The word is about what the scarf does, not what it's made of or why it's worn.
In old texts, the same word was used for a curtain or screen between people.
Think of something that keeps things out of sight.
questions.fun_fact: World Hijab Day has been held every year on February 1 since 2013.

quality.notes: “Hijab” literally means something closer to a screen or partition, from a root meaning “to cover”, so “Cover” is acceptable. “Silk” is a weak distractor. The description is flat, and the question reads like a dictionary test. It shares the answer word with rock-11 (a song “cover”), but that is a different fact.

questions.description: Slippers so stylish they get their own market street.
questions.question: These pointed leather slippers, called babouches, are sold in huge piles in the markets of which country?
hints: The country is a short boat trip from Europe.
Its busy markets are called souks.
Marrakesh and Fez are famous cities there.

media.note: Close-up of the pointed toes of colorful leather babouche slippers, no shop signs or text.

questions.fun_fact: Babouches have no stiff back, so you can slip them off quickly before entering a home or a mosque.

quality.notes: Commons very likely has a clear photo of babouche slippers.

questions.description: Two cities, two giant parties, zero reasons to stay home.
questions.question: Rio de Janeiro's carnival is famous for samba. What is the carnival of Venice most famous for?
hints: Think about what people wear at the party in Venice.
They hide who you are.
You put one over your face.
questions.fun_fact: One old Venetian style, the bauta, has a pointed chin so the wearer can eat and drink without taking it off.

quality.notes: Tango and flamenco are clearly the wrong kind of thing for Venice, so the real choice is only between masks and fireworks. An illustrative Venice image would also have been safe.

questions.description: A cloth that was woven at home and ended up changing a nation.
questions.question: You spin cotton thread at home on a small wheel to weave khadi cloth, as millions of Indians did in the 1920s. Who started this movement?
hints: He wanted India to stop buying British cloth.
He believed in peaceful protest.
He led the famous Salt March in 1930.
questions.fun_fact: For decades, Indian law said the national flag had to be made of khadi.

quality.notes: The 'You spin…' setup is a little long-winded but acceptable. Hint 2 (peaceful protest) is already strong. Flag-code fun fact is true (khadi was required until 2021–22).

questions.description: The most-folded, most-crumpled face in the whole United States.
questions.question: Whose portrait is on the front of the US one-dollar bill?
hints: He lived in the 1700s and wore his hair white and tied back.
He was a general before he was a president.
He was the very first president of the United States.
questions.fun_fact: A US one-dollar bill lasts only about six to seven years in use before it wears out and is replaced.

quality.notes: Whose face is on US banknotes is US-specific knowledge; international families mostly guess, so age_fit 3. Fairly dry recall. Shares the answer (Washington) with us-presidents-14 but asks a different fact.

questions.description: He never became president, but he got a hit musical, which is arguably better.
questions.question: This man is Alexander Hamilton, the first US Treasury Secretary. He was never president, yet his face is on a US banknote. What is its value?
hints: It's not the smallest bill, but it's far from the biggest.
Its value is a round number with two digits.
Count your fingers to get the number.

media.note: A painted portrait of Alexander Hamilton (e.g. by John Trumbull), without any banknote showing.

questions.fun_fact: Hamilton is one of only two non-presidents on US banknotes in use today; the other is Benjamin Franklin on the $100 bill.

quality.notes: Knowing US banknotes is US-specific; outside the US it's a pure guess, so age_fit 3. The question is long. The media isn't truly essential (the question names Hamilton), so it should be illustrative. Hint 3 ('count your fingers') basically gives the answer, which is allowed for the third hint.

questions.description: The world's most important backup player, always ready on the bench.
questions.question: If the US president suddenly can no longer do the job, who moves into this house and takes over?
hints: This person is elected together with the president.
This person casts the deciding vote when the Senate is split in a tie.
This person is second in command.

media.note: A clear photo of the White House, no people or captions.

questions.fun_fact: Nine US vice presidents have become president in the middle of a term; the first was John Tyler in 1841.

quality.notes: 'The First Lady' and 'the oldest senator' are weak wrong options. Fun fact checks out (nine vice presidents, the first was Tyler). Civics recall, moderately fun.

questions.description: A mountain so big it makes its own weather and probably has its own fan club.
questions.question: This snowy volcano, Mount Rainier, is in the only US state named after a president. Which state is it?
hints: The state lies on the Pacific coast.
The state shares a border with Canada.
It shares its name with the US capital.

media.note: A clear photo of Mount Rainier; no signs or text naming the state.

questions.fun_fact: Georgia is named after a king, George II of Great Britain, not after a president.

quality.notes: Easy to reason out ('named after a president' → Washington). The media is labeled essential but is really illustrative. Good wrong options (Georgia, Virginia).

questions.description: Aliens who took a video game recording as a very rude letter.
questions.question: In the film “Pixels” (2015), the heroes who fight giant game characters had once been arcade champions. In which decade?
hints: The film's monsters come from very old, blocky arcade games.
It was the golden age of arcade halls, before home consoles took over.
Pac-Man and Donkey Kong were brand new hits back then.
questions.fun_fact: In the film, aliens think a recording of arcade games sent into space is a declaration of war.

quality.notes: The 2010s can't fit 'had once been' in a 2015 film, and the 1960s predate arcades, so both are weak; the 1970s would be a better wrong option. The fun fact repeats the description. An arcade image would be a better illustrative choice than movie theater seats.

questions.description: The only good thing about your internet going down.
questions.question: Your internet is down and you play Chrome's dinosaur game. After a while, what starts flying at the dinosaur besides the cactuses?
hints: They only show up once your score gets high enough.
You have to duck or jump to avoid them.
They're flying reptiles with big wings.
questions.fun_fact: The game's secret code name was “Project Bolan”, after Marc Bolan, the singer of the band T. Rex.

quality.notes: Facts are right: pterodactyls show up at higher scores, and Project Bolan is named after Marc Bolan of T. Rex. Most kids know the game, but the pterodactyl detail fits about 5 better than 4. Since the question doesn't name the answer, a desert image could have been illustrative instead of decorative.

questions.description: A game that changed its name but kept its jersey.
questions.question: The soccer video game series EA Sports FC had a different name until 2023. What was it?
hints: It's just four letters.
Many players still call the game by its old name.
It's also the name of the group that runs the World Cup.
questions.fun_fact: The first game in the series, “FIFA International Soccer”, came out in 1993.

quality.notes: The rename happened in 2023 and the first game came out in 1993, so the facts hold. Hint 3 nearly gives the answer away, which is allowed. football-history-14 mentions FIFA but asks a different fact.

questions.description: Two old rivals finally agreed to race each other with medals on the line.
questions.question: The first “Mario & Sonic at the Olympic Games” came out in 2007, made for the next Summer Olympics. Which city held them?
hints: The host city is a national capital.
The host country is in Asia.
The main stadium was nicknamed the “Bird's Nest”.
questions.fun_fact: It was the very first game where Mario and Sonic, once fierce rivals, appeared together.
questions.concept: Mario & Sonic at the Olympic Games

quality.notes: Players have to reason from 2007 to the 2008 Games, and young teens may not know that 2008 was Beijing. Tokyo also fits hints 1 and 2, which is fine. The fun fact is true: this was the first official crossover.

questions.description: A best friend who says only one word, again and again.
questions.question: I'm Ash's yellow best friend in the Pokémon cartoon, and I always say my own name. What type of Pokémon am I?
hints: My tail looks like a bolt.
My red cheeks can spark.
I use Thunderbolt in battles.
questions.fun_fact: Pikachu's name mixes two Japanese sounds: “pika” for a spark and “chu” for a mouse's squeak.

quality.notes: Very young kids know Pikachu, but the idea of a Pokémon "type" puts it slightly above 1. The meaning of "pika" and "chu" in the fun fact is correct.

questions.description: A desk where nobody does homework, only pickaxes.
questions.question: I'm one of the first blocks you make in Minecraft, and I give you a 3-by-3 grid to build tools. What am I made from?
hints: You get my ingredient from the first thing you punch in the game.
You need four of them in a square.
Chop a tree and turn its logs into them.
questions.fun_fact: You can't make a pickaxe in your small inventory grid: it needs the bigger 3-by-3 grid of a crafting table.

quality.notes: The recipe (4 planks) is correct. The decorative 'video game controller' image is generic. A Minecraft landscape would show the topic, but it might show a crafting table.

questions.description: A song so catchy it gets stuck in your head, then beats you up.
questions.question: I'm “Megalovania”, the famous battle music of the fight against Sans in Undertale. Who composed me?
hints: He wrote an early version of me years before the game came out.
He made almost the whole game by himself.
His last name is a clever animal with a bushy tail.
questions.fun_fact: An early version of Megalovania first appeared in 2008, in a fan-made hack of the game EarthBound.

quality.notes: I'm slightly unsure whether the EarthBound hack (Radiation's Halloween Hack) came out in 2008 or 2009. Hint 3 is a pun on the English word "fox", so it won't travel well into other languages. Young adult gamers know this widely, so I'd put it a little below 13.

questions.description: Mario's favorite forest food, but please don't pick your own.
questions.question: In Super Mario games, what does a mushroom that looks a lot like this one do to Mario?
hints: Mario starts the game small.
After eating it, he can take one hit without losing a life.
He grows to twice his height.

media.note: A clear photo of a red mushroom with white spots (fly agaric).

questions.fun_fact: Once Mario is big, he can smash brick blocks with his head.

quality.notes: Wikimedia Commons is very likely to have a clear photo of a fly agaric, so the essential image works. Hint 3 comes close to the answer, which is allowed.

questions.description: A volcano that retired so long ago it forgot how to erupt.
questions.question: Arthur's Seat, a hill in Edinburgh, Scotland, is an extinct volcano. When did it last erupt?
hints: “Extinct” means it is not expected to erupt ever again.
Back then, the land that is now Scotland lay close to the equator.
It was before the dinosaurs even existed.
questions.fun_fact: Edinburgh Castle stands on another old volcanic rock, the plug of an ancient volcano.

quality.notes: About 340–350 million years (Carboniferous) is right, and so is the equator hint. Few people know this; it's mostly a guess unless the hints are used. That makes it hard for 10, and it's close to an obscure fact. Arthur's Seat is a regional landmark that many families outside the UK won't know.

questions.description: Do not try to cool this down by blowing on it.
questions.question: This glowing orange stuff flows out of volcanoes. What is it really?
hints: When it cools down, it becomes hard and dark.
It used to be solid stone deep under the ground.
It is the same stuff mountains are made of, but super hot.

media.note: Close-up of glowing orange molten lava flowing, no people or text.

questions.fun_fact: Lava can reach about 1,200 °C (2,200 °F), about twice as hot as a wood-fired pizza oven.

quality.notes: "About twice" a pizza oven is loose: 1,200 °C is roughly 2.5 times 450–500 °C. A clear lava photo is easy to find. The question is a basic fact. The fun fact touches on lava temperature, which is what q-0730 asks, but the question itself asks something different.

questions.description: Fashion tip: when you visit lava, dress like you're about to walk on the Moon.
questions.question: Suits like this one let people get very close to lava and fire. What is the shiny outer layer made of?
hints: The shiny layer bounces heat away like a mirror.
It is a light metal, not a heavy one.
You can find the same metal as a thin foil in your kitchen.

media.note: Person wearing a shiny silver heat-protective (aluminized) suit with hood.

questions.fun_fact: A shiny aluminum coating can reflect around 90% of the heat that hits it.

quality.notes: Aluminized proximity suits are probably on Commons. The shiny photo makes silver and aluminum the obvious picks, but silver is still a fair trap.

questions.description: The sky's most elegant clouds, and they know it.
questions.question: Cirrus clouds are thin and wispy, float very high, and are made of ice crystals. What does their Latin name mean?
hints: Think about what they look like.
Their shape is long and thin, like strands.
Something you find on your head.
questions.fun_fact: Luke Howard gave clouds their Latin names in 1802: cumulus means “heap”, stratus “layer” and nimbus “rain cloud”.

quality.notes: Using the other cloud names as wrong answers is clever. The description is not very funny and is barely a full sentence. Most players can't know the Latin, though they can reason from the wispy shape, so I put it nearer 11. The question is a bit long.

questions.description: It sunbathes all day and still counts as working.
questions.question: I sit on roofs and on satellites, and I turn sunlight into electricity. What am I?
hints: I work best on a cloudless day.
I don't need wind, water or fuel.
I am a flat, dark-blue panel facing the Sun.
questions.fun_fact: Vanguard 1, launched in 1958, was one of the first satellites powered by solar cells, and it is still circling the Earth.

quality.notes: Hint 3 says 'panel', which is part of the answer word. The riddle is simple and not very surprising. The image query 'sunlight through clouds' is really just decorative.

questions.description: A storm with so many names it needs a passport.
questions.question: Typhoons are giant spinning storms. In which ocean do they form?
hints: The same storm is called a hurricane in another ocean.
Typhoons often hit Japan and the Philippines.
This ocean's name means “peaceful”, which these storms are not.
questions.fun_fact: A typhoon, a hurricane and a cyclone are the same kind of storm; only the ocean where it forms changes the name.

quality.notes: Typhoons form in the northwest Pacific specifically. The fun fact simplifies things: the name depends on the region, not just the ocean. The question reads like a dry geography fact. An illustrative image would have been safe, so decorative wasn't needed. It only shares a topic with q-0015 (largest ocean).

questions.description: A superhero whose bad mood ruins everyone's picnic.
questions.question: I fly with the X-Men and call down lightning and rain. Before joining them, I was worshipped as a rain goddess. On which continent?
hints: My white hair makes me easy to spot.
My mother was a princess from a long line of priestesses.
The continent of the Sahara and the Nile.
questions.fun_fact: Storm first appeared in the comics in 1975, and Halle Berry played her in the first X-Men film in 2000.

quality.notes: Storm's Kenyan backstory is correct. Fans of the films know it, but younger players mostly won't. It fits loosely in the weather category. Different fact from oscars-10 (X-Men).

questions.description: A dish so nice they named it twice.
questions.question: I'm couscous: tiny balls of wheat, steamed over a pot of stew. Where was I first made?
hints: I'm often served with lamb, chickpeas and vegetables.
I'm part of the same world as the Sahara desert.
Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia all call me their own.
questions.fun_fact: In 2020, UNESCO added couscous to its world heritage list, shared by Algeria, Mauritania, Morocco and Tunisia.

quality.notes: The wrong answers are far-off regions that are easy to rule out; Middle East or Southern Europe would be more tempting. Hint 2 (Sahara) almost gives it away. Fairly dry origin question. A picture of couscous would have been safe as illustrative.

questions.description: A dessert with more layers than a winter outfit.
questions.question: I'm a cake made of chocolate sponge layers, whipped cream and cherries. What am I?
hints: I come from a land famous for cuckoo clocks.
The real recipe adds a cherry brandy called kirsch.
My region's dark pine trees gave me my name.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany, a cake may only be sold as a real Black Forest cake if it contains kirsch, a cherry brandy.

quality.notes: The clue fits this one cake well. The kirsch rule in Germany is true.

questions.description: A bread with a built-in pocket, for people who want a sandwich without the hard work.
questions.question: This flatbread has been baked around the eastern Mediterranean for thousands of years. It puffs up into a hollow pocket you can fill with falafel. What is it?
hints: It's eaten a lot in Greece, Turkey and the Middle East.
It's often cut in half and stuffed.
You can buy it as a pocket bread for gyros or kebabs.
questions.fun_fact: The pocket forms because water in the dough turns to steam in the hot oven and blows the bread up like a balloon.

quality.notes: 'Thousands of years' is a bit loose. The question is about 150 characters, long for reading aloud. The pocket plus falafel makes it fairly easy.

questions.description: A bird so big it shows up on money, flags and coats of arms.
questions.question: I glide over the Andes on huge wings, and a famous Andean song is named after me. Which group of birds am I in?
hints: My head has almost no feathers.
I clean up nature by eating animals that have already died.
I'm the Andean condor.
questions.fun_fact: An Andean condor was once tracked flying more than 160 km (100 mi) without flapping its wings once.

quality.notes: The Andean condor is a New World vulture, so the answer is correct. Q-0995 (hyena, vulture and condor are all scavengers) is related but asks a different fact. Few teens know the condor is a vulture, so I rate it nearer 9.

questions.description: A chat app where everyone has their own server, but nobody brings you snacks.
questions.question: The chat app Discord launched in 2015. Which group of people was it first made for?
hints: Think of people who team up online.
They often wear headsets and shout “Behind you!”
Players use it during matches of Minecraft or Fortnite.
questions.fun_fact: Discord's little logo mascot has its own name: Clyde.

quality.notes: The facts hold up: Discord launched in May 2015 for gamers. The logo mascot really is called Clyde, but the name is also used for Discord's bot, so the fun fact is a bit fuzzy. The distractors are weak. Office workers and music bands are easy to rule out, and the question nearly answers itself for anyone who has heard of Discord. Hint 2 (headsets, “Behind you!”) already makes it obvious. The fun fact is mild. Discord is meant for 13 and up, so younger kids may not know it, but teens and adults will.

questions.description: The version of YouTube where the comments section takes a nap.
questions.question: You're setting up the YouTube Kids app. Its oldest age group is for children up to what age?
hints: It stops before the teenage years really start.
Kids in this group are around the end of primary school.
It's one year below 13, the age for a regular YouTube account.
questions.fun_fact: YouTube Kids launched in 2015, and it has no comments section at all.

quality.notes: The 'Older' group (9–12) is correct today, but product settings change, which breaks the house rule against facts that change often. Hint 3 says 13 is the age for a regular account, but that age differs by country, and the hint nearly gives the answer away (allowed for hint 3). Hint 1 already points strongly to 12. This is a dry product-settings fact that nobody enjoys learning. It is not surprising, and players would only guess it, not reason their way to it. Few kids or parents know the exact group limits, so it is harder than difficulty 4.

questions.description: A race to the other side where your best move is building walls in your opponent's way.
questions.question: On a 9-by-9 board, you race your pawn across while placing walls to block the other player. What is this 1997 Mensa award winner called?
hints: It was made by the French game company Gigamic.
In a two-player game, each player has 10 walls to place.
Its name comes from a word for a long hallway.
questions.fun_fact: In Quoridor you may never wall a pawn in completely: every player must always have a way left to reach the other side.

quality.notes: Facts check out: Mensa Mind Game 1997, Gigamic, 10 walls each in a two-player game. The clue is a dry specialist name-recall that few players can reason towards. The decorative query 'wooden board game pieces' could pull up a Gigamic wooden game, maybe even Quoridor itself, but the image is blurred, so the risk is small. Hint 3 ('corridor') is close but allowed.

questions.description: The pie you collect slice by slice, and you can't even eat it.
questions.question: The board game where you fill a round token with six colored wedges was invented in 1979 by two journalists. In which country?
hints: Both inventors worked for newspapers in the same city.
The idea came when they found pieces missing from their Scrabble set.
They lived in Montreal.
questions.fun_fact: Chris Haney and Scott Abbott invented Trivial Pursuit, which went on to sell well over 100 million copies around the world.

quality.notes: Trivial Pursuit, Haney and Abbott, Montreal 1979, the missing Scrabble pieces: all correct. A fun meta question, and the options are all plausible English-speaking countries.

questions.description: That face you make when someone opens the fridge after a long holiday.
questions.question: Disgust makes you pull a face and step back. What is this feeling mainly good for?
questions.answer: Keeping you away from germs and rotten food
wrong_answers: Keeping you warm on cold days
Helping you run away from loud noises
hints: Think of moldy bread or a smelly trash can.
It makes you not want to touch or eat something.
Things that feel “yucky” can often make you sick.
questions.fun_fact: The disgusted face, with a wrinkled nose and raised upper lip, helps block smells and is understood by people all over the world.

quality.notes: The distractors are clearly silly (sleep, warmth). Even kids can rule them out without knowing anything, so they don't really compete with the answer. human-body-1 also has 'germs' as its answer, but it asks about a different fact.

questions.description: A hat full of wires that can tell when you're daydreaming.
questions.question: It uses small sensors stuck on your head, it draws your brain's electrical activity as wavy lines, and doctors use it to study sleep. What is this test called?
hints: It listens to the tiny electric signals of nerve cells.
Its sister test does the same thing for the heart.
Its name contains the Greek word for “brain”: encephalon.
questions.fun_fact: The German doctor Hans Berger recorded the first human brain waves in 1924.

quality.notes: Feels like a school test. The question says 'brain', and 'encephalo' in the option points there for anyone who knows Greek roots, but the ECG/EMG distractors are good. Hint 3 nearly gives the answer away, which is allowed.

questions.description: Some people forget their keys; these people supposedly forget nothing at all.
questions.question: Film geniuses and detectives often have me: one glance at a page and they can recall every word. What am I?
hints: I'm about things you've seen, not things you've practiced.
I'm said to last for years, not just a few seconds.
It's as if your eyes took a snapshot.
questions.fun_fact: Many scientists doubt that a true photographic memory exists in adults; record-breaking memorizers use tricks instead.

quality.notes: Hint 1 ('things you've seen') already points strongly to 'photographic'. Kids under 9 may not know the term, so this is slightly harder than rated.

questions.description: Two halves, one head, and a lot of teamwork.
questions.question: Look at this organ. Its right half mostly controls the movements of which side of your body?
hints: The organ is the brain.
Its wiring crosses over on the way down.
It's like a mirror: right controls the opposite.

media.note: A clear photo or model of a human brain seen from above, both halves visible, no labels or text.

questions.fun_fact: The nerve paths cross over in the lower brainstem, which is why a problem in one side of the brain affects the other side of the body.

quality.notes: 'Neither side, only thinking' is a weak, odd distractor, so the question is really a 50/50 between left and right. The essential photo isn't truly needed (it works as an illustration). Hint 3 basically states the answer.

questions.description: A film about napping that keeps you awake for hours afterwards.
questions.question: In the film “Inception”, five minutes of sleep in the real world become about how long in the first dream level?
hints: In the dream, time stretches out, not shrinks.
Each deeper level stretches time even more.
Cobb explains it: five minutes outside gives you much more time inside, but less than a day.
questions.fun_fact: Christopher Nolan worked on the idea for “Inception” for about ten years before making the film in 2010.

quality.notes: The '5 minutes to 1 hour' line is correct. Hint 1 rules out 10 minutes and hint 3 rules out a day and a week, so the hints give the answer away together. The question is film-detail recall; the 'school' lens doesn't fit. A spinning top hints at Inception without giving the answer away.

questions.description: Some car badges are cute. This one means serious business.
questions.question: A prancing horse is to Ferrari as which animal is to Lamborghini?
hints: Like Ferrari, Lamborghini is a sports car brand from Italy.
The founder's star sign was Taurus.
It's a big farm animal with horns, the male of the cow.
questions.fun_fact: Before he built sports cars, Ferruccio Lamborghini made tractors, and many of his cars are named after famous fighting bulls.

quality.notes: The Taurus hint is strong but fine. The decorative racetrack image might show a Lamborghini with its badge, but it is blurred. Car-brand knowledge goes slightly beyond what an average 11-year-old knows.

questions.description: A candy with a secret inside, and it's not very good at keeping it.
questions.question: He's the round, cheerful yellow M&M's character. What is inside him?
hints: The red M&M's character is plain milk chocolate inside.
He's rounder and bumpier than the plain ones.
It's a nut that grows underground.
questions.fun_fact: Plain M&M's came out in 1941, and the peanut kind followed in 1954.

quality.notes: M&M's characters are a US brand mascot, mostly known from US ads, so families elsewhere may not know them (international angle). It's a dry brand fact. Almond and hazelnut M&M's exist, but the yellow character is clearly the peanut one. Hint 3 nearly gives the answer away.

questions.description: A logo so famous it gets stared at on runways, handbags and very expensive sunglasses.
questions.question: The Versace logo shows the head of which figure from Greek myth?
hints: In the myths, she lived far away with her two sisters.
Instead of hair, she has something that hisses.
One look into her eyes and you turn to stone.
questions.fun_fact: Gianni Versace first saw her face as a boy, carved on ancient ruins in southern Italy.

quality.notes: Hint 2 (hair that hisses) already gives it away to anyone who knows the myth. Rated a bit harder than 9, because young teens rarely know the logo.

questions.description: The only rabbit that prefers chocolate to carrots.
questions.question: I came out in 1948, I'm a sweet brown powder, and my mascot is a bunny. What are you supposed to do with me?
hints: You use me at breakfast.
You need a glass and a spoon.
I turn a white drink brown and chocolatey.
questions.fun_fact: In the United States, Nesquik was first sold under the shorter name “Quik”.

quality.notes: 'Sprinkle it on ice cream' is something people really do with cocoa powder, though milk is clearly the main use. Distractors are weak for anyone who knows the product. Brand-recall question with little surprise.

questions.description: A plane built by a whole continent's worth of neighbors.
questions.question: Airbus builds its planes mainly in four European countries. Which of these is NOT one of them?
hints: Airbus was a European team effort to compete with American plane makers.
The fourth Airbus country is an island nation that builds the wings.
This country is shaped like a boot.
questions.fun_fact: Airbus parts are so big that the company flies them between its factories inside a giant whale-shaped plane called the Beluga.

quality.notes: The four core countries are right (France, Germany, Spain, UK). Italian suppliers do make Airbus parts, so 'mainly' is doing a lot of work. A rather dry odd-one-out; the Beluga fun fact is nice.

questions.description: A scent of sea breeze, a ship's deck and a bottle full of history.
questions.question: Old Spice was launched in 1937, and its bottles show old sailing ships. Who was its very first fragrance made for?
hints: The answer surprises most people today.
The line for men only came a year later, in 1938.
The very first product was a sweet, flowery perfume.
questions.fun_fact: Old Spice was created by a small company called Shulton and was bought by Procter & Gamble in 1990.

quality.notes: The 1937 women's line ('Early American Old Spice') is correct. 'Babies' is a filler option. Old Spice is mostly a US brand with uneven fame elsewhere (weak in Latin America), so it travels less well. Hint 3 nearly gives the answer, which is acceptable.
