questions.description: The loudest way to say “Happy New Year” ever invented.
questions.question: I'm small, red and very loud, and I pop all night at Chinese New Year. Legend says I'm lit to scare away what?
wrong_answers: A thunder god called Lei Gong
A fox spirit called Huli Jing
hints: It's a creature that was said to come out once a year.
It was said to be afraid of loud noises and the color red.
Its name is also the Chinese word for “year”.
questions.fun_fact: Firecrackers were first made in China long ago by throwing bamboo into a fire, where it burst with a loud bang.

quality.notes: Nian is well known in East Asia but less so elsewhere, so rated a little harder. Hint 2 points strongly to it. The lens tag 'colombia' looks wrong.

questions.description: A city name so long, the mail carrier needs a snack break halfway through.
questions.question: Bangkok's full ceremonial name is the longest name of any capital city. About how many letters does it have in English letters?
hints: It is far longer than any normal city name.
It would fill a few lines of text.
It is more than 100 but much less than 500.
questions.fun_fact: Thai people usually call their capital “Krung Thep”, meaning “City of Angels”, which is just the start of its full name.

quality.notes: Bangkok's ceremonial name is 168 letters in Guinness's romanization, so the facts hold. “About 1,000” is too absurd to tempt anyone, and “About 20” is close to it. Hint 3 leaves only one option, which is allowed for hint 3.

questions.description: A city that got the crown, lost it, and still dresses like royalty.
questions.question: Peter the Great moved Russia's capital to Saint Petersburg. Which city lost the title then, and won it back in 1918?
hints: It is a very old city on a river with the same name.
Its fortress has red walls and towers topped with red stars.
St. Basil's Cathedral, with its colorful onion domes, stands there.
questions.fun_fact: Saint Petersburg has changed its name three times: Petrograd, then Leningrad, then back to Saint Petersburg in 1991.

quality.notes: Knowing that Moscow is today's capital is enough to answer, so this is a little easier than 6. It reads like a school fact. The hints share St. Basil's with famous-landmarks-7, but that question asks a different fact.

questions.description: A skyscraper that looks like it's waiting to be dropped into a giant's car.
questions.question: Which car brand has its headquarters in a Munich tower shaped like four engine cylinders?
hints: This brand comes from Bavaria, in southern Germany.
Its logo is a circle with blue and white quarters.
Its name is short for “Bavarian Motor Works” in German.
questions.fun_fact: Before it built cars, BMW began by making engines for airplanes.

quality.notes: Hint 1 (Bavaria) also fits Audi from Ingolstadt, so it is weak but not wrong. Many young teens won't connect Munich with BMW.

questions.description: A cat so big it needs its own sofa, not just a corner of yours.
questions.question: Stewie, a Maine Coon, once held the world record for the longest pet cat. About how long was he from nose to tail tip?
hints: Maine Coons are one of the biggest cat breeds.
He was much longer than a normal house cat, but not as long as a bed.
Think of the height of a child about seven years old.
questions.fun_fact: Maine Coons have big, furry paws that work a bit like snowshoes in the cold winters of their home in the northeastern United States.

questions.description: Cats spent thousands of years becoming perfect hunters, and still pick the cheapest seat in the house.
questions.question: It hides a cat and helps it calm down when it's scared, and cats squeeze into it even when it's far too small. What is it?
hints: It often arrives at your door with a delivery.
It has four walls and an open top.
It's made of thick brown paper.
questions.fun_fact: In a study at an animal shelter, cats that were given a box to hide in got used to their new home faster than cats without one.

questions.description: A tiny bottle with a big personality and an even bigger price tag.
questions.question: What do people use a little spray bottle like this one for?
hints: You use it on your skin, not on things in the house.
You spray just a little on your neck or wrists.
Your nose loves what is inside.

media.note: A clear photo of an elegant perfume bottle with a spray top, with no brand name visible.

questions.fun_fact: Many perfumes have three “layers” of scent: the first notes fade within minutes, while the base notes can last for hours.

quality.notes: This is a simple identification question with little surprise. The distractors are good because they are other uses of spray bottles.

questions.description: Chemistry's most famous seating chart, where every element knows exactly where to sit.
questions.question: How many elements does the periodic table have today?
hints: It is more than 100.
The last four were officially named in 2016.
The heaviest one, oganesson, has an atomic number equal to the total.
questions.fun_fact: About 90 elements are found in nature; the rest have been made by scientists, often just a few atoms at a time.

quality.notes: This is a plain school-count question. The number could change if new elements are made, but it has been stable since 2016.

questions.description: An ice cube's worst summer day, told in one short sentence.
questions.question: You leave an ice cube in the sun. It melts and turns from a solid into a…
hints: You can pour it into a glass.
It takes the shape of whatever it is in.
Water, milk and juice are all this.
questions.fun_fact: Water is one of the few things that takes up more space as a solid than as a liquid, which is why ice floats.

quality.notes: Fun: a plain school fact with no twist. Description: an accurate sentence, but it isn't funny. An ice-cube image may show meltwater, which is a small nudge. 'Crystal' is a slightly odd option, since ice itself is a crystal, but it doesn't make the question ambiguous.

questions.description: A gemstone that left the royal crowns behind for a steady job on your wrist.
questions.question: Many expensive watches, like this one, have a “glass” made of lab-grown sapphire. Why?
questions.answer: It is very hard to scratch
hints: Think about what a watch bumps into every day.
Sapphire is one of the hardest natural materials; only diamond is much harder.
Keys and coins in your pocket can't harm it.
questions.fun_fact: Sapphire and ruby are the same mineral, corundum: red ones are called rubies, and all other colors are sapphires.

quality.notes: Hint 2 ('one of the hardest materials') nearly gives the answer away at the middle step. Players can reason their way to the answer, which is good.

questions.description: The fluffiest math problem ever, and nobody cares about the final answer.
questions.question: I'm an old trick: you picture fluffy sheep jumping over a fence and count them one by one. What am I for?
wrong_answers: Passing time in a long line
hints: People try me in bed at night.
I'm meant to make your mind slow down and get bored.
Use me when you can't close your eyes and drift off.
questions.fun_fact: Scientists at Oxford found that counting sheep doesn't help much; picturing a calm, relaxing scene puts people to sleep faster.

quality.notes: Very easy; it's closer to a 1 than a 2. It fits loosely under children's songs, but it's fine as a question. The Oxford fun fact is accurate (2002 study).

questions.description: A tiny box that plays the same song forever and never gets tired.
questions.question: I'm a little box with a metal comb that plays a tune. I was invented in 1796 in Geneva. Which country is that city in today?
hints: That country has four official languages.
It's a small country with no sea.
It is famous for the Alps, watches and chocolate.
questions.fun_fact: A music box plays by a turning cylinder with tiny pins that pluck the teeth of a metal comb.

quality.notes: Fun: the music-box setup is just padding. The real question is 'which country is Geneva in?', which is dry. Hint 3 (Alps, watches, chocolate) nearly names the country, which is allowed. Several candidates share the answer Switzerland but ask different facts.

questions.description: Left, right, left, right… don't stop now, the tuba is watching you.
questions.question: A march has a steady left-right beat, and bands play it at parades. Who was this kind of music first made for?
hints: These people often had to travel long distances on foot.
The steady beat helped big groups move with the same step.
These people wear uniforms and carry flags.
questions.fun_fact: The Ottoman army's mehter band, one of the oldest military bands in the world, inspired Mozart's famous “Turkish March”.

quality.notes: Hint 3 ('uniforms and flags') also fits the marching bands in the image, so it's a bit loose. 'Left, right' in the description and question hints at soldiers. manners-and-customs-17 has the same answer, Soldiers, but asks about a different fact.

questions.description: Where music lives before anyone gets to hear it.
questions.question: A script is to an actor as what is to a musician?
hints: The actor reads lines from the script.
It's printed on paper and full of little dots and lines.
It shows the notes the musician has to play.
questions.fun_fact: In 1501 in Venice, Ottaviano Petrucci printed the first book of music for several voices using movable type.

quality.notes: Fun: a simple analogy with little surprise. Hint 2 ('dots and lines on paper') nearly gives the answer away. Choosing a decorative image is reasonable, since most music images would show sheet music.

questions.description: Curtains: great for windows, bedrooms and splitting up the planet.
questions.question: During the Cold War, Europe had its Iron Curtain. What was the matching barrier around Mao's China called?
hints: Like its European cousin, it's named after a material.
The material is a plant.
Giant pandas love to eat it.
questions.fun_fact: The “Cactus Curtain” really existed too: it was the name for the line between Cuba and the US base at Guantánamo Bay.

quality.notes: Rated too hard: most players can work out 'bamboo' from China plus the Iron Curtain pattern, so it's easier than 12. Nice fun fact: it turns the Cactus distractor into a real curtain.

questions.description: A plane so old that its pilots' grandparents may have flown it too.
questions.question: This US Air Force giant with eight engines first flew in 1952 and still flies today. What was it built as?
hints: Its wings are so long that they have small extra wheels near the tips.
During the Cold War, some were kept in the air day and night, ready for a nuclear war.
A rock band and a beehive hairstyle were named after it: the B-52s.

media.note: A clear photo of a B-52 Stratofortress flying, with no bombs or missiles visible and no text naming the plane.

questions.fun_fact: The B-52 is planned to stay in service until the 2050s, about 100 years after its first flight.

quality.notes: Correct: hint 3 is a slight stretch. The beehive hairstyle was named after the plane's nose, and the band was named after the hairstyle. Players can guess 'bomber' just from the Cold War topic. The text already describes the plane fully, so the 'essential' photo isn't really needed. The photo must avoid visible weapons and 'B-52' markings, and the note covers this.

questions.description: A physicist whose career took a very sharp turn.
questions.question: Before becoming the Soviet Union's most famous dissident and winning the 1975 Nobel Peace Prize, Andrei Sakharov helped build what?
wrong_answers: The first Soviet nuclear power plant
hints: He was a brilliant physicist.
Later in life, he warned the world about the very thing he had helped make.
It's a weapon even stronger than the atomic bomb.
questions.fun_fact: Sakharov wasn't allowed to travel to Oslo to collect his Nobel Peace Prize, so his wife Yelena Bonner accepted it for him.

quality.notes: Most adults wouldn't know Sakharov's work on the H-bomb; it's well-read-adult knowledge, so 13 rather than 12.

questions.description: Digging a hole just to listen to other people's phone calls.
questions.question: The CIA and Britain's MI6 once dug a secret tunnel under Berlin to listen in on Soviet phone lines. In which decade?
hints: It was early in the Cold War.
The Soviets knew about it from the start, thanks to a double agent.
Elvis was a brand-new star back then.
questions.fun_fact: The Soviets learned about the tunnel from a spy before it was even dug, but let it run for almost a year to protect him.

quality.notes: Facts check out: Operation Gold/Stopwatch, tunnel used 1955–56, George Blake was the double agent. Age fit: few 16-year-olds know this; most adults could only reason from 'early Cold War' (hint 1, which points strongly to the 1950s). That is closer to 11 than to 9.

questions.description: The day footwear joined world politics.
questions.question: At the United Nations, Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev famously banged his shoe on his desk. In which year?
hints: Earlier that year, an American U-2 spy plane was shot down over the Soviet Union.
Rome hosted the Summer Olympics that year.
It happened the year before the Berlin Wall went up.
questions.fun_fact: Although the story is famous, no clear photo or film of Khrushchev actually banging his shoe has ever been found.

quality.notes: October 1960 is correct, and the hints are accurate. Correct: there is no authentic photo of the shoe-banging (a known doctored image exists), so the fun fact is true but the event itself is debated. Age fit: the exact year of the shoe incident is beyond 'most adults'; closer to 13 than 12.

questions.description: Some countries choose their friends; these had theirs chosen for them.
questions.question: It's a country that is officially independent, but whose government follows orders from a bigger power, like Poland or Hungary under Moscow. What is it called?
hints: The term was used a lot during the Cold War.
The name comes from space.
The Moon is one for the Earth.
questions.fun_fact: Warsaw's Palace of Culture and Science was a “gift” from the Soviet Union to Poland, finished in 1955.

quality.notes: Hint 2 ('the name comes from space') is already very strong for a second hint. Image and fun fact are fine.

questions.description: The fanciest color in history smelled surprisingly fishy.
questions.question: Ancient royal purple dye was made from the animal whose shell you see here. What kind of animal is it?
hints: It lives in the sea and moves very slowly.
It's not a fish, but it is related to clams.
It's a cousin of the garden snail.

media.note: A close-up of a spiny murex shell (Bolinus brandaris or Hexaplex trunculus), no labels.

questions.fun_fact: It took thousands of these snails to dye a single robe, which is why only rulers could afford it.

quality.notes: Distractors: once players see a shell photo, a squid and coral (no snail-like shell) are easy to rule out, so it's easier than rated. Hint 2 ('related to clams') also fits squid. Correct: 'thousands per robe' is about right; the classic estimate is around 10,000 snails per gram of dye. A clear murex photo is very likely on Commons.

questions.description: Pick the wrong color on the trail map and your legs will remember it all week.
questions.question: On ski slopes in Europe and North America, who is a run marked with black meant for?
hints: Ski runs get colors that show how hard they are.
Black is the top of the scale.
These runs are the steepest and hardest.
questions.fun_fact: In North America the hardest runs use a black diamond, and the very hardest get two of them.

quality.notes: Hints 2–3 pretty much give it away. Many families worldwide don't ski, but 'black = hardest' can be worked out.

questions.description: A controller that makes you lean sideways on the couch without even noticing.
questions.question: This close-up shows part of a game controller. What kind of controller is it?
hints: You hold it with both hands.
You turn it left and right.
It often comes with pedals for your feet.

media.note: A photo of a video game racing wheel, at least part of the round rim with its buttons visible, clearly a gaming wheel; no game titles visible.

questions.fun_fact: Some racing wheels push back against your hands, so you can feel the bumps of the track.

quality.notes: Description: 'lean sideways' hints at steering, which points to the wheel. Fun: once the round rim is visible, it's a plain identify question. Commons very likely has a clear essential photo.

questions.description: Sega's answer to the Game Boy, with a screen full of colors.
questions.question: You put six fresh AA batteries into a Sega Game Gear in 1991. About how long can you play?
hints: Its color screen was lit from behind, which uses a lot of power.
Its rival, the Game Boy, lasted far longer with fewer batteries.
It was less than a single afternoon.
questions.fun_fact: The original Game Boy, with its simpler green-and-black screen, could run for over 10 hours on just four AA batteries.

quality.notes: Correct: about 3–5 hours on six AA batteries is right. Hint 3 ('less than an afternoon') basically gives the answer. Description: a plain statement, not funny. Fun: niche retro trivia that's a bit dry, though the fun fact comparison helps.

questions.description: Two tiny motors live in your hands, and they're not there to drive anywhere.
questions.question: PlayStation controllers have two small motors inside. What are they for?
hints: You feel it in your hands, you don't see it.
It happens when you crash or get hit in a game.
The controller's old name, DualShock, is a clue.
questions.fun_fact: Each motor spins a small off-center weight, and that wobble is what makes the controller shake.

quality.notes: The off-center weight in the fun fact describes DualShock-era rumble motors. The current DualSense uses voice-coil haptic actuators, so “two small motors” isn't strictly true of every PlayStation controller.

questions.description: Half phone, half game console, and you had to hold it sideways to make a call.
questions.question: This phone was also a game console. In which country is the company that made it based?
hints: The company is from northern Europe.
It also made the famous phones with the game Snake.
Its capital is Helsinki.

media.note: A clear photo of the original Nokia N-Gage game phone (2003), showing its wide shape with the keypad and game buttons on either side of the screen; the Nokia logo may be visible.

questions.fun_fact: People called the N-Gage the “taco phone”, because you had to hold its edge against your ear to talk.

quality.notes: The Nokia logo allowed in the essential photo turns the question into “where is Nokia from?”. Many adults and older teens know that, so 10 is closer than 11. The “Country” overlap candidate is unrelated.

questions.description: Its cartoon cousin spins like a tornado, but the real one prefers to just yell.
questions.question: Today, this animal lives in the wild mostly on an island south of Australia. What kind of animal is it?
hints: Its babies are born very tiny.
Most of its relatives live in Australia and nearby islands.
Its babies grow up in a pouch.

media.note: A close-up of a Tasmanian devil's face and front body, without the full animal; no text.

questions.fun_fact: For its size, the Tasmanian devil has one of the strongest bites of any mammal.

quality.notes: q-2012 (diprotodon → marsupials) asks the same kind of question with the same answer, but about a different animal, so it only borders on overlap. The Taz reference in the description identifies the animal but not its group.

questions.description: The little voice in the car that never gets tired of saying “turn left.”
questions.question: GPS tells your phone where you are, even in deserts or the middle of the ocean. Where do its signals come from?
hints: Its parts are very, very high up.
They are not on the ground at all.
They circle the Earth in space.
questions.fun_fact: Your phone needs signals from at least four GPS satellites to work out exactly where you are.

quality.notes: Phones also use cell towers to help find position (assisted GPS), so one distractor is half-true, though GPS itself is satellite-based. The question is fairly school-like and dry. The wording of hint 1 (“Its parts”) is awkward.

questions.description: A ball so neatly sewn it could get a job in a tailor's shop.
questions.question: The hard red ball used in cricket has a raised seam around its middle. How many rows of stitches run along that seam?
hints: The rows sit side by side, so the seam is quite wide.
It's more than four.
It's one row fewer than the number of days in a week.
questions.fun_fact: Bowlers polish one side of the ball on their trousers so it swings in the air.

quality.notes: Six rows of stitching is the standard description, but this is an obscure count that only cricket fans could know, and the fact is close to unknowable in non-cricket regions such as the Americas. It's a dry count with little fun, and hint 3 is pure arithmetic that gives the answer away.

questions.description: When the sky starts crying, the math teachers take over the match.
questions.question: Cricket's rain rule resets the target when a match is cut short. It's named after how many statisticians?
hints: The rule's full name is just a row of surnames joined by dashes.
Each surname belongs to a statistician who worked on the method.
It started with two names in 1997, and one more was added in 2014.
questions.fun_fact: Frank Duckworth and Tony Lewis created the method in 1997, and Steven Stern's name was added in 2014.

quality.notes: Duckworth-Lewis-Stern is right, but the dates are blurry: D/L was first used in 1997 and the Stern rename came in 2014–15. Asking for a count of names is a gimmick, and the numeric distractors are weak. Hint 1 gives the answer away to anyone who has heard the name. The method is cricket-only knowledge that isn't familiar in many regions.

questions.description: A green guy who can never decide what to wear: fur, feathers or scales.
questions.question: Which green-skinned member of the Teen Titans can turn into any animal?
hints: This hero is the jokester of the team.
This hero's best friend on the team is Cyborg.
The hero name has a word for a wild creature in it.
questions.fun_fact: In the comics, Beast Boy turned green because of a serum his scientist parents gave him to cure a rare illness.

quality.notes: The answer's name (“Beast”) fits the clue about turning into animals, so players can guess it from the name alone.

questions.description: Most families keep a big old clock to tell the time, but this family has other plans.
questions.question: In many Batman stories, what does Bruce Wayne use the old grandfather clock in Wayne Manor for?
questions.answer: To open the way to the Batcave
wrong_answers: To lock away the family jewels
To send secret messages to Alfred
hints: It isn't really about telling the time.
Batman needs a quick, secret way to his gear.
Behind it there are stairs going down into the dark.
questions.fun_fact: In the 1960s Batman TV series, the secret way down was opened by tilting the head of a Shakespeare bust.

quality.notes: The answer is a bit more specific than the distractors but doesn't really stand out. q-0312 shares only the Batcave topic.

questions.description: Who needs a flashlight when your eyes come with extras?
questions.question: Superman can shoot red beams from his eyes. What is this power called?
hints: It's a superpower, not a gadget.
He can use it to cut and weld metal.
It's the opposite of his freezing breath.
questions.fun_fact: In his first comics in 1938, Superman had no heat vision at all and couldn't even fly: he could only jump very high.

quality.notes: X-ray vision is also one of Superman's powers, but it doesn't shoot beams, so it is clearly wrong.

questions.description: Batman, but with more jokes and far fewer frowns.
questions.question: In which 2017 animated film does Batman live alone, adopt Robin by mistake and team up with the Joker?
wrong_answers: Teen Titans Go! To the Movies
hints: It's an animated film full of jokes.
Everything in it is built from little bricks.
Batman is the star, not a side character.
questions.fun_fact: This Batman first showed up in “The Lego Movie” in 2014 and was so popular he got his own film.

quality.notes: “Lives alone” is loose, since Alfred lives in the manor with him; the film's point is that Batman feels alone. Hint 2 (bricks) narrows the options to the two Lego films.

questions.description: A man who asked the whole world to imagine things, and the world actually listened.
questions.question: I was born in Liverpool, I wore small round glasses, and I wrote the song “Imagine”. Who am I?
hints: I was one of the four members of a very famous band.
That band was the Beatles.
My first name is John.
questions.fun_fact: Liverpool's airport is named after him: Liverpool John Lennon Airport.

quality.notes: All four Beatles were born in Liverpool, so only the glasses and "Imagine" separate the options. That's fine. Yoko Ono has been officially credited as co-writer of "Imagine" since 2017, a small nuance. The description just repeats "imagine" from the question and adds no joke of its own. Most 13-year-olds don't know who wrote "Imagine", so 7 is too low.

questions.description: Three days of music, mud and very questionable fashion on a dairy farm.
questions.question: The famous Woodstock music festival took place on a farm in New York State. In which year?
hints: It was the age of hippies and flower power.
It happened the same summer people first walked on the Moon.
It was the last year of the 1960s.
questions.fun_fact: Around 400,000 people showed up, far more than the organizers had planned for.

quality.notes: Woodstock is US-centred but famous worldwide. Young teens rarely know its year, so 9 is slightly low. The Moon landing hint is a nice way to reason towards it. The image query is generic but safe.

questions.description: Science finally proved what your car radio already knew.
questions.question: When you need cheering up, science has an answer: a 2015 study named this Queen song the most feel-good song ever. Which?
hints: It's fast, joyful and full of energy.
Freddie Mercury sings that he's having a good time.
He says he's like a shooting star and asks nobody to stop him.
questions.fun_fact: The study was done by a Dutch brain scientist, who even worked out a formula for a feel-good song.

quality.notes: The study is real (Jacob Jolij, 2015, commissioned by a brand rather than a peer-reviewed paper). "When you need cheering up, science has an answer:" is filler before the actual question. "Another One Bites the Dust" and "The Show Must Go On" are clearly not feel-good songs, so anyone who knows the songs can rule them out easily. Hint 3 almost quotes the title, which is allowed for hint 3.

questions.description: Hollywood's favorite hobby: dressing actors up as rock stars.
questions.question: At a night of music films: “Bohemian Rhapsody” is to Freddie Mercury as “Rocketman” is to…
hints: Both films tell the life story of a British star.
This star is famous for his piano and his wild glasses.
He sang “Your Song” and wrote songs for “The Lion King”.
questions.fun_fact: Rami Malek won the Oscar for Best Actor for playing Freddie Mercury in “Bohemian Rhapsody”.

quality.notes: The "At a night of music films:" setting is padding. It has the same answer as disney-films-6 (Elton John), and hint 3 mentions The Lion King, but the fact asked is different.

questions.description: Borrowing someone else's homework, but with a guitar and permission.
questions.question: Writing your own song is to an “original” as playing someone else's song in your own version is to a…
hints: Talent show singers do this all the time.
Many famous hits are new versions of older songs.
The word is also what goes on the front of a book.
questions.fun_fact: “Hallelujah” by Leonard Cohen has been covered by hundreds of artists.

quality.notes: The analogy is clunky and long to read aloud. Hint 3 (the front of a book) is an English pun and doesn't carry over to other languages (Spanish says "portada").

questions.description: A box of tiny pebbles with a very important job that nobody wants to talk about.
questions.question: Since the 1940s, homes all over the world have bought bags of clay grains like these. What are they mostly used for?
hints: The grains soak up liquid very well.
A furry pet uses them every day.
It goes in a box that a cat visits.

media.note: Close photo of loose grey clay cat litter granules, without packaging, box or cat visible.

questions.fun_fact: In 1947 Edward Lowe gave a neighbor some dried clay to use instead of sand or ashes for her cat, and that started the modern cat litter business.

quality.notes: Essential photo: loose litter granules with no box are fairly easy to find, but they might look like plain gravel. 'Road salt' isn't clay, so it's a slightly weaker distractor.

questions.description: A stone so famous that the crayon box named a color after it.
questions.question: “I'm an opaque blue-green stone, often with brown veins, and a color between blue and green carries my name.” What am I?
hints: I'm popular in silver jewelry.
My color is like a tropical sea.
Swimming pools are often painted this color.
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from an old French word meaning “Turkish”, because the stone reached Europe through Turkey.

quality.notes: Knowing the color name 'turquoise' is a bit beyond most 9–10-year-olds, so slightly above 4.

questions.description: Same rock, three names, depending on how far it has fallen.
questions.question: Meteor is to “streaking through the sky” as meteorite is to “lying on the ground”. What goes with “a small rock drifting through space”?
hints: It's the same rock before it reaches our air.
An asteroid is much bigger than this.
The word starts like the other two and ends in “-oid”.
questions.fun_fact: Most shooting stars are made by meteoroids no bigger than a grain of sand.

quality.notes: A clean but dry vocabulary analogy. The '-oid' hint depends on the word form, but it carries over to Spanish and German.

questions.description: A grey soup that becomes a sidewalk if you wait long enough.
questions.question: Builders mix grey cement powder with water, sand and gravel, pour it into a mold, and a few days later it's hard as rock. What have they made?
hints: Bridges, dams and sidewalks are made of it.
A truck with a spinning drum brings it to building sites.
Its name starts like “con…”.
questions.fun_fact: The dome of the Pantheon in Rome, built about 1,900 years ago, is still the largest dome in the world made of concrete without steel bars.

quality.notes: A fairly plain 'what is it' question. Hint 3 ('con…') only works in English (Spanish hormigón, German Beton), so it needs reworking when translated.

questions.description: A boring-looking rock with a party going on inside.
questions.question: This close-up shows crystals lining a hollow inside a rock. What is the whole rock called?
hints: From the outside it looks like a plain round stone.
You have to crack it open to see the surprise.
Shops sell them cut in half, often with purple amethyst inside.

media.note: Close-up of the crystal-lined inside of a geode, showing only the crystals in the hollow, not the whole cut rock.

questions.fun_fact: The Pulpí geode in Spain is so big that several people can stand inside it among giant gypsum crystals.

quality.notes: Geodes are familiar from gift shops and science kits, so probably easier than 8. The query might return a whole cut geode, but the note covers that.

questions.description: Rocks go through more makeovers than a reality TV star.
questions.question: This speckled rock is granite, often used for kitchen countertops. Which of the main rock types in the rock cycle is it?
hints: Its crystals grew big because it cooled very slowly.
It started out as melted rock deep underground.
Its name comes from the Latin word for fire.

media.note: Close-up of polished or natural granite showing speckled interlocking crystals (pink, white, black).

questions.fun_fact: Mount Rushmore in the USA was carved into granite.

quality.notes: 'Meteoritic' is not a rock type in the rock cycle, so it's an obvious filler distractor. The image isn't essential because the question already says it's granite. A dry school question. It shares a topic with q-0884 (granite's minerals) but asks a different fact.

questions.description: Tiny white cubes that make fries happy and snails very unhappy.
questions.question: This white stuff is made by drying out seawater. What do people use it for most at home?
hints: You find it on the dinner table.
It sits next to the pepper.
It makes potato chips taste salty.

media.note: Close photo of a pile of white sea salt crystals, no labels or shakers with text.

questions.fun_fact: Your body needs salt to make your muscles and nerves work.

quality.notes: Very easy and not very surprising. Fine at level 1.

questions.description: The floor is lava? No, the floor is baked clay.
questions.question: Tiles like these are made of baked clay with a shiny coating. Why are they so popular on bathroom and kitchen walls?
hints: Think about what splashes in a bathroom.
You can wipe them clean easily.
They stay dry under the shower.

media.note: Photo of shiny glazed ceramic tiles on a wall.

questions.fun_fact: About 4,600 years ago, Egyptians decorated rooms under the Step Pyramid of Djoser with blue glazed tiles.

quality.notes: A practical question that's fine but not exciting. The description's joke is about floors, but the question is about wall tiles. The image isn't truly essential.

questions.description: The ancient Roman way of saying “I won, and the whole city is coming to watch.”
questions.question: This carving on an arch in Rome shows an emperor riding in a victory parade. What did the Romans call such a parade?
hints: Arches like this one were built to remember these parades.
The winning general rode a chariot pulled by four horses up to the temple of Jupiter.
Today the same word means a great victory or success.

media.note: Close-up of the relief inside the Arch of Titus in Rome showing Titus riding a four-horse chariot, crowned by Victory. No captions or signs.

questions.fun_fact: According to the Roman writer Pliny, the winning general's face was painted red, like the statue of Jupiter.

quality.notes: Solid. Players can work the answer out from the English word “triumph”, so it's slightly easier than 11. The relief photo works better as illustrative than essential, but it does no harm.

questions.description: Live long and prosper, and mind where you put your fingers.
questions.question: Leonard Nimoy, who played Spock, based this Star Trek greeting on a blessing he saw as a boy. Who gives that blessing?
hints: Nimoy grew up in Boston, in a family that came from Ukraine.
The blessing comes from the Hebrew Bible.
He saw it during a service in a synagogue.

media.note: Photo of a real hand making the Vulcan salute (fingers split between the middle and ring finger). No Star Trek characters, logos or costumes.

questions.fun_fact: With both hands, the gesture looks like the Hebrew letter shin, the first letter of a name for God.

quality.notes: Great surprising fact. Hint 2 (the Hebrew Bible) already gives the answer away. The description is only a weak joke.

questions.description: Zero to hero, with a soundtrack full of singing ladies.
questions.question: You're watching Disney's “Hercules”. Which of these groups does NOT show up in the film?
hints: The film is set in ancient Greece.
Hercules' father Zeus lives on Mount Olympus with his family.
Nobody in the film sails around looking for buried treasure.
questions.fun_fact: The film uses the Roman name Hercules, even though the story is Greek and the Greeks called him Heracles.

quality.notes: Pirates is plainly the odd one out, so the question is easy to reason but dry. Young kids may not know the words “Titans” or “Muses”. The description hints at one wrong option (the Muses) without ruling anything out.

questions.description: A planet so far away that the Sun looks like just a bright star from there.
questions.question: “I am deep blue, I am the planet farthest from the Sun, and I share my name with the Roman god of the sea.” What am I?
hints: I am one of the four giant planets.
The Roman sea god carries a trident.
The Greeks called the sea god Poseidon; the Romans used another name.
questions.fun_fact: Neptune takes about 165 Earth years to go once around the Sun.

quality.notes: The riddle stacks three clues, so it's a fairly standard school question. The description is a bit off: from Neptune the Sun is still far brighter than any star, and the line isn't very funny.

questions.description: Earth's next-door neighbor, and it's not in a peaceful mood.
questions.question: Which planet, named after the Roman god of war, comes right after Earth counting from the Sun?
hints: It's the fourth planet from the Sun.
Robots called rovers drive around on it.
It's known as the Red Planet.
questions.fun_fact: Mars looks red because its dust is full of iron oxide, the same stuff as rust.

quality.notes: A dry school fact. The same answer (Mars) appears in q-0051 and q-0352, but they ask different facts. Hint 3 repeats q-0051.

questions.description: Sleeping Beauty's name lights up the sky, even when she's asleep.
questions.question: Sky lights like these share their name with Princess Aurora from “Sleeping Beauty”. Where do you see them most?
questions.answer: Near the North and South Poles
hints: They are best seen on long, dark winter nights.
Countries like Norway, Finland and Canada are famous for them.
You need to go very far north or very far south.

media.note: Photo of green northern lights over a dark landscape, with no text.

questions.fun_fact: Aurora was the Roman goddess of the dawn, so Sleeping Beauty is named after the morning itself.

quality.notes: The deserts and rainforests distractors are weak, and the answer is longer than the other options. Hint 2 nearly gives it away. Strictly, auroras show up in a ring around the magnetic poles rather than at the poles themselves, but “near” is fair.

questions.description: A man so big and so fast that defenders saw him in their nightmares, and then on the scoreboard.
questions.question: Usain Bolt is to athletics as Jonah Lomu is to…
hints: He played on the wing for a team dressed all in black.
He became world famous at the 1995 World Cup, running over England's defenders.
His team performs the haka before every match.
questions.fun_fact: Jonah Lomu was about 1.96 m (6 ft 5 in) tall and weighed around 120 kg (265 lb), yet he could run 100 m in under 11 seconds.

quality.notes: Solid analogy. Hints 1–2 (team in black, 1995 World Cup) narrow it to rugby fairly early, but that's acceptable. Lomu is little known outside rugby countries, so 12 is fair. q-0430 (Bolt's 100 m record) asks a different fact.

questions.description: A sport where the wheelchairs come with dents as badges of honor.
questions.question: Wheelchair rugby, a full Paralympic sport since Sydney 2000, was invented in Canada in which decade?
hints: The first Paralympic Games were held in 1960, before this sport existed.
It was invented in the city of Winnipeg.
It was invented in 1977.
questions.fun_fact: Wheelchair rugby is one of the few Paralympic team sports where men and women play on the same team.

quality.notes: The facts are correct: Winnipeg, 1977, full medal sport at Sydney 2000, mixed-gender teams. Hint 1 already rules out two options, leaving only 1970s and 1990s, and hint 3 states the exact year. A guess-the-decade question is somewhat dry.

questions.description: A giant letter standing at the end of the field, waiting for someone to spell something.
questions.question: I stand at each end of a rugby field, shaped like a giant letter H. Where must a kicked ball go to score points?
questions.answer: Over the bar, between the posts
wrong_answers: Under the bar, between the posts
Around the outside of the posts
Into a net behind the posts
hints: It is not like scoring a goal in soccer.
The posts reach far up into the sky for a reason.
The ball has to fly higher than the crossbar.
questions.fun_fact: The crossbar of a rugby goal is 3 m (about 10 ft) above the ground, but the posts can be more than 16 m (52 ft) tall.

quality.notes: The riddle voice is muddled: 'I' am the posts, yet the question asks where the ball goes. The description repeats the 'giant letter' clue from the question. The fun fact's '16 m posts' is true only for some unusually tall posts; the rules set a minimum height of 3.4 m.

questions.description: A final so tense, even the trophy needed extra time to calm down.
questions.question: South Africa won the 1995 Rugby World Cup final at home, with a drop goal in extra time. Which team did it beat?
hints: The losing team had the tournament's biggest star, Jonah Lomu.
The final score was 15–12.
This team performs the haka before its matches.
questions.fun_fact: Nelson Mandela handed the trophy to captain François Pienaar while wearing a Springbok jersey with Pienaar's number 6.

quality.notes: A strong question, helped by the film Invictus and the Mandela fun fact. Hint 1 (Lomu) nearly solves it for rugby fans. It touches the same tournament as rugby-0 (Lomu at 1995), but asks a different fact.

questions.description: A fly-half whose boots probably deserve their own trophy cabinet.
questions.question: Dan Carter ended his All Blacks career by winning the Rugby World Cup in England. In which year?
hints: He played for New Zealand from 2003 on.
New Zealand won the World Cup twice in a row, and this was the second time.
It was four years after New Zealand won at home in 2011.
questions.fun_fact: After that 2015 final, Dan Carter was named World Rugby Player of the Year for the third time, after 2005 and 2012.

quality.notes: The facts are correct (2015 at Twickenham; Player of the Year in 2005, 2012 and 2015). Knowing 'England hosted 2015' or the four-year cycle helps you reason. A Twickenham photo could show event signage with a date. q-2146 (England's 2003 win) is a different fact. Somewhat dry.

questions.description: Some people say it shows an ancient astronaut; archaeologists say it shows a king with excellent taste in stonework.
questions.question: This carved stone lid covers the tomb of the Maya king Pakal. In which ancient city was it found?
hints: The city lies in the rainforest of southern Mexico.
The tomb was hidden deep inside a pyramid called the Temple of the Inscriptions.
Its name is Spanish and sounds a bit like “palisade”.

media.note: Show the carved sarcophagus lid of King Pakal from the Temple of the Inscriptions, without any caption or sign naming the site.

questions.fun_fact: Archaeologists found Pakal's tomb in 1952 after clearing a secret staircase that had been filled with rubble for more than 1,000 years.

quality.notes: Solid hard question. The lid of Pakal's sarcophagus is well photographed on Commons. The essential role is a bit generous, since the question text names the tomb anyway.

questions.description: A mountain so holy that the pilgrims politely walk around it instead of climbing it.
questions.question: Pilgrims walk all the way around Tibet's Mount Kailash, about 52 km (32 mi), without climbing it. What is the word for walking around a holy place as worship?
hints: The word comes from Latin for “walking around”.
Muslims do the same thing seven times around the Kaaba.
It begins with the same Latin root as “circle”.
questions.fun_fact: Mount Kailash is holy to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and followers of Bon, and nobody is known to have climbed to its top.

quality.notes: The answer is a rare English/Latin technical word. In German or Spanish ("Umrundung", "circunvalación") it becomes a vocabulary test, so it is tied to one language. Hints 1 and 3 say nearly the same thing. Players can guess the answer from "circum-", which is fine but makes it a bit dry. The description mostly repeats the question.

questions.description: A fisherman who ended up with one of the longest walking routes in Europe named after him.
questions.question: I fished on the Sea of Galilee before becoming one of Jesus's twelve apostles. Today pilgrims walk across Spain to my tomb. Who am I?
hints: My brother John was also an apostle.
My tomb is said to be in a city in northwestern Spain.
In Spanish, I am called Santiago.
questions.fun_fact: Santiago de Compostela's cathedral swings a giant incense burner, the Botafumeiro, so high it almost touches the ceiling.

quality.notes: Good. Peter and Andrew were also fishermen, so they are fair distractors, and the Spain tomb clue makes the answer unique.

questions.description: A city where the old streets have seen more walkers than any shopping mall.
questions.question: Pilgrims walk the Way of the Cross through its old streets, where Jesus is said to have carried his cross. Its Old City is holy to three religions. Which city is it?
hints: It is in the Middle East.
Its Old City has the Western Wall and the Dome of the Rock.
Its name begins with the letter J.
questions.fun_fact: The Way of the Cross has 14 stations, and many churches around the world have 14 small pictures on their walls to copy the walk.

quality.notes: Cairo is a weak distractor. The question is a bit long, at about 150 characters. The description is generic. A decorative image works, but a safe illustrative one would have been possible too.

questions.description: A minaret that looks like a giant stone corkscrew, with no elevator in sight.
questions.question: You're climbing the spiral ramp around the minaret of the Great Mosque of Samarra, in Iraq. In which century was it built?
hints: It was built for the Abbasid caliphs, who briefly made Samarra their capital.
This was the time of Baghdad's golden age and the stories of the Thousand and One Nights.
It was finished around the year 850.
questions.fun_fact: The spiral minaret, called the Malwiya, is about 52 m (171 ft) tall, and for a while the mosque was the largest in the world.

quality.notes: Asking for the century is fairly dry. The "You're climbing" setup adds nothing. Hint 3 gives the year, which is allowed.

questions.description: Rome has a whole second city underground, and nobody lives in it anymore.
questions.question: You're walking through dark tunnels under Rome lined with ancient graves. Pyramid is to pharaohs as these catacombs are to…
hints: They lived in Rome almost 2,000 years ago.
Their tombs are decorated with fish and doves.
They followed the teachings of Jesus.
questions.fun_fact: Rome's catacombs together stretch for hundreds of kilometers of tunnels under the city.

quality.notes: Mixing a scenario with an analogy is clunky. Rome also has Jewish catacombs, but early Christians is the standard answer. "Viking warriors" and "Greek philosophers" are weak distractors. The "hundreds of kilometers" in the fun fact may overstate it: common estimates are about 150–170 km, though some go higher.

questions.description: A wall that holds back a whole lake and still keeps the lights on.
questions.question: This dam makes electricity. Inside it, falling water spins which machines?
hints: The water rushes down through big pipes inside the dam.
One machine spins like a giant fan in the water.
The spinning part is connected to a machine with magnets and wire coils.

media.note: A clear photo of a large hydroelectric dam with its wall and reservoir.

questions.fun_fact: People have used falling water to do work for thousands of years, with water wheels that ground grain.

quality.notes: The photo isn't really needed to answer, so the role should be illustrative, not essential. “Pumps” could be argued for pumped-storage dams. The answer is fairly dry.

questions.description: A wheel that never touches the road but still does the heavy lifting.
questions.question: What is this simple machine mainly used for?
hints: You often see it on building sites and old wells.
A rope runs over its wheel.
You pull down on one side, and something goes up on the other.

media.note: A clear photo of a pulley wheel with a rope running over it.

questions.fun_fact: Legend says Archimedes used pulleys to pull a fully loaded ship onto land all by himself.

quality.notes: The distractors (measuring speed, cutting wood) are weak, so once you see the pulley the answer is clear. The Archimedes ship story is a legend from Plutarch, and the fun fact says so.

questions.description: The straightest friend in your pencil case.
questions.question: I'm flat and straight, with little lines and numbers along my edge. What do you use me to measure?
hints: You find me at school.
You also use me to draw straight lines.
My numbers are often centimeters.
questions.fun_fact: Ancient Egyptians measured with the cubit: the length from the elbow to the fingertip.

quality.notes: A plain riddle for small kids. The decorative “school desk” image may well show a ruler, though it is blurred.

questions.description: The only vegetable that makes grown-ups cry in the kitchen.
questions.question: Cutting an onion breaks its cells, which release an invisible gas that stings your eyes. Why does the onion make it?
questions.answer: To scare off animals that bite it
hints: The onion can't run away.
Think of it as the onion's weapon.
It only appears when the onion gets damaged.
questions.fun_fact: Chilling an onion before you cut it slows the reaction, so you cry less.

quality.notes: The defense explanation is the accepted one. The description says “only vegetable”, which isn't literally true, but it's a joke. Hint 2 is strong.

questions.description: Nature's way of saying “who needs batteries?”
questions.question: Fireflies do it, deep-sea anglerfish do it, and some mushrooms do it too: they make their own light. What is this called?
hints: The light comes from a chemical reaction inside the living thing.
The first part of the word means “life”.
The second part comes from the Latin word for light.
questions.fun_fact: Most of the animals that live in the deep sea can make their own light.

quality.notes: The fun fact rests on the roughly 75% figure for animals seen in the deep water column, so “most” is acceptable.

questions.description: Playground equipment, but make it physics class.
questions.question: At the playground, a slide is to inclined plane as a seesaw is to…
hints: All four options are simple machines.
A seesaw is a bar that turns around a fixed point in the middle.
A crowbar and a bottle opener work the same way.
questions.fun_fact: Archimedes said: “Give me a place to stand, and I will move the Earth.”

quality.notes: Good analogy. Hint 1 adds little.

questions.description: The office toy that keeps clicking long after you've stopped working.
questions.question: Lift one ball of this desk toy and let it go, and one ball flies out on the other side. What does it show?
questions.answer: Energy passing from ball to ball
hints: The middle balls barely move.
Each ball hits the next one and hands something on.
Lift two balls, and two fly out on the other side.

media.note: A clear photo of a Newton's cradle desk toy with its row of hanging steel balls.

questions.fun_fact: The toy is named after Isaac Newton, whose laws of motion explain how it works.

quality.notes: Physicists would also say momentum is passed on, but the answer is fine as a simplification. The answer is a bit longer than the distractors. The question describes the toy in words, so the image could be illustrative.

questions.description: The bathroom gadget that's honest even when you don't want it to be.
questions.question: You stand on me in the bathroom, and I tell you how heavy you are. What am I?
hints: Doctors have one too.
I show a number in kilograms or pounds.
At the market, I weigh fruit and vegetables.
questions.fun_fact: People in ancient Egypt weighed things with balance scales more than 4,000 years ago.

quality.notes: Very easy riddle with little surprise. It is close to inventions-9 (the balance scale, used for weighing), but the object is different.

questions.description: A string that can't sit still, and that's exactly why it sounds good.
questions.question: Pluck this guitar string and you hear a note. What is the string doing to make the sound?
hints: Look closely: the string looks blurry after you pluck it.
Touch it with your finger, and the sound stops.
It moves back and forth very fast.

media.note: A clear close-up photo of guitar strings on a guitar.

questions.fun_fact: Hummingbirds are named after the humming sound their super-fast wings make.

quality.notes: A still photo adds nothing here, so the role should be illustrative, not essential. The hummingbird fun fact only loosely connects to the question.

questions.description: The invisible force that ruins every attempt to slide across the kitchen in socks.
questions.question: I'm the force that slows you down when you slide, and I'm weakest on smooth surfaces. Where would you slide farthest?
hints: I'm called friction.
Rough surfaces make me stronger.
Skaters glide here.
questions.fun_fact: Without friction you couldn't even walk: your feet would just slide.

quality.notes: The riddle voice (“I'm the force”) clashes with a question about a place, which reads awkwardly. A frozen-lake image would be safe as illustrative, so decorative isn't needed.

questions.description: The sky's own camera flash, with very loud sound effects.
questions.question: It flashes bright, a loud boom follows, and it comes during storms. Where does lightning usually come from?
hints: Look up during a storm.
They are dark and full of rain.
The same place the rain falls from.
questions.fun_fact: Light travels much faster than sound, so you see lightning before you hear its thunder.

quality.notes: Very easy and plain. The question mostly repeats what the description already says.

questions.description: A tiny cylinder with a big promise printed on its side.
questions.question: What does the “1.5 V” printed on this battery tell you?
questions.answer: How strongly it pushes electric current
wrong_answers: How much energy it stores in total
How fast electrons move inside it
hints: The V stands for a unit named after an Italian scientist.
A car battery has 12 of these.
It is often compared to water pressure in a pipe.

media.note: A clear photo of an AA battery with “1.5 V” readable on its label.

questions.fun_fact: The volt is named after Alessandro Volta, who built the first battery in 1800.

quality.notes: “Pushes electric current” is a simplification of voltage that experts could quibble with. Energy stored is related to voltage, but it is clearly a different idea. The fun fact repeats Volta and 1800 from q-0444, but the question asks something else. It reads a bit like a school test.

questions.description: Lemonade for your gadgets.
questions.question: Stick a copper coin and a zinc nail into a lemon and it becomes a battery. About how many volts does it give?
hints: You can touch it safely with your fingers.
It isn't enough to charge a phone.
It's a little less than one ordinary AA battery.
questions.fun_fact: Potatoes work as batteries too, and boiled ones work even better.

quality.notes: The distractors are spread very wide (12, 120, 1,000), and hint 1 rules out the high ones, so it is easier than the stated 7. The description is very short and not very funny.

questions.description: The superhero version of a mom's handbag: there's always something useful inside.
questions.question: Batman's belt is yellow, sits around his waist and is full of little pouches. What does he keep in them?
hints: He has no superpowers, so he needs help from somewhere.
Think of the bat-shaped things he throws.
A grappling hook to climb buildings is in there too.
questions.fun_fact: Batman's utility belt first appeared in the comics in 1939, the same year as Batman himself.

quality.notes: The answer is easy to guess: 'Gadgets and tools' is the only serious-sounding option, and 'Spare masks' and 'Snacks' feel like jokes. The 'yellow, sits around his waist' detail is filler. Fairly dry.

questions.description: The official shoe of the beach, the pool and lazy Sundays.
questions.question: They're light, they float in the pool and they bend easily. What are most flip-flops made of?
hints: Getting them wet is no problem at all.
It's the same kind of stuff as a bath toy.
Car tires are made of something similar.
questions.fun_fact: Ancient Egyptians already wore sandals with a strap between the toes, some made of papyrus.

questions.description: Shoes that decided to keep going up your leg.
questions.question: These shoes cover your ankle, keep your feet dry in rain or snow, and cowboys love them. What are they?
hints: They're great for jumping in puddles.
They're taller than most other shoes.
Puss in a famous fairy tale wears them.
questions.fun_fact: The oldest leather shoe ever found is about 5,500 years old and was discovered in a cave in Armenia.

quality.notes: The Areni-1 shoe fact is correct. The description's 'up your leg' already hints at boots.

questions.description: Shoes that make you taller without growing.
questions.question: These shoes lift your heel high off the ground, make you look taller and go click-clack on the floor. What are they?
hints: They're often worn to parties.
It's hard to run in them.
The back of the shoe stands on a thin spike.
questions.fun_fact: High heels were first worn by horse riders in Persia, and later by European men in the 1600s.

quality.notes: Hint 3's 'thin spike' doesn't fit every heel, but that's a small point.

questions.description: A tiny bodyguard that lives inside a boot.
questions.question: I'm a hidden cap of steel inside a work boot. When a brick falls on the boot, I take the hit. What part of you do I protect?
hints: You'll find me at the end of the boot.
The part I guard has ten pieces in total.
You wiggle them in the sand.
questions.fun_fact: Safety boots are tested by dropping a heavy weight right onto the toe cap.

quality.notes: Shares only the topic 'boots' with shoes-and-accessories-8. Easy enough to work out.

questions.description: A unit that weighs almost nothing but costs a fortune.
questions.question: Colombia is famous for its green emeralds. What unit is used to weigh gems like these?
hints: It's used for diamonds too.
The same word, spelled a bit differently, tells how pure gold is.
It sounds like an orange vegetable.
questions.fun_fact: One carat is 0.2 grams, and the name comes from carob seeds, once used to balance jewelers' scales.

quality.notes: Hint 3 ('sounds like an orange vegetable', i.e. carrot) and hint 2 (karat/carat spelling) only work in English. In Spanish it's 'quilate' and in German 'Karat', so the hints don't travel. 'Dram' is an obscure distractor, and 'Ton' is easy to rule out.

questions.description: A god who traded his island for a very cold room far beyond Neptune.
questions.question: The people who carved these statues worshipped a creator god. Which god gave his name to a dwarf planet beyond Neptune?
hints: These stone giants stand on a lonely island in the Pacific Ocean.
The island is Rapa Nui, also called Easter Island.
The dwarf planet was found around Easter 2005, which is why it got a Rapa Nui god's name.

media.note: A clear photo of the moai stone statues on Easter Island (Rapa Nui), with no text or signs.

questions.fun_fact: Before it got its official name, the team that found Makemake nicknamed it “Easterbunny”.

quality.notes: Facts check out: Makemake was found just after Easter 2005 and nicknamed “Easterbunny”. Pluto is also a god who gave his name to a dwarf planet beyond Neptune, but the moai photo narrows it down, and Pluto isn't among the options. The text in effect asks two linked things. Pele is a good Polynesian distractor.

questions.description: A shiny ball with four long whiskers that started a race to space.
questions.question: This metal ball with four long antennas went into orbit in 1957 and beeped back to Earth. What was it called?
hints: It was launched by the Soviet Union.
It was the first artificial satellite ever.
Its name means “fellow traveler” in Russian.

media.note: A clear photo of a Sputnik 1 replica: polished metal sphere with four long antennas; no labels or text.

questions.fun_fact: Radio fans all over the world could hear Sputnik's simple “beep-beep” signal with their own radios.

quality.notes: Photos of the replica may carry museum labels. “1957” plus “race to space” makes it fairly easy for adults.

questions.description: Jupiter travels with two fan clubs, and they still haven't forgiven each other.
questions.question: Jupiter's Trojan asteroids move in two swarms, one ahead of the planet and one behind. The swarm ahead is mostly named after whom?
hints: The names come from the war told in Homer's “Iliad”.
The swarm behind Jupiter is named after the other side of that war.
Achilles is one of the asteroids in this swarm.
questions.fun_fact: A few asteroids ended up in the “wrong” camp: Trojan Hektor sits among the Greeks, and Greek Patroclus among the Trojans.

quality.notes: Correct: L4 is the Greek camp, 588 Achilles is in it, and Hektor and Patroclus are the famous misplaced ones. Once hint 1 is given, it is a coin flip between Greek and Trojan heroes.

questions.description: Twelve signs that claim to know your personality before you've even said hello.
questions.question: This close-up shows signs like a ram, a bull and twins. Which practice says these signs shape your personality?
hints: It is not a science, even though it uses the sky.
Horoscopes in magazines come from it.
Its name sounds almost like the science of stars, but it is about fortunes.

media.note: A close-up of an old zodiac wheel showing a few signs such as the ram, bull and twins; no written words.

questions.fun_fact: Because Earth slowly wobbles, the Sun no longer sits in the same constellations on the dates horoscopes use.

quality.notes: Medieval zodiac wheels usually have Latin inscriptions, so a picture with no words is unlikely. Families meet horoscopes in everyday life, so this is easier than 9.

questions.description: The invisible guest at every beach party who never brings sunscreen.
questions.question: Sunlight splits into colors like these, but it also has invisible rays. Which invisible rays can give you sunburn?
hints: Sunscreen is made to block them.
They are still strong on cloudy days.
They are often written with two letters: U and V.

media.note: A photo of white light passing through a glass prism and splitting into a rainbow of colors; no text.

questions.fun_fact: Bees can see ultraviolet light, and many flowers have hidden UV patterns that guide bees to the nectar.

quality.notes: The prism photo isn't really essential (illustrative would fit), but it does no harm. q-0388 (ozone layer) mentions UV but asks a different fact.

questions.description: Planets don't run in circles, no matter what your school poster says.
questions.question: “Kepler showed I'm the path of every planet around the Sun, and the Sun sits at one of my two focus points.” What shape am I?
hints: A circle has only one center, so it is not that.
It looks like a slightly squashed circle.
You can draw it with a loop of string around two pins.
questions.fun_fact: Earth's orbit is so close to a circle that you could not tell it is an ellipse if you drew it on paper.

quality.notes: The description rules out the “circle” option, and hint 1 does too. Elliptical orbits are core school physics, so about 10 rather than 12.

questions.description: The most expensive Christmas present ever unwrapped in space.
questions.question: In which year was the James Webb Space Telescope launched into space?
hints: It is newer than the Hubble telescope.
It launched not long after the COVID-19 pandemic began.
It launched on Christmas Day, between 2020 and 2022.
questions.fun_fact: Webb's gold-coated mirror is 6.5 m (21 ft) wide and had to fold up like origami to fit inside its rocket.

quality.notes: A plain launch-year question, quite dry. The “Christmas” description is fine. Hint 3 nearly gives the year, which is allowed.

questions.description: A planet so big it makes Earth look like a marble in a beach ball.
questions.question: Jupiter is a gas giant. About how many Earths could fit inside it?
hints: Jupiter is the biggest planet in the solar system.
About 11 Earths would fit side by side across Jupiter.
Eleven times wider means about 11 × 11 × 11 times the space inside.
questions.fun_fact: Jupiter has no solid ground: if you tried to land on it, you would just sink into thicker and thicker gas.

quality.notes: Correct: about 1,321 Earths, about 11 Earths wide. Good hints that let players reason their way to the answer.

questions.description: The Moon has a bumpy face because space keeps throwing rocks at it.
questions.question: “I'm a round hole on the Moon, made when a space rock crashed into it.” What am I?
hints: The Moon is covered with thousands of me.
You can see some of me with binoculars.
My name starts with “cra…”.
questions.fun_fact: Because the Moon has no wind or rain, astronaut footprints there can last for millions of years.

quality.notes: Hint 3 (“starts with cra…”) depends on the language and will break in translation. Otherwise a good kids' question.

questions.description: Named after the goddess of arguments, and it really did start one.
questions.question: “I roam the scattered disc beyond Neptune, I'm the heaviest known dwarf planet, and I'm named after the Greek goddess of strife.” Who am I?
hints: My discovery in 2005 started a big debate among astronomers.
That debate ended with Pluto no longer being a planet.
In myth, I threw a golden apple that led to the Trojan War.
questions.fun_fact: Eris is about the same size as Pluto but more massive, and its moon is named Dysnomia, the daughter of strife.

quality.notes: The question already says “goddess of strife”, so anyone who knows Greek myth gets it. That is fair, but it makes the question easier than 14.

questions.description: Three planets would sink in the bathtub; one would just bob around.
questions.question: Three of these planets are denser than water. Which one is less dense than water?
hints: It is a gas giant.
It is the second-biggest planet.
It is the one famous for its huge rings.
questions.fun_fact: In a bathtub big enough to hold it, Saturn would float, though it would leave a ring!

quality.notes: A well-known, fun fact. The bathtub image is close to a metaphor, but here it is the classic illustration of the fact, so it's acceptable.

questions.description: Not ice cream, not icebergs, but giants made of ice.
questions.question: How many planets in our solar system are ice giants?
hints: They are the two farthest planets from the Sun.
Both look blue or blue-green.
One of them spins tipped on its side.
questions.fun_fact: The “ice” in ice giants is mostly water, ammonia and methane, and it is not cold at all deep inside.

quality.notes: A dry count question. Hint 1 already gives away the number.

questions.description: Somebody had to be the one to turn off the lights on the way out.
questions.question: This astronaut, photographed on the Moon in December 1972, was the last person to climb back into the lunar lander. Who is he?
hints: He flew on Apollo 17, the final Moon landing.
He was the commander of his mission, and his partner was a geologist.
His first name is a short form of Eugene.

media.note: The NASA Apollo 17 photo of Gene Cernan in his spacesuit next to the US flag on the Moon (face hidden behind the visor); no caption or name visible.

questions.fun_fact: Before leaving, Gene Cernan wrote his daughter's initials in the Moon dust.

quality.notes: The daughter's-initials story comes from Cernan's own account and is widely repeated, but it is hard to verify, so correct is 4. The photo can't identify a man whose visor hides his face, so it is illustrative, not essential. A query with his name may return captioned images. 'Last man on the Moon' is well-known space trivia, so about 14 rather than 15.

questions.description: A shoe print that's very far from your front door.
questions.question: This famous footprint was not made on Earth. Who left it?
hints: The grey dust in the photo is on the Moon.
This person needed a rocket to get there.
They wear a big white suit and a helmet.

media.note: Close-up of the famous Apollo 11 bootprint in grey lunar dust, no people or text visible.

questions.fun_fact: There is no wind or rain on the Moon, so footprints there can last for millions of years.

quality.notes: The distractors are weak: once you hear 'not made on Earth', only one option makes sense. That's acceptable at difficulty 2.

questions.description: A dessert that never melts, no matter how long you leave it on the table.
questions.question: “I'm crunchy and dry, I never melt, and you buy me in science museum shops.” Who is this ice cream named after?
hints: Its makers say it was made for people on a very long trip.
Those people traveled far above the clouds.
They wear helmets and ride rockets.
questions.fun_fact: This freeze-dried ice cream was made for NASA, but astronauts almost never ate it in space, because its crumbs could float into equipment.

quality.notes: It's disputed whether this ice cream ever flew at all (Apollo 7 claims), but the fun fact hedges with 'almost never', so it holds. A decorative 'science museum gift shop' image could show packs labeled 'Astronaut Ice Cream'. The description repeats 'never melts' from the riddle.

questions.description: Good morning! And good morning! And good morning again!
questions.question: How often do astronauts on the International Space Station see a sunrise?
hints: The station is much faster than Earth's spin.
It flies around the whole Earth many times a day.
They see about 16 sunrises in a single day.
questions.fun_fact: The station travels at about 28,000 km/h (17,500 mph), fast enough to circle Earth in about an hour and a half.

questions.description: The shiniest towel at the finish line.
questions.question: Runners often get shiny foil blankets like these after a marathon. Where were these blankets first meant to be used?
hints: They were made in the 1960s.
NASA helped develop them.
In many languages they are named after the place where rockets go.

media.note: Runners wrapped in shiny silver foil blankets after a race; no text mentioning space or NASA.

questions.fun_fact: The foil blanket is so thin that it can be folded to the size of a wallet, yet it reflects most of your body heat back to you.

quality.notes: English speakers who know the name 'space blanket' get it easily. Other languages (Spanish 'manta térmica', German 'Rettungsdecke') don't carry that clue, so the difficulty varies by language. The photo works as illustrative rather than essential.

questions.description: When you're outside the spaceship, you can't just pop back in to use the bathroom.
questions.question: Astronauts wear a special diaper under their suit on a spacewalk. About how long does a spacewalk usually last?
hints: Getting dressed in the suit alone takes a long time.
Spacewalks are planned like a long work shift.
It's longer than a school morning, but shorter than a whole day.
questions.fun_fact: NASA's official name for the space diaper is “Maximum Absorbency Garment”.

quality.notes: 'About 3 days' is clearly impossible, and the diaper in the question already hints at a long walk, so the distractors are weak.

questions.description: The most expensive vacation ever, and you couldn't even open the window.
questions.question: In 2001, American businessman Dennis Tito paid about 20 million dollars to become the first space tourist. In which country did his rocket lift off?
hints: NASA didn't want to fly him, so he traveled with Russia.
He rode a Soyuz rocket to the space station.
He launched from Baikonur, the same place as Yuri Gagarin.
questions.fun_fact: Dennis Tito spent about eight days in space and later said it was “paradise”.

quality.notes: Hint 1 names Russia, which isn't an option, so it nudges strongly toward Kazakhstan. That's acceptable for a hint.

questions.description: A jetpack that would make every superhero jealous.
questions.question: In 1984, astronauts flew freely in space with a jetpack called the Manned Maneuvering Unit. What did its small thrusters puff out?
hints: It was not burned, just let out under pressure.
It's a safe gas that doesn't catch fire.
It's the gas that makes up most of the air you breathe.
questions.fun_fact: Bruce McCandless flew the jetpack about 100 m (320 ft) away from the shuttle with no safety line.

quality.notes: It reads as a dry technical fact. Hint 2 rules out oxygen and hydrogen, and hint 3 all but names nitrogen. The lens 'pop_culture' is mislabeled.

questions.description: Three letters, 98 meters tall, and very loud.
questions.question: NASA's giant SLS rocket launched the Artemis I mission around the Moon in 2022. What do the letters SLS stand for?
hints: The name is quite plain and businesslike.
It is meant to be a whole system, not one ship.
The first word is the place where it goes.
questions.fun_fact: The SLS reuses engines very similar to the ones that once flew on the Space Shuttle.

quality.notes: Expanding an acronym is a dry, school-test-style question. The plainest-sounding option is easy to guess, especially with hint 1, so it's easier than 13. The fun fact understates the engine link: Artemis I flew refurbished Space Shuttle RS-25 engines themselves, not just similar ones.

questions.description: The question every kid asks an astronaut first.
questions.question: “Instead of water, I use strong suction, like a vacuum cleaner, because in space nothing falls down.” What am I?
hints: Every astronaut needs me several times a day.
I have a seat.
On Earth, you flush me.
questions.fun_fact: On the space station, urine is cleaned and turned back into drinking water.

quality.notes: None of the fridge, washing machine or oven fits 'instead of water … suction', and the description hints at the famous kids' question about toilets in space. Easier than 6.

questions.description: The only place where staring at screens all day is your actual job.
questions.question: You're at a desk full of screens on Earth, talking by radio with astronauts during their flight. Where are you?
hints: The astronauts call this room “Houston” in many films.
Dozens of experts watch every part of the flight from here.
The room guides and watches over the whole mission.
questions.fun_fact: During the Apollo 13 emergency, mission control teams worked day and night to bring the crew safely home.

quality.notes: A fairly plain 'what is this place' question; probably easier than 7. The decorative 'rocket launch countdown' image is mood only, which is reasonable here.

questions.description: Something you can spot from your backyard, and it waves back if you're lucky.
questions.question: This bright line was made by something that crosses the whole sky in about five minutes and shines steadily, never blinking. What is it?
hints: It's lit by the Sun, even when it's dark where you stand.
A meteor is gone in seconds, and planes have blinking lights.
People live and work inside it.

media.query: ISS pass long exposure night sky
media.note: Long-exposure photo of the night sky with a single bright, unbroken streak from a space station pass; no text or labels.

questions.fun_fact: The International Space Station is big enough that you can see it without a telescope from almost anywhere on Earth.

quality.notes: Other bright satellites also fit the clue, but none is an option. Hint 2 rules out two options at once. A long-exposure streak photo is likely on Commons, but it doesn't show the 'no blinking' detail by itself.

questions.description: A sandwich in space needs a little rethinking.
questions.question: It's flat, round and soft, it makes almost no crumbs, and astronauts wrap their food in it instead of bread. What is it?
hints: Crumbs are a big problem when everything floats.
It comes from Mexican cooking.
You use it to make tacos and burritos.
questions.fun_fact: Floating crumbs can get into astronauts' eyes or into machines, so bread is rarely eaten in space.

quality.notes: The clue also fits other flatbreads (pita, wraps), though none is an option. The decorative image of astronauts eating may show tortillas, but it's blurred. food-history-1 also has the answer tortillas but asks a different fact.

questions.description: A zodiac sign that goes headfirst into everything, horns included.
questions.question: Aries is a zodiac sign, a constellation, and in a Greek myth it had a Golden Fleece. What animal does its name mean?
hints: It's a farm animal.
It has thick wool you can make sweaters from.
It's a male sheep with curly horns.
questions.fun_fact: Aries is the first sign of the zodiac because the Sun used to be in it at the start of spring in ancient times.

quality.notes: Golden Fleece plus the hint about wool points strongly to the ram. The description's 'horns' only rules out Lion.

questions.description: The universe is getting bigger, and it's not because of all the snacks.
questions.question: “In 1929, I used the redshift of galaxies' light to show that they're flying away from us.” Who am I?
hints: He was an American astronomer working at Mount Wilson Observatory.
His work showed the universe is expanding.
A famous space telescope launched in 1990 carries his name.
questions.fun_fact: Before becoming an astronomer, Edwin Hubble trained as a lawyer.

quality.notes: Galileo is a weak distractor for a 1929 discovery. 'Trained as a lawyer' is roughly right: he studied law at Oxford, and his claims to have practiced are doubtful.

questions.description: A hole in the sky that isn't a hole, just very bad at shining.
questions.question: “I'm the most famous dark nebula you can see without a telescope: a black patch right next to the Southern Cross.” What am I?
hints: You can only see me well from the Southern Hemisphere.
I'm a cloud of dust that blocks the stars behind me.
My name sounds like a bag of black fuel for a fireplace.
questions.fun_fact: Some Aboriginal Australians see the Coalsack as the head of an “emu in the sky” made of dark clouds.

quality.notes: A southern Milky Way image may well show the Coalsack itself. That's harmless, but it could have been illustrative instead of decorative.

questions.description: A cosmic soap bubble with a name that got it all wrong.
questions.question: “I'm a glowing shell of gas thrown off by a dying star like the Sun.” What small, hot star is left at my center?
hints: I'm a planetary nebula, though I have nothing to do with planets.
The star left behind is about the size of Earth.
Its color name is the same as snow.
questions.fun_fact: Planetary nebulas got their name because, in old telescopes, they looked round like planets.

questions.description: A building with a roof that opens like a giant eye.
questions.question: You're at an observatory on a clear night. Which of these can you NOT see through its big telescope?
hints: Think about what time it is.
One of these only shows up during the day.
It's the star that gives us daylight.
questions.fun_fact: Many observatories are built on high mountains, above the clouds, so the air is clearer for watching the stars.
