quality.notes: Very easy, since 'night' plus the Sun is instant. Hint 1 almost gives it away. Not much surprise. Also, you'd never look at the Sun through a normal telescope anyway.

questions.description: An astrophysicist with a mustache, a smile and his own sky indoors.
questions.question: Neil deGrasse Tyson, host of the TV series “Cosmos”, became director of which New York planetarium in 1996?
hints: It's part of a famous natural history museum.
That museum is right next to Central Park.
Its name starts with an H.
questions.fun_fact: Tyson decided to become an astrophysicist after visiting that very planetarium as a 9-year-old.

quality.notes: US-centric: it asks for the name of a specific New York institution, which families elsewhere won't know. 'Zeiss Planetarium' is a brand or German venue, not a New York one, so it's an odd distractor. Hint 3 (first letter) is lazy. Dry name recall.

questions.description: A zodiac sign that takes up more of the sky than all its neighbors.
questions.question: It's the biggest constellation of the zodiac, it's drawn as a young woman holding wheat, and its brightest star is Spica. Which is it?
hints: Its birthdays fall in late August and September.
It comes just after Leo, the lion.
Its name is the Latin word for maiden.
questions.fun_fact: Virgo is the second-largest constellation in the whole sky, beaten only by Hydra, the water snake.

quality.notes: 'Young woman' points to Virgo/maiden for anyone who knows the signs. The wheat image repeats a clue already in the question.

questions.description: Light your eyes can't see, but a gold-plated telescope can.
questions.question: The James Webb Space Telescope was built to see mostly which kind of light?
hints: This light lets it peer through clouds of dust.
Warm things give off a lot of it.
Night-vision cameras and TV remotes use it.
questions.fun_fact: Webb has to stay colder than about −220 °C (−370 °F), or its own warmth would blind it.

quality.notes: Same answer as physics-13 (Infrared), and hint 3 uses the same TV remote clue, but this asks a different fact (what JWST observes).

questions.description: A star you can catch, and it plays very catchy music.
questions.question: You're playing Super Mario and grab a flashing star. What happens to Mario?
questions.answer: He can't be hurt for a while
hints: He starts flashing in bright colors.
Enemies he touches get knocked away.
For a few seconds, nothing can harm him.
questions.fun_fact: While the star power lasts, the music speeds up into a fast, happy tune.

quality.notes: Fun fact is slightly off: the music switches to a separate star theme rather than 'speeding up'.

questions.description: Hollywood called a scientist, and the black hole got a glow-up.
questions.question: “I won a Nobel Prize, and I helped the film “Interstellar” show the glowing disk of gas around its black hole as it would really look.” Who am I?
hints: I'm an American physicist from Caltech.
My Nobel Prize in 2017 was for detecting gravitational waves.
My first name is short and sounds like a nap.
questions.fun_fact: The computer images of the black hole Gargantua were so accurate that they led to real science papers.

quality.notes: Hint 3 is English wordplay ('kip' = nap, which is British slang). It won't travel to other languages and many US players won't get it. Nested curly quotes around the film title inside the riddle quote are clumsy when read aloud.

questions.description: Stars that blink in rhythm, and a scientist who read the beat.
questions.question: Who found in 1912 that how fast a Cepheid variable star pulses shows how bright it truly is, so we can measure its distance?
hints: She worked at Harvard College Observatory, studying photos on glass plates.
Edwin Hubble later used her discovery to measure the distance to other galaxies.
Her middle name is a bird that lives on lakes and rivers.
questions.fun_fact: She was paid about 30 cents an hour for work that later helped show the universe is expanding.

quality.notes: Hint 3 (swan as a bird) works when translated. Fine expert question.

questions.description: Astronomers rank stars like a race, but the winners get the smallest numbers.
questions.question: You spot a “first magnitude” star on a clear night. Calling the brightest stars “first” and the faintest “sixth” goes back to which era?
hints: It's much older than the telescope.
The idea is linked to the astronomer Hipparchus.
Ptolemy kept the scale in his star catalog, the Almagest.
questions.fun_fact: The scale runs backwards: the brighter the star, the lower the number, and Sirius even has a negative magnitude.

quality.notes: The opening scenario sentence adds length for nothing. The Industrial Revolution is an implausible era for naming stars. Hints 2–3 (Hipparchus, Ptolemy) almost give it away.

questions.description: A crab drew a line around the world, and nobody stopped it.
questions.question: This line on the world map runs through Mexico, Egypt and India and is named after the zodiac crab. What is it called?
hints: It's in the Northern Hemisphere.
On the June solstice, the Sun is right overhead at noon there.
It shares its name with the fourth zodiac sign.
questions.fun_fact: It got its name about 2,000 years ago, when the Sun was in the constellation Cancer at the June solstice.

quality.notes: An 'old world map globe' image may have the tropics labeled on it.

questions.description: Two people punch each other for fun, and then someone rings a bell like it's school.
questions.question: You're watching an Olympic boxing match, and the bell rings to end round 1. What happens next?
questions.answer: The boxers rest in their corners
wrong_answers: The boxers shake hands and leave
hints: The match isn't over yet: more rounds are coming.
Boxing is tiring, so the fighters need a short break.
Each boxer goes back to a stool where a coach gives water and advice.
questions.fun_fact: Olympic boxing bouts have three rounds of three minutes each, with a one-minute rest between them.

quality.notes: The wrong answers are weak: anyone who knows the match goes on for more rounds can rule out 'announce the winner' and 'leave', and swapping gloves is silly. The question is fairly flat and plays like an everyday-logic test.

questions.description: Packing a sports bag is easy, as long as you don't pack the wrong sport.
questions.question: You're packing your bag for a soccer game. Which of these do you NOT need?
hints: In soccer, you mostly use your feet.
Only the goalkeeper may use hands, and never a tool.
This thing is held in your hand to hit a ball.
questions.fun_fact: Soccer has been part of the Summer Olympics since 1900, longer than almost any other team sport.

quality.notes: Very easy odd-one-out with little surprise. The tennis racket stands out as the only item from another sport, which suits difficulty 1 but makes it dull. The fun fact claim 'longer than almost any other team sport' is loose: water polo, rugby and cricket were also at the 1900 Games, and soccer was missing in 1932.

questions.description: A race where someone keeps putting furniture in your way on purpose.
questions.question: You're running an Olympic hurdles race. How many hurdles must you jump over before the finish?
hints: It's more than a handful, but not dozens.
It's the same number in the 100 m, 110 m and 400 m hurdles.
It's the number of fingers on your two hands.
questions.fun_fact: Knocking a hurdle over is allowed: runners are only disqualified if they knock one down on purpose or go around it.

quality.notes: The wrong numbers 3, 25 and 50 are far from the answer, so players can estimate their way to 10 easily. The fun fact simplifies the rule: disqualification is for knocking a hurdle down deliberately with hand or foot, or for going around one. A dry number question.

questions.description: A sport where your feet do most of the talking, and they talk very high up.
questions.question: Which Olympic combat sport comes from Korea and is famous for high and spinning kicks?
hints: Fighters wear a white uniform and a padded vest.
It's the national sport of South Korea.
Its name begins with “Tae”.
questions.fun_fact: In Olympic taekwondo, the vests have sensors that score points automatically when a kick lands.

quality.notes: Hint 3 gives the first syllable, which is nearly the answer. Hint 1 (white uniform) also fits karate and judo. The question is fairly direct and school-like. Karate is a strong wrong option that young players may pick.

questions.description: A boat so tight you basically wear it like trousers.
questions.question: Which people first built this kind of boat, for hunting in icy Arctic waters?
hints: They lived where the sea is cold and the winters are long.
Their first boats were made of animal skins stretched over wood or bone.
They live in places like Greenland, northern Canada and Alaska.

media.note: A clear photo of a person paddling a kayak (closed deck, double-bladed paddle).

questions.fun_fact: The word “kayak” comes from an Inuit word meaning “hunter's boat”.

quality.notes: The meaning of 'kayak' is often given as 'man's boat' or 'hunter's boat', and the source is debated. Aleut and Yupik peoples also built kayaks, but 'the Inuit' is clearly the best of the four options. A clear kayak photo is easy to find, so the essential image is fine.

questions.description: Flying backwards over a bar is a perfectly normal thing to do at work, for some people.
questions.question: This athlete is doing an event from which group of Olympic sports?
hints: The event takes place inside a big stadium.
The same group includes sprints and the marathon.
Its events are run on a track or held on the field inside it.

media.note: A clear photo of an athlete clearing a high jump bar, landing mat visible.

questions.fun_fact: The high jump world record of 2.45 m (8 ft 0.5 in) by Javier Sotomayor has stood since 1993.

quality.notes: The fun fact repeats the Sotomayor record that q-1065 asks about, but the question itself asks something different. A fairly plain classification question.

questions.description: A brand that has been helping tired cooks pretend they spent all day on dinner since 1838.
questions.question: I was founded in Germany in 1838 by Carl Heinrich Knorr, and you'll find me in kitchen cupboards worldwide. What am I best known for?
hints: You usually add hot water to me.
I'm often used to give flavor to rice, stews and sauces.
Think of a little cube that dissolves into broth.
questions.fun_fact: Before soups, Carl Heinrich Knorr's business roasted chicory, a root that people drank as a cheap coffee substitute.

quality.notes: Facts are correct: Heilbronn, 1838, and he started out with chicory. The question rests almost entirely on knowing the Knorr brand, which is a brand-recognition test more than trivia. The brand is known in many countries but not everywhere, and kids rarely know it, so 8 fits better than 7. It reads like a dry brand quiz. The 'tired cooks' description points toward convenience food, which slightly helps both the answer and the frozen-pizza option.

questions.description: Zebra stripes that only a laser can read.
questions.question: I'm a row of black and white stripes on almost every package, and the checkout goes “beep” when it reads me. What am I?
hints: You find me printed on the box, not stuck on later.
A red light at the checkout scans me.
My lines have different widths and hide a number.
questions.fun_fact: The first product ever scanned by its barcode at a store was a pack of chewing gum, in 1974 in the United States.

quality.notes: Solid question. The fun fact about Wrigley's gum in 1974 is correct. 'Black and white stripes' plus the beep make it very easy, so a 2–3 is right. The QR code distractor works well.

questions.description: Tiny bouncers that stand at the door of your head.
questions.question: Look at the photo: some swimmers put these in their ears. What do they mainly keep out?
hints: It's all around you in the pool.
It can make your ears feel blocked after a swim.
You swim in it.

media.note: A clear photo of a pair of swimming earplugs (silicone or rubber), no packaging text.

questions.fun_fact: Water stuck in the ear can cause “swimmer's ear”, an itchy infection of the ear canal.

quality.notes: The answer is close to obvious once the question says swimmers wear these. “Sunlight” and “cold air” are weak options for ears in a pool. A recognisable earplug photo is likely to exist, although swimming earplugs look like ordinary ones. It feels a bit like a dry school question.

questions.description: A race so long you could finish a whole film series while doing it.
questions.question: You're training for an Ironman triathlon. The swim is to 3.8 km (2.4 mi) as the run is to…?
hints: The run comes last, after the swim and a long bike ride.
The run alone is a famous race distance.
It's a full marathon.
questions.fun_fact: The first Ironman, in Hawaii in 1978, had only 15 starters, and 12 of them finished.

quality.notes: The analogy and the “You're training…” scenario are unneeded framing: the question really just asks how long the Ironman run is. Hint 2 points fairly strongly to the marathon. The facts are correct, including the 1978 race with 15 starters and 12 finishers.

questions.description: Your skin's favorite umbrella comes in a bottle.
questions.question: You rub it on your skin before playing outside at the pool, it comes in a bottle and it stops you from turning red. What is it?
hints: You use it on sunny days.
It protects your skin.
Its name has the word “sun” in it.
questions.fun_fact: You should put sunscreen on again after swimming, because water washes much of it away.

quality.notes: “Before playing outside at the pool” reads awkwardly. Shampoo, toothpaste and hand soap are clearly wrong for something that stops sunburn. Hint 3 depends on the word in each language; it works in Spanish and German, so it is acceptable. Simple, low surprise.

questions.description: The only donut you're happy to see thrown at you.
questions.question: I'm a ring hung by pools and on ships, ready to throw to someone in trouble in the water. Why am I so brightly colored?
hints: It has to do with your eyes.
Think of waves and a person far away.
Bright colors stand out against blue water.
questions.fun_fact: Many life rings have reflective strips so they shine in a flashlight beam at night.

quality.notes: “So I float better” is a reasonable distractor, though a few kids might argue for it. The facts are solid: life rings do carry reflective strips.

questions.description: Three steps, three swimmers, and only one gets the shiny top spot.
questions.question: On the Olympic podium, first place is to gold as third place is to…?
hints: It's a metal.
It's brown-orange in color.
Second place gets silver, and third gets the next one.
questions.fun_fact: Olympic gold medals are mostly silver, covered with a thin layer of gold.

quality.notes: This is common knowledge with little surprise, though the fun fact is good. Hint 3 almost says the answer outright.

questions.description: A board that bounces you higher than your expectations.
questions.question: In Olympic diving, the platform is to 10 m (33 ft) as the springboard is to…?
hints: The springboard is lower than the platform.
It's less than half the platform's height.
It's about as high as a single floor of a house.
questions.fun_fact: Divers from the 10 m platform hit the water at about 50 km/h (30 mph).

quality.notes: The analogy framing is forced; it is really a plain recall question. Many players will guess from hint 2. The facts are correct: the Olympic springboard is 3 m, and a 10 m dive hits the water at about 50 km/h.

questions.description: The stuff that makes surfers look like seals.
questions.question: It's stretchy, it's full of tiny gas bubbles, and wetsuits are made of it. What is neoprene?
hints: It's made in factories, not grown.
It's also used for laptop sleeves and mouse pads.
It's a cousin of the stuff in car tires, made in a lab.
questions.fun_fact: Neoprene was invented in 1930 by scientists at the US company DuPont.

quality.notes: The question lists features of neoprene and then asks what neoprene is, which is a clumsy structure. Hint 3 (the tire comparison) is near the answer, which is allowed for hint 3. The facts are correct (DuPont, 1930).

questions.description: Braces, thick glasses and a brain sharper than everyone else's in the office.
questions.question: Which telenovela, about Beatriz Pinzón Solano, a brilliant secretary at a fashion company, holds the Guinness record as the most successful telenovela ever?
hints: It was made in Colombia at the end of the 1990s.
It has been remade in more than 20 countries, from India to Germany.
The US remake starred America Ferrera and was called “Ugly …”.
questions.fun_fact: Germany, Russia, India, China and the United States all made their own version of Betty's story.

quality.notes: Guinness record (2010) is right. Telenovela knowledge leans heavily on Latin America: families outside it mostly know only the remake 'Ugly Betty', so a 9 is too low. The question is also long (well over 160 characters) and dry. The answer is longer than the other options, which makes it stand out a little.

questions.description: Countless soap heroes have run here at the last second, usually without a ticket.
questions.question: Romeo and Juliet's most famous scene is to a balcony as the famous final goodbye in the film “Casablanca” is to…
hints: The film came out in 1942 and is set during the Second World War.
Ilsa leaves while Rick stays behind in the fog.
She leaves on a plane bound for Lisbon.
questions.fun_fact: The famous line “Here's looking at you, kid” is said several times in “Casablanca”, including in that final farewell.

quality.notes: The analogy is forced: a balcony is a scene's setting, not a real relation, so it is really just 'where does the Casablanca goodbye happen?'. Most teens have never seen Casablanca, so it is closer to an adult 11. The description's 'without a ticket' points softly toward travel places.

questions.description: A love story that really didn't plan its arrival.
questions.question: I'm the heroine of the K-drama “Crash Landing on You”: a rich South Korean swept into North Korea by a sudden storm. What was I flying?
hints: I was enjoying an outdoor sport, not traveling for work.
I had no engine at all.
I hung under a big fabric wing, with my feet in the air.
questions.fun_fact: When she lands, she is caught in a tree and found by a North Korean army officer, who later falls in love with her.

quality.notes: The facts are right: Yoon Se-ri is swept away while paragliding and lands in a tree. Players can reason toward it (blown by a storm, no engine). A hot-air balloon is a fair distractor. The 'language' lens tag doesn't fit.

questions.description: The villain's favorite hiding place: the bottom of a drawer, for twenty years.
questions.question: In a soap, the villain hides me for years. When the heroine finally finds me, she learns her true love never left her on purpose. What am I?
hints: I was meant to be delivered, not hidden.
I come in an envelope.
Someone wrote me to explain everything.
questions.fun_fact: The lost letter trick is much older than TV: in Shakespeare's “Romeo and Juliet”, a letter that never arrives changes the whole ending.

quality.notes: A generic soap cliché, a bit flat. Only a letter fits 'learns he never left on purpose', so it can be reasoned out, but there is little surprise. The Romeo and Juliet fun fact is accurate and nice.

questions.description: The star of the show, if the show were only sound.
questions.question: I never appear on screen, but when a telenovela travels to another country, the heroine speaks with my voice. Who am I?
hints: I work in a studio, not on the set.
I have to match my words to the actor's lips.
My job is called dubbing.
questions.fun_fact: The Mexican telenovela “The Rich Also Cry” became a huge hit in Russia in the early 1990s, dubbed into Russian.

quality.notes: 'The Rich Also Cry' was a real hit in Russia, but it was shown with a voice-over track, not lip-synced dubbing, so 'dubbed' is loose. A narrator also lends a voice, but 'the heroine speaks with my voice' makes voice actor clear. The 'history' lens doesn't fit. Somewhat dry.

questions.description: She lives on the beach, and her best friend has fleas.
questions.question: I'm Marimar, a poor girl who lives on the beach with my dog Pulgoso. In 1994, which Mexican pop star played me?
hints: She also sang the show's theme song.
She starred in two more famous telenovelas about poor girls named María.
She is married to music boss Tommy Mottola.
questions.fun_fact: “Marimar” was so loved in the Philippines that it was remade there twice, in 2007 and 2015.

quality.notes: Strong Latin American focus: Marimar is famous in Latin America and the Philippines, not to families in most other places. Shakira is ruled out by 'Mexican pop star' for anyone who knows she is Colombian. The description's 'fleas' joke rests on the Spanish name Pulgoso, which non-Spanish speakers won't get. All facts check out.

questions.description: Before telenovelas had faces, they only had voices and a lot of bubbles.
questions.question: Daily radio dramas of the 1930s gave us the name “soap opera”. Where does the “soap” come from?
questions.answer: Soap makers paid for the shows
hints: It has to do with money, not with the stories.
The ads during the show were for washing products.
Companies selling soap sponsored them to reach listeners at home.
questions.fun_fact: Soap and cleaning companies like Procter & Gamble sponsored so many of these radio dramas that the name stuck.

quality.notes: A good origin-of-a-name question, and it is reasonable to think through. Fair distractors.

questions.description: Same tears, same love triangles, different country.
questions.question: Telenovela is to Mexico as what is to South Korea?
hints: Its name starts with the first letter of the country.
It is a cousin of K-pop.
Shows like “Squid Game” and “Crash Landing on You” belong to this group.
questions.fun_fact: The worldwide boom of South Korean shows and music even has its own name: the “Korean Wave”, or Hallyu.

quality.notes: Hint 1 ('starts with the first letter of the country') only works in languages that spell Korea with K; in Spanish it is 'Corea', so the hint breaks in translation. 'Dizi' is a nice distractor. Shares the K-drama topic with telenovelas-and-soaps-2, but it asks a different fact. A fairly plain analogy.

questions.description: In soaps, nobody is ever completely sure who their dad is.
questions.question: Which of these films does NOT have a big secret about a parent or child at its heart?
hints: In three of them, someone learns a surprise about their family.
One of them has a famous line about being someone's father.
In the odd one out, the father knows exactly who his son is and swims across the ocean to find him.
questions.fun_fact: Darth Vader's line in “The Empire Strikes Back” is “No, I am your father”, though many people misquote it as “Luke, I am your father”.

quality.notes: Finding Nemo is easy to spot as the odd one out, so I'd put it lower than 8. Hint 2 and the fun fact touch the Vader line asked in q-0315, but this question asks a different fact. Hint 3 nearly gives the answer, which is allowed.

questions.description: The only time of year when it's normal to put a tree in your living room.
questions.question: On Christmas morning, what do children hope to find under a tree like this one?
hints: They come wrapped in shiny paper.
Santa Claus brings them.
You open them and say “Thank you!”

media.note: A decorated Christmas tree with lights and ornaments, with nothing underneath it.

questions.fun_fact: The tradition of bringing a decorated tree indoors at Christmas started in Germany hundreds of years ago.

questions.description: A staircase that goes straight into the river, and nobody thinks that's strange.
questions.question: In Varanasi, people walk down long stone steps like these to bathe in the holy Ganges. What are these steps called?
hints: The word comes from Hindi.
Varanasi has more than 80 of them along the river.
The word sounds a bit like “gates”.

media.note: Photo of the stone river steps in Varanasi with people bathing in the Ganges, without signs naming the ghats.

questions.fun_fact: Varanasi is one of the oldest cities in the world that has been lived in without a break.

quality.notes: Hint 3 (“sounds like gates”) is an English sound joke and won't work in translation. Fairly dry vocabulary question.

questions.description: A bathtub for babies that never leaves the church.
questions.question: Riddle: “I'm a stone bowl in a church, and babies are held over me while water touches their heads.” What am I?
hints: I'm used at a ceremony that welcomes new Christians.
I'm often near the church entrance.
The ceremony is baptism.
questions.fun_fact: Some old baptismal fonts had lids with locks, so nobody could steal the holy water.

quality.notes: Few 13-year-olds know the term “baptismal font”; rated too low. The question opens with “Riddle:”, which is close to announcing its clues.

questions.description: Millions of travelers, one destination, and nobody needs to ask for directions.
questions.question: The Hajj, the journey to Mecca that every Muslim who can should make once, is one of Islam's five what?
hints: The other four include prayer and fasting.
They are the basic duties of every Muslim.
They hold up a building, like columns.

media.note: Photo of Hajj pilgrims dressed in white at Mount Arafat, without the Kaaba in view.

questions.fun_fact: Millions of people make the Hajj each year, making it one of the largest gatherings on Earth.

quality.notes: The media role should be illustrative, not essential, because the photo isn't needed to answer. Dry. The Five Pillars are fairly well known, so maybe an 11.

questions.description: Four tournaments, four cities, and one very tired champion.
questions.question: They're played in Melbourne, Paris, London and New York, and winning all four in one year is tennis's greatest feat. What are they called?
hints: They're the four biggest and oldest events in tennis.
Wimbledon is one of them.
The name is also used in baseball and in card games for a huge win.
questions.fun_fact: The name was borrowed from the card game bridge, where a “grand slam” means winning every trick.

quality.notes: “Davis Cup tournaments” is a forced distractor: the Davis Cup is one team competition, not a set of tournaments. Tacking “tournaments” onto every option looks artificial. The bridge origin of the name is the usual account. Asks a fairly dry definition. guinness-world-records-11 mentions Grand Slam but asks about Nadal, so it's a different fact.

questions.description: Being Swiss and great at tennis, without being Roger Federer.
questions.question: Swiss player Stan Wawrinka won three Grand Slam singles titles with his famous one-handed backhand. In which decade?
hints: He had to beat Federer, Nadal and Djokovic at their peak.
He won the Australian Open, the French Open and the US Open.
His first big title came in Melbourne in 2014.
questions.fun_fact: Wawrinka and Roger Federer won Olympic gold together for Switzerland in men's doubles in Beijing in 2008.

quality.notes: A niche player's decade: hard because the fact is obscure, not because it's widely known. Players mostly guess between the 2000s and 2010s. Dry trivia with no reasoning hook. Hint 1 (Federer/Nadal/Djokovic at their peak) and the Federer mention in the description already narrow it to two decades.

questions.description: The only moment in tennis when you get to throw the ball at yourself.
questions.question: You're about to serve in a tennis match. Which of these is NOT a rule of the serve?
questions.answer: The ball must bounce before you hit it
wrong_answers: You stand behind the back line
You get two tries to get it in
It must land in the box across from you
hints: Think about how a serve starts: you toss the ball up.
Most players hit the ball high in the air.
A serve is hit before the ball ever touches the ground.
questions.fun_fact: The fastest serves in men's tennis travel at more than 250 km/h (155 mph).

quality.notes: The answer is the longest option and the only one phrased as “The ball must…”, so it stands out a little. Hint 1 (“you toss the ball up”) already points strongly to it. A fairly plain rules question.

questions.description: The referee's eyes, upgraded with lots of cameras.
questions.question: I'm made of many cameras. When a player challenges a call, I replay the ball's path on the big screen to show in or out. What am I?
hints: I was first used at big tennis tournaments in the 2000s.
Cricket uses me too.
I'm named after a bird with very sharp eyesight.
questions.fun_fact: Hawk-Eye says it can place the ball to within just a few millimeters.

quality.notes: Cyclops was a real tennis line-calling machine, so it's a good distractor. It only beeped on serves and didn't replay the ball's path, so it stays clearly wrong.

questions.description: A shot hit with the back of your hand leading the way.
questions.question: For a right-handed tennis player, forehand is to the right side as backhand is to…
hints: “Back” tells you which part of the hand faces the ball.
Your racket has to cross your body.
It's the opposite side to the forehand.
questions.fun_fact: Many players hit the backhand with both hands, while others, like Roger Federer, used just one.

quality.notes: Weak distractors: “The right side” repeats the forehand half of the analogy, and above the head or below the knees are not sides. A dry left/right question. brain-and-mind-9 has the same answer, but it's a different fact.

questions.description: Some kids have the best seats in the stadium, but they never sit down.
questions.question: These young people run around the court during big tennis matches. What is their job?
hints: They crouch near the net and at the back of the court.
Players never have to bend down while they're there.
They're called ball kids.

media.note: Ball kids in uniform on a tennis court, crouching or holding tennis balls.

questions.fun_fact: At Wimbledon, ball kids train for months before they're allowed on court.

quality.notes: The photo of ball kids holding balls nearly shows the answer. Hint 3 (“They're called ball kids”) is very close to giving it away. Fairly plain.

questions.description: Boxes you can't put anything in, except a fast ball.
questions.question: Look at this tennis court from above. How many service boxes does it have?
hints: The serve must land in one of these boxes.
They're the boxes closest to the net.
There are two on each side of the net.

media.note: A tennis court seen from directly above, with all lines clearly visible.

questions.fun_fact: A serve must always land in the service box diagonally across from the server.

quality.notes: A counting task from a photo; you only need to know what a service box is. A bit dry. Hint 3 nearly gives the answer away.

questions.description: Some courts are soft, some are green, and one doesn't forgive your knees.
questions.question: Wimbledon is to grass as the US Open is to…
hints: The Australian Open is played on the same kind of surface.
It's often painted blue or green.
It's made of concrete or asphalt with a coating on top.
questions.fun_fact: The US Open has been played on several surfaces, including grass and clay, before switching to hard courts in 1978.

quality.notes: Carpet and sand are weak distractors. Fewer people know the US Open's surface than know Roland-Garros is on clay, so it's more like a 10 than an 8.

questions.description: The longest walk ever taken just to throw away a piece of jewelry.
questions.question: In “The Lord of the Rings”, Frodo's journey begins in the Shire. Where must it end, so the One Ring can be destroyed?
hints: It's in the dark land of Mordor.
The Ring was made there, in fire.
It's a volcano.
questions.fun_fact: In the films, Mount Doom was played by Mount Ngauruhoe, a real volcano in New Zealand.

quality.notes: The image query “old hardcover books” is safe but only loosely related to the question; a volcano picture would work but would give the answer away. Fine as it is.

questions.description: Every wizard needs a walking stick, and not because of bad knees.
questions.question: You're watching the films: Gimli is to his axe as Gandalf is to his…
hints: Gandalf is a wizard.
He holds it high and it can glow with light.
It's a long stick made of wood.
questions.fun_fact: Gandalf's staff changes with him: grey and wooden as Gandalf the Grey, white and shining as Gandalf the White.

quality.notes: The wrong answers are weak: no LOTR fan pictures Gandalf with a bow, shield or hammer. “You're watching the films:” is an unneeded scenario. The question is a plain analogy. Sharing the word “staff” with the music-staff question is not an overlap.

questions.description: A nickname that's only half nice.
questions.question: It's a word used in Gondor, it appears in Boromir's dream, and it refers to someone's size. Who are the “halflings”?
hints: Think of who is about half as tall as a man.
They walk barefoot and love second breakfast.
Frodo is one of them.
questions.fun_fact: Tolkien wrote that hobbits are usually between 2 and 4 feet (about 60 to 120 cm) tall.

quality.notes: The question stacks three clues as padding, and once you hear “halfling” the meaning is close to obvious. Hint 2 (second breakfast) nearly gives it away. It is easier than the stated 8.

questions.description: One arrow, one dragon, and suddenly you're royalty.
questions.question: Bard is a hero of “The Hobbit”. Which of these titles was NEVER his?
hints: Three of these titles are true.
That missing title belonged to dwarves like Thorin.
Bard ruled a city of Men, not a dwarf kingdom.
questions.fun_fact: Bard killed Smaug with a single black arrow that had been in his family for generations.

quality.notes: Hint 1 (“three of these are true”) adds nothing. Hint 2 points straight at the dwarf title. “Slayer of Smaug” describes something Bard did more than it is a formal title, but it is not a real ambiguity.

questions.description: Elves and Men team up, a rare event, like everyone agreeing on dinner.
questions.question: How long before Frodo's quest did the Last Alliance of Elves and Men fight Sauron?
hints: That's when Isildur cut the Ring from Sauron's hand.
Elrond was there, and Elves live a very long time.
In the film, Elrond says: “I was there, Gandalf…”
questions.fun_fact: The battle ended the Second Age of Middle-earth, and the Third Age began.
questions.concept: Última Alianza de Elfos y Hombres

quality.notes: The famous film line in hint 3 continues “…3,000 years ago”, so hint 3 is very strong. That is allowed for hint 3.

questions.description: Before the fish-eating, the whispering and the bad posture, he was just a normal guy.
questions.question: Before the Ring changed him, Sméagol lived by a great river and loved fishing and digging roots. Gandalf says his people were related to which folk?
hints: Think of a small folk who love simple homes.
Gandalf saw it in Sméagol's riddles and habits.
Bilbo and Frodo belong to this folk.
questions.fun_fact: Sméagol got the Ring when his cousin Déagol found it while fishing in the river.

quality.notes: In the book Gandalf calls Déagol Sméagol's “friend”. “Cousin” comes from other versions, so the fun fact is slightly shaky.

questions.description: The ultimate retirement home: far away, no Ring, plenty of Elves.
questions.question: Ring-bearers were allowed to go there, Elves sail there from the Grey Havens, and it lies far over the sea to the West. Which land is it?
hints: It's also called the Undying Lands.
Frodo, Bilbo and Gandalf sail there at the end.
Its name starts with “Val”.
questions.fun_fact: Sam, also a Ring-bearer for a short time, is said to sail West too, many years after Frodo.

quality.notes: Strictly, mortal Ring-bearers went to Tol Eressëa next to Valinor (the “Undying Lands”). This is a minor nitpick. Númenor also lay far over the sea to the West, but the other clues tell them apart.

questions.description: Leaving a trail of breadcrumbs, but make it fashion.
questions.question: I was carried off by orcs, and I dropped the leaf-shaped brooch of my elven cloak so my friends could follow me. Who am I?
hints: I'm a hobbit.
Aragorn finds the brooch and knows I'm still alive.
My full name is Peregrin Took.
questions.fun_fact: The elven cloaks of Lórien could hide their wearers so well that they looked like stones or grass.

questions.description: A wizard with a box of rockets at a hobbit party: what could go wrong?
questions.question: Gandalf's fireworks lit up Bilbo's farewell party in the Shire. Which birthday was Bilbo celebrating?
hints: Hobbits can live a long time.
Bilbo was very old, but still lively.
The number has three of the same digit.
questions.fun_fact: Tolkien called 111 an “eleventy-one” birthday, a funny hobbit way of saying it.

quality.notes: 999th and 11th are not believable answers. Hint 3 (three of the same digit) also fits 999.

questions.description: A tiny blade with a very pointy name.
questions.question: It's an Elvish blade that men would call a dagger, it glows blue when orcs are near, and Bilbo named it after fighting giant spiders in Mirkwood. What is it called?
hints: Bilbo later gives it to Frodo.
Its name is a short English word.
Think of what a bee or a wasp does.
questions.fun_fact: Bilbo named the sword after the spiders of Mirkwood, whom he fought alone in the dark.

quality.notes: This is a base question, but hints 2 and 3 depend on the English word “sting”. The sword is called Dardo in Spanish and Stich in German, so the hints don't carry over to other languages. The question text is also long.

questions.description: A village where every front door is perfectly round, and the doorbell is probably round too.
questions.question: You're visiting the Hobbiton movie set in New Zealand. About how many hobbit holes with little doors are there?
hints: It's a real village set on a sheep farm.
There are more than a few, but you can walk past them all in one tour.
The number is between 40 and 50.
questions.fun_fact: Some of the hobbit holes at Hobbiton were built smaller than others, to make actors look bigger or smaller in the films.

quality.notes: The number 44 is the commonly given figure, but it depends on the source. A tourist-set count is fairly dry trivia, and the “You're visiting…” scenario is unneeded.

questions.description: The fabric in your jeans has a passport.
questions.question: The word “denim” comes from the French “de Nîmes”. What is Nîmes?
hints: “De” means “from” in French.
The cloth was named after where it was made.
It's a place in the south of France.
questions.fun_fact: Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis got a patent for jeans with metal rivets on May 20, 1873.

quality.notes: The fun fact (Levi Strauss rivet patent, 1873) brushes against the same fact as q-1604, but the question itself asks something different. Players can reason to the answer from "de".

questions.description: A dress with a built-in way of telling you about its owner's love life.
questions.question: This dress has a fitted top, a wide skirt and an apron, and women wear it at beer festivals in the Alps. Where is it from?
hints: Think of mountains with snowy peaks.
Its name is dirndl.
Munich's Oktoberfest is full of them.
questions.fun_fact: By tradition, a bow tied on the left of the apron means the woman is single, on the right that she's taken.

quality.notes: "Beer festivals in the Alps" is loose, since Munich is near the Alps rather than in them. The apron-bow fact is good. With "Alps" and "beer festivals" in the question it is fairly easy to work out.

questions.description: A tunic and skirt that dress up for school and for weddings alike.
questions.question: Ao dai is to Vietnam as baju kurung is to…
hints: “Baju” means “clothes” in the language of this country.
Its capital has the famous Petronas Towers.
Its capital is Kuala Lumpur.
questions.fun_fact: Many schoolgirls in Malaysia wear a baju kurung as their school uniform.

quality.notes: The baju kurung is also worn in Brunei, Indonesia and Singapore, but none of these is an option. The question is dry, and the description is not very funny.

questions.description: Stripes this bold could only belong to a very serious job.
questions.question: Soldiers in puffy blue, red and yellow striped uniforms, carrying long axes on poles, guard whom?
hints: Their home is the smallest country in the world.
They are called the Swiss Guard, though they don't work in Switzerland.
They live in Vatican City.
questions.fun_fact: People often say Michelangelo designed the uniform, but it was actually designed in 1914 by a guard commander.

quality.notes: It is about a different fact from the other pope questions. The fun fact (the 1914 redesign, not Michelangelo) is good. A halberd photo would be safe as an illustrative image, so decorative is the wrong role.

questions.description: The biggest chair in town, and nobody ever asks him to get up.
questions.question: I'm a giant marble statue of a seated man in Washington, D.C. Martin Luther King Jr. gave his “I Have a Dream” speech on my steps. Who do I show?
hints: He was president during the US Civil War.
He is often shown with a beard and a tall black hat.
He ended slavery in the United States and gave the Gettysburg Address.
questions.fun_fact: The memorial has 36 columns, one for each US state at the time of Lincoln's death in 1865.

quality.notes: Mainly US knowledge; families outside the US know the Lincoln Memorial and the speech's location less well, so 7 is a bit low. Hint 2 (beard and tall hat) almost gives it away. The decorative image is a reasonable choice, because any memorial photo would show Lincoln.

questions.description: A political insult that went so badly, it got its own mascot.
questions.question: This animal became the symbol of the US Democratic Party after opponents mocked an 1828 candidate by calling him one. Who was he?
hints: He became the 7th president of the United States.
He was a famous general before he was president.
His face is on the US $20 bill.

media.note: A clear photo of a single donkey, no text or party logos.

questions.fun_fact: Instead of being offended, Jackson used the donkey on his own campaign posters, and cartoonist Thomas Nast later made it famous.

quality.notes: US political trivia that is hard outside the US. The 'jackass' origin is correct, and Nast made it popular later. Hint 3 (the $20 bill) is fine as the strong hint.

questions.description: Imagine designing a house and having a different family move in every four or eight years.
questions.question: Which Irish-born architect designed this famous building in the 1790s?
hints: He won a design competition held in 1792.
He was born in Ireland, and some say the building looks like a mansion in Dublin.
His first name is the same as that of several kings of England and Scotland.

media.note: A clear photo of the White House in Washington, D.C., with no signs or captions naming the architect.

questions.fun_fact: Hoban also helped rebuild the White House after British troops burned it in 1814.

quality.notes: Pure name recall that very few could reason towards; this is near the 'nobody could know it' edge, though a specialist might enjoy it. US-centric. Hint 2 repeats 'born in Ireland', which the question already says. The distractors are strong (Thornton, Latrobe, L'Enfant).

questions.description: A memorial with curtains made of steel, so nobody can pull them shut.
questions.question: This memorial to President Dwight D. Eisenhower in Washington, D.C., opened in 2020. Which famous architect designed it?
hints: The architect was born in Canada and worked mostly in the United States.
He's famous for wild, curvy buildings covered in metal.
He designed the Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao, Spain.

media.query: Dwight D. Eisenhower Memorial Washington tapestry
media.note: Photo of the Eisenhower Memorial showing the large steel tapestry; no sign naming the architect.

questions.fun_fact: The giant steel “tapestry” shows the cliffs of Normandy in France in times of peace.

quality.notes: The facts are correct (it opened in 2020, and the tapestry shows the Normandy coast in peacetime). The distractors are good architects.

questions.description: Most grandparents celebrate with cake; this one preferred falling from a plane.
questions.question: Former president George H. W. Bush celebrated several birthdays doing what this photo shows. How old was he on the last of these birthdays?
hints: He kept doing it long after he left the White House in 1993.
He jumped on his 75th, 80th and 85th birthdays too.
He was born in 1924 and made his last jump in 2014.

media.note: A clear photo of a tandem parachute jump in the sky; any people, no captions.

questions.fun_fact: As a young Navy pilot in the Second World War, Bush first used a parachute to escape his plane over the Pacific.

quality.notes: A fun fact, but mostly a guess unless you know the news story. US-centric. Hint 3 lets you work out the answer by arithmetic, which is fine for hint 3.

questions.description: A tall hat, a beard and a face worth exactly one cent.
questions.question: You find a US penny with Abraham Lincoln's face on it. In which century was he president?
hints: The United States became independent in 1776, before he was president.
He was president during the US Civil War.
He died in 1865.
questions.fun_fact: Lincoln was the first real person shown on a regular US coin, the penny of 1909.

quality.notes: The penny image shows its minting year (1900s or 2000s), which could mislead players. Knowing Lincoln's era is mostly US school knowledge. The question is dry; the 'You find a penny' setup adds little.

questions.description: A party so big that the bus drops everyone off from the sky.
questions.question: In a standard Fortnite Battle Royale match, about how many players jump onto the island at the start?
hints: It's a lot more than a soccer team.
Only one player or team is left at the end.
It's a nice round number with three digits.
questions.fun_fact: The first Fortnite World Cup in 2019 was won by a 16-year-old called Bugha, who took home 3 million dollars.

quality.notes: Hint 1 rules out 10 and hint 3 (three digits) leaves only 100, but hint 3 is allowed to come that close. The Free Fire candidate asks a different fact.

questions.description: Little round-headed people who are always ready for bowling night.
questions.question: In Wii Sports you bowl and play tennis as cartoon people you can design to look like yourself. What are they called?
hints: You can make one for everyone in your family.
Nintendo still uses them on the Switch.
Their name sounds just like the console's name.
questions.fun_fact: Wii Sports came packed with the Wii in most countries and sold more than 80 million copies.

quality.notes: Small point: the Wii was not sold with Wii Sports in Japan, but the fun fact says “most countries”, so it is correct.

questions.description: Ski goggles that went to computer school.
questions.question: A virtual reality headset like this shows each eye a slightly different picture. Why?
wrong_answers: To protect your eyes from light
To show two games at once
hints: Your own two eyes see the world from slightly different spots.
It's the same trick 3D movie glasses use.
It's about depth: what's near and what's far.

media.note: A clear photo of a generic VR headset, without readable brand names.

questions.fun_fact: One of the first VR headsets, built in 1968, was so heavy it had to hang from the ceiling.

quality.notes: The photo isn't really needed to answer, so the image is illustrative rather than essential. A generic VR headset photo is easy to find.

questions.description: A ticket that makes you climb a ladder of prizes.
questions.question: I'm a battle pass in Fortnite: you buy me for one season and climb my tiers by playing. What do I give you?
hints: I don't make you win more often.
It's all about how you look.
Think outfits, emotes and backpacks.
questions.fun_fact: A Fortnite battle pass can pay for itself: it includes enough V-Bucks to buy the next one.

quality.notes: How many V-Bucks a battle pass gives can change between seasons, so the fun fact may go out of date. The question reads like a dry rules check. The description is fine but not very funny.

questions.description: Saving up your pocket money for a second chance.
questions.question: In the classic Super Mario Bros., how many coins does Mario have to collect to get an extra life?
hints: The counter on screen has only two digits.
When it fills up, it starts again from zero.
It's the smallest three-digit number.
questions.fun_fact: A green mushroom with spots also gives Mario an extra life.

quality.notes: It is close to retro-games-5 (100 rings for an extra life in Sonic): a different game, but the same idea and the same number. Hint 3 nearly states the answer, which is allowed.

questions.description: A spiky little animal that went to Hollywood and got very, very fast.
questions.question: Which video game hero, star of his own movies since 2020, is based on this animal?
hints: He is blue and loves to run.
He collects golden rings.
His full name ends with the name of this animal.

media.note: A clear photo of a real hedgehog, no cartoon characters.

questions.fun_fact: Sonic's look in the first film was redrawn after fans disliked the first trailer, so the film came out three months later.

quality.notes: Several earlier questions also have Sonic as the answer (q-1512, q-0875, retro-games-5), but they ask other facts. A hedgehog photo is easy to find.

questions.description: Planet Earth, served as a dessert.
questions.question: If Earth were a peach, the thin skin would be the crust and the pit would be the core. What is the juicy fruit part?
hints: It is the thickest layer between the surface and the center.
It is mostly hot rock that flows very, very slowly.
Its name sounds like a cloak worn over the core.
questions.fun_fact: The mantle is about 2,900 km (1,800 mi) thick and makes up around 84% of Earth's volume.

quality.notes: The ozone layer is not part of the solid Earth, so it's a weak distractor. The description is a fragment, not a full sentence. Hint 3's cloak link works in English, German and Spanish.

questions.description: A love song so slow it takes millions of years to get to the chorus.
questions.question: In a Pixar short film, a lonely singer lives in the middle of the ocean, plays a ukulele tune and waits millions of years for love. What is the singer?
hints: The singer is very, very big and never moves.
The singer is hot-headed in the most literal way.
The film's title is the hot stuff that flows out of it.
questions.fun_fact: The short “Lava” played in cinemas before Pixar's “Inside Out” in 2015, and its song was inspired by Hawaiian music.

quality.notes: The volcano doesn't really play the ukulele; the ukulele only backs its song. Hint 2 ('hot-headed') already points strongly to the answer. Lava is less widely seen than full Pixar films.

questions.description: A volcano that wears a cape under its national park.
questions.question: Yellowstone, in the USA, sits on top of a “supervolcano”. What makes a volcano “super”?
questions.answer: It can throw out over 1,000 km³ of rock and ash at once
wrong_answers: It is the tallest volcano on its continent
It erupts at least once every single day
It sits deep under the ocean floor
hints: It is about the size of its eruptions, not its height.
Its eruptions can cover whole countries in ash.
Think of an eruption thousands of times bigger than a normal one.
questions.fun_fact: Yellowstone's Old Faithful geyser shoots hot water into the air roughly every hour and a half.

quality.notes: Close to mountains-2 (same Yellowstone supervolcano, but that one asks when it last erupted), so a different fact. The answer is the only option with a number and unit, which makes it stand out a little. It reads like a definition, so it's a bit dry.

questions.description: Islands with a very warm basement.
questions.question: The islands of Hawaii are really the tops of what?
hints: They grew up from the bottom of the ocean.
Some of them are still growing today.
Their beaches can be black because of cooled lava.
questions.fun_fact: Measured from the seafloor, Hawaii's Mauna Kea is over 10,000 m (33,000 ft) tall, taller than Mount Everest.

quality.notes: Coral reefs grow on Hawaii's volcanoes, but the answer is still clear. A photo of the cliffs may show black volcanic rock.

questions.description: A tunnel dug by something much hotter than a mole.
questions.question: Scientists think caves like this one could shelter astronauts on the Moon and Mars. What kind of cave is it?
hints: No water dug this tunnel.
It formed when the outside of a hot river hardened and the inside flowed away.
It was made by an eruption.

media.note: Inside of a lava tube: a long, smooth, round rock tunnel, no signs or text.

questions.fun_fact: Kazumura Cave in Hawaii is the longest known lava tube on Earth, about 65 km (40 mi) long.

quality.notes: Hint 1 already rules out two options. Lava tube photos are easy to find on Wikimedia Commons.

questions.description: Real estate on Mars: three giant volcanoes, great views, no air.
questions.question: This NASA picture shows three giant volcanoes in a row on Mars. What is the huge volcanic region they sit on called?
hints: The same region also holds the tallest mountain in the solar system.
Its name comes from a faraway land mentioned in the Bible.
The three volcanoes are called the ... Montes: Arsia, Pavonis and Ascraeus.

media.note: NASA view of Mars showing the three volcanoes Arsia, Pavonis and Ascraeus Mons in a row, without labels.

questions.fun_fact: The Tharsis bulge is so heavy that scientists think it may have tilted the whole planet Mars.

quality.notes: Elysium is also a volcanic region on Mars, but the three volcanoes in a row point clearly to Tharsis. This is a dry fact to memorise, with little to reason towards, and only for specialists. The 'history' lens doesn't fit. Hint 3's '... Montes' gives the answer away, as hint 3 may.

questions.description: A mountain with a very bad cough.
questions.question: Which of these does NOT come out of an erupting volcano?
hints: Three of them are hot, one is cold.
The odd one falls from clouds in winter.
It is white and you can build a man out of it.
questions.fun_fact: Some active volcanoes, like Mount Etna in Italy, have snow on top while lava flows below.

quality.notes: The odd one out is obvious even to small children, so it's a simple check rather than a fun puzzle. Decorative media fits here.

questions.description: A place where the wind never got the memo that it's allowed to stop.
questions.question: Explorer Douglas Mawson called it “the home of the blizzard”. It also holds the record for the coldest temperature ever measured. Where is it?
hints: It is far from any big city.
Penguins live there, but polar bears don't.
It is the icy land around the South Pole.
questions.fun_fact: At Cape Denison, where Mawson camped, the wind blew at an average of about 80 km/h (50 mph) for a whole year.

quality.notes: Hint 2 (penguins, but no polar bears) all but settles it already. Most young teens know that the coldest place is Antarctica, so it is a little easier than 7.

questions.description: The sky is throwing a tantrum, and it brought ammunition.
questions.question: Listen: what is falling from the sky and hitting this car?
hints: It comes from big storm clouds.
It is made of frozen water.
Small balls of ice that bounce when they land.

media.note: Recording of hailstones clearly hitting a car roof or metal surface, a hard pattering of ice.

questions.fun_fact: The biggest hailstone measured in the US fell in South Dakota in 2010: about 20 cm (8 in) wide.

quality.notes: Hail on a car roof can sound like heavy rain. The recording needs to be clearly hard and icy. The fun fact is about the US only, but it is fine.

questions.description: Somewhere, 30 degrees means a hot beach day; somewhere else, it means wear a coat.
questions.question: Which of these countries does NOT use degrees Celsius in its everyday weather forecasts?
hints: This country uses another temperature scale named after a German-born scientist.
There, a hot summer day can be “90 degrees”.
Its forecasts use degrees Fahrenheit.
questions.fun_fact: Anders Celsius first made his scale upside down: 0 was boiling water and 100 was freezing.

quality.notes: Hint 1 calls Fahrenheit “German-born”. He was born in Danzig and spoke German, so this is arguable. A few other countries also use Fahrenheit, but none of them is an option. Families outside the US may find this slightly harder than 6.

questions.description: The season when your nose turns into an ice cube.
questions.question: In a place with four seasons, about how many months does winter last?
hints: A year has 12 months.
The four seasons share the year fairly.
Divide 12 by 4.
questions.fun_fact: When it is winter in Europe, it is summer in Australia, so many Australians eat Christmas lunch at the beach.

quality.notes: Feels like a dry school-math question, and the hints just walk you through the division. How long winter lasts really varies from place to place. Children in tropical places don't live with four seasons. The 'colombia' lens is odd for a base question. The 1 and 9 distractors are weak.

questions.description: Weather that can't decide whether to bother.
questions.question: A breeze is a gentle wind. A drizzle is a gentle…
hints: It falls from gray clouds.
It makes you think about an umbrella.
Tiny drops of water falling softly.
questions.fun_fact: Drizzle drops are tiny, less than half a millimeter wide, so they seem to float more than fall.

quality.notes: A plain vocabulary analogy. Young kids may not know the word 'drizzle', so it is closer to 4. Translating it into other languages should work.

questions.description: A god whose hammer comes back like a very loyal boomerang.
questions.question: This painting shows Thor, the god of thunder, with his hammer. From the myths of which region does he come?
hints: His stories were told by people who sailed in longships.
His father is Odin.
Vikings told these stories.

media.query: Winge Thor's Fight with the Giants
media.note: The public-domain painting “Thor's Fight with the Giants” by Mårten Eskil Winge, showing Thor with his hammer.

questions.fun_fact: In English, Thursday is named after Thor: it means “Thor's day”.

quality.notes: The painting isn't really essential, because the text already names Thor; 'illustrative' would fit better. The Thursday fun fact only works in English (and German). Many kids know Thor from Marvel but not the region his myths come from.

questions.description: A roof so big and round, even the clouds come to visit.
questions.question: This famous dome sits on top of which church?
hints: The church is in Europe.
Michelangelo designed this dome.
The Pope often speaks to the crowds in the square in front of it.

media.note: Close-up of the dome of St. Peter's Basilica in Vatican City (dome and lantern only, no square or signs with names).

questions.fun_fact: Michelangelo designed the dome, but he died before it was finished, and others completed it in 1590.

quality.notes: Telling St. Peter's from St. Paul's from a close-up of the dome alone is hard. Most 13-year-olds couldn't do it, so this is rated too low. It's a fairly dry 'name the building' question. Shares a topic with famous-landmarks-9 (the Vatican's domed church), but that one asks a different fact.

questions.description: A building that looks ready to sail away, but never leaves the dock.
questions.question: This sail-shaped tower stands on its own small island by the sea. What is it used as?
hints: It's in the Middle East.
It has a helicopter pad near the top.
You book a room to sleep there.

media.note: Clear photo of the Burj al Arab in Dubai, the sail-shaped tower on its island, without visible name signs.

questions.fun_fact: The Burj al Arab opened in 1999 and stands on an artificial island built about 280 m (920 ft) off the coast of Dubai.

quality.notes: 'Opera house' works well as a decoy because of the Sydney sails. Hint 3 almost says the answer, which is allowed.

questions.description: The king of the gods needed a seat, and someone had to carve it.
questions.question: This old engraving shows the giant Statue of Zeus at Olympia, one of the Seven Wonders. Which Greek sculptor made it?
hints: He worked in Athens in the 400s BC.
He also oversaw the sculptures of the Parthenon.
His name begins with “Ph”.

media.query: Statue of Zeus at Olympia engraving
media.note: An old engraving or drawing of the seated Statue of Zeus at Olympia (e.g. by Fischer von Erlach or Maarten van Heemskerck), without a caption naming the sculptor.

questions.fun_fact: Archaeologists found his workshop at Olympia, including a little cup scratched with the words “I belong to Phidias”.

quality.notes: Pure name recall, so fairly dry. Old engravings on Commons often carry captions, which risks showing the sculptor's name. Hint 3 is a spelling hint, which is fine as the last hint.

questions.description: Two giants sat in a cliff for centuries without ever getting bored.
questions.question: These giant Buddhas were carved into a cliff about 1,500 years ago, on the Silk Road. In which country did they stand?
hints: The valley lies high in the Hindu Kush mountains.
The statues were blown up in 2001, which shocked the world.
The country's capital is Kabul.

media.note: Historical photo of one of the Bamiyan Buddhas standing in its cliff niche, before 2001, without captions naming the place.

questions.fun_fact: The taller of the two Bamiyan Buddhas was about 55 m (180 ft) high, taller than the Statue of Liberty from heel to torch.

quality.notes: Rated too hard: many adults remember the 2001 destruction in Afghanistan, so it's about a 12, not a 14. Hint 2 (blown up in 2001) is already very strong. It also touches on a destructive event; that's acceptable but borderline in tone.

questions.description: A monster with a very important job: spitting on people when it rains.
questions.question: This stone creature sticks out from a church roof and spits out rainwater. What is it called?
hints: You can find many of them on old cathedrals in Europe.
The water runs through its open mouth.
Its name comes from an old French word for “throat”.

media.note: Close-up of a stone gargoyle sticking out from a Gothic cathedral wall, ideally with its mouth as a water spout.

questions.fun_fact: A true gargoyle is a drain pipe; stone monsters that only decorate a roof and carry no water are called grotesques or chimeras.

quality.notes: 'A totem' is a weak decoy because totems don't sit on church roofs.

questions.description: The most romantic gift ever: a whole mountain of plants on your roof.
questions.question: “Legend says I built terraced gardens full of trees for my wife, who missed the green hills of her home.” Who am I?
hints: My gardens became one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
I was a king in Mesopotamia, in today's Iraq.
My city was Babylon.
questions.fun_fact: Archaeologists have never found clear proof that the Hanging Gardens existed, and some think they were really in the city of Nineveh.

quality.notes: Caesar and Genghis Khan are easy to rule out, so it often comes down to Nebuchadnezzar vs Ramesses. The Ishtar Gate image points to Babylon, but that only helps players who already know the answer.

questions.description: Paris's most famous lady has a very strong skeleton.
questions.question: Gustave Eiffel's company built this tower for the 1889 World's Fair in Paris. What is it made of?
hints: It's a metal.
Workers paint it again every few years so it doesn't rust.
A magnet sticks to it, and Earth's core is mostly made of it.

media.note: Clear photo of the whole Eiffel Tower, showing its metal lattice.

questions.fun_fact: On hot summer days the Eiffel Tower can grow about 15 cm (6 in) taller, because its iron expands in the heat.

quality.notes: Iron is right (puddled iron), but many sources wrongly say 'steel', so some players may argue. The role is set to essential, but the question already names the tower, so illustrative would fit better.

questions.description: A road that hangs from giant ropes and still doesn't swing like a hammock.
questions.question: This famous bridge hangs from two huge cables. In which city is it?
hints: It's on the west coast of the United States.
It's named after the strait it crosses, not after its color.
The city is famous for its cable cars and steep hills.

media.note: Clear photo of the Golden Gate Bridge, with no city name or signs visible.

questions.fun_fact: The Golden Gate Bridge's famous color has an official name: “International Orange”.

quality.notes: The text clue 'hangs from two huge cables' fits many suspension bridges; only the photo pins it down. A routine landmark question. Hint 2 points at the name 'Golden Gate'.

questions.description: An island where the stone heads outnumber the coffee shops.
questions.question: You walk all around Easter Island counting the giant stone heads, the moai. About how many do you find?
hints: There are far more than a hundred.
Most were carved in one single quarry on the island.
It's close to a thousand.
questions.fun_fact: Most moai don't look out to sea: they face inland, watching over the villages of the people who carved them.

quality.notes: The 'you walk around counting' framing is a mild bit of invented story. Hint 3 nearly gives the answer away, which is allowed.

questions.description: A statue with the best view in town, and arms wide open to enjoy it.
questions.question: The Christ the Redeemer statue stands on top of Corcovado mountain in Rio de Janeiro. About how high is the mountain?
hints: It's lower than one kilometer.
It's about twice as high as the Eiffel Tower.
It's more than 500 m.
questions.fun_fact: The statue on top is 30 m (98 ft) tall, and its arms stretch 28 m (92 ft) from hand to hand.

quality.notes: A dry height estimate. The Sugarloaf image could show Corcovado in the background, which is harmless but a little confusing. Hints 1 and 3 together pin down the answer.

questions.description: A place so special, the whole world promised to look after it.
questions.question: In 1978, these islands became one of the very first World Heritage Sites. Where are they?
hints: They lie in the Pacific Ocean.
Charles Darwin studied their animals.
They belong to Ecuador.

media.note: Photo of a marine iguana on black lava rock by the sea, without any place name visible.

questions.fun_fact: On UNESCO's World Heritage List, the Galápagos Islands carry the number 1.

quality.notes: The marine iguana photo is really the main clue rather than the 1978 date. That's acceptable, but nature fans will find it much easier.

questions.description: Some people get flowers; some get a building the whole world travels to see.
questions.question: The Taj Mahal is to Mumtaz Mahal as the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus is to…
hints: Both buildings are tombs.
His tomb was so famous that its name became the word for any grand tomb.
His name hides inside the word “mausoleum”.
questions.fun_fact: Shah Jahan, who built the Taj Mahal for Mumtaz Mahal, was later buried right next to her inside it.

quality.notes: A nice question to reason out, since 'mausoleum' contains the name. Hint 2 already gives a lot away.

questions.description: A giant ice cube that drops pieces into a lake as big as buildings.
questions.question: This Argentine glacier, the Perito Moreno Glacier, is named after whom?
hints: He traveled through Patagonia in the 1800s.
He helped settle the border between Argentina and Chile.
“Perito” was his nickname, Spanish for “expert”.

media.note: Photo of the ice front of the Perito Moreno Glacier rising from the lake, without signs or text.

questions.fun_fact: Francisco Moreno earned the nickname “Perito”, meaning “expert”, for his work as Argentina's expert in the border talks with Chile.

quality.notes: The decoys are weak: 'explorer' is the obvious guess for a glacier's namesake, so it's easier than the stated 11. The fun fact repeats hint 3 (Perito = expert). The description's grammar is odd: it reads as if the lake is 'as big as buildings'.

questions.description: The only cook in the family that works best outdoors and smells of smoke.
questions.question: I stand outside in the garden, I have metal bars, and I cook sausages over hot coals. What am I?
hints: You often use me at summer parties.
I can make smoke.
People flip burgers on me with tongs.
questions.fun_fact: People have cooked meat over open fire for hundreds of thousands of years, long before anyone built a kitchen.

quality.notes: A straightforward riddle that is pleasant but not surprising. The description is a bit clumsy ("the only cook in the family"), and hints 1 and 2 are weak.

questions.description: Some cheeses wait patiently for months, and one just can't wait at all.
questions.question: Three of these cheeses are left to ripen for weeks or months before you eat them. Which one is eaten fresh?
hints: The fresh one is soft and white.
It's full of small, soft lumps called curds.
It often comes in a tub and goes great with fruit.
questions.fun_fact: Real Parmesan must ripen for at least 12 months, while cottage cheese can be ready in about a day.

quality.notes: Kids around 11 rarely know which cheeses are aged, and cottage cheese is not familiar everywhere, so 6 is too low. Young gouda ripens for only a few weeks, but it is still ripened, so the answer holds. The question reads like a dry fact.

questions.description: A hot bath for potatoes, and they come out crunchy.
questions.question: You're in the kitchen: soup is cooked in water, and fries are cooked in…?
hints: It's slippery and greasy.
It makes food golden and crispy.
It often comes from olives or sunflowers.
questions.fun_fact: Many cooks fry potatoes twice: first to cook them soft inside, then again to make them crispy.

quality.notes: Honey and juice are too easy to rule out, even for kids. A photo of fries in a paper cone is fine. A simple analogy with not much fun in it.

questions.description: A bread so soft it doubles as a spoon.
questions.question: You're tearing off a piece of naan to scoop up your curry. In which country is naan NOT a traditional bread?
hints: Naan belongs to South and Central Asia.
The odd one out is in Africa.
Its traditional bread is a big, spongy pancake called injera.
questions.fun_fact: Naan is often baked by slapping the dough onto the hot inside wall of a clay oven called a tandoor.

quality.notes: It is easy to reason out: three Asian countries and one African country. The "You're tearing off a piece of naan" scene adds length without adding a clue. The fun fact about the tandoor is nice.

questions.description: A diet that makes cows, pigs and chickens breathe a sigh of relief.
questions.question: Lisa Simpson is one, and so are millions of people in India. What does a vegetarian not eat?
hints: It's not something that grows in a garden.
A vegetarian says no to sausages.
Burgers and chicken nuggets are made of it.
questions.fun_fact: India has more vegetarians than any other country in the world.

quality.notes: The wrong answers are weak: "Vegetables" is obviously wrong given the word "vegetarian". The Lisa Simpson detail adds some charm.

questions.description: A party where the guest of honor is a big pile of glowing embers.
questions.question: Cowboys called gauchos made me famous: meat grilled slowly over embers in Argentina and Uruguay. What am I called?
hints: I'm usually a long Sunday get-together with family and friends.
The person cooking me tends the fire for hours.
My name means “roasted” in Spanish.
questions.fun_fact: Uruguay and Argentina are among the countries that eat the most beef per person in the world.

quality.notes: The topic is Latin American and very easy for Spanish speakers, where "asado" literally means "roasted". It is much less known to families elsewhere, so the difficulty differs a lot between language versions.

questions.description: Cartoon chefs wave it around, but real chefs use it to make pizza flat.
questions.question: Three of these kitchen things use heat to cook food. Which one is only for flattening dough?
hints: It never gets hot.
It's a long stick, often made of wood.
You roll it back and forth over cookie dough.
questions.fun_fact: Some rolling pins have patterns carved into them, so they print pictures onto cookies.

quality.notes: Very easy and a little dry. The description repeats the "flat" clue from the question.

questions.description: The oven's favorite hobby, as long as nothing melts.
questions.question: You're baking in a hot oven. Which of these do you NOT bake?
hints: One of these must stay very cold.
It would melt in the oven.
You eat it from a cone.
questions.fun_fact: There is a dessert called baked Alaska: ice cream covered in whipped egg white and baked so fast that the inside stays frozen.

quality.notes: "As long as nothing melts" in the description gives a nudge towards ice cream. That is acceptable at difficulty 1, but it is still a giveaway. The baked Alaska fun fact is good.

questions.description: A bird that gets nervous every November.
questions.question: This big bird comes from the Americas, makes a “gobble gobble” sound, and is roasted for Thanksgiving. What is it?
hints: It's much bigger than a chicken.
It has a red, floppy piece of skin on its face.
It shares its name with a country.
questions.fun_fact: Wild turkeys can fly short distances and run at about 40 km/h (25 mph).

quality.notes: The question leans on Thanksgiving, a US holiday, and the description ("nervous every November") does too, so it has a US bias. Hint 3 ("shares its name with a country") only works in English. Overlap with q-1016 (the turkey-sound audio question) is mild: it shares the gobble sound, but the question is different.

questions.description: A tiny island country with a very big wallet.
questions.question: Baht is to Thailand as what is to Singapore?
hints: Singapore was a British colony for a long time.
Its neighbor Malaysia uses the ringgit.
Australia and Canada use money with the same name.
questions.fun_fact: Since 1967, Singapore and Brunei have let their dollars be used at the same value in each other's country.

quality.notes: Fun: a dry analogy, close to a school-test question. Age fit: many adults know the Singapore dollar, so 11 feels a bit high. The fun fact is true (1967 interchangeability agreement with Brunei).

questions.description: Money that retired in 2002 and now lives only in grandparents' drawers.
questions.question: Before the euro, the franc was to France what which currency was to Spain?
hints: Its name means something like “little piece.”
Spain used it from 1868 until 2002.
Its name sounds like a small version of Mexico's money.
questions.fun_fact: When Spain switched to the euro, one euro was worth exactly 166.386 pesetas.

quality.notes: Fun: a fairly dry analogy. It leans slightly towards the Spanish-speaking world, but the peseta is known widely enough. The Puerta del Sol image may show shop signs, though old peseta prices are unlikely.

questions.description: An engineer who builds traps for package thieves with more care than most people build houses.
questions.question: You're watching Mark Rober catch package thieves with a glitter bomb. Where did he work as an engineer before YouTube?
hints: His old job was about things very far from home.
He helped build a robot that drives on another planet.
He worked on the Curiosity rover, which landed on Mars.
questions.fun_fact: Mark Rober worked at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory for about nine years before becoming a full-time YouTuber.

quality.notes: Strictly, JPL is run by Caltech for NASA, but saying 'NASA' is the usual way to put it, and his roughly nine years there on Curiosity are well documented. Kids and teens around the world know Mark Rober well. The rover candidate q-0195 shares only a topic.

questions.description: A prank that promises one thing, then never gives you up.
questions.question: To “rickroll” someone, you trick them into opening Rick Astley's song “Never Gonna Give You Up”. In which decade did the song come out?
hints: The song is much older than YouTube.
Think of big hair, shoulder pads and cassette tapes.
It's from the same decade as the first Super Mario Bros. game.
questions.fun_fact: In 2021, the music video for “Never Gonna Give You Up” passed 1 billion views on YouTube.

quality.notes: The song came out in 1987, the first Super Mario Bros. in 1985, and the video passed 1 billion views in 2021, so all facts check out. Hint 1 already rules out the 2000s. The decorative image is a reasonable choice.

questions.description: A YouTuber who gives away money faster than a broken cash machine.
questions.question: Each dollar fans gave to MrBeast's 2019 challenge got one of me planted, and over 20 million of me went into the ground. What am I?
hints: I grow slowly but can live for hundreds of years.
Birds build nests in me.
Lots of me together make a forest.
questions.fun_fact: MrBeast ran the challenge, called Team Trees, together with fellow YouTuber Mark Rober.

quality.notes: Wrong answers are weak: nobody plants 20 million rose bushes or cacti in a charity drive, and 'planted' plus the scale point to trees. The description is about MrBeast's money, not about trees or the challenge, so it is only loosely linked. The Team Trees facts are correct.

questions.description: A dance that makes you look like you're riding a horse that isn't there.
questions.question: It's sung by PSY, its dance looks like riding a horse, and in 2012 it was the first YouTube video to reach 1 billion views. Where is “Gangnam Style” from?
hints: The singer comes from Asia.
The same country makes Samsung phones.
Its capital city is Seoul.
questions.fun_fact: Gangnam is a wealthy district of Seoul, and the song gently makes fun of its fancy lifestyle.

quality.notes: The question is long, about 170 characters, with three facts before the actual question. The song is from 2012, so many kids today don't know it, which pushes the difficulty above 4. The facts are correct: PSY, the horse dance, and the first video to reach 1 billion views in December 2012.
